https://semiwiki.com/semiconductor-manufacturers/intel/370512-intel-18a-vs-intel-18a-p-what-is-the-difference-and-why-does-it-matter/ Intel 18A-P also introduces additional transistor options, including enhanced RibbonFET variants sometimes referred to as “Power Boost” devices. These allow designers to optimize different sections of a chip for maximum speed, lower leakage, or improved efficiency. The process also includes interconnect enhancements that reduce resistance, helping signals travel more efficiently through the chip. 
Another significant improvement is thermal performance. Intel has indicated that 18A-P reduces thermal resistance by approximately 20% to 40% compared with 18A. Better thermal behavior means heat can be removed more effectively from the silicon, allowing chips to sustain higher performance levels without exceeding thermal limits.

articles.title: Cette compacte électrique premium voit son prix baisser de 6 000 euros quelques semaines après son lancement
articles.text:
Le groupe Volkswagen est en pleine offensive sur le marché des véhicules électriques en Europe. Si on a souvent abordé les nouveautés de Skoda, Volkswagen et Cupra avec des modèles citadins, Audi n’est pas en reste puisque la marque a relancé l’A2 en version électrique. L’Audi A2 e-tron est désormais éligible à la prime Coup de pouce CEE, ce qui devrait bien aider ses ventes en France.
Une voiture premium éligible à l’aide
Généralement, les voitures premium dépassent les critères pour profiter du bonus écologique, désormais appelé Coup de pouce CEE. Elles doivent rester sous un tarif de 47 000 euros, mais l’Audi A2 e-tron s’y maintient pour plusieurs versions. Mais ce n’est pas tout, il faut aussi valider l’éco-score, qui favorise les voitures produites en Europe. Parfait, l’Audi A2 e-tron est produite à Ingolstadt, en Allemagne.
Tous les feux étaient au vert pour l’obtention du bonus écologique. Et la publication au Journal officiel du 22 octobre 2026 valide son éligibilité à l’aide à l’achat d’une voiture électrique en France. De ce fait, elle profite d’une prime pour tous de 3 535 euros, de 5 890 euros si votre revenu fiscal par part est compris entre 11 251 et 16 880 euros et jusqu’à 6 145 euros si votre revenu fiscal de référence par part est inférieur à 11 250 euros.
Une voiture efficiente et relativement bien placée
Rares sont les voitures électriques premium à être éligibles au bonus écologique. Seules les versions d’entrée de gamme de la Mercedes CLA et du GLB électrique arrivent à rester sous les 47 000 euros. Du côté d’Audi, le choix de rester en 400 volts et la plateforme MEB commune avec la Volkswagen ID.3 Neo, permettent d’avoir des tarifs d’accès contenus.
La version de 170 chevaux avec batterie de 52 kWh débute à 38 600 euros au catalogue, pour une autonomie de 423 km WLTP. Ce qui réduit son prix pour tous à 35 065 euros avec l’aide du bonus écologique. Si cette autonomie vous semble trop juste, il est judicieux de s’intéresser à la version de 231 chevaux à propulsion, utilisant une batterie de 84 kWh pour une autonomie allant jusqu’à 646 km WLTP, grâce au très bon travail d’optimisation aérodynamique d’Audi sur l’A2 e-tron. En se contentant du premier niveau de finition, cette version dotée de la plus grande autonomie du catalogue est proposée à partir de 46 900 euros, ce qui la rend éligible au bonus et donc à un tarif de 43 365 euros pour tous.
Une bonne nouvelle pour Audi, qui va avoir fort à faire avec cette Audi A2 e-tron, qui arrive sur un marché très concurrentiel : celui des compactes électriques.

articles.title: Firefox 159 est là et corrige 167 failles de sécurité : à vos mises à jour !
articles.text:
Mozilla vient de mettre à jour Firefox pour corriger une série de vulnérabilités, dont certaines pouvaient permettre à du code malveillant de s'échapper des processus isolés du navigateur. Les correctifs sont disponibles sur ordinateur et Android, sans qu'aucune exploitation active ait été signalée.
Depuis septembre, Mozilla publie une nouvelle version de Firefox tous les quinze jours, et à en juger par la dernière fournée de patchs livrée avec la version 159, on ne s’en plaindra pas. La fondation vient en effet de corriger 167 vulnérabilités, dont 108 présentant un risque élevé. Du moteur JavaScript au rendu graphique en passant par la gestion de la mémoire, les failles touchent de nombreux composants du navigateur, jusque dans les protections censées empêcher une page web compromise d’accéder au reste du système. Vous savez ce qu’il vous reste à faire.
Treize failles qui pouvaient faire céder la sandbox
Le point le plus sensible concerne treize vulnérabilités de type sandbox escape. Pour limiter les dégâts en cas d'attaque, Firefox exécute le contenu des pages web dans des processus isolés aux permissions restreintes. Même si un site piégé parvient à exploiter une faille, cette séparation doit l'empêcher d'accéder librement aux ressources de l'ordinateur.
Les défauts corrigés permettaient justement de contourner ces restrictions, notamment à travers des composants chargés de la navigation ou de la gestion des formulaires. Une sortie de sandbox ne donne pas automatiquement le contrôle du système, mais elle peut considérablement aggraver une première compromission, par exemple lorsqu'un attaquant est déjà parvenu à exécuter du code malveillant. Mozilla ne mentionne toutefois aucune exploitation active de ces failles.
Des erreurs de mémoire à la pelle, mais un décompte à relativiser
Les problèmes de mémoire occupent également une belle place dans le bulletin, avec 97 vulnérabilités de type use-after-free. Ces erreurs surviennent lorsqu'un programme réutilise une zone de mémoire déjà libérée et peuvent, selon les circonstances, provoquer un plantage ou ouvrir la voie à l'exécution de code malveillant.
Mozilla a par ailleurs corrigé des failles d'élévation de privilèges, qui pouvaient accorder à certains processus plus de droits que prévu, ainsi que des contournements de la politique de même origine, censée empêcher un site d'accéder aux données d'un autre. D'autres vulnérabilités risquaient d'exposer des informations sensibles, notamment dans les composants chargés des communications réseau et du traitement audio-vidéo.
À noter que la fondation a récemment revu sa façon de publier ses avis de sécurité et attribue désormais un identifiant CVE distinct à chaque faille de sécurité mémoire découverte en interne, alors qu'elle pouvait auparavant en regrouper plusieurs sous une même référence. Une évolution qui contribue à expliquer le nombre particulièrement élevé de vulnérabilités recensées dans Firefox.
Firefox installe normalement ses mises à jour de façon automatique, mais vous pouvez aussi prendre les devants en ouvrant le menu des réglages > Paramètres > À propos de Firefox. Le navigateur recherche alors la dernière version disponible et propose un redémarrage pour achever l'installation. Sur Android, la mise à jour passe par le Play Store.
Les versions à support prolongé ont également reçu leurs correctifs : Firefox ESR 153.6.0 comble 145 vulnérabilités, contre 80 pour Firefox ESR 115.44.0. Cette dernière continue de recevoir des mises à jour de sécurité sur Windows 7, 8 et 8.1 ainsi que sur macOS 10.12 à 10.14, Mozilla ayant prolongé sa maintenance jusqu'en mars 2027.
- 100 % développé en interne
- Fiable, efficace et stable
- Fonctionnalités d'optimisation de l'interface et de l'expérience utilisateur

articles.title: Cloudera and Mistral connect open-weight models to data - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cloudera and Mistral bring open-weight models closer to enterprise data
Open-weight models are giving enterprises more choice in how they put proprietary data to work. Turning that flexibility into useful applications requires models and enterprise data systems to work together.
Cloudera Inc.’s partnership with Mistral AI SAS brings those pieces together. The collaboration pairs Cloudera’s enterprise data foundation with Mistral’s customizable models, according to Marjorie Janiewicz (pictured, right), chief revenue officer of Mistral AI.
“Companies need to be able to control where those models get deployed,” she said. “They need to own those models so that the day somebody decides to unplug them, they have business continuity. So open weights from an approach perspective is very important.”
Janiewicz and Abhas Ricky (left), chief business officer and general manager of Applied AI at Cloudera Inc., spoke with co-hosts Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed model deployments, enterprise data and secure deployment. (* Disclosure below.)
Open-weight models meet enterprise context
The model portfolio includes Mistral Large 4, with joint engineering teams helping customers choose models and infrastructure for specific use cases. For enterprises, using models trained on public sources through an application programming interface is only a starting point, according to Ricky.
“You want to be able to ground that with your domain-specific context, with your domain-specific information,” he said. “Oftentimes, that’s actually sitting in closed firewall environments, and that context is critical for high-fidelity outputs whether using a model or an agentic solution.”
Demand spans financial services, public sector and manufacturing as organizations explore open-weight models. Customizing those models with proprietary information can help businesses develop new solutions from their existing intellectual property, according to Janiewicz.
“When you touch the heart of those businesses, think [know your customer processes] in financial services, as an example, or crash testing in automotive,” she said. “You are at the heart of the business. You need a solution that’s safe [and] secure, and you need to be independent in your ability to construct those systems.”

articles.title: Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
articles.text:
Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
At TechSparks 2026, Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, advised entrepreneurs to think globally from day one, tackle difficult problems, and stay committed for the long term.
AI has made it easier to build products, but entrepreneurs still need to decide what to build and whether they can stay committed long enough to turn an idea into a sustainable business.
For Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, the answer is to solve difficult problems, stay focused, and avoid chasing the next big thing.
Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Shaam spoke about building Omio, which operates across 56 countries, and why Indian entrepreneurs should think globally from the beginning.
“If I were to rebuild Omio today, I would start here because there is so much growth and opportunity in India today. But the principles remain the same. You need to go after really hard problems and focus on solving them for a very long time,” he told YourStory.
Shaam founded Omio after identifying a problem in global transportation: operators had separate systems for trains, buses, and ferries. After moving to Germany, he spent two and a half years working on the supply side before launching the company's first product.
“Building a billion-dollar business is really hard. The stories of companies going from zero to a billion dollars very quickly are rare. Don’t get inspired by the exceptions as for most, it is a daily grind,” he said.
Think global from day one
Shaam believes entrepreneurs need not wait until they have succeeded in India before expanding overseas. While some businesses cater to local needs, sectors such as education, healthcare, and deeptech offer opportunities across markets.
“If your problem statement is already global, you should start early. We entered 30 countries in our first three or four years, even though people told us to win Germany first. That bet, despite the capital required and the mistakes we had to correct, probably helped make us become the company we are today,” he said.
AI has also made international expansion easier. Shaam recalled that when Omio expanded in Germany, it employed around 30 people to handle translations. That work is now done by AI.
However, lower barriers to entry also make it easier for competitors to copy products. Shaam believes entrepreneurs must therefore be more careful about where they invest their time and resources.
“The onus moves from bias to action to judgement: what should I focus on? Which industry has a bigger moat? What will that moat look like 10 years from now? Starting is easy now but choosing what to pursue and committing to it is the hard part,” he said.
AI may change distribution, but trust remains important
Shaam said AI agents could change digital commerce, including how people book travel. However, widespread adoption will depend on bringing down costs and finding sustainable business models.
“Consumers need these agents to be very cheap before they penetrate the market. There is a cost barrier and a business-model problem to solve. I see this as a major transformation and not an overnight event,” he explained.
Even as more transactions move to AI agents, Shaam believes businesses will still need to deliver reliable services in the physical world.
“Real life happens outside the internet. If an agent buys something or orders food, people need to trust that it will arrive every single time. Businesses that can solve these operational problems at scale will have something valuable to build on,” he said.
For aspiring founders, his advice was to focus on solving a problem rather than on the appeal of becoming an entrepreneur.
“Find a great problem. Don’t become an entrepreneur simply because you want to be one. This is a journey with long periods of darkness, and you need to be passionate enough about what you’re solving to keep going,” Shaam concluded.

articles.title: Oops! Apple just put its first laptop touchscreen on the wrong MacBook
articles.text:
Oops! Apple just put its first laptop touchscreen on the wrong MacBook
Out of reach
Well, it’s finally happened: Apple has got with the times and finally made a laptop with a touchscreen. However, while the new MacBook Pros with PROLED screens look like fantastic devices, I think Apple has made a mistake by putting its first laptop touchscreen on the more expensive MacBook Pro, rather than the more mainstream MacBook Air… or even the MacBook Neo.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499. That’s a big ask for most people, especially these days.
Of course, MacBook Pros, as the name suggests, are aimed at professionals, and thanks to their high-end components, they should really be seen as investments that allow you to speed up your workflow.
Interestingly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros come with Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. If you want Apple’s latest M6 chip, you’ll need to go for the non-touchscreen 14-inch MacBook Pro that was announced a few days earlier. Perhaps confusingly, the M6 is less powerful than the M5 Pro and M5 Max, and so far there are no hints that Apple is preparing to release M6 Pro and M6 Max chips.
My point is that by putting its first-ever laptop touchscreen on its most powerful — and expensive — MacBooks, Apple is severely limiting the potential audience for the technology. Had it instead put a touchscreen on the more affordable MacBook Air, it could have had a real hit on its hands.
Who’s it for?
As someone who has used plenty of Windows laptops and Chromebooks with touchscreens in the past, I know how useful they can be for certain tasks, and I often miss them when using a MacBook.
Being able to scroll down a website with a finger, turn a page in an ebook, or quickly tap a menu item feels natural and intuitive, and I’m sure it will on the new MacBooks. My daughter, who grew up with touchscreens on everything, would also instinctively poke an often sticky, grubby (kids, you’ve got to love them!) finger at a MacBook screen and be surprised when nothing happened.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
These are all pretty simple tasks and gestures. What I've never used touchscreens on laptops for, however, is for complex tasks and tools, such as recording and editing music in Ableton Live, or editing videos in Adobe Premiere Pro.
Instead, for things that needed precision or complexity, nothing beat the good old combo of keyboard and touchpad (or even better, keyboard and a mouse), as well as other external peripherals such as MIDI controllers and drawing tablets. Which leads me to wonder why Apple picked the MacBook Pro, a device that’s supposedly designed for exactly those type of tasks, to showcase its first laptop touchscreen.
If you’re dropping $3,000+ on a touchscreen laptop to mostly just to use the touchscreen for browsing websites, then you’re either super-rich or you should get help with your budgeting.
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and no touchscreen starts at $2,999 / £2,999 / AU$4,799. As the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR touchscreen with the same specs costs $400 / £400 / AU$700 more, that’s quite a premium for the touchscreen.
Yes, I know the PROLED XDR screen offers better image quality as well thanks to its tandem OLED tech (check out our explainer on why this is a big deal), but if you don’t need that additional image quality, which includes better contrast, higher brightness levels, and support for the Adobe RGB color gamut, and are just interested in the touchscreen, then essentially yeah, you’re paying $400 extra for it.
If you’re a professional, especially one in the creative industry, you’ll need to think long and hard if that investment is worth it. Meanwhile, the likes of the MacBook Air and MacBook Neo aren’t really used for complex creative tasks, and instead used for casual day-to-day use, where touchscreens are much more useful.
Granted, adding an extra $400 / £400 / AU$700 to the price of a MacBook Neo or MacBook Air wouldn’t be great, especially as they’ve just had a price bump earlier this year, but Apple wouldn’t need to include the OLED tech and advanced image-quality options included in the MacBook Pro. A touchscreen MacBook Neo for $899, say, could be a real hit, especially if Apple was to also keep the non-touchscreen model for people who still want the ultimate affordable way to get into the Mac ecosystem.
This isn’t just an Apple problem, of course. The new laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark SoC, which are aimed at the same creative professionals and heavy local AI users as the MacBook Pro (with similarly high price tags), come with touchscreens. I’ve spent a decent amount of time with each one at various events, and I found that the touchscreen was the least-used part of the laptop — in fact, I often forgot those laptops had one. Because there aren’t cheaper, non-touch, models, though I didn’t resent its inclusion.
As I said, I do get the appeal of touchscreen laptops, but I find the technology is best used in 2-in-1 devices where the keyboard can be flipped behind the screen (or removed entirely) so that it can be used as a tablet-like device.
In an ideal world, then, Apple would have put its touchscreen on an entirely new 2-in-1 MacBook, but I can’t see that happening any time soon. Apple sort of has a device like that — the powerful iPad Pro, which can be paired with a Magic Keyboard that turns it into a touchscreen laptop. The problem there, however, is that despite coming with Apple’s powerful M-series chips, the same you’ll find in MacBooks, the iPad Pro is limited to the iPadOS operating system and mobile apps.
Put macOS on that bad boy, however, and allow us to run full desktop applications on it, and hey presto: Apple has a touchscreen MacBook that utilizes the tech in a way that’s actually useful. Until then, I’ll stick with my standard MacBook Pro, and just try to remember not to prod it with my sausage fingers too often.

articles.title: ChatGPT ahora tiene su propio manual de ética y valores como un humano: de la fidelidad al respeto
articles.text:
OpenAI publicó el 29 de octubre una versión actualizada del Model Spec, el documento público donde describe cómo quiere que se comporten sus modelos de inteligencia artificial. El texto ahora se organiza en torno a cinco valores, incorpora guías sobre contexto, supervisión humana y autonomía de las personas, y elimina la mayor parte de sus indicaciones detalladas de estilo.
Los cinco valores son la fidelidad a la intención humana, la reducción del daño, la honestidad y la transparencia, el respeto a la autonomía de las personas —que la empresa llama “agencia humana”— y el cuidado. Según OpenAI, estos principios ya estaban presentes en el documento, y la reorganización busca explicar por qué el modelo debe actuar como lo hace.
La empresa presenta la fidelidad a la intención humana como la base de su enfoque. Según su descripción, OpenAI redacta el documento y fija los límites; los desarrolladores dirigen sus aplicaciones dentro de esos límites, y los usuarios orientan el trabajo del modelo dentro de las restricciones anteriores.
Para OpenAI, la fidelidad no significa obedecer al pie de la letra. Implica entender lo que quieren y valoran la empresa, los desarrolladores y los usuarios, y actuar con criterio cuando esa comprensión es incompleta.
El documento ofrece un ejemplo: al ayudar a comparar ofertas de trabajo, el modelo puede usar prioridades mencionadas previamente por la persona, como tener horarios previsibles, siempre que haga visibles esos supuestos y permita corregirlos.
Las incorporaciones al documento
El registro de cambios del Model Spec en GitHub resume las novedades. Se añade la sección “Consider context carefully” (“considerar el contexto con cuidado”), sobre cómo usar el contexto, la memoria y la personalización de forma proporcionada y con respeto por la privacidad y el control del usuario.
También se incorporan principios para reforzar la capacidad de las personas de entender, elegir y actuar, así como para seguir las normas sociales pertinentes.
El control y la comunicación de efectos secundarios pasan a ser un principio de nivel de usuario, con indicaciones más claras sobre autorización y compromisos entre objetivos. Además, el documento suma una guía explícita para apoyar la supervisión y la corrección humanas y actualiza la llamada cadena de mando, que establece qué instrucciones se aplican y cómo se resuelven los conflictos entre ellas.
Cambios en las pautas de estilo y la nomenclatura
OpenAI retiró la mayor parte de las pautas detalladas de estilo. Argumenta que la forma de responder debe adaptarse a las preferencias de cada usuario, según el idioma, la cultura y las particularidades de cada persona, y que los comentarios y el contexto del usuario son la prueba de esas preferencias.
Se mantienen algunos criterios más firmes, como abordar las preguntas con objetividad. Los usuarios y los desarrolladores pueden pedir de forma explícita que el modelo adopte una perspectiva determinada, pero no debe deducir esa preferencia solo a partir de lo que cree que la persona quiere oír.
Otro cambio es de nomenclatura. Ante la variedad de usos y entornos en los que se despliegan sus modelos, el documento ahora se refiere al modelo como “GPT” y ya no como “el asistente”. La versión anterior, del 18 de agosto, había añadido aclaraciones sobre las interacciones con adolescentes y una sección sobre las capacidades y los límites del modelo.
OpenAI advierte que el Model Spec describe el comportamiento al que aspira y que sus modelos todavía no lo reflejan por completo. La empresa informó que mejorará el documento y los modelos a partir de la investigación, el uso real y los comentarios del público, e invitó a opinar sobre los valores y los equilibrios propuestos.
Además, la compañía informó que explora nuevos métodos de entrenamiento para que sus modelos aprendan esos valores y entiendan los principios concretos del documento. Según OpenAI, compartirá los resultados de ese trabajo en futuras actualizaciones, sin precisar una fecha.

articles.title: GitHub ha tenido que hacer algo a gran escala para seguir el ritmo de la IA. Sus cifras explican hasta qué punto
articles.text:
Estamos acostumbrados a hablar de la inteligencia artificial en términos de plo que puede hacer por nosotros: escribir una función, corregir un error o ayudarnos a terminar una aplicación. Sin embargo, cada vez que ese trabajo se traduce en cambios compartidos, entra en juego una infraestructura que rara vez vemos. Hay que registrar versiones, atender solicitudes y coordinar el trabajo de personas y sistemas automáticos, muchas veces al mismo tiempo. La expansión de los agentes está haciendo que esa parte menos visible del desarrollo merezca tanta atención como el propio código.
Cuatro millones de núcleos adicionales. La magnitud de ese trabajo empieza a entenderse cuando miramos lo que GitHub ha incorporado a su infraestructura en lo que va de 2026. Según los datos publicados por la propia plataforma, ha sumado cuatro millones de núcleos de CPU, 160 petabytes de almacenamiento de alta velocidad y 50 terabits por segundo de capacidad de red. No hablamos de cuatro millones de procesadores físicos ni de la capacidad total de GitHub, sino de recursos adicionales para atender una actividad creciente. La compañía sitúa a los agentes de IA entre los factores que explican esta presión.
Una actividad que se ha disparado. Para entender por qué GitHub necesita tantos recursos, tenemos que mirar primero cuánto ha crecido el trabajo que pasa por sus sistemas. Según Octoverse 2026, la plataforma pasó de registrar 12.900 millones de commits anuales a 34.300 millones en los doce meses terminados en septiembre de 2026, incluyendo repositorios públicos y privados. Solo en ese último mes, GitHub registró 7.380 millones de commits. Cada uno representa una versión guardada de los cambios en un proyecto, aunque puede contener modificaciones de muy distinto tamaño. Es una distinción importante: hablamos de actividad registrada, no de líneas de código generadas.
Los agentes cambian las reglas. Una parte de esta aceleración se entiende al observar cómo está cambiando el trabajo de los programadores. Según GitHub, en septiembre más del 40% de las pull requests, las propuestas para incorporar cambios a un proyecto, comenzaron con un borrador elaborado por un agente de IA que la plataforma pudo detectar; en marzo eran el 17%. La compañía también observó que los repositorios nuevos con archivos de configuración para agentes registraron, de media, ocho veces más commits que aquellos sin esos archivos. Es una asociación significativa, aunque estos últimos también pueden utilizar IA y la comparación no demuestra por sí sola una mejora equivalente de productividad.
El problema no es solo almacenar. Pensemos en un agente que recibe una tarea, revisa un repositorio, propone cambios y, tras nuevas comprobaciones, vuelve a modificarlo. Aunque el resultado final sea una única mejora, sincronizar ese trabajo con GitHub puede implicar múltiples envíos de cambios, lecturas y comprobaciones automatizadas. Si muchos agentes trabajan en paralelo, la plataforma no solo tiene que guardar más información, también debe moverla y procesarla con suficiente rapidez. Esa es la parte menos intuitiva del fenómeno: el desafío no consiste únicamente en el tamaño del código, sino en la frecuencia con la que se trabaja sobre él.
Los límites ya se han notado. El aumento de actividad también ha dejado al descubierto problemas de capacidad. El 17 de agosto de 2026, GitHub sufrió una interrupción de siete horas y 47 minutos que afectó a varios de sus servicios. Según explicó la propia compañía, el incidente comenzó cuando el tráfico alcanzó un nuevo máximo y un componente crítico de su centro de datos en Estados Unidos no consiguió escalar para responder a la demanda. GitHub reconoció que no había ampliado determinados recursos con suficiente antelación, aunque no atribuyó directamente aquella caída a los agentes de IA.
Más capacidad no será suficiente. GitHub también está modificando la arquitectura que sostiene sus repositorios para evitar que el incremento de actividad termine convirtiéndose en un problema permanente. La empresa está migrando hacia una infraestructura distribuida entre varias regiones de Microsoft Azure y trabaja en separar el almacenamiento del procesamiento, de manera que ambos recursos puedan ampliarse de forma independiente. También busca reducir las operaciones que necesitan coordinarse entre sí. En pruebas internas, la nueva arquitectura ha conseguido multiplicar hasta por 35 la capacidad de escritura, aunque ese resultado todavía no representa el rendimiento general de la plataforma.
Una infraestructura para otra forma de trabajar. La experiencia de GitHub permite observar una consecuencia menos evidente de la expansión de la inteligencia artificial. Generar propuestas de código con mayor facilidad no significa que todo ese trabajo pueda incorporarse automáticamente a un proyecto. Los desarrolladores todavía necesitan revisar los cambios, comprobar que funcionan y decidir cuáles merecen conservarse, mientras que los servicios que utilizan deben ser capaces de gestionar una actividad cada vez más automatizada.
Imagen destacada ｜ Markus Winkler

articles.title: Meeting Room Tech Mistakes That Make Every Video Call Start Late - Tech Guide
articles.text:
In today’s fast-paced business environment, video calls have become indispensable for communication and collaboration. Whether connecting with remote teams, clients, or partners, organisations rely heavily on video conferencing to maintain productivity and foster relationships. However, despite widespread adoption, many companies face persistent challenges causing video calls to start late. These delays waste valuable time, disrupt workflow, reduce employee morale, and create poor impressions on clients and colleagues.
Understanding common pitfalls in meeting room technology is crucial for businesses aiming to streamline their video conferencing experiences and ensure punctuality. From technical glitches to user errors, various factors contribute to late call starts. Addressing these issues proactively leads to smoother meetings, better collaboration, and improved business outcomes. This article explores the most frequent meeting room tech mistakes that cause video calls to begin behind schedule and offers practical solutions to overcome them.
Common Causes of Video Call Delays
One frequent reason video calls start late is technical issues with the meeting room setup. These problems range from faulty hardware connections to software incompatibilities. For example, cables may be loose or incorrectly connected, the wrong input source might be selected on displays, or devices may fail to pair properly. Such issues often result in frustrating delays as users scramble to identify and fix problems before the meeting can proceed.
In some cases, video conferencing software may not be correctly configured or updated, leading to unexpected errors when attempting to connect. Compatibility issues between different platforms or outdated software versions can cause crashes or connectivity failures. These technical challenges highlight the importance of having a well-maintained and properly configured meeting room environment.
A surprising number of companies underestimate the importance of professional support for their IT infrastructure within meeting rooms. Leveraging the expertise of managed IT experts at Edgeworx can significantly reduce these technical hiccups by ensuring all equipment is installed correctly, updated regularly, and maintained proactively. Managed IT providers typically monitor systems remotely to address problems before they impact meetings, allowing video calls to start as scheduled. Their proactive approach includes routine health checks, timely software updates, and rapid troubleshooting, collectively minimizing downtime and disruptions.
Equipment and Setup Issues
Inadequate or outdated equipment is another common culprit behind late video call starts. Many organisations attempt to save costs by using consumer-grade webcams, microphones, or speakers, which often lead to poor audio and video quality. This results in repeated adjustments and retests before the meeting can begin, frustrating participants and consuming valuable time.
Moreover, insufficient bandwidth or network issues can cause lag, jitter, or disconnections, further prolonging video call start times. Network congestion, limited Wi-Fi coverage, or outdated routers can all negatively affect the quality and reliability of video conferencing sessions. Without a robust and optimised network infrastructure, even the best hardware cannot perform to its full potential.
A well-planned meeting room setup incorporates reliable, business-grade hardware and a network environment optimised for video conferencing. For instance, using dedicated video conferencing endpoints instead of relying solely on laptops can enhance stability and ease of use. These endpoints are designed specifically for video calls and typically offer better audio and video quality, simplified user interfaces, and seamless integration with conferencing platforms.
Organisations that invest in such solutions usually experience fewer delays and smoother call initiations. Additionally, ensuring that the network supports Quality of Service (QoS) prioritisation for video traffic can help reduce latency and packet loss, making calls more stable and responsive.
The Role of User Training and Support
Even with the best technology in place, user error remains a significant factor in late starts. Many employees are not fully trained on how to operate meeting room systems, leading to confusion and last-minute troubleshooting. This issue is especially prevalent when multiple platforms or devices are involved, requiring users to navigate different interfaces, sign-in procedures, and settings.
For example, users may struggle with starting the call, sharing their screens, or adjusting audio and video settings. In some cases, they may not know how to troubleshoot common issues such as muted microphones or disconnected cameras, which can delay meetings further.
Providing comprehensive training and ongoing support can drastically improve meeting punctuality. Companies that engage with Foresight IT’s technical expertise benefit from tailored training programs that empower employees to use video conferencing tools confidently and efficiently. These programs often include hands-on workshops, quick reference guides, and video tutorials that cater to varying levels of technical proficiency. Additionally, having IT support readily available to assist during meetings ensures that any issues are resolved quickly without causing lengthy delays.
Beyond initial training, fostering a culture that encourages employees to familiarise themselves with meeting room technology and report issues promptly contributes to smoother operations. Regular refresher sessions and updates on new features or changes in software also help maintain user competence and reduce errors.
Importance of Regular Maintenance and Updates
Neglecting routine maintenance and software updates is another factor causing video calls to start late. Outdated software may be incompatible with the latest video conferencing platforms or contain bugs that hinder connectivity. Similarly, hardware that is not regularly checked may fail unexpectedly during calls, causing interruptions and delays.
Firmware updates for cameras, microphones, and other peripherals often include performance improvements and security patches. Skipping these updates can leave devices vulnerable to malfunctions or cyber threats. Likewise, failing to update video conferencing applications can result in missing critical compatibility fixes or new features designed to enhance user experience.
Scheduling regular maintenance and updates as part of IT management helps prevent these problems. Managed service providers often include these tasks in their offerings, ensuring that both hardware and software remain in optimal condition. This proactive approach reduces downtime and supports timely video call starts.
Routine maintenance also involves checking physical components such as cables, connectors, and power supplies for wear and tear. Environmental factors like dust accumulation or temperature fluctuations can impact equipment longevity and performance, making regular inspections vital.
Environmental and Room Design Factors
The physical environment of a meeting room can influence how quickly video calls commence. Poor lighting, background noise, or inadequate acoustics can necessitate adjustments or relocation before a meeting can proceed. For instance, harsh backlighting may make participants’ faces difficult to see, while excessive ambient noise can interfere with audio clarity.
Additionally, rooms not ergonomically designed for video conferencing may require repositioning of cameras and microphones or rearranging furniture to ensure all participants are visible and audible. Such last-minute changes can delay call starts and reduce overall meeting efficiency.
Investing in meeting room design that considers these factors can enhance overall efficiency. For example, installing sound-absorbing materials and adjustable lighting can create a conducive environment for video calls. Dedicated meeting rooms with properly placed cameras, microphones, and displays allow participants to join calls quickly without needing constant adjustments.
Moreover, incorporating features like automatic camera framing and noise-cancelling microphones can further streamline meeting setups. These technologies reduce the need for manual intervention and help meetings begin promptly.
Data-Driven Benefits of Optimising Meeting Room Technology
Statistics underline the significant impact these issues have on business productivity and employee satisfaction. According to a report by ZK Research, 70% of employees say they lose time due to meeting technology problems, with an average of 20 minutes wasted per meeting setup failure. This lost time accumulates rapidly across organisations, leading to decreased efficiency and increased frustration.
Another study from Wainhouse Research found that poor audio and video quality is the top reason for video conference dissatisfaction, affecting 35% of users. Such dissatisfaction can reduce engagement, hinder communication, and ultimately impact decision-making during meetings.
Furthermore, a Microsoft report highlights that organisations with optimised meeting room technology see a 15% increase in meeting efficiency. This improvement translates to faster decision cycles, better collaboration, and a more positive workplace culture.
These statistics demonstrate that investing in the right technology, training, and support not only prevents delays but also enhances overall organisational performance.
Conclusion
Delays at the start of video calls can be frustrating and costly, but they are largely preventable. By addressing common meeting room technology mistakes-such as inadequate equipment, lack of user training, poor maintenance, and suboptimal room design-businesses can ensure their video calls begin promptly and run smoothly.
Engaging professional IT support, like the , and benefiting from can provide the expertise needed for seamless video conferencing experiences. These partnerships help organisations implement best practices, maintain systems proactively, and empower users with the knowledge to operate technology confidently.
Investing in the right technology, training, and environment not only saves time but also enhances communication and collaboration in today’s digital workplace. As remote and hybrid work models continue to evolve, optimising meeting room technology is essential for maintaining productivity and fostering strong professional relationships.

articles.title: Fortinet turns its firewall footprint into an AI security on-ramp - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Fortinet turns its firewall footprint into an AI security on-ramp
The fastest way to bring a new security capability into the enterprise has never been a new product. It’s a new license for something the customer already owns. Fortinet Inc. understands this better than most, as it has continued to add features to its FortiGate firewall.
This week, the company announced it is applying that strategy to the most pressing security problem facing information technology leaders today: securing artificial intelligence.
On Monday, the company announced the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service, a cloud-delivered subscription that brings AI-specific inspection and guardrails to FortiGate firewalls. Customers turn it on, and FortiGate begins inspecting prompts, model responses and Model Context Protocol tool traffic in real time, without the customer having to deploy and manage a separate AI security stack. The engine behind the service is FortiAIGate, Fortinet’s AI gateway, which received a new set of capabilities, including technology from the Virtue AI acquisition the company closed in August.
AI security has shifted from a niche to a land grab in under two years. Palo Alto Networks Inc. bought Protect AI; Check Point Software Inc. acquired Lakera; F5 Inc. purchased CalypsoAI; and Cisco Systems Systems Inc. procured Robust Intelligence. Forrester tallied more than $2 billion in spending by major vendors on AI security startups over an 18-month period.
Every platform vendor now has an AI security story. The question for buyers is no longer who has the technology, but who can deploy it across the organization fastest and at the lowest operational cost. That’s the question Fortinet is trying to answer.
Here are some takeaways that should matter to chief information officers and chief information security officers:
Platform is the strategy
Most AI security products on the market today require customers to stand up something new: a proxy, a gateway, an API integration for every AI application, or a browser extension on every endpoint. Each of those is a project, and projects stall. In my conversations with security leaders, the gap between “we bought an AI security tool” and “we have AI security coverage” is often measured in quarters, which is why the security industry is filled with shelfware.
Fortinet’s approach mitigates that by riding on the FortiGate installed base, one of the largest in the industry. The firewall already sits in the traffic path at branches, campuses and data centers, so turning on AI inspection becomes a policy decision rather than an infrastructure deployment. Software-defined wide-area network integration was the primary reason the company went from a minority-share player in WAN connectivity to a market leader in just a few years.
Organizations need AI security that can scale as quickly as AI is deployed. By extending advanced AI inspection and guardrails through FortiGate, Fortinet is making AI security available within existing security infrastructure, which is the right move for the company and its customers.
Midmarket companies and distributed enterprises, such as retailers, healthcare systems and manufacturers, are adopting AI as quickly as anyone, but they lack the staff to run a dedicated AI security program. Delivering protection via an appliance they already manage lowers the barrier considerably. It’s the same model that made FortiGate the default choice for secure SD-WAN, and it’s likely to work here for the same reasons.
Inspection is moving from ‘who’ to ‘what’
The first wave of AI security products focused on discovery, identifying which employees are using ChatGPT, which SaaS apps have embedded AI, and whether sensitive files are being uploaded. Useful but shallow. Knowing that someone used an AI tool tells you nothing about whether the interaction was dangerous.
The new service goes further by inspecting the content of AI interactions. FortiAIGate applies multilayered guardrails across prompts, model responses, MCP tool calls and responses, API activity and agent actions. The inspection covers text, images, audio, video and code. Expanded data loss prevention detects 35 types of personally identifiable information and confidential data, and can trigger alerts, deny or redact them before they leave the organization.
This is the shift that will enable businesses to deploy AI safely. Traditional security tools focus on IP addresses, signatures, and payloads. AI threats, such as prompt injection and poisoned tool responses, live in natural language. A firewall that understands only packets will miss them. One that understands intent is better aligned with where AI is headed.
The real test will be accuracy at scale. Fortinet claims low latency and minimal false positives, and Virtue AI’s guardrail technology should help, but security teams have long memories of DLP tools that blocked everything or nothing. I’d want to see proof in production before buying the marketing.
AI cost control is now a security function
The capability I found most interesting has little to do with traditional threats. FortiAIGate lets administrators set model permissions, budgets, spending limits and rate limits at the organization, workspace, project or user level. Administrators are alerted as spending approaches a limit, and requests are blocked once the limit is exceeded. Intelligent routing sends each request to the appropriate model based on content, policy and cost, without requiring application re-architecting.
Fortinet also highlights “Denial-of-Wallet” attacks, in which malicious or runaway prompts burn through tokens and GPU compute. That threat category didn’t exist three years ago and is now a real budget risk. As agents run around the clock and machine token consumption outpaces that of humans, an uncontrolled agent loop can generate a five-figure inference bill over a weekend.
The bigger point is organizational. AI spending today is scattered across business units, developer credit cards, and cloud accounts. Finance can’t see it, IT can’t govern it and security doesn’t own it. Placing spend controls in the same gateway that enforces security policy gives CIOs a single control point for both risk and cost. I expect token governance to become a standard line item in AI security evaluations in 2027, and Fortinet is early to make it a core feature.
Agents are the new shadow IT
Shadow IT took a decade to bring under control. Shadow AI is emerging in months, and shadow agents will be even harder to manage because agents don’t just consume data; they act on it. They call APIs, invoke tools, connect to MCP servers, and trigger workflows, often with credentials that no one in security has reviewed.
FortiAIGate’s expanded agent visibility shows which agents are operating across the business and how they interact with enterprise applications, APIs, tools, data and MCP servers. Combined with Virtue AI’s capabilities to discover unsanctioned agents, scan MCP tools and block malicious tool calls, Fortinet is building a solid foundation for agent governance.
Visibility is step one, not the finish line. Enterprises need to treat agents as identities, with owners, least-privilege access and continuous monitoring. Fortinet’s broader Security Fabric, spanning network, identity, endpoint and security operations, provides a credible path to connect agent visibility with enforcement. The company needs to demonstrate that those dots are connected in practice, not just in architecture slides.
Flexibility on where AI traffic is processed is a must-have
Not every organization will be comfortable sending prompts and model responses through a cloud service. Regulated industries, governments and companies with data sovereignty requirements often need inspections to occur within their own environment. Fortinet addresses this with self-hosted FortiAIGate, which can run on-premises, in the customer’s cloud or on Kubernetes with Nvidia Corp. graphics processing units, keeping prompts, responses, data and logs within the environment.
The company also includes more than 50 predefined compliance policies covering AI governance frameworks, data privacy laws, industry regulations and security frameworks, along with detailed logs of every prompt, output and tool call for auditors. As the EU AI Act and a patchwork of state and industry rules take shape, that audit trail will be worth as much as the guardrails themselves.
The dual model is smart. The cloud-delivered service is the on-ramp for the broad base, while self-hosted FortiAIGate is the destination for customers with demanding performance, privacy or sovereignty needs. It also addresses an important blind spot. A firewall sees only traffic that passes through it, but a growing share of agent activity occurs cloud-to-cloud or within application tiers that never cross a FortiGate. A gateway placed next to the AI workload closes that gap.
A note on earnings
On a related note, Fortinet announced its third-quarter results on Wednesday. By almost any operational measure, it was a strong quarter, with revenue up 20%, to $2.08 billion, beating the $2.06 billion consensus. Product revenue jumped 37%, to $765 million, and billings grew 29%, to $2.34 billion.
Investors seemed fixated on a single line item: Service revenue grew only 13%, to $1.31 billion, and Fortinet trimmed its full-year services forecast to $5.15 billion to $5.17 billion, down from $5.18 billion to $5.22 billion. The stock fell more than 20% on Thursday, pulling other cybersecurity names down with it.
I think the market overreacted, and I’m not alone. Rosenblatt Securities analyst Catharine Trebnick titled her post-earnings note “Selloff Overdone” and maintained her Buy rating. Large enterprise customers typically buy hardware first and activate services in stages, which Chief Financial Officer Christiane Ohlgart called “really a timing issue.” Trebnick agrees, writing that “the leading indicators support that read”: Service billings grew 26%, total deferred revenue rose 19%, and short-term deferred revenue grew 14.5%, its fastest pace in five quarters.
More important, the product surge is being driven by customers moving to higher-end FortiGates with the computing power to run new functions such as AI security. Every one of those boxes is a future subscription, including the AI service announced this week. Trebnick called the new FortiGuard service “the clearest path we have seen for AI security to show up in service revenue rather than hardware.” Product revenue today becomes service revenue tomorrow, and investors who sold on a one-quarter timing gap are looking at the wrong number.
Final thoughts
Fortinet’s move reflects a broader truth about the AI security market, namely that the technology is converging and the battle is shifting to distribution and operational simplicity. Every major vendor now offers some form of prompt inspection, guardrails and agent visibility. Fortinet’s edge is that it can deliver those capabilities to a massive installed base with little more than a license and a policy change, a meaningful advantage in a market where most organizations are still figuring out where to start.
There are open questions. Inline inspection of AI traffic depends on TLS decryption, which many organizations still don’t enable broadly, so the service’s effectiveness is limited by the customer’s inspection posture. Pricing and packaging will determine how quickly the service spreads beyond early adopters. Fortinet will need to prove its accuracy claims against rivals that have been selling AI guardrails longer.
For buyers, I’d focus on four things. First, if you already run FortiGate, evaluate the service against your actual AI traffic before buying a standalone tool; you may already have the control point you need. Second, revisit your TLS inspection policies, because AI security without decryption is AI visibility at best. Third, bring finance into the conversation now and set token budgets and rate limits before agent spending surprises you. Finally, build an agent inventory with an owner for every agent, because you can’t secure what you can’t see, and you can’t hold accountable what no one owns.
AI will create more security work, not less. The vendors that make that work easiest to absorb will win, and Fortinet has made a strong case for being among them.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: Sony fait revenir la 3D sans lunettes, mais pas là où on l'attendait
articles.text:
Des années après l'échec des téléviseurs 3D, Sony veut rendre l'affichage en relief plus abordable. Avec son nouvel ELF-MN1, un écran miniature de 6 pouces, le constructeur japonais entend donner vie à des personnages virtuels et des objets numériques, directement chez soi.
Présenté au Japon le 28 octobre, le Sony ELF-MN1 appartient à la famille Spatial Reality Display, jusqu'ici surtout destinée aux professionnels de la création 3D. Cette fois, Sony change d'approche : plutôt que de proposer un grand écran pour la conception ou la visualisation de projets, il mise sur un accessoire compact, conçu pour faire apparaître des avatars et des figurines numériques comme s'ils étaient réellement posés devant l'utilisateur.
Un écran miniature qui suit vos yeux pour créer le relief
L'ELF-MN1 repose sur une dalle LCD de 6 pouces dotée de microlentilles qui dirigent une image différente vers chaque œil. Un système de suivi oculaire adapte l'affichage aux mouvements de la tête, afin de préserver l'illusion de profondeur sans lunettes. Sony a même intégré un capteur infrarouge pour améliorer ce suivi dans les environnements sombres.
Avec sa définition de 1 080 × 2 160 pixels et ses 403 pixels par pouce, une densité record pour la gamme, le petit écran promet un affichage particulièrement fin. Son support transparent en acrylique contribue à donner l'impression que les personnages se trouvent directement sur le bureau.
L'expérience reste toutefois individuelle : une seule personne peut profiter du relief à la fois, à une distance comprise entre 30 et 80 cm. L'écran nécessite par ailleurs un ordinateur ou un smartphone compatible, connecté en USB-C, ainsi qu'une application adaptée. Il ne transforme donc pas n'importe quelle vidéo en contenu 3D.
Des figurines virtuelles pour environ 300 euros
Sony cible notamment les amateurs d'animation japonaise avec HoloModel, un service de Gugenka proposant des figurines numériques de personnages sous licence. L'idée est de retrouver son personnage favori en relief, sans avoir besoin d'une figurine physique.
Le constructeur prévoit aussi un SDK compatible avec Unity pour permettre aux développeurs de créer leurs propres expériences. De quoi ouvrir la porte à d'autres usages, au-delà des avatars et des personnages d'animation.
Mais la véritable évolution concerne le prix. En 2020, le premier Spatial Reality Display de Sony était annoncé à 4 999 dollars. L'ELF-MN1 est proposé au Japon à 53 900 yens TTC, soit environ 306 euros à titre indicatif. Les deux produits n'ont évidemment pas les mêmes ambitions, mais cette différence illustre le changement de positionnement de Sony.
Les précommandes sont ouvertes au Japon, avec une sortie prévue le 11 décembre 2026. Aucune commercialisation française n'a été annoncée.
La 3D sans lunettes ne reviendra peut-être pas dans nos salons sous la forme de téléviseurs géants. Sony semble désormais lui imaginer un avenir plus personnel, sur nos bureaux, aux côtés de nos objets et personnages préférés.

articles.title: Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
articles.text:
Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
Can AI run the entire software show? At TechSparks 2026, ForgeCode CEO Tushar Mathur explained how AI agents can automate software development while engineers focus on quality and results.
AI can generate code faster than ever, but getting it tested and reviewed and into production is a different challenge.
Engineering teams are increasingly using AI agents to write code, fix bugs, and build features. But faster coding does not necessarily mean faster software delivery.
As code generation accelerates, reviews pile up, testing slows down, and teams struggle to coordinate the growing volume of changes.
At TechSparks 2026, Tushar Mathur, CEO of Forge Code, explored this problem in his session, Anatomy of a software factory. He explained how AI-native engineering organisations can move beyond automating individual coding tasks to building systems that manage the entire software development lifecycle.
“Just because code is becoming easy and faster to generate doesn't mean your overall SDLC becomes faster,” Mathur said.
From coding assistants to software factories
The traditional software development process focused heavily on writing code efficiently. Teams spent time defining requirements, preparing specifications and designing architecture to reduce the effort needed during implementation, he said.
With AI taking over more coding work, the bottlenecks are moving elsewhere.
Mathur described how organisations can end up with large volumes of pull requests awaiting review, longer testing cycles and more bugs than existing regression suites can catch.
Hiring more engineers or running more AI agents is not necessarily the answer. More people can increase coordination costs, while adding agents without effective feedback loops can generate code that overwhelms the systems responsible for reviewing and testing it.
“The reason why this happens is because there's no signal,” Mathur said, explaining why simply connecting automated steps does not create an effective software factory.
An assembly line that learns
Mathur presented Forge Code as a software factory that coordinates AI agents across the development lifecycle. The process begins with triaging requests, creating specifications and implementing features.
Agents then verify changes before they move towards deployment, with human engineers stepping in when decisions or feedback are needed.
The system also monitors production, using the resulting insights to inform future tasks. This creates a feedback loop in which the factory can identify problems, improve its workflows and generate new work from what it learns.
Mathur said Forge Code was running around 100 agents in the background during his presentation, working on features, compatibility and bug detection.
He outlined six principles for an effective software factory: autonomous operation, scalability, cost efficiency, measurability, self-improvement and alignment with business goals.
The last principle is particularly important.
Instead of treating every request as a coding task, the factory should work towards outcomes such as improving customer retention or meeting compliance requirements. Teams can then prioritise features based on the value they deliver.
Engineers become supervisors
In this model, engineers spend less time directing every task and more time monitoring outcomes, reviewing signals and improving the system. Business leaders can also contribute requests and priorities directly, allowing the factory to translate organisational goals into a development backlog.
Writing code faster is great. Shipping better software is the real win.
For engineering teams, the trick is turning AI-powered speed into reliable products, measurable gains and business results.

articles.title: La Diplomate saison 5 : Netflix confirme la suite de sa série politique culte
articles.text:
La Diplomate saison 5 : Netflix confirme la suite de sa série politique culte
Le drame politique récompensé aux Emmy Awards n'a pas terminé sa course sur Netflix.
La Diplomate n'a pas dit son dernier mot sur Netflix. Au terme d'une saison 4 qui a laissé les fans en haleine, la plateforme de streaming a décidé de reconduire la série avec Keri Russell pour une cinquième saison.
Une saison 5 officiellement confirmée
Le thriller politique La Diplomate est revenu le 15 octobre dernier avec une quatrième saison sous haute tension. Son récit a en effet vu la présidente Grace Penn (Allison Janney) et le vice-président Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell) comploter pour voler l'arme la plus puissante de la Russie, précipitant au passage les États-Unis vers la guerre.
Une situation que l'ambassadrice Kate Wyler (Russell) a tenté tant bien que mal de gérer jusqu'au final explosif de la saison, qui a laissé l'avenir de tout ce beau monde en suspens au beau milieu du G7.
Les fans peuvent cependant être rassurés : la série aura droit à une saison 5 et ce cliffhanger ne demeurera donc pas sans réponse.
Mais en attendant de savoir ce qui attend l'administration Penn dans cette future saison, il faut noter que la créatrice de la série, Debora Cahn (À la Maison Blanche), a encore bien des choses à raconter.
Elle a en effet indiqué au micro du Hollywood Reporter que, pour elle, l'histoire ne fait que commencer.
"J’ai grandi avec la télévision classique, où une saison comptait 22, voire 25 épisodes ; j’ai donc l’impression que nous ne faisons que commencer," a expliqué Cahn. "Je n’ai pas le sentiment d’en être à la quatrième saison. J’ai plutôt l’impression d’être là où les choses deviennent vraiment passionnantes."
C'est la première fois depuis la première saison que Netflix reconduit La Diplomate après l'arrivée de nouveaux épisodes. En effet, les saisons 3 et 4 avaient été annoncées avant la diffusion des saisons 2 et 3. La saison 4 est actuellement dans le top 10 des séries les plus vues sur Netflix dans 63 pays.

articles.title: La Guerra de las Galaxias real está empeorando tanto que una empresa quiere ponerle "guardaespaldas" a los satélites
articles.text:
Los acercamientos entre satélites con fines defensivos, ofensivos o de espionaje son cada vez más comunes. Generalmente se trata de ensayos, por lo que todos los dispositivos implicados pertenecen a la misma agencia. Sin embargo, todas las alarmas saltaron recientemente cuando se detectó a un satélite ruso acercándose a un satélite de radar de la compañía finlandesa ICEYE, que aporta datos de inteligencia a Ucrania. Es la primera vez que se detecta algo así contra un satélite comercial que apoya a este país . Por eso, sus naciones aliadas han mostrado preocupación y una compañía especializada en limpieza orbital no ha tardado en proponer una solución: una flota de guardaespaldas para satélites militares.
China y Rusia a la cabeza. Si bien son muchos los países que han hecho maniobras de acercamiento en órbita, ninguna ha logrado superar las cualidades de China y Rusia. Como relatan en Space, ambos países tienen la mejor tecnología en ese aspecto; por lo que, si llega el momento de dejar los ensayos y pasar a la acción, estarían en clara ventaja. Por eso, la compañía Astroscale propone crear naves guardaespaldas que protejan a los satélites sin necesidad de acoplarse o capturarlos. Según ha explicado su jefe de defensa, Alex Godfrey, en un evento en Londres, Europa podría ser de los territorios más beneficiados, pues sus tecnologías de acercamiento son mucho más débiles que la rusa o la china.
Su propuesta consiste en desarrollar una flota de naves que protejan a los satélites desde cerca, pero sin necesidad de tocarlos o acoplarse con ellos.
Mucho más barato. Al no ser necesario un acoplamiento más allá de las maniobras de proximidad, la propuesta no es demasiado cara. De hecho, desde Astroscale señalan que poner en marcha estas naves costaría un 1% de lo que cuesta la flota Skynet, usada en Reino Unido para facilitar las comunicaciones en el ámbito militar.
¿Por qué una empresa de limpieza? Astroscale no deja de ser una empresa de limpieza de basura espacial, pero lo cierto es que eso es lo que la hace tan especial. Para poder retirar chatarra de la órbita terrestre, es necesario acercarse mucho a ella. Por eso, esta empresa es muy buena fabricando naves con tecnologías de acercamiento de precisión. En este caso, ni siquiera sería necesario acercarse muchísimo, solo lo justamente necesario.
Antecedentes. La tecnología, en principio, estará basada en la que ya usó Astroscale en su misión ADRAS-J. En este caso, se eligió una pieza de basura espacial real, concretamente la etapa superior descartada de un cohete japonés, y se pusieron a prueba con éxito maniobras de proximidad.
Teniendo en cuenta que parten de un conocimiento que ya se ha probado, la compañía asegura que podría tener lista una primera nave guardaespaldas en solo 3 años. Puesto que el gobierno del Reino Unido promete financiación para el desarrollo del control espacial a partir de 2030, esperan tener un prototipo preparado ese mismo año. Después, si todo va bien, estos guardaespaldas del espacio podrían distribuirse estratégicamente por toda la órbita terrestre.

articles.title: 267 ventes par mois : le nouveau SUV électrique chinois de Volkswagen vire au fiasco total
articles.text:
Pour tenir le rythme, Volkswagen développe continuellement une gamme dédiée au marché chinois. Mieux encore, la marque allemande s’est carrément alliée à Xpeng pour cerner au mieux les attentes locales. Elle pensait alors avoir trouvé la recette magique pour renouer avec le succès. Hélas, la mayonnaise a bien du mal à prendre puisque le premier modèle de cette collaboration s’avère être un échec.
Les chiffres de ThinkerCar sont sans appel : avec 267 exemplaires vendus chaque mois, l’ID. Unyx 08 est complètement à la traîne. Par rapport aux objectifs de Volkswagen qui étaient fixés à 3 622 modèles par mois, c’est la douche froide. Le constructeur allemand, qui a vu ses ventes fortement chuter en Chine, comptait pourtant beaucoup sur cette nouvelle génération de modèles pour remonter la pente.
L’alliance avec Xpeng : l’espoir déchu de Volkswagen
Cela semble malgré tout très insuffisant pour contrer la concurrence locale qui bataille à feu et à sang à coup de prix ultra agressifs. De fait, les performances commerciales de Volkswagen sont passées de 4,2 millions de voitures en 2019 à seulement 2,69 millions l’année passée. Les affaires ne risquent donc pas de s’améliorer. L’ID. Unyx 08 avait pourtant réuni tous les ingrédients pour réussir.
Basé sur l’imposant Xpeng G9, le SUV allemand en reprend les technologies pour se positionner ouvertement sur le segment premium. Son prix est par ailleurs bien placé avec un ticket d’entrée fixé à environ 32 000 €. Attrayant, mais pas encore assez pour espérer tailler des croupières aux stars du marché : les Xiaomi YU7 et Zeekr 7X demeurent moins chers et plus largement distribués en Chine.
Des tarifs attractifs, mais déjà dépassés par la réalité du marché
Alors que l’ID. Unyx 08 est uniquement vendu chez les concessionnaires Volkswagen, le Xiaomi YU7 peut se trouver chez des revendeurs multimarques plus facilement accessibles. Pour les clients cherchant à se procurer le plus rapidement possible une nouvelle voiture, ça peut énormément jouer. On pensait l’accord avec Xpeng une opportunité rêvée pour se mettre au niveau des modèles chinois. Mais l’allemand est en réalité déjà dépassé.
Le Xiaomi YU7 profite par exemple d’un ensemble de capteurs bien plus avancés au service de la conduite autonome. Le Zeekr 7X, lui, fait valoir sa recharge rapide ultra efficace réduisant les temps d’attente. Puisque les concurrents en offrent plus pour moins cher, les clients ne voient aucun intérêt à aller vers l’ID. Unyx 08. Cela aurait possiblement fonctionné il y a vingt ans de cela. Malheureusement pour Volkswagen, le monde a changé…

articles.title: LattePanda Launches LattePanda Sigma 2: The Embeddable AI Single Board Server
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
LattePanda Launches LattePanda Sigma 2: The Embeddable AI Single Board Server
The LattePanda Team today launched LattePanda Sigma 2, an x86 single-board server designed to bring high-performance local AI computing directly into intelligent products and systems. Built around the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H processor with Intel Arc B390 graphics, LattePanda Sigma 2 delivers up to 180 TOPS of total AI performance at INT8 in a compact form factor.
As "The Embeddable AI Single Board Server," LattePanda Sigma 2 combines high-performance computing, up to 64 GB of memory, high-speed networking, flexible expansion, and real-time hardware control in a single board. Rather than sitting alongside a product, it is designed to be integrated directly into the product itself, supporting applications from autonomous robots and vision systems to professional instruments and private AI appliances.LattePanda Sigma 2 combines the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, Intel Arc B390 GPU, and integrated NPU to deliver up to 180 TOPS of total AI performance at INT8. It features a 16-core CPU with up to 4.8 GHz clock speed, a 12 Xe-core Intel Arc B390 GPU delivering up to 122 TOPS of INT8 AI performance, and an NPU capable of up to 50 TOPS.
With up to 64 GB of LPDDR5X-8533 RAM and 136.5 GB/s memory bandwidth, LattePanda Sigma 2 provides the capacity and throughput required for demanding local AI workloads. Up to 59 GB of VRAM can be allocated for AI workloads, providing enough room for 35B-class quantized MoE models and the KV cache required by long-context AI agents. With INT4 quantization and OpenVINO, the system can run the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model locally at around 30 tokens per second.
Built for Local AI Systems
LattePanda Sigma 2 is designed to support both individual AI workloads and multi-agent local AI systems. Developers can expand compute capacity through M.2, OCuLink, or Thunderbolt 4, connecting additional AI accelerators as workloads grow. An integrated RP2350 microcontroller adds GPIO connectivity and real-time hardware control, allowing AI applications to interact with sensors and actuators. Preloaded MicroPython firmware provides a programmable interface for intelligent devices and automation systems.
Server-Class Expansion in an Embeddable Form Factor
LattePanda Sigma 2 provides extensive connectivity for storage, networking, and acceleration. It includes three M.2 M-Key slots, one M.2 E-Key slot, PCIe 4.0 x2 via OCuLink, and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. Dual 10GbE Ethernet supports high-bandwidth networking, while USB 3.2 Gen 2, USB 2.0, HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 2.1, and eDP 1.5 provide flexible system integration options. These interfaces allow LattePanda Sigma 2 to operate as a compact local AI server or integrate directly into larger intelligent systems.
Ready for Local AI Development and Deployment
LattePanda Sigma 2 supports Windows 11 and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or later, with compatibility for OpenVINO, llama.cpp, and Ollama. It ships with Ubuntu, GPU and NPU drivers, OpenVINO Model Server (OVMS), OpenClaw, and local AI models pre-installed on the onboard SSD, reducing setup time for local AI deployment.
Designed for Product Integration
LattePanda Sigma 2 is designed for product-level integration and long-term deployment, offering a guaranteed 3+ year product lifecycle, custom boot logos and BIOS customization options, and direct engineering support for integration projects. Its combination of local AI compute, high-speed I/O, flexible expansion, and real-time control supports a wide range of applications, including:
- Local AI Appliances—Run private RAG and AI agents while keeping sensitive data on premises.
- All-in-One Homelabs—Combine NAS, virtualization, media services, and local AI in one system.
- Professional Instruments—Capture and process high-speed data streams directly inside compact professional equipment.
- Mobile Autonomous Robots—Unify perception, navigation, planning, and real-time control on one platform.
"Local AI is moving beyond development and into the products and systems people use every day," said Youliang Yu, Product Manager of LattePanda Sigma 2. "With LattePanda Sigma 2, we are combining the computing performance, memory capacity, expansion, and real-time hardware control needed to run AI locally in a compact, embeddable platform. The goal is to give developers a practical way to put local AI directly into the products they build."
Key Specifications
- Processor: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H
- AI Performance: Up to 180 TOPS (CPU + GPU + NPU, INT8)
- NPU: Up to 50 TOPS
- CPU: 16 cores (4P + 8E + 4LPE), up to 4.8 GHz, 18 MB cache
- GPU: Intel Arc B390, 12 Xe-cores, up to 122 TOPS (INT8)
- Memory: Up to 64 GB LPDDR5X-8533 RAM, 136.5 GB/s bandwidth
- Storage & Expansion: 3× M.2 M-Key, 1× M.2 E-Key, OCuLink PCIe 4.0 x2
- Networking: 2× 10GbE RJ45
- Thunderbolt: 2× Thunderbolt 4 Type-C
- USB Type-A: 2× USB 3.2 Gen 2, 2× USB 2.0
- Display: HDMI 2.1, DP 2.1 via USB Type-C, eDP 1.5
- Co-Processor: RP2350
- Operating System: Windows 11, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or later
- Dimensions: 146 × 102 mm
For more information about LattePanda Sigma 2, please visit the LattePanda website. During the pre-sale period through mid-November, the LattePanda Sigma 2 is available at a promotional price of $2,599. Following the conclusion of the pre-sale period, the price will return to $2,799.

articles.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX buying out 418 homes near flagship AI data center, but only if they drop participation in lawsuit — report claims the company is targeting an entire neighborhood, but will only buy from people who don't pursue noise pollution complaints
articles.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceX buying out 418 homes near flagship AI data center, but only if they drop participation in lawsuit — report claims the company is targeting an entire neighborhood, but will only buy from people who don't pursue noise pollution complaints
18 homeowners have reportedly agreed to the deal already.
SpaceXSI, Elon Musk’s data center business powering Grok, is reportedly buying 418 properties in Colonial Hills, Southaven, which sits about half a mile from the powerplant that the company will use to power its data centers in the area. According to The Guardian, real estate agents have been going door to door, offering owners deals on behalf of the company provided that they do not join a class-action lawsuit over the noise pollution coming from the gas turbines that power its GPUs.
MZX, the SpaceXSI subsidiary that operates the Colossus II site, circulated an open letter to nearby residents, saying that it “requires property for its business purposes,” with Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite saying that they will be used to house SpaceXSI staff that the company will need as it expands operations. Musk himself is reportedly staying in the area in an Airstream trailer four nights per week to personally oversee the data center build-out needed to power Grok AI.
The bigger issue here, though, is the requirement that sellers must sign an agreement that prevents them from joining the ongoing case against the company for noise pollution. The Colossus 1 and 2 sites have been in hot water since they started operating, primarily for their use of unpermitted turbines and the air pollution that they bring. SpaceXSI has since promised that it will remove all its unpermitted turbines in a year, especially as its 1.2-gigawatt powerplant comes online. However, this apparently hasn’t resolved the noise pollution issue that the community has been complaining about.
“It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud. I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry,” piano teacher Elizabeth Rose, who lives a couple of miles from the site, told the publication. One of the plaintiffs in the class-action, Jason Haley, also said to The Guardian, “There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house. It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep; I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.”
The company has denied all the allegations against it, saying that it has adjusted its power output and installed sound-dampening walls to reduce the impact on the neighborhood. Musselwhite also said that city monitors have not detected the site breaching the local ordinance limit of 70 decibels, although some experts say that persistent noise as low as 50 decibels could have adverse health impacts.
Opposition against the noise pollution and Musk’s purchases aren’t unanimous, though. Some residents aren’t as affected by the noise pollution, while local businesses are experiencing increased activity. Other people have also agreed to sell just so they could get away from the noise. The mayor says that the buyout isn’t intended to turn Colonial Hills into a company town. “The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as negative,” Musselwhite said.
