articles.title: Samsung advierte: la crisis de RAM está a un paso de volverse mucho peor
articles.text:
Si creías que la crisis de RAM que está haciendo que todos tus dispositivos favoritos sean cada vez más caros no podía volverse más grave, estabas en lo equivocado. En la más reciente presentación de resultados financieros, Samsung advirtió que la situación será peor en 2027 y que las consecuencias se seguirán sintiendo en 2028.
La alta demanda de componentes críticos para servidores y centros de datos de inteligencia artificial permitió a Samsung lograr ingresos trimestrales récords, que rondaron el equivalente a unos 146.300 millones de dólares. El negocio de semiconductores de la compañía coreana incrementó sus ventas en un 15 % e ingresó más de 110.000 millones de dólares en el período.
Si bien Samsung está generando más dinero que nunca en plena crisis de RAM, también advierte que la provisión de componentes continuará muy ajustada el próximo año. La firma ha revelado que toda su producción de memoria de alto ancho de banda HBM4 para 2027 ya está vendida.
Samsung también menciona que en la primera mitad del próximo año comenzará la fabricación a escala de memoria HBM4E y que la incrementará durante el segundo semestre. Asimismo, la empresa habla de una creciente demanda de módulos DDR5 y de discos de estado sólido para servidores. Pero más allá de las proyecciones favorables para su negocio, los coreanos reconocen que la crisis de RAM puede agravarse en 2027.
Aún no hemos visto lo peor de la crisis de RAM, según Samsung
En una de las diapositivas de la presentación de resultados financieros de Samsung se ofrece una referencia directa a la crisis de RAM y sus consecuencias. "El gasto de capital en infraestructura de IA se acelerará a medida que se expanda el ecosistema de inteligencia artificial. Es probable que el fuerte aumento de la demanda impulsada por la IA agrave aún más la escasez de oferta en comparación con el año calendario 2026", indican los asiáticos.
Pero los coletazos de la escasez de RAM y almacenamiento se extenderán hasta 2028, pues allí también se sentirán las consecuencias de la crisis. Samsung considera que los efectos se seguirán viendo después de 2027, incluso aunque incremente su inversión en infraestructura.
"En medio del creciente traslado de la producción de bits desde la DRAM convencional hacia la HBM, creo que esto actuará como una restricción física sobre la oferta", mencionó un ejecutivo de la firma asiática.
Si la advertencia de Samsung se cumple, la industria de los semiconductores continuará fuertemente enfocada en abastecer la infraestructura de IA. Esto limitará la cantidad de hardware disponible para la electrónica de consumo y lo encarecerá, por lo que tendremos crisis de RAM para rato.

articles.title: Winzig, aber heikel: Nasa-Rover Perseverance entdeckt ultrafeine Staubpartikel auf dem Mars
articles.text:
Gefahr für Astronauten? Nasa-Rover Perseverance entdeckt ultrafeine Staubpartikel auf dem Mars
Über 1645 Marstage hinweg hat der Nasa-Rover Perseverance feine und ultrafeine Marsstaubpartikel gemessen, die sich auf mitgeführten Proben von Raumanzugmaterialien abgesetzt hatten. Einige dieser Partikel sind theoretisch klein genug, um tief in die Lunge vorzudringen und womöglich sogar in den Blutkreislauf überzugehen. Jetzt wurden die Ergebnisse in den Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences veröffentlicht.
Feine und ultrafeine Partikel
Frühere Messungen erfassten Marsstaubpartikel mit einem Durchmesser von bis zu etwa 3 Mikrometern. Das „Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry“ (PIXL) an Bord von Perseverance wies jetzt zwei noch kleinere Partikelklassen nach: feine Partikel mit einer Größe von 2,5 Mikrometern und ultrafeine, etwa 100 Nanometer große – oder wohl eher kleine – Partikel. Zum Vergleich: Die ultrafeinen Partikel sind rund 700-mal dünner als ein menschliches Haar. Die PIXL-Ergebnisse sind die ersten Vor-Ort-Messungen von feinen und ultrafeinen Partikeln auf dem Mars.
Welcher Stoff hält den Marsstaub besser ab?
Die winzigen Partikel könnten tief in die Lunge von Astronaut:innen vordringen, in den Blutkreislauf übertreten und unter Umständen lebenswichtige Organe beeinträchtigen. Hinzu kommt die Sorge, dass die Bedingungen auf dem Mars und die Eigenschaften des Staubs Raumanzüge zersetzen könnten. Deshalb hatte der Perseverance-Rover Proben von potenziellen Raumanzugmaterialien an Bord, darunter die Kunstfaser Vectran und die Schutzbeschichtung Teflon.
Vectran schien die größeren Staubpartikel zurückzuhalten. Auf der Teflonprobe lagerte sich weniger Staub ab. Die dort haftenden Partikel waren allerdings kleiner. Das könnte auf unterschiedliche elektrostatische Eigenschaften der Materialien zurückzuführen sein, die beeinflussen, welche Partikelgrößen an ihnen haften bleiben. „Wir haben keine Beweise dafür, dass der Staub die Raumanzugmaterialien beschädigt hat, sondern lediglich, dass die Materialien dazu neigten, unterschiedlich mit dem Staub zu interagieren“, sagte Scott VanBommel von der Washington University in St. Louis, Autor der Studie.
Der Mars ist nicht zu gefährlich
Die Ergebnisse könnten künftig bei der Entwicklung von Raumanzügen und Habitaten, bei Verfahren zur Staubentfernung sowie bei Gesundheitsstandards für Marsbesatzungen berücksichtigt werden. „Eine geringere Partikelgröße macht Staub nicht unbedingt gefährlicher, aber kleinere Partikel können potenziell tiefer in den menschlichen Körper eindringen und sind für den Körper schwerer auszuscheiden“, sagt VanBommel.
Das Gesundheitsrisiko der Partikel, die der Nasa-Rover entdeckt hat, muss allerdings weiter untersucht werden. Zusätzlich erweitern die Erkenntnisse die Richtlinien und Protokolle, die die Nasa für toxikologische Risiken aufgestellt hat. Die Ergebnisse dieser Studie würden nicht bedeuten, dass der Mars für Menschen zu gefährlich ist, sagt VanBommel. „Marsstaub ist eine Gefahr, die bei der Planung berücksichtigt werden muss, genauso wie Strahlung und die Entfernung zur Erde.“

articles.title: How Edge AI Helps Humanoid Robots React Faster Than a Central GPU - EE Times
articles.text:
STMicroelectronics argued that humanoid robots should use onboard sensors and cameras to handle fast reactions on the robot, and leave only whole-body coordination to a central GPU, because a round trip to the GPU adds latency a moving robot cannot afford. The chipmaker is still weighing whether to build more powerful MCUs or MPUs for the task, a decision it says depends on how the robotics market develops.
“Every millisecond counts,” Allan Lagasca, director of STMicroelectronics’ robotics segment strategic program, told EE Times. “If you want a fast reaction, you should move the processing to the edge. If you want the entire system to work together, that is where the GPU comes in.”
Running inference closer to the task can reduce the workload sent to a central GPU and avoid delays associated with transferring data and returning commands, Lagasca said. In robotics, those delays can affect physical movement.
When two hands coordinate to transfer an object, for example, a delayed command can cause a joint to miss its target. Even if individual joints miss their targets by only a few millimeters, the combined movement can be affected.
“If inference is performed at the edge, the system can send the necessary command locally and respond faster,” he said.
The central GPU, which Lagasca called the robot’s “larger brain,” still has to synchronize the head cameras, machine vision, and navigation, and coordinate joints whose sensors are not connected to one another. Without that coordination, he said, “the robot could move both feet forward at the wrong time.” STMicroelectronics does not make GPUs.
The chipmaker’s current AI inference products are based on its neural processing unit (NPU) and microprocessor unit (MPU), Lagasca said. Whether it develops more powerful chips depends on how the market evolves.
Robotics is still a low-volume market, while STMicroelectronics, as an integrated device manufacturer, targets high-volume production. “By following this market, we will better understand which technologies are needed,” he said.
Where the hand does its own thinking
In a robotic hand demonstration at electronica India, a camera captured an image of a human hand, and an AI model identified 21 points to recognize the gesture. The system then translated that information into commands for a robotic hand with six motors. Gesture recognition ran on STMicroelectronics’ STM32N6 32-bit microcontroller.
“The mapping is not simple,” Lagasca said. “It is not even a one-to-one or one-to-two relationship, and it must run continuously as the hand moves.”
The work starts with the camera. Its module combines an image sensor to capture images, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to determine the camera’s position and orientation, and a time-of-flight (ToF) sensor to measure distance. “Capturing an image is not enough; you also need to measure the distance,” Lagasca said. The ToF reading tells the hand when to close its fingers.
Inference also runs mainly onboard the camera, partly for privacy, Lagasca said. As long as an image is used for inference without being stored or sent elsewhere, the system can meet privacy and cybersecurity requirements, he added.
The camera’s output then has to be translated into commands the motors can use. Lagasca said the gesture recognition demonstration used a standard PLC to bridge AI outputs and robotic control. “The difficulty lies in translating the data generated by AI into a format that can be transferred to a standard PLC to control the robot,” he said.
The same edge approach enables the hand to adjust its grip. Humans adjust their hold on a water bottle almost instinctively; a robot has to compute the required grip.
In another example, Lagasca described a hand that identifies a water bottle, determines its distance, and adjusts its grip to avoid crushing it or letting it slip. “The MCU, in this case the STM32, performs this inference,” he said.
Each part of the robot handles its share. Most sensors have their own MCUs, Lagasca said, as do the motion and motor-control functions, while AI inference has its own NPU. “This creates a distributed architecture rather than putting everything into a single processor,” he said.
Integrating robotic modules and simplifying hardware
Humanoid robot manufacturers may source hands, joints, and cameras from different suppliers. Integrating these components can create problems with camera placement, board space, and motor control. A camera mounted on top of a hand may require the robot to reposition its hand before lifting an object, while one mounted underneath may strike the table during pickup.
STMicroelectronics said it is exploring ways to integrate camera technology and other functions into the humanoid hand itself. Although the company does not manufacture camera modules, it can combine its technologies with those of its partners. Earlier this year, STMicroelectronics and camera-module maker Leopard Imaging introduced a multimodal vision module for humanoid robots that combines STMicroelectronics’ imaging technology, 3D depth-mapping, and motion sensors. The module connects over Ethernet through Nvidia’s Holoscan Sensor Bridge to Nvidia’s Jetson computers and Isaac robot development platform. It is designed to fit the size, weight, and power limits of humanoid robots.
Lagasca said the broader approach is to divide the robot into modules, including hands, joints, feet, and eyes, that can be adapted to different applications and form factors.
Packaging the required functions within these modules presents another challenge. Designers must fit processing, motor control, and connectivity into the available board space. Lagasca cited a customer requirement for a 6 × 6-centimeter board.
Choosing MCUs, motor drivers, and connectivity parts separately could produce a design measuring 140 × 330 mm, far larger than the board, he said. For its robotic hand, ST integrated six MOSFETs and three drivers into one package, so a manufacturer can mount one part instead of nine.
Safety remains an open question
The distribution of intelligence across a robot also raises safety concerns. Lagasca said existing safety frameworks include Safety Integrity Level (SIL) requirements for industrial applications and Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) requirements in the automotive sector. These requirements may become relevant as companies from the automotive, industrial automation, smartphone, and home appliance markets enter robotics.
However, compliance with a standard doesn’t guarantee that the entire robot is safe.
“If a sensor fails, the robot could still cause an injury, even if it meets the relevant SIL or ASIL standard,” Lagasca said.
AI can introduce additional risks if a system fails to make a decision or makes the wrong one, he said. All these elements must be considered together to assess a robot’s functional safety.
Lagasca added that many existing standards were developed for fixed equipment rather than moving robots. The industry still needs to determine which standards and regulatory requirements are appropriate for humanoid systems, particularly those that interact directly with people.
The chipmaker’s role in the humanoid bill of materials
Lagasca said that STMicroelectronics can address approximately 600 positions in a humanoid robot’s bill of materials (BOM), covering more than 500 components. The share of a robot’s total cost that this represents depends on its design, including how many joints, sensors, and AI functions the robot has, he added.
As an illustration, he said that if a robot’s BOM were worth $600 and STMicroelectronics supplied all of it, the chipmaker’s share would be 100%. If the BOM grew to $1,000 while the chipmaker’s parts remained valued at $600, its share would fall to 60%.
Entry-level robots may cost less and have fewer degrees of freedom, while mid-range and high-end systems may require more sophisticated capabilities. Depending on the design, Lagasca said STMicroelectronics could potentially address 800 or more positions as the number of joints, sensors, cameras, and AI-processing requirements increases.
From demonstrations to deployment
Despite the growing number of humanoid robot demonstrations, Lagasca said many applications remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Automotive manufacturing and logistics are among the early areas of interest because manufacturers can justify the cost of automation and adjust production lines to meet market demand.
He cited Boston Dynamics’ association with Hyundai and Figure AI’s relationship with BMW as examples of links between humanoid robotics and the automotive industry. Hyundai, which owns Boston Dynamics, plans to start deploying Atlas robots at its Georgia plant in 2028, while BMW has conducted trials for Figure robots in its Spartanburg, S.C., body shop.
Moving beyond demonstrations presents several challenges. Training data is one of them. Activities such as drilling, soldering, cooking, and sewing can be recorded and uploaded to create datasets, Lagasca said.
Battery technology doesn’t yet support 24-hour operation, he said, making downtime a practical consideration for developers.
The applications that reach the market will also depend on safety and regulatory requirements. Lagasca said direct physical interaction between humanoid robots and people presents additional challenges, particularly in healthcare.
Cybersecurity is another concern. Lagasca said that chipmakers and device manufacturers must account for the EU Cyber Resilience Act and other applicable requirements at both the product and application levels. “You do not want 10,000 robots operating in the real world only for someone to hack into them,” he said.
How intelligence is ultimately distributed between the edge processors and the central GPU may depend on a question the industry has not settled: What a humanoid robot should look like. The system architecture “has not stabilized,” Lagasca said. “Some developers ask why a robot should have only two hands rather than six, or only two legs.”
“We do not yet know what the final configuration will be,” he said.

CES 2026 Signals the Year Physical AI Was Born

articles.title: Ransomware on a Home PC vs a Work Laptop: Same Click, Very Different Consequences - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Understanding the Threat Landscape
Ransomware attacks have become one of the most widespread cybersecurity threats globally, targeting both individuals and organizations. While many users may view ransomware as a personal issue affecting only individual devices, the reality is far more complex. The consequences of a ransomware attack on a home PC can be severe, but when the same attack hits a work laptop, the stakes rise dramatically, impacting not just the user but entire organizations and their stakeholders.
Ransomware typically involves malicious software encrypting files on a device, making them inaccessible until a ransom is paid. However, the impact varies greatly depending on the environment. The difference between a home PC and a work laptop is not only ownership but also the scope and scale of the damage that can follow. Understanding these distinctions is critical for effective prevention and response strategies.
The Home PC Scenario: Personal Data at Risk
When ransomware strikes a home PC, the primary victims are the individual user and their personal data. Photos, documents, and other files can be locked away, causing frustration and potential loss of irreplaceable memories or essential information. The financial impact is often limited to the ransom demand and possible costs for recovery software or professional help, but the emotional and practical toll can be significant.
Many home users rely on their computers for online banking, tax filing, managing sensitive personal documents, or even running small side businesses. A ransomware infection can lock access to these critical files and expose users to identity theft and financial fraud. According to Cybersecurity Ventures, ransomware attacks are predicted to occur every 2 seconds by 2031, highlighting the increasing frequency of these incidents.
Despite the personal impact, home users often have more control over recovery options. Backups, antivirus tools, and professional IT support can help mitigate damage. However, many individuals lack adequate backups or technical expertise, which can lead to permanent data loss. Engaging with a trusted provider like Auxzillium can provide tailored managed IT services that improve security posture and response strategies for both individuals and businesses.
Additionally, ransomware infections on home PCs can serve as launchpads for further attacks. Infected personal devices connected to home networks can inadvertently compromise other devices, including smart home systems, phones, or work laptops used remotely. This interconnectivity underscores the need for vigilance and robust security measures even in home settings.
Work Laptop: A Target with Corporate Consequences
Ransomware on a work laptop has far-reaching implications beyond the individual user. In corporate environments, a single infected device can act as a gateway to an entire network, potentially crippling business operations and exposing sensitive company data. Intellectual property, customer information, employee records, and financial data can be compromised or held hostage, posing significant risks to organizational viability.
The financial impact for businesses is substantial and escalating. The average ransom payment rose by 43% in 2023, reaching over $200,000 per incident, according to Sophos. Beyond ransom costs, downtime from ransomware attacks can lead to significant revenue loss, reputational damage, and regulatory penalties for failing to protect customer data. Some businesses report losses exceeding millions due to operational disruptions and remediation efforts.
Organizations must implement stringent cybersecurity measures, including routine employee training, multi-factor authentication, robust backups, and network segmentation. An article by Creative Consultants Group outlines a proactive five-step defense plan businesses can adopt to stop ransomware in its tracks. Such strategies are essential to reduce vulnerability and ensure rapid recovery.
Furthermore, ransomware attacks on corporate devices can trigger cascading effects. Supply chains may be disrupted, client trust eroded, and long-term partnerships jeopardized. In some cases, attackers combine ransomware with data theft and threaten to release sensitive information publicly if ransom demands are unmet, adding pressure on organizations to respond swiftly.
The Role of User Behavior and Awareness
User behavior is a critical factor in ransomware infections on both home PCs and work laptops. Cybercriminals frequently exploit human error-phishing emails, malicious links, and deceptive downloads are common attack vectors. A single click on a disguised link or attachment can unleash ransomware that spreads rapidly.
In workplace settings, employees often face sophisticated phishing campaigns designed to bypass traditional security measures. Attackers use social engineering tactics tailored to specific industries or roles, increasing breach likelihood. Training and awareness programs tailored to business environments are vital to mitigating these risks. IBM reports that human error contributes to 95% of cybersecurity breaches.
Conversely, home users may lack the knowledge or resources to identify and avoid threats effectively. Many individuals do not regularly update software or use strong, unique passwords, increasing vulnerability. Raising awareness about safe browsing habits, recognizing suspicious communications, and implementing basic security hygiene is crucial in both scenarios.
Organizations investing in continuous cybersecurity education see measurable reductions in phishing susceptibility, emphasizing the importance of human factors in defense. Meanwhile, home users benefit from accessible educational resources and tools that simplify security best practices.
Recovery and Mitigation: Different Approaches for Different Environments
Recovery from ransomware differs significantly between personal and corporate contexts. For home PC users, restoring data from backups or using decryption tools can often resolve the issue without extensive disruption. Nonetheless, emotional toll and potential data loss remain concerns. Some ransomware variants resist decryption, and paying ransom does not guarantee recovery.
In contrast, businesses require comprehensive incident response plans covering technical recovery, legal considerations, communication strategies, and regulatory compliance. Incident response teams must act quickly to isolate affected systems, assess damage, and restore operations. Partnering with cybersecurity firms specializing in ransomware response can expedite restoration and limit damage.
Both individuals and organizations benefit from investing in preventative measures. Regular software updates, endpoint protection, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring are essential components of a resilient cybersecurity strategy. Collaboration with a can provide managed IT services designed to safeguard critical assets and support robust, tailored recovery plans.
Moreover, organizations increasingly adopt cyber insurance policies to mitigate financial losses from ransomware. These policies often require adherence to strict security protocols, incentivizing stronger defenses and preparedness.
Legal and Compliance Implications
Ransomware attacks on businesses have legal and compliance consequences beyond financial and operational impacts. Regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) impose strict data protection and breach notification requirements. Failure to comply can result in hefty fines, legal action, and reputational damage.
For instance, under GDPR, organizations must notify authorities within 72 hours of detecting a data breach, including ransomware incidents compromising personal data. Non-compliance can lead to fines of up to 4% of annual global turnover. Similarly, HIPAA mandates timely breach notification for protected health information, with penalties for violations.
While home users face fewer regulatory burdens, they remain vulnerable to privacy violations and identity theft repercussions. Understanding these legal dimensions is vital for organizations to develop compliant and effective cybersecurity policies. Businesses must integrate legal counsel into incident response planning to navigate these requirements effectively.
The Growing Threat and Evolving Tactics
Ransomware attacks continue to grow in sophistication and scale. Cybercriminals now use advanced tactics such as double extortion, where data is stolen before encryption and threatened with public release. Additionally, ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) models enable less technical attackers to rent ransomware tools, increasing attack volume.
According to Cybersecurity Insiders, 68% of organizations experienced a ransomware attack in 2023, with 37% paying the ransom. This trend highlights the importance of proactive defenses and robust incident response.
The rise of remote work expands the attack surface. Work laptops used outside secure corporate networks are more vulnerable, emphasizing the need for endpoint security solutions and VPN usage.
Conclusion: The Same Click, Different Worlds
A single click can unleash ransomware, but the aftermath depends heavily on context. On a home PC, the damage is personal-often frustrating but generally contained. On a work laptop, the consequences ripple through entire organizations, affecting employees, customers, and stakeholders.
Mitigating ransomware risks requires a multifaceted approach. Businesses must adopt proactive defense plans, invest in employee training, enforce strict access controls, and partner with cybersecurity experts. Individuals need vigilance, education, regular backups, and professional support when necessary.
By recognizing the stark differences between personal and professional environments, users can better appreciate the importance of cybersecurity measures tailored to their unique risks. Whether protecting cherished memories or safeguarding critical corporate data, the right strategies make all the difference after that fateful click.

articles.title: Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI
articles.text:
Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI — how we can measure throughput of agentic AI workloads without any GPU involved
The future of agentic AI lies in CPUs, or so the story goes. Here’s our first attempt to measure that.
Agentic AI has set off a firestorm in the world of CPUs over the past six months, yet it’s an area of performance that still doesn’t have solid, repeatable benchmarks to evaluate where the latest hardware falls. We’ve been working on an internal set of tests to evaluate at least one aspect of contentious agentic loops end-to-end, isolating CPU and memory performance from the accelerator to understand how these components contribute to the agentic loop.
This is still a work in progress, but we wanted to bring Tom’s Hardware Premium readers behind the scenes to understand how we’re going about tackling this problem, our methodology for testing, and detail what we’ve learned about agentic loops along the way. We've prototyped the test and settled the central design, but there's still work to do before the numbers it produces hold up to scrutiny.
Given that this area of computing is bleeding-edge and rapidly evolving, we undoubtedly have blind spots here. That’s OK. The testing we’re doing is built to look at how agentic performance scales across the CPU as sessions increase, providing an ideal throughput for each chip that provides as many agent sessions as possible while remaining interactive.
Toward the end of this article, we've included a section on some of the shortfalls of this approach, as well as some ideas we’re toying with to tackle things like multi-turn agentic flows. And keep in mind that these tests aren't meant to replace our other testing of local AI, but to supplement it. As this space continues to evolve and the hardware characteristics are better defined, we’ll be able to make more informed decisions about where this testing goes in the future.
Defining an agentic AI loops
"AI agents" imply some little workers that, strapped with an LLM, can go and handle whatever task you throw at them. It's a fine description, but we'll need a bit more a technical definition if we're going to benchmark the performance of agentic AI.
There are two parts here that are important. First are functions. With agentic AI, we give the LLM access to tools, which, in the case of popular agentic frameworks like LangGraph, are Python functions. The tool may be reading or writing a file, querying a database, running tests on code, or just about anything else you can define in a function. Here's a basic example.
@tool
    def run_command(command: str) -> str:
        """Run a build or test command in the repository root. Allowed: make [targets], python -m pytest [args]."""
return traced("run_command", {"command": command}, lambda: ws.run_command(command))
This is how you write a tool call with LangGraph inside of Python, and it's an example of a tool call that the we've given the LLM access to through our LangGraph persona. We identify the function as a tool the LLM can call with "@tool," and then we define the function like normal Python with "def run_command," passing through the command as an argument. The extra "-> str" on the end notes that the argument will be a string, and the function should return a string.
That's followed up by a description of the tool that the LLM can read (triple quotes just allow you to space this across multiple lines in Python). We're prompting the LLM that it can run build or test commands using make or pytest. For this example, we wrap the function up with the anonymous lambda function and pass it back to an overarching trace function. That's not important right now, however. The goal is to illustrate what a tool call looks like.
This is only one of a handful of tools available to our coding agent. It can also read and write files, edit files, and search code using regular expressions, all defined in the same way with Python functions. Agentic AI is often described as a "loop," however, and that's because the task often requires calling a tool multiple times and/or calling different tools.
If we're working a Python project, for instance, we may prompt the LLM to "debug this Python script." It may call the "list files" tool to evaluate what Python script we're talking about first. Then, it will call the "read file" tool to understand it, or maybe "search code" to find a spot to start troubleshooting. Then it might run "edit file" and "run command," and if the file isn't fixed, it may loop back over these tools a few times.
This is the agentic loop. We prompt the LLM, it evaluates and starts calling tools it needs to form an answer. Then, it gets back the information from the tool calls, it re-evaluates, and then it may call more.
Starting with concurrency
We’ll dig into the specific tests and what they’re doing later in this article, but it’s good to set the stage with why our benchmark is designed the way it is. We developed the test on an Nvidia DGX Spark (GB10) featuring 128 GB of unified memory, a Blackwell GPU, and the relatively weak Arm-based Grace CPU. Above, you can see the time spent running these agent loops on the GB10 with gemma4-26b-a4b. The model isn’t super important here as long as we're able to call tools, and we’re able to re-record the tests using different models as they continue to release.
The point here is the share of time spent, not the model or the specific work the agents are doing (though that does provide useful context). Each result here is a list of sequential tasks for the agent to execute against the model, and nearly all of the time is spent on the GPU. Even relatively demanding CPU tasks, like with our coding agent, represent just a small fraction of the computational time. Running one or even a few agents isn’t a problem for the CPU when we have access to a large, powerful GPU with a sufficiently large model running on it.
Looking closer at one specific set of tasks, you can see that there are plenty of tasks for the CPU to execute during the window, but those tasks happen so quickly that it barely registers in the overall time spent.
These tasks aren’t evenly spaced, either. Depending on when the agent needs to call tools, the shape of the workload can look very different. Above, for example, you can see our document agent, which is tasked with scanning and extracting information from a set of PDF files. Nearly all of the agent time is spent at the very beginning of the task, after which it’s almost pure GPU inference.
Obviously, a more powerful GPU will churn through the inference step faster, but we’d have to create a severe imbalance between the CPU and GPU for the CPU portion of a single agentic loop to create a bottleneck — at least with these common tools. Agents don’t just handle a sequential list of tasks, however. They spawn sub-agents, and if multiple sessions are running on the same system in sandboxed environments, contention for limited resources becomes a real issue.
Instead of designing the test platform in such a way that creates a severe CPU/GPU imbalance, we looked toward concurrency. The idea is to sweep across the chip with concurrent sessions running a list of tasks in a loop in their own processes. As the sweep scales up, contention across the CPU starts to appear, and minor differences in tool calls, code execution and compilation, web browsing, and the variety of other tasks our agents do pile on.
How the benchmark works
With concurrency as our north star, we can start breaking down the design of the benchmark and how it works internally. The overall design is simple. Custom agents built with LangGraph have a list of 30 tasks to execute in sequence against a llama.cpp server running gemma4-26b-a4b. Instead of going directly to the server, however, the agents go through a proxy server that records a trace.
During live recording, the agent communicates with the proxy server, which passes a live call to the llama.cpp server. The proxy server meanwhile writes every logged request to the LLM and the response from it to an overarching JSON. Tool calls bypass the server chain and are logged to their own JSON files. Finally, for each task, a correct response is generated, hashed, and stored as its own JSON.
Recording everything allows us to remove the live model entirely from the equation. The agents still run as normal, but instead of running against a live LLM, they run against that proxy, replaying the traces captured. The requests and tool calls are all happening live, but the agents are immediately handed back a response from the trace based on the live inference capture.
Starting with the request from the agent, it’s matched by session label and hash to ensure it’s accurate before the response is looked up in the master JSON. If there’s a mismatch, the run stops and is marked as invalid. If everything checks out, the response is passed back, and the agent session(s) call the tools they need. The tool calls are compared to the JSONs generated during recording, and the recorded result is passed back. This is critical.
The test compares the live tool call to the recorded result, but it always passes back the recorded result to keep the test from drifting, even if the tool call is correct. True tool mismatches are logged. The test proceeds, but it’s marked as invalid for each level with tool mismatches.
This setup makes redesigning and expanding the benchmark simple. We can write a new persona in Python using LangGraph, or expand to other frameworks like CrewAI. Additionally, we can rerecord traces against different models in the future, perhaps some with expanded capabilities. As long as we’re communicating over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, we can mix and match pieces of our testing to represent a broader range of workloads.
The test starts at a single worker process and scales up to the maximum thread count of the CPU, running three repeats per level. Each worker process operates off a list of 30 tasks, with new worker processes starting at the next point in the list. So, worker session one would start at task one, worker session two would start at task two, and so on. Tasks do not take an equal amount of time, so this offset creates imbalanced contention as tasks overlap.
What this actually measures
The metric we get out of the test is sessions per second. A session is a single task completed from end-to-end, and we measure the number of sessions completed per second at each level. Naturally, at lower levels, we complete fewer sessions per second, often falling below 1, meaning the task takes longer than one second to complete. The tasks are completed sequentially. What we’re looking for is how chips diverge as sessions increase, measuring the throughput of agentic work on the CPU.
We derive two headline scores from the sweep. First is peak throughput, which is the highest sessions per second we recorded, as well as the concurrency level at which it was recorded. Next is ideal throughput, which is the point at which the slowest 5% of sessions take no longer than 1.5x the time it takes for a single session to complete at the base concurrency level. We expect that tasks will take longer as the number of sessions increases, but past that 1.5x mark, the length of the task gets significantly longer, and depending on the processor’s topology, throughput can start to degrade.
It’s worth highlighting again that there is no GPU delay in this concurrency sweep. We’ve removed the GPU entirely, throwing as much concurrent work at the CPU as possible to determine where that peak throughput point lies. However, the GPU still plays a significant role, so the results should be viewed in a realistic context.
As more agents work on the CPU, they’ll compete for resources on the chip, but this balance can easily shift. If there isn’t enough GPU horsepower, agents may queue for a slot, and that’s not effectively utilizing the compute on either processor. Our testing is more than theoretical throughput from napkin math, but it’s less than a true end-to-end system. There are too many variables to account for in that setup for us to produce any useful numbers that are broadly applicable.
However, we can run the sweep with live inference to evaluate system-level performance. For live runs, the responses handed back to agents are still served from the recording to keep runs equal. However, the request is recorded by the llama.cpp server, which generates the same number of tokens before being discarded. This accounts for the normal inference pipeline, including prefill, decode, and cache performance, as well as agents queuing for a slot.
Both numbers are important. Live sweeps are a realistic look at local AI across the entire system, while frozen replays measure the peak throughput a CPU is capable of with access to all the GPU compute (theoretically) that it could want.
Our starting agent personas
We’ve defined six agent personas. A “persona” is a Python script built with LangGraph that defines what the agent can do. The agents tool calls are Python functions, defined in that main script that connects our LangGraph nodes. Each persona is working off its own unique list of tasks from local documents. For example, the research persona is able to answer questions by searching in a Wikipedia corpus of about 50,000 articles.
| Persona | Sub-Tasks | Description | Tools | 
| Analyst | Planner, analyst, writer | Answer questions about a fake retail company by searching DuckDB with SQL and write a report. | List tables, describe tables, run SQL query, make chart from query | 
| Coding | Coder, reviewer | Fix bugs in one of four small projects (two C, two Python) from an issue report. | List files, read files, code search, file edits, command execution, test review | 
| Documents | Intake, extractor, auditor | Scans purchase orders, invoices, and other accounting documents and matches invoices against purchase orders. | List documents, extract text from PDF, extract tables from PDF, Tesseract OCR, basic arithmetic | 
| Research | Planner, researcher, writer | Searches local English Wikipedia corpus to answer questions. | Query corpus | 
| Support | Triage, researcher, responder | Answer support tickets for a fictional company using a knowledge base. | Knowledge base search, read articles | 
| Web | Planner, browser agent, writer | Find products that meet specified criteria in a headless Chromium session. | Open URL, click web element, enter text, select option, go back, read more of page | 
Above, you can see an overview of each persona. For five out of the six, we start with some sort of planning stage, followed by the main agent loop, and finish with a report. For the analyst persona, for instance, the planner takes the questions and splits them into structured output with two to four steps. Analysts then run in parallel, searching the database, and the writer turns those findings into a response.
The one exception is the coder persona, which works a bit differently. It’s working off four projects, attempting to address a bug from an issue report (similar to a GitHub issue report). The coder finds the bug, runs tests to confirm the fix, and then passes it off to a reviewer step. The reviewer step (naturally) reviews the fix before applying it.
For each of the personas, the current test setup looks at single-turn tasks. Agents make multiple loops to the LLM depending on the task, and often use tools several times, but it’s all to resolve a single task with no previous context. For instance, when a customer support query comes up, the agent may take multiple passes at the knowledge base to answer that query. However, once the agent has answered the query and moved on to the next, it’s treated as a separate action without context from the first query.
This is not completely representative of agentic workflows, which are often multi-turn processes. We're able to script multi-turn tasks, but that creates greater divergence risk, as well as risk of a crash. Running this locally, it's not hard to spill over the context window after a few turns of complex interactions. It's possible to do, but it's not on the top of our list of priorities right now.
We won’t cover all of the tasks the current personas do because, frankly, it’s a lot and most of it isn’t that interesting. Still, we want to provide at least one example for each persona so you can get an idea of what’s going on under the hood.
| Persona | Example Task | Source of Truth | 
| Analyst | “How do discounts affect gross margin across categories?” | DuckDB warehouse | 
| Coding | Invoice project – Saturday due dates move to Sunday, not Monday | PyTest, make | 
| Documents | Approve correct invoices from purchase orders based on a price from a list of six documents across four scans. | Faux PDF invoices, purchase orders, and goods received notices with errors planted | 
| Research | “What causes earthquakes and how are they measured?” | 50,000-article English Wikipedia corpus | 
| Support | “How long a two-factor code stays valid” | Knowledge base for fictional smart home company | 
| Web | Highest-rated 55L backpack and lightest waterproof boots | Local website for an outdoor gear store | 
All of the other tasks are very similar to what you can see in the examples above. With the documents persona, for example, the agent is always approving the correct invoices, but the mix of documents and types of errors change between sets. Similarly, the support persona is always answering support questions, but they focus in different areas. Some ask to troubleshoot error codes, others (like the example above) ask about policies, and more still include multiple questions within one query, tasking the agent with piecing together multiple areas of the knowledge base.
Shortcomings of the current approach
Although we’ve tried to create a broad range of agentic work here, there are some shortcomings of the current version of this test. Most notably, our testing and recordings only come from two types of systems: a 64-core Threadripper test bed with 128GB of DDR5-6000 RDIMMs, and a DGX Spark.
As we continue to test other platforms, we may need to adjust the tests, rerun recordings, or swap the model. We’d have to re-gather all of our results if we make those changes. By other platforms, we’re not just talking about an Intel system, either. We’ve seen a variety of different local AI setups, from Mac Studio clusters to GPU-ridden workstations. The load on the CPU completely changes depending on the GPU performance, model, quantization level, and server settings.
The other shortcoming is API performance. The test is designed in such a way that we can easily connect to any model from a frontier lab through their API. Although that model runs in the cloud, the tools themselves run locally unless you’re using an entirely cloud-based sandbox. If you’re working through an AI-assisted development workflow on a budget laptop, for instance, all of the compilation, testing, and agent code still runs on your machine.
Although we have plans to look into this hybrid model with a weaker host PC and a cloud API, we didn’t explore it too much during initial development. API usage is expensive, and we don’t want to be throwing away tokens trying to get the initial test suite set up correctly.
Finally, sandboxing. The current test is isolated through a Docker image, which introduces negligible overhead (<2%) compared to a bare-metal run. We’ll need to explore the overhead of sandboxing local agents via different means in the future, which is an area we really haven’t explored much in this test.
Continuing to learn
Agentic AI is rapidly evolving, so much so that you’ll get different definitions of what characterizes agentic workloads and hardware built for agentic workflows depending on who you ask. Add on top of that rapid hardware and model changes, and it’s obvious that we could never define a bulletproof benchmark that can stand the test of time. That’s a fool’s errand. What we have here is our starting point, which we will continue to build on top of.
From what we have now, the next steps are to get the first real numbers. We've done some basic tests to ensure the system is set up correctly (for instance, running a free-threaded version of Python to test GIL impact within a single session), but the focus here was getting the basic system in place to record traces and replay them.
We're also relying exclusively on LangGraph here. We need to explore other frameworks like CrewAI, as well as the "one-click" agents like Hermes and OpenClaw.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Braun introduce un microprocesador y una pantalla en su nueva afeitadora: así es la Braun Nevo que cuesta casi 700 euros
articles.text:
Braun lleva años lanzando numerosos dispositivos para el cuidado de la barba, con varias gamas y un gran repertorio de generaciones a sus espaldas. Y la nueva afeitadora trae algo que resulta atractivo para ir "hecho un pincel": un microprocesador y la nueva Nevo Smart Display.
Una afeitadora que ofrece información y recomendaciones
La Braun Nevo es la nueva afeitadora de la marca que se sitúa en la gama prémium, por lo que ya os adelantamos que no es especialmente barata. Y si hay algo a destacar de esta nueva afeitadora, es que incorpora una pantalla inteligente para tener un mayor control del cuidado de la barba.
Dicha pantalla muestra información y recomendaciones personalizadas, y lo hace en tiempo real. Para ello, se vale de los sensores que vienen integrados en un cuerpo unibody de acero inoxidable, y el objetivo es que la máquina pueda regular la potencia en función de la densidad de la barba y los contornos faciales. Todo ello sin necesidad de conectarnos a una aplicación.
También incorpora la tecnología denominada AeroTouch, un sistema de afeitado que la marca promete ofrecer un deslizamiento ligero y suave sobre la piel, evitando de esta forma que la piel se irrite con la fricción de la afeitadora o que podamos crear arrugas al estirar y contraer la piel.
Junto a la máquina, se incluye un centro de cuidado que es capaz de limpiar, lubricar y recargar la afeitadora de forma automática, sin que tengamos que preocuparnos de ello. Además, la garantía ofrecida por la marca es de cinco años y también incluye acceso a BraunCare+, un servicio diseñado para tener una experiencia de cuidado más personalizada.
En cuanto a su disponibilidad, la afeitadora Braun Nevo ya está disponible por un precio de 679 euros, aunque ahora mismo está de oferta y hay disponibilidad en varios packs:

‘Shaking from head to toe’ — How the facial recognition blame game leaves shoppers stranded
articles.text:
‘Shaking from head to toe’ — How the facial recognition blame game leaves shoppers stranded
Inside the ‘Kafkaesque nightmare’ of clearing your name
Mary could tell that her husband was “distraught” the moment he was wrongly accused of shoplifting and ordered to leave Home Bargains. The ordeal left him feeling “isolated”. “I was scared to go into a shop,” he said. They had only popped out to pick up some vitamins.
Elsewhere, a woman’s husband was left “shaking from head to toe” after she was told to leave Budgens on account of stealing “loads of meat” the week before. “My mind was racing,” she said. They hadn’t been to that shop for months.
Facial recognition is an inherently personal and intimate technology. It scans your features, processes your biometric data and, depending on its results, can stop you from entering a particular space.
It might all happen in an instant but its impact extends far and can be surprisingly long lasting — something that is made all the worse by a dizzying lack of clarity about who is to blame when something goes wrong.
‘Taste the indifference’
Earlier this week, in a cramped room in the House of Commons, people wrongly accused of shoplifting by facial recognition technology met to discuss their experiences with Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, Dr Allison Gardner.
The event, sponsored by the civil liberties group Big Brother Watch, was designed to give people an opportunity to air their grievances with politicians, the media, and the companies involved.
Above all, perhaps, it gave everyone the chance to get some answers about how the system works, who is to blame when it doesn’t work as intended, and to start planning how best to move forward.
Big Brother Watch invited Facewatch, the company behind the technology, to attend. It also invited representatives from Sainsbury’s, a company that is currently in the process of introducing facial recognition to 200 of its stores.
Neither company sent representatives to the event.
On hearing details of one specific case, Dr Gardner said she “had so many questions.” Was it an algorithm glitch, a shop worker making an honest mistake, or something else? Unfortunately, there was no one to answer the specifics.
“You can taste the indifference,” someone at the back of the room said.
“Sainsbury’s is happy to scan its customers’ faces but won’t face the people its technology has harmed,” Jack Coulson, Head of Advocacy at Big Brother Watch, later told TechRadar.
Each of the testimonies from people wrongly flagged by the technology shared striking similarities. A routine activity was suddenly transformed into a confusing, public ordeal of having to defend themselves against allegations they did not immediately understand. People said they felt “bewildered”, “isolated” and “confused.”
However, while the emotional impact was consistent, the specifics of each case were often not.
Some people were stopped the moment they walked through the shop doors. Others were confronted at the tills with a full basket. The errors were equally unpredictable. One person was a victim of mistaken identity, while another saw their face flagged on an overhead screen. One woman was wrongly intercepted simply because the system had identified the people walking in directly behind her.
There was talk of algorithms, of bias and poorly configured training data, of mechanisms for redress, and off-the-record chats about how some managed to gather more information.
The overarching feeling was one of bureaucratic exhaustion. Shoppers were left with no clear path to clear their names. “I didn’t know who to turn to,” one person said.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday.
The corporate defence
TechRadar reached out to all the companies mentioned in this article. Booker Group, which owns the Budgens brand, refused to comment on record. Sainsbury’s did not respond, and neither did Home Bargains.
Facewatch said it gave the invitation “serious consideration” but cited concerns about the balance of the event “given the tone of Big Brother Watch’s campaign messaging to date”. The company said that it had provided an explanation to the organizers and parliamentary co-chair, offering to answer questions after the session.
When asked who is liable when the system produces an error, Facewatch said it "takes responsibility for its technology and processes, and retailers are responsible for how their staff interact with customers” though it said legal liability “depends on the facts and it cannot responsibly be determined by providing a blanket answer”.
The company also said that when a false alert occurs, it initiates a “safeguarding process with the retailer to establish exactly what happened”.
Facewatch added: “We challenge campaign messaging that uses those incidents to create a disproportionate impression of the risk to ordinary shoppers. Facewatch operates discreetly and successfully in thousands of stores across the UK every day. Presenting exceptional incidents as representative of that everyday operation is misleading and risks creating unnecessary fear.”
‘Salt in the wound’
The lack of clarity that follows when someone is mistakenly flagged by the facial recognition system is the “salt in the wound of being publicly humiliated,” Big Brother Watch’s Coulson said.
When TechRadar visited a South London Sainsbury’s earlier this month, we found that there was no viable way of opting out of the facial recognition system and that security had little information about how the system works. There are signs with QR codes at the entry of the shops, though attendees said these contained insufficient information following a dispute.
Big Brother Watch offers some respite for the affected people, helping individuals navigate Subject Access Requests (SARs) — a statutory mechanism under UK data protection law used to force companies to disclose what data they hold. But the process is slow, demands that victims surrender even more personal data, and offers no guarantee that a face will actually be removed from watchlists.
“It’s the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation,” Coulson told TechRadar.
The UK’s data privacy regulator, the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), acknowledged the severity of the testimonies, calling the experiences "harrowing". It said it hoped to share more concrete insights into the commercial use of the technology soon.
But for now, the confusion remains and the blame for when it goes wrong is still unclear.
Following the event, Dr Gardner told TechRadar that she is "extremely concerned at the poor implementation and lack of governance" surrounding the technology and will be raising the issue with ministers and contacting companies directly.
She added that she would “like to know what redress is being given to wrongly accused individuals that is proportionate to the upset caused. Who is accountable and can be held liable.”
Until those questions are answered, the lack of clarity isn't just acting as a regulatory loophole; it risks creating a chilling effect for the wider public. If one person was “frightened to go to a shop” for weeks after, then perhaps you would be too.
Names have been changed to protect affected peoples’ privacy.
Sam is VPN Managing Editor at TechRadar. He has worked in the VPN industry since 2018 and has previously written for CNN, Al Jazeera, WIRED, and Deutsche Welle as a freelance journalist. He focuses on VPNs and digital privacy, cybersecurity and internet freedom.
Before joining TechRadar, Sam carried out research on global digital rights issues at Top10VPN. His research has been cited by the United Nations and UK Parliament, as well as publications such as The Guardian, Washington Post and BBC.

articles.title: Lighthouse Communities Foundation lists on BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to scale youth livelihoods
articles.text:
Lighthouse Communities Foundation lists on BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to scale youth livelihoods
Lighthouse Communities Foundation has joined BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to raise funds to help 500 young people in Pune build career confidence and job-ready skills.
For many young people, finding a job begins long before they enter a classroom. Understanding their strengths, identifying career options and building the confidence to pursue them can be just as important as acquiring skills.
Lighthouse Communities Foundation (LCF), a non-profit working to improve livelihood opportunities for underserved youth, has marked its listing on the Bombay Stock Exchange’s (BSE) Social Stock Exchange (SSE). The listing follows a public issue of Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instruments held from September 30 to October 14, 2026.
The foundation marked the milestone with a bell-ringing ceremony at BSE on October 29, attended by government officials, corporate partners, philanthropic organisations and its leadership.
A new route to fund social impact
The listing gives Lighthouse Communities Foundation access to a regulated platform through which corporates, corporate social responsibility (CSR) partners and impact-focused supporters can fund its work.
ZCZP instruments differ from conventional investments. They pay no interest and return no principal, meaning subscribers contribute towards defined social outcomes rather than receiving financial returns. The platform also requires organisations to report how funds are used and the progress achieved.
“Models that combine career guidance, skilling and employer linkages, supported by transparent funding, are exactly what our youth need to find stable livelihoods,” said Manisha Verma, IAS, Additional Chief Secretary, Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department, Government of Maharashtra, who attended the ceremony as chief guest.
The listing comes as LCF looks to expand a model that combines government infrastructure and corporate support to deliver livelihood programmes.
Helping young people find the right career path
LCF’s Lighthouse programme begins by helping participants understand their aspirations and strengths before they choose a vocational training pathway. The foundation works with partner organisations offering courses aligned with available employment opportunities.
Since its establishment in 2015, LCF has reached more than 2.9 lakh young people across six states. Its Lighthouse programme operates 51 centres, with women accounting for nearly 60% of enrolments. According to the foundation, 77% of placed youth remain employed a year after placement.
The model brings together state and local governments, which provide infrastructure, and corporate partners, which fund operations and implementation.
Dr Ganesh Natarajan, Co-Founder and Chairman of LCF, said the listing was an important milestone in the organisation’s work with underserved youth.
“Ringing the bell at BSE today is a proud moment for everyone who has been part of the Lighthouse journey, from our young people and partner organisations to the corporates and governments who backed us early,” he said.
He added that LCF aims to reach one million young people nationally, helping them choose and build the careers they aspire to.
Pune is the next focus for expansion
The proceeds from the issue will support LCF’s work in Pune, with a target of helping 500 young people develop career awareness, confidence and job-readiness skills to access sustained livelihoods.
In Maharashtra, the foundation works with the Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department and the Directorate of Vocational Education and Training under a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2023.
Its initiatives include a Lighthouse centre at ITI Mulund and Model Career Centres in Thane and Nagpur. The partnership has provided career counselling to more than 5,500 young people, skilling to over 2,075 and placement support to more than 3,200.
The next phase is expected to extend the programme to additional Model Career Centres and industrial training institutes, including those in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Amravati.
Lighthouse Communities Foundation will report its progress through the Social Stock Exchange’s disclosure framework. For the foundation, the listing creates an opportunity to connect funding with measurable outcomes as it works to expand access to meaningful and sustained livelihoods.

articles.title: Les agents IA « Dots » de ChatGPT s'invitent dans Google Messages et iMessage
articles.text:
Inaugurés le mois dernier par OpenAI, les « ChatGPT Dots » sont des assistants personnels autonomes fonctionnant en arrière-plan pour gérer certaines tâches pour vous. Jusqu’à présent cantonnés à l’interface de ChatGPT, Slack ou Microsoft Teams, ils débarquent enfin dans l’application de messagerie de votre smartphone. Plus besoin de lancer l’application dédiée, donc, vous pouvez parler à l’assistant directement depuis Google Messages ou iMessage.
Parlez avec ChatGPT Dots dans votre application de messagerie
Votre ChatGPT Dot peut vous envoyer des messages de son propre chef. Si vous lui avez par exemple demandé de surveiller l’évolution du tarif d’un produit ou de suivre un projet de voyage, il vous prévient dès qu’il détecte un changement qu’il juge digne d’intérêt. Les notifications ne se limitent d’ailleurs pas simplement au texte, l’agent peut par exemple vous envoyer des photos ou des notes vocales.
 By popular request, you can now text your dot.
Give it a task to take off your plate or something to keep an eye on, using text, photos, or even voice notes. It will text you proactively with relevant updates.
Safe, secure texting via iMessage or RCS. You’re the only one who can text your dot, and your dot can only text you. Rolling out now as a preview for Pro users in the US.
— ChatGPT (@ChatGPT) October 28, 2026
L’intérêt d’un tel outil réside dans la continuité de l’historique, puisque votre assistant conserve le contexte des discussions menées ailleurs et garde accès aux mêmes plugins connectés. Vous pouvez donc commencer à planifier un sujet sur l’interface principale de ChatGPT pour finir par en discuter par SMS sans avoir à réexpliquer toute la situation à zéro. Pour configurer la liaison, il suffit d’ouvrir le profil du Dot concerné et de sélectionner l’option de messagerie.
Confidentialité et disponibilité
Côté confidentialité, OpenAI se veut évidemment rassurant en indiquant que les échanges restent cloisonnés entre vous et votre Dot, l’activation de cette option ne donnant en aucun cas à l’outil un droit de regard sur vos autres conversations privées. La fonctionnalité repose donc sur un canal sécurisé où vous êtes la seule personne en mesure de contacter votre agent, et inversement.
À lire : Après Muse de Meta et ChatGPT Dot, Anthropic s’aligne et dévoile Claude Duet
Pour l’instant, cette nouveauté est réservée aux abonnés payants qui ont ChatGPT Pro, uniquement aux États-Unis. Reste à voir quand OpenAI étendra cette fonctionnalité au reste du monde et aux utilisateurs d’autres formules, gratuites ou payantes.

articles.title: Mistral releases open weights for Mistral Large 4, providing sovereign control for the company’s ‘Le Chonk’ AI model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Mistral releases open weights for Mistral Large 4, providing sovereign control for the company’s ‘Le Chonk’ AI model
Mistral AI SAS today announced the availability of the open weights of its frontier model Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the company’s most capable large language model to date, initially released in preview three weeks ago.
With 1 trillion parameters and 52 billion active parameters, ML4 is natively multimodal and has received three additional weeks of reinforcement training and customer testing. The company says it’s becoming one of the best open agentic coding models in the world, offering leading performance at a small fraction of the token cost with state-of-the-art cyber defense capabilities.
“ML4 OSS showcases our science team’s ability to innovate at speed,” said Vice President of Science Pierre Stock. “Building on the ML4 Preview, the open-weight version continues reinforcement learning training and delivers substantial gains with no signs of saturation.”
The company trained ML4 on 3,800 Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell graphics processing units in its European data centers to achieve high-fidelity performance for tool use and coding, driven by end-to-end control of its infrastructure and the ability to optimize for hardware during model development.
Open weights mean companies can take the model and deploy it on their own hardware, within their own firewalls, and run sensitive data without exposing it to the cloud or outside parties. With Mistral’s model, companies will have a Western-developed model to compete with the multitude of ultra-large Chinese coding models on the market, such as the GLM family from Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co. Ltd. and the Kimi family from Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co. Ltd.
“Open source is essential to ensure state-of-the-art AI does not end up concentrated in the hands of a few actors,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Arthur Mensch. “Other labs have raised hundreds of billions to develop equivalent capabilities; in three years, Mistral raised roughly $6 billion.”
Because of its training regimen, ML4 stands out among many other frontier models, rivaling even top models such as Chinese-built GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.
On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests agentic coding in the terminal, ML4 climbed from 28% to 41%, tying GLM-5.3 as the best model for coding agents.
Mistral offers three reasoning modes for ML4: low, medium and high. Teams can use this to match reasoning depth to the task without adjusting prompts, which can be less effective, allowing reasoning to fit quick everyday tasks to deep work on extremely complex problems. This allows developers and enterprise users to control token use per task.
The company said the release of ML4 represents a new generation of Mistral models spanning all modalities. It follows the recent launch of Voxtral 3, a family of voice models and voice agents. Mistral plans to continue to release additional models from this family in the coming months.

articles.title: Test de Tom The Postgirl, un jeu aux allures de conte aussi mignon qu'absurde
articles.text:
En cette période excitante d’Halloween, l’envie de regarder des films d’horreur (y compris en famille), de lire des romans d’épouvante ou de jouer à des jeux qui font peur est plus forte qu’habituellement. Depuis le changement d’heure, le soleil se couche plus tôt, et l’ambiance est de plus en plus propice à expérimenter des œuvres plus noires que d’habitude
Mais attention, il n’y a pas besoin pour autant de lancer Silent Hill 2 pour se retrouver plongé dans un univers étrange, ou d’aller jouer à Hellraiser: Revival pour ressentir quelque chose de viscéral. Parfois, un petit jeu indépendant sorti de nulle part suffit à nous mettre dans une ambiance lynchienne, idéale pour une soirée d’Halloween.
C’est justement la proposition de Tom the Postgirl, jeu aussi étrange que loufoque, qui ressemble à un épisode de Twin Peaks qui aurait croisé le chemin d’un livre pour enfants bizarre. Tom the Postgirl sort ce jeudi 29 octobre sur PC et Mac via Steam, ainsi que sur Nintendo Switch. Il est vendu 9,99 €. Le jeu est l’œuvre du petit studio suisse Oopsie Daisies, qui le coproduit avec Arte France. Voici notre test, sans divulgâchage, du jeu le plus déroutant de ce mois d’octobre.
Points forts
- Un humour noir qui fait mouche
- Une direction artistique originale
- Quelques surprises dans l’aventure
Points faibles
- Un gameplay limité
- Une durée de vie très courte
- Peu de rejouabilité
Il était une fois… on ne sait pas trop
Tout commence par une belle journée d’une saison non identifiée, au hasard, le printemps, et Tom, une petite fille malicieuse en parka rouge, cousine inavouée de Kenny dans South Park, se fait embaucher par la poste de son village pour livrer des paquets aux habitants. Jusqu’ici, tout va bien.
Sauf que Tom n’est pas une petite fille comme les autres, et que son petit village tranquille en apparence est le théâtre, dans l’ombre, de multiples petits vices à la fois mignons, étranges, coquins, voire carrément flippants.
Avec son mélange d’ambiances, on ne sait pas trop comment prendre Tom the Postgirl, ni sur quel pied danser tout au long de l’aventure. D’un côté, ses graphismes tout en crayonné noir et blanc et l’aspect cartoon du jeu, à la fois très simplement animé et mignon tout plein, font sourire. De l’autre, les rencontres et événements qui se déroulent ponctuellement font lever plus d’un sourcil interrogateur.
Un ver de terre rigolo côtoie des enfants maltraités et tenus en laisse, tandis que le fermier d’à côté couche avec ses poules (oui, il ne dort pas qu’avec), et qu’un des voisins de Tom collectionne des photos d’elle pour une raison inconnue. Humour très noir, donc, pour ce conte sous acide à ne surtout pas faire avec ses enfants, malgré sa tête d’album jeunesse. Le jeu est d’ailleurs classé PEGI 16.
Si l’aventure prête régulièrement à sourire au fur et à mesure des péripéties, un certain malaise s’installe durant les quelques heures nécessaires pour boucler l’histoire. On en ressort content, comme après un bon épisode de Twin Peaks ou une balade au musée René Magritte, et c’est un compliment. Le grotesque qui épice l’aventure est également accentué par l’excellent sound design qui privilégie les grognements et autres bruits de bouche aux dialogues.
En quête de sens
Il n’y a pas grand-chose à dire sur le gameplay de Tom the Postgirl. Vous déplacez le personnage avec le stick directionnel et interagissez avec les éléments via une seule et unique touche. Ah si, en appuyant sur la gâchette droite, vous pouvez faire courir le personnage. Enfin, courir est un grand mot puisque Tom passe d’une allure très lente où elle traîne les pieds à une allure moins lente où elle traîne un peu plus vite les pieds.
Pour le reste, une touche permet de consulter la carte et une autre de vérifier si vous avez bien tout fait dans le coin. Car oui, la carte se compose de nombreuses zones dans lesquelles vous entrez pour livrer vos précieux colis. Ces zones regorgent de petits détails (crapauds qui explosent, nains de jardin à envoyer balader d’un coup de pied ou fermier zoophile), et un radar vous indique quels méfaits il reste à commettre, ou quelle incongruité vous n’avez pas encore vu.
Vous avez alors le choix de ratisser les zones et de semer la pagaille, le tout sans aucune forme de récompense, ou de livrer vos paquets comme une bonne factrice, en résistant à la tentation de jeter un coup d’œil dans les colis. Vous l’aurez compris, vous pouvez créer un maximum de bazar dans votre village, mettre le feu à quelques buissons au passage, et tout simplement ne pas faire votre travail correctement.
Le principal intérêt du jeu est bien sûr de provoquer le rire ou le malaise, selon la situation. Vos actions sont toutefois très limitées, soyons d’accord, mais le peu que le jeu propose suffit à donner envie de continuer à pousser plus loin le curseur de l’absurde, et d’assister à davantage de moments comiques.
« L’exquise tentation du voyeurisme »
Arte et Oopsie Daisies décrivent si bien leur jeu qu’il n’y a pas besoin d’en dire plus : sur sa page Steam, ils promettent « l’exquise tentation du voyeurisme ». Les mots creepy et cosy reviennent aussi dans la bouche des développeurs, une équipe suisse de cinq amis qui « explorent les contes de l’enfance et les souvenirs un peu gênants ».
Si vous prenez votre temps, Tom the Postgirl peut se faire en 3 heures à tout casser. Vous pouvez également parcourir le jeu en une vingtaine de minutes montre en main, mais ce serait du gâchis. Le titre ne possède pas une énorme rejouabilité, mais une fois l’aventure principale finie, on peut éventuellement y retourner via un new game plus (oui oui) pour trouver des détails amusants que l’on aurait ratés la première fois, et refaire certains choix différemment (plusieurs fins, des succès et des profils à débloquer pour les plus curieux). Mais pas de quoi fouetter un chat. Autrement dit, Tom the Postgirl est surtout l’aventure d’une fois, idéalement le temps de deux soirées.
Si l’École des loisirs, la maison d’édition française spécialisée dans les albums jeunesse, décidait de rendre la lecture du soir plus stimulante pour les parents, elle éditerait Tom the Postgirl, non sans quelques problèmes. Le jeu coproduit avec Arte réussit son pari du cosymalaise, pour peu qu’on aime les aventures étranges teintées d’humour noir, mais pas trop. À 9,99 € toutefois, réfléchissez bien avant d’acheter un titre qui ne dure que le temps de deux ou trois soirées.
Pour vous faire une idée avant de payer, une démo gratuite est disponible sur Steam.
Le verdict
Tom the Postgirl
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Un humour noir qui fait mouche
- Une direction artistique originale
- Quelques surprises dans l’aventure
On a moins aimé
- Un gameplay limité
- Une durée de vie très courte

articles.title: Google lança Gemini 4 Carbon com avanços em cibersegurança, mas você ainda não pode usá-lo • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Google lança Gemini 4 Carbon com avanços em cibersegurança, mas você ainda não pode usá-lo
Modelo supera números da Anthropic e OpenAI em testes gerais da Artificial Analysis e avança em capacidades de segurança.
Apenas duas semanas após o anúncio do Gemini 4 Argon, o Google já lançou o que considera o seu novo modelo de fronteira. O Gemini 4 Carbon é destinado a tarefas avançadas de programação e cibersegurança, incluindo identificação de vulnerabilidades em ambientes controlados e correção de códigos.
O modelo, apresentado nesta quarta-feira (29/10), não chega ao público geral por enquanto. Como tem sido comum desde o Claude Mythos 5 para modelos com tamanho poder, o Carbon será inicialmente restrito a especialistas de defesa digital enquanto conduz avaliações de segurança com autoridades dos Estados Unidos.
O Google prevê liberar os primeiros acessos por API entre daqui a uma e duas semanas, enquanto ainda não há prazo para a chegada ao aplicativo Gemini ou à interface para navegadores. O preço da API deve seguir a mesma tabela do modelo Argon: US$ 2 (cerca de R$ 10) por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 10 (R$ 53) por milhão de tokens de saída.
O Google destaca o avanço da IA em benchmarks. No índice da consultoria independente Artificial Analysis, que mede o desempenho próximo do uso real da IA, o Gemini 4 Carbon alcançou 59 pontos. O número o coloca à frente de rivais como Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), com 58, do GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), com 57, e do Gemini 4 Argon, com 50.
Segundo o Google DeepMind, um dos principais avanços está em tarefas mais longas: em testes internos, o Carbon conseguiu trabalhar durante dias sobre problemas complexos de software, retomando etapas e buscando alternativas quando encontrava caminhos sem solução.
Ainda assim, há tarefas em que desempenhou menos do que concorrentes. No benchmark FrontierSWE 2, voltado a agentes de programação, ficou abaixo do GPT-6 Astra e do Opus 5.5. Perdeu para a IA da Anthropic também no OSWorld-2.1, um dos principais testes de capacidade de operação autônoma de computadores.
O foco maior do Gemini 4 Carbon é o setor de cibersegurança. Nos testes apresentados pela companhia, ele obteve:
Com o avanço, o Google afirma que o modelo consegue atuar desde o encontro de vulnerabilidades até uma possível correção. A atenção da indústria a esse tópico, vale lembrar, ocorre após casos seguidos de “fuga” de ambientes de testes por diferentes modelos da OpenAI, Anthropic e Meta.
O Carbon também se mostrou bastante resistente a ataques de prompt injection, algo que tem sido um problema especialmente em empresas e órgãos públicos que têm atribuído etapas de trabalho à IA. O teste não conseguiu enganar o modelo do Google em nenhuma das tentativas de ataque.
