articles.title: HP and Asus are moving PC production back to China as soaring component costs force a rethink
articles.text:
What we know so far: When US-China trade relations reached an all-time low last year, many global electronics manufacturers made a beeline for alternative low-cost manufacturing locations such as Thailand, Vietnam, and India. However, with skyrocketing component costs squeezing profit margins, some of these companies are reportedly shifting at least part of their PC manufacturing operations back to China.
According to Nikkei Asia, American PC giant HP and Taiwanese consumer electronics firm Asus have already moved some of their manufacturing operations back to China. Another leading PC OEM, Dell, is also said to be evaluating whether to follow suit and shift some of its PC production back to the Asian nation to offset rising component costs.
The renewed preference for China as a PC manufacturing hub underscores broader, systemic pressures gripping the global electronics supply chain. According to the report, PC makers expect that moving production back to China will allow them to leverage established infrastructure and benefit from lower input prices than those available in alternative destinations.
The resurgence of China as a hub for PC manufacturing also highlights the challenges faced by emerging low-cost destinations, both in terms of pricing power and infrastructural readiness. The move would also likely delay the much-hyped return of domestic electronics manufacturing to the US despite the announcement of several financial and other incentives.
Following the imposition of sanctions and tariffs on China in 2024 and 2025 by both the Biden and Trump administrations, PC makers started to look for safer destinations in countries that have a friendlier relationship with the US. While Thailand, Vietnam, and India emerged as potential alternatives, none of them have established supply chains or expertise in mass manufacturing, unlike China.
It is worth noting that PC makers are not officially discarding their stated goal of diversifying manufacturing operations beyond China. In fact, many are even buying memory chips from Chinese companies like CXMT instead of from established suppliers like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, largely due to the significantly lower prices they offer.
The report noted that the shift back to China is adversely affecting the suppliers that invested in Southeast Asia. An unnamed manager at an unidentified PC component supplier told the publication that the company built multiple factories in Thailand for its PC clients, but now he doesn't know whether they will ever become profitable or instead have to be written off as a one-time loss.

articles.title: ZHITAI Joins Forces with Phantom Blade Zero on Collaboration SSD Gift Box
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
ZHITAI Joins Forces with Phantom Blade Zero on Collaboration SSD Gift Box
ZHITAI, the consumer memory brand of YMTC, announced a strategic partnership with Phantom Blade Zero, the highly anticipated AAA action game that has captured global attention. Under the theme "Unleash Your Edge," the two brands have joined forces to introduce the ZHITAI × Phantom Blade Zero Collaboration Gift Box, combining high-performance memory technology with Eastern wuxia aesthetics to deliver an immersive experience in the Phantom World for gamers around the world.
With its distinctive Kungfu-punk aesthetic and intense, fast-paced combat, Phantom Blade Zero has emerged as one of the year's most anticipated AAA action titles. The partnership's theme, "Unleash Your Edge," draws inspiration from the game's protagonist, Soul, and his unwavering resolve in the face of adversity. This theme bridges the game's lightning-fast combat with ZHITAI's relentless pursuit of peak storage performance—reflecting both Soul's unyielding conviction and ZHITAI's dedication to continuous innovation and exploration.As the official designated global memory partner of Phantom Blade Zero, ZHITAI is committed to providing professional, high-performance storage solutions. Drawing on years of technological expertise, ZHITAI aims to bring gamers worldwide a smooth, responsive storage experience that lets them fully immerse themselves in their martial arts adventures.
To further enhance the experience of exploring the Phantom World, the Collaboration Gift Box houses the ZHITAI TiPlus9100 SSD. Powered by next-gen YMTC Xtacking 4.0 TLC NAND flash, the TiPlus9100 supports PCIe 5.0 and delivers sequential read speeds of up to 12,000 MB/s and sequential write speeds of up to 10,700 MB/s. Its DRAM-less architecture and single-sided PCB design offer versatile compatibility across gaming laptops, ultrabooks, and DIY desktops. For AAA games such as Phantom Blade Zero, where fast-paced combat and seamless scene transitions are essential to the gaming experience, the TiPlus9100 delivers stable performance under demanding workloads while helping reduce loading times and delays during scene transitions. This allows players to stay focused on every move and every moment of combat, fully immersed in the Phantom World.
Crafted for gamers, the ZHITAI × Phantom Blade Zero Collaboration Gift Box brings the Phantom World to life. Defined by a dark wuxia aesthetic, it offers an immersive unboxing experience—combining high-performance storage, custom setup accessories, and exclusive collectibles. The box houses five custom items adorned with co-branded artwork: a ZHITAI TiPlus9100 SSD with a themed sleeve, a storage box, a screwdriver, a metal sticker, and a lenticular card. By translating the Phantom Blade Zero universe into functional and collectible gear, ZHITAI seamlessly bridges high-performance hardware with the player's personal gaming space.
From PC hardware to collectible accessories, this collaboration goes beyond bringing together high-performance memory technology and AAA action gaming. It reflects ZHITAI's ongoing commitment to combining technological innovation with gaming culture. Through its partnership with Phantom Blade Zero, ZHITAI aims to further strengthen its presence among gamers worldwide, bringing advanced memory technology and high-quality products to a broader global audience. Looking ahead, ZHITAI will continue to explore new opportunities across international markets, delivering innovative memory solutions that meet the evolving needs of consumers around the world.
The ZHITAI × Phantom Blade Zero Collaboration Gift Box is coming soon, with further details on its launch date and availability to be announced. Stay tuned to ZHITAI's official channels for the latest updates.

articles.title: El primer MacBook con pantalla OLED ya está aquí y que se queme la pantalla sería mi última preocupación
articles.text:
Apple ha tardado más de la cuenta en realizar dos movimientos que esperábamos hace años: meter una pantalla OLED y, además, táctil en un MacBook. El resultado es el nuevo MacBook Pro PROLED XDR, el MacBook más sofisticado de la marca y uno con una pantalla de hasta 2.000 nits. Y claro, aparte del elevadísimo precio, la pregunta que ha surgido es... ¿se quemará el panel?
Y yo, si tuviese los 3.349 euros que cuesta y quisiera uno, no tendría esa preocupación.
La intranquilidad. Es lógico porque, durante años, hemos visto casos de quemado y de algo más grave: el apagado total de algunos píxeles. En un panel OLED, los píxeles emiten luz por sí mismos y se desgastan por el uso al ser un elemento orgánico. El quemado viene cuando un elemento fijo se muestra durante muchas horas en la pantalla, ya que esos píxeles envejecen más que los de alrededor.
El resultado es una "sombra" permanente de un logo, una barra o parte de la interfaz que no se va cuando se apaga la pantalla. Y si esto preocupa en un televisor, en un monitor de ordenador en el que hay elementos fijos horas, horas y horas como la barra de menú y búsqueda de un navegador, el dock o la barra de herramientas, más aún.
Evolución de las defensas. Teniendo en cuenta que la preocupación tiene lógica (y en los comentarios del tema de presentación del portátil lo hicisteis saber), hay cosas que debemos tener en cuenta. A lo largo de las generaciones, las defensas en estos paneles han ido aumentando y se dividen en tres caterogías:
- Software. Los fabricantes usan varios nombres comerciales y demás, pero en esencia, hay tres grandes avances para evitar el quemado de elementos estáticos. Por un lado, desplazar la imagen unos píxeles a intervalos para que ninguno cargue siempre con el peso de reproducir el mismo contenido. Otros recalibran el panel durante unos minutos, por ejemplo al apagarlos, y también se puede reducir el brillo en elementos concretos como puede ser la barra de tareas. Asus, Samsung o MSI lo hacen en sus monitores.
- Hardware. También están los propios paneles y los disipadores. Las marcas han ido añadiendo mejores disipadores para que los píxeles se calienten menos y asís e minimicen los riesgos, pero MSI tiene un sensor de presencia que sabe si hay alguien delante para iniciar el proceso de cuidado del panel si te alejas.
- Respaldo comercial. Por último, los fabricantes saben que los paneles OLED tienen esa contrapartida y, aunque no siempre son los primeros en añadir años a la garantía, Asus y MSI dan tres años de garantía. Esto ya aplica menos a Apple porque depende de cada fabricante.
Los paneles de Apple. Lo que sí tiene que ver con la compañía de la manzana es que, aunque no sabemos aún qué tipo de OLED monta este MacBook Pro, sí sabemos que en el iPad Pro incluyeron la tecnología OLED en tándem. Apilan dos capas emisoras para repartir la carga entre ambas capas, haciendo que sea más difícil ese quemado.
La tecnología no es perfecta. Rtings es un analista especialista en pantallas que estos últimos años se ha convertido en una de las referencias a la hora de analizar OLED y detallar los cuidados que debemos tener con ellos. Este verano publicaron un artículo con un titular preocupante en el que afirmaban que el quemado de los paneles había evolucionado peor de lo que esperaban, con quemados en prácticamente todos los paneles.
El asterisco es que, sin quitar una coma al artículo de Rtings que prácticamente es un análisis científico, es cierto que estas pruebas las hacen de una forma brutal. Por ejemplo, reproduciendo durante 18.000 horas la CNN para ver dónde aparecían los quemados y en qué porcentaje.
Esas 18.000 horas sería como ver el mismo canal cinco horas seguidas diarias durante diez años. Nadie usa así el televisor (o casi nadie), y la propia Rtings comentó que esa prueba no equivale a diez años de uso normal y que, si ves contenido variado, el quemado sigue siendo improbable.
Mis dos centavos. Dicho esto, entiendo perfectamente por qué persiste la idea de que el quemado de los paneles OLED sigue siendo un problema. Es lo típico de "cría fama y échate a dormir", pero en este caso tiene sentido porque una tele, monitor o portátil OLED es algo muy, muy caro (y en el caso del MacBook, ni te cuento). Sin embargo, nadie usa el equipo como los analistas de los medios especializados en este ámbito.
En el caso de un portátil, es cierto que tenemos elementos fijos en el dock o en la barra superior. Si como yo estás todo el día en el navegador, pues la barra de Firefox. Pero claro, siempre ves un vídeo y se elimina tanto el dock como la barra superior, o sales al escritorio, o cargas otro escritorio...
Es decir, aunque estén muchas horas reproduciendo lo mismo, si sales de esa app a hacer otra cosa, es probable que hagas que algún elemento se refresque para eliminar la posibilidad del quemado. Y eso, de nuevo, sin saber qué tecnologías aplica Apple para luchar contra esto. La conclusión es que, si te llama la atención y tienes el dineral que cuesta, no me preocuparía ni un poco por ese quemado.

articles.title: Amazon reported booming cloud revenue but otherwise missed expectations | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday and missed analysts’ expectations for both its total revenue and earnings per share. There were other murky numbers in the report that scared investors, too, including how much cash the company is burning through.
But the report did have a big, bright spot: Its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, beat revenue expectations and grew a whopping 39% compared to the year-ago quarter.
Here are the numbers:
- Net sales increased 12% to $201.9 billion. But analysts were expecting $202.2 billion, according to FactSet.
- Fully diluted earnings per share were $1.89. Analysts were expecting $1.97.
- AWS sales reached $45.98 billion. Analysts were expecting $45.29 billion. In addition, Amazon said that AWS operating income grew to $17.8 billion, compared with $11.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025.
But here’s the biggest ouch of the report: Free cash flow fell to a negative of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12 months — meaning the company was spending far more cash than it generated. This compares to positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion for the trailing 12 months ended September 30, 2025.
The big spending was driven largely by Amazon’s investments in AI, the company said. With one quarter left in its fiscal year, Amazon reiterated that it still expects to end its 2026 with cash capital expenditures of about $220 billion.
To put that in perspective, the company forecast fourth-quarter net sales of between $240 billion and $247 billion. The fourth quarter is typically a retailer’s biggest, thanks to the holiday shopping season. That means Amazon expects to spend almost as much on capital expenditures, largely for AI, over the full year as it expects to bring in from sales in the fourth quarter.

articles.title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
articles.text:
The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.
Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC, Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour, and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara.
The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote.
The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May.
Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.
“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

articles.title: Tu Motorola Edge 70 Pro acaba de recibir Android 17: estas son las novedades más importantes
articles.text:
Mototola ha comenzado el despliegue de Android 17 para el Motorola Edge 70 Pro. A unas semanas de hacer lo propio con el Edge 70, la compañía lanzó la esperada actualización para uno de sus móviles premium que debutó este año. La nueva versión del sistema operativo ya comenzó a ofrecerse en Europa y llega con cambios visuales, mejoras de productividad y nuevas funciones de seguridad.
Un usuario de Reddit reportó que recibió la notificación de actualización para la versión europea del Motorola Edge 70 Pro. El paquete de 3,42 GB corresponde a la versión de software A171WMH.44-25 y forma parte de un despliegue escalonado, por lo que los propietarios de este móvil podrían recibir el aviso durante las próximas semanas. Desde hace un tiempo que la compañía prometió que agilizaría los tiempos de despliegue de sus actualizaciones, ya que siempre ha sido de las últimas en ofrecer la versión más reciente de Android en sus terminales.
En la notificación, Motorola señala que Android 17 ofrece un diseño renovado y más expresivo, notificaciones más inteligentes, una experiencia multitarea optimizada y nuevos controles enfocados en la protección de los datos del usuario. Entre los cambios más notorios se encuentra un rediseño de las notificaciones y los ajustes rápidos, así como el soporte para Live Activities, que muestra información en tiempo real de llamadas, mensajes o permite controlar el reproductor multimedia sin que abras cada aplicación por separado.
La actualización será el primero de tres saltos de versión que prometió Motorola para el Edge 70 Pro. La marca ha intentado alinearse con Google y Samsung en la oferta de actualizaciones para sus dispositivos más recientes, por lo que también será compatible con Android 18 y Android 19 en el futuro.
¿Qué hay de nuevo en Android 17 para los Motorola?
El Motorola Edge 70 Pro recibirá todas las características que anunció el fabricante hace unos meses. Android 17 ofrece varias novedades que mejoran la interacción con el móvil y la organización de la información. Un ejemplo son los widgets apilables, que permiten combinar varios widgets en un único espacio de la pantalla de inicio para ahorrar espacio y alternar entre ellos mediante gestos.
Los íconos temáticos también cambian y ahora es posible que más elementos del sistema adopten automáticamente los colores seleccionados por el usuario. Aquellos que usen el diseño clásico de los ajustes rápidos podrán ocultar las etiquetas de texto para ganar espacio en la pantalla.
Pasando a las notificaciones, la novedad que más nos gusta de esta actualización son las Live Updates. Esta característica reduce el exceso de notificaciones, ya que muestra información en tiempo real dentro de una misma. En caso de que no atiendas el móvil y recibas muchas alertas, el Motorola Edge 70 Pro podrá hacer un resumen automático para que no tengas que leerlas todas, o separar las importantes del resto usando IA.
El resto de funciones incluyen un control avanzado del brillo HDR, en el cual se puede limitar la intensidad máxima cuando veas fotografías o vídeos. También debuta Tap to Share, que permite compartir archivos acercando dos teléfonos, mientras que Quick Drop ayuda a enviar documentos a grupos.
La actualización de Android 17 para el Motorola Edge 70 Pro desplegará una notificación en pantalla una vez que esté disponible en tu país. Si aún no la recibes, deberás acceder a Ajustes > Información del teléfono > Actualización de software para comprobar si la versión está disponible. Recuerda que las actualizaciones de Android se despliegan de forma escalonada, por lo que algunos usuarios tendrán que esperar más tiempo para acceder a ellas.

articles.title: How Rogers Xfinity Internet is helping Canadians protect their connected homes at no additional cost
articles.text:
From smart doorbells to connected TVs, our homes are becoming more high-tech by the day. As the number of devices connected to our home WiFi grows, so does the need to keep them protected from online threats.
According to IDC Canada, 37 per cent of Canadian households use home automation devices, while 39 per cent use smart security devices.* These technologies can make everyday life more convenient, whether you’re checking a camera while away from home or controlling your lights from your phone, but they also add more connected devices to keep track of and protect.
That’s where network-level cybersecurity can make a difference for your home WiFi network. Rather than relying on individual security measures for every device, Rogers Xfinity Internet offers Advanced Security, a built-in feature designed to help protect every connected device in the home from cyberthreats.
Peace of mind for your connected home
Rogers Xfinity Advanced Security provides an additional layer of protection by monitoring your home WiFi network from online threats in real time. It helps block devices from accessing known malicious websites and content, while also alerting you to suspicious activity.
The feature is designed to help protect all devices connected to your home network, including computers, smartphones, smart TVs, streaming devices, cameras, doorbells and gaming consoles. It can also help prevent family members from accidentally visiting malicious sites that may contain malware, spyware, ransomware or viruses.
For Rogers Xfinity Internet customers, the protection is included at no additional cost, with no extra hardware to install. It can also complement traditional antivirus software, adding another layer of defence across your smart devices.
That built-in protection makes a meaningful difference, with Rogers Xfinity Advanced Security blocking more than 40 million cyberthreats each month for Rogers Xfinity customers.
Keeping security simple as technology evolves
With so many devices connecting to the internet, managing cybersecurity can quickly become complicated. Rogers Xfinity Advanced Security helps simplify protection by working at the home network level, allowing multiple connected devices to benefit without requiring a separate security setup for each one.
Customers can manage their home network through the Rogers Xfinity app, where they can also view security alerts and set parental controls. Advanced Security is optional and can be turned on or off through the app, giving customers control over whether they want to use the feature.
For the best experience, Rogers Xfinity Gateways and WiFi Pod extenders are designed to work together as a unified WiFi system. Using third-party extenders or mesh WiFi systems can affect device connections and limit the visibility and protection available through Advanced Security.
A timely reminder to protect your devices
As Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the holiday shopping season approach, many Canadians will be looking to add new technology to their homes. Whether it’s a smart speaker, a connected doorbell or a new gaming console, every new device is another reason to think about online security.
As more devices connect to your home network, Rogers Xfinity Internet with Advanced Security offers a simple way to stay ahead of potential threats, with an extra layer of protection across the connected home at no additional cost.
To learn more about Rogers Xfinity Internet and its built-in, always on WiFi security, visit the Rogers website.

articles.title: Qué códigos de Free Fire se pueden redimir hoy 29 de octubre de 2026 y conseguir diamantes gratis
articles.text:
Garena habilitó una nueva serie de códigos de Free Fire para este jueves 29 de octubre de 2026, con recompensas que pueden incluir diamantes, trajes, skins de armas y otros objetos dentro del videojuego. Los beneficios están sujetos a la disponibilidad, la región y la vigencia de cada combinación alfanumérica.
La dinámica suele concentrar una alta cantidad de intentos en poco tiempo. Por ese motivo, los jugadores deben ingresar los códigos con rapidez y verificar que la cuenta esté vinculada a una plataforma autorizada antes de comenzar el trámite en el sitio oficial de recompensas.
Cuáles son los códigos de Free Fire disponibles para finales de octubre de 2026
La lista reúne 15 combinaciones de letras y números. Cada clave debe copiarse sin modificaciones, con respeto por las mayúsculas y sin espacios adicionales. Garena puede limitar su uso por región o por cantidad de usuarios. Estos son los códigos disponibles:
- F2Q7W1E5R9T3Y6U4.
- F5A9S3D7F1G4H8J2.
- F6Z1X5C2V8B4N9M3.
- F3H8J4K1L7P5O2I9.
- F9S2D6F3G7H1J4K8.
- F1L5P9O3I7U2Y4T8.
- F4Q8W2E6R1T5Y9U3.
- F7A1S5D9F2G6H3J7.
- F2Z6X3C7V1B5N8M4.
- F5H9J1K8L4P2O6I3.
- F8S3D7F4G1H5J9K2.
- F3L7P2O6I4U8Y1T5.
- F6Q1W5E9R3T7Y2U4.
- F9A4S8D2F6G3H7J1.
- F1Z5X9C3V7B2N6M8.
En qué portal se canjean los códigos de Free Fire
El intercambio se realiza únicamente en el portal oficial de recompensas de Garena. El sitio solicita iniciar sesión antes de habilitar el campo para ingresar las combinaciones disponibles.
Una vez dentro de la página, el usuario debe seleccionar el método de acceso asociado a su perfil de juego. El sistema admite cuentas vinculadas con Google, Facebook, Apple, Huawei o VK. Tras pegar el código, corresponde confirmar la operación y esperar la validación del portal.
Para recibir los premios es necesario tener una cuenta de Free Fire registrada y asociada a uno de los proveedores admitidos. Las cuentas de invitado no pueden participar del sistema de canje, aunque el jugador tenga instalado el videojuego y disponga de códigos vigentes.
Quienes juegan como invitados deben vincular el perfil a una plataforma autorizada antes de intentar el trámite. Esa vinculación permite identificar la cuenta que recibirá los objetos y evita que las recompensas queden sin un destinatario asignado dentro del juego.
Qué hacer si el código aparece como inválido o expirado
El mensaje “código inválido o expirado” indica que la combinación ya no está disponible. Puede ser porque concluyó su período de vigencia, alcanzó el límite de usos o no funciona en la región desde la cual se intenta realizar el canje.
Asimismo, es posible que el sistema rechace el pedido por un error de escritura. Los códigos combinan letras y números, así que se debe revisar cada carácter antes de confirmar. Una letra omitida, una mayúscula alterada o un número equivocado pueden impedir la acreditación del beneficio.
Cuándo se acreditan los diamantes y los demás objetos en Free Fire
Las recompensas suelen llegar al buzón interno del videojuego en un plazo inferior a 24 horas. Los jugadores deben revisar esa sección luego de completar el trámite, porque los objetos no siempre aparecen de forma inmediata en el inventario principal.
El sistema de premios contempla diamantes, accesorios, elementos coleccionables, atuendos y skins de armas. Los diamantes figuran entre los incentivos más buscados porque permiten acceder a contenido de pago y realizar compras dentro de Free Fire, aunque el premio final depende de cada código validado.
Qué medidas ayudan a evitar problemas de seguridad al jugar Free Fire
Expertos sugieren utilizar solo el sitio oficial para canjear códigos y descargar el juego desde tiendas verificadas. Para instalar la aplicación en Android, la vía indicada es Google Play Store; en dispositivos de Apple, corresponde usar App Store. Otra clave es usar una conexión estable, porque reduce el riesgo de interrupciones durante la validación.
Es clave evitar las aplicaciones modificadas, los enlaces no oficiales y los programas que prometen beneficios automáticos pueden comprometer la seguridad de las cuentas. Ese tipo de archivos puede exponer datos personales, facilitar el robo de perfiles o incorporar errores que las versiones oficiales ya corrigieron mediante actualizaciones.

articles.title: AWS's Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents' mistakes
articles.text:
AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes
Earlier this month, the team behind Hydro developed a new way to check that a distributed system still works correctly when it resends messages after a failure.
This produced what Shadaj Laddad described to me as “like a 5000 line PR.” Hydro is an open-source Rust framework for distributed systems, the software that runs across many machines at once, and agents now write most of it with humans driving. The PR was difficult to split into smaller pieces as its components worked together.
That’s a lot of code to review for a tool developers count on to catch bugs. Laddad, research lead for the Hydro team at AWS, says it’s something the team spends a lot of time thinking about. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose. He was set to give a keynote the next day where he was going to argue code review can’t keep pace with how agents write code.
Agents have let the team aim higher, Laddad told me, saying PRs arrive faster and run longer. “You can have the feature work well in isolation, then you mix it with something else, and suddenly the guarantees break down,” he said.
And you can’t just trust the tests. In most agent workflows, he says, the agent writes both the code and the unit tests. “Agents are great, but they’re unpredictable,” Laddad said. That unpredictability is part of what makes them creative, and it makes it hard for a human to review all those tests and confirm they do what the team wants.
His answer is shared Correctness checks outside the agent’s “zone of trust,” such as those enforced by a compiler. Rust’s borrow checker is his example: It catches race conditions before the code ever runs. Hydro does something similar for distributed systems, catching several types of bugs at compile time so an agent gets instant feedback on mistakes it introduced. The wider goal, which the team is still exploring, is domain-specific guardrails that agents can share.
To find candidates, the team studies historical projects for recurring patterns. Idempotency, ensuring a retried request doesn’t run twice, comes up repeatedly in design reviews, so the team is asking whether it can become a general-purpose guardrail. Laddad sees this as the next rung on an old ladder. C spared programmers from mangling function calls in assembly. Java took memory allocation off their plate. Agents, he argued, make the next layer more urgent.
Compilers have limits, though. As The New Stack reported in August, AI-generated Rust can compile perfectly and still be wrong.
The same team also built Infinity, an open-source agent runtime AWS announced on October 23. It suspends an agent while it waits on a tool call or a CI job instead of keeping it running. Laddad cited a benchmark showing 75,000 concurrent agents on a single Raspberry Pi. According to the AWS announcement, that figure is extrapolated from a server test in which each idle agent used about 100 KB.
Hydro itself is an early release, built for teams running high-throughput, low-latency services who are constantly worried about distributed systems bugs. Laddad noted that users should expect rough edges and a learning curve right now. The payoff is the confidence to change a system without fearing it will break a few months later.
Hydro and Infinity are open source at hydro.run, built jointly by AWS and UC Berkeley.

articles.title: Major US Homeland Security breach exposes details on 41,000 employees — undercover ICE agents and contractors unmasked in ‘Icepick’ data dump
articles.text:
Major US Homeland Security breach exposes details on 41,000 employees — undercover ICE agents and contractors unmasked in ‘Icepick’ data dump
Numerous employees and contractors have had personal details exposed
- DHS data breach exposes personal details of over 41,000 employees and contractors
- The information includes personal information on ICE agents, as well as details of surveillance operations and tools used by undercover agents
- Numerous high-level officials across US government agencies have been named within the breach
The details of over 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has surfaced online, including staffers at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection, following an apparent data breach.
The leak contains sensitive information such as email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses for employees alongside internal information on how Homeland Security conducts undercover operations and surveillance programs.
The archive was published by a group calling itself the Department of Peace. They dubbed the leak ‘Icepick’, and shared a note stating, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”
‘Icepick’ data dump exposes agents and contractors
The DHS has been locked in a battle with activists, protestors, and anonymous social media users who have been tracking and cataloguing the movements and behavior of ICE employees.
In response to protests and activist activity, the DHS has expanded its definition of “doxing” - the malicious exposure of personal information such as home addresses - to include basic information such as names.
The Icepick data leak has since been turned into a searchable database by Swiss cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew, who said, “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them.”
“The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular,” crimew said. “The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government’.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Of the 41,000 records exposed, around 10,000 belong to ICE employees, 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and a further 1,000 are Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency accounts.
Details on DHS operations contains references to “Keyhole” - an undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups that took place earlier this year - alongside references to a Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).”
Tools used by employees have also been revealed in the breach, which include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform, the PenLink platform used to analyze phone records and social media, and AI platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot.
According to the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, who verified the leak on behalf of Wired, the data was obtained from the DHS's Okta login system. An Okta spokesperson said, “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
A DHS spokesperson said that the agency is “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available”

Benedict holds an MA (Distinction) in Security, Intelligence, and Diplomacy from the University of Buckingham Centre for Security and Intelligence Studies (BUCSIS), with his specialization providing him with a robust academic framework for deconstructing complex international conflicts and intelligence operations, and the ability to translate intricate security data into actionable insights.

articles.title: How to Make Artificial Intelligence More Environmentally Sustainable
articles.text:
IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, and electricity use at Microsoft and Google has climbed because of AI, according to their own reports. Charles Humble spoke about Green AI at GOTO Copenhagen, where he argued sustainability ought to be a top-level architectural concern. Amongst his recommendations: use pre-built and smaller models, run compute where low-carbon electricity is abundant, and train on renewable energy.
Humble quoted the International Energy Agency (IEA), which has stated that the combined electricity use from Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta has more than doubled between 2017 and 2021, rising to around 72 terawatt-hours in 2021. Microsoft’s 2024 environmental report mentioned that its total carbon emissions have risen 30% since 2020, primarily due to the construction of data centers to meet demand for AI. Google’s emissions had surged about 50% since 2019 and 13% year on year in 2023 alone, according to their own reporting, largely driven by artificial intelligence.
The emission that these reports talk about is mainly carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Since the Industrial Revolution we’ve been increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, trapping more heat, Humble said. We want to keep our warming to 1.5 degrees by 2100, but projections suggest that it will be between about 2.5 and 3 degrees.
The IT industry contributes a lot to this problem, partly through electricity use as Humble explained:
The IEA estimated that global data centre electricity consumption in 2022 is about 240 to 340 terawatt hours, 1 to 1.3% of global electricity demand. Networks add another 260 to 360 terawatt hours. That’s 700 terawatt hours, about the same as Brazil’s 726 terawatt hours in the same time period.
IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, where aviation is 3%, Humble said. But while the aviation industry is working quite hard to try and cut its emissions, we as an industry are doing the opposite.
There are several questions Humble suggested asking for putting AI into a business context:
- Do you really need it?
- Do you need to train a new model from scratch, or can you use a pre-built one?
- If you can relax part of your SLA, does that allow you to run your workloads in a greener location?
- Can you use demand shaping?
If we need to train a custom model, Humble suggested thinking about how much data we actually need to collect. Sometimes, smaller models work better, he argued. He also suggested using open-source data sets and, if possible, demand shifting to collect data when and where there is green energy available.
In theory, training can be on 100% renewable energy all the time, which can reduce carbon emissions somewhere between 45% and 99%, Humble mentioned.
He argued that most of the energy may actually be spent when we deploy a model into production and maintain it, and mentioned four steps to make all computing greener:
- Use the smallest hardware configuration that can safely execute the job.
- Run compute in areas where low-carbon electricity is abundant and where there are credible plans to make the grid even cleaner.
- Use cloud services from cloud providers that have data centers in green locations and provide good tooling to help reduce your footprint.
- Optimize the execution time of jobs to further reduce the carbon footprint.
Sustainability ought to join cost, performance, security, regulatory concerns, and reliability as one of the top-level considerations for your computing workloads, Humble concluded. We should think about how to build systems in a more environmentally sound way.
InfoQ interviewed Charles Humble after his talk.
InfoQ: How does location matter when it comes to reducing carbon emissions?
Charles Humble: A compute workload uses a fixed amount of energy, but the carbon cost of that energy varies enormously by place and time depending on the sources of electricity that is powering the data centre. Assuming the data centre is using grid power in a region running mostly on hydro, solar, nuclear and wind (for example Norway, Sweden and France), running a workload here can be many times cleaner than one dependent on coal or gas. Carbon intensity also changes during the day and over the course of the year as wind, solar and demand vary.
In carbon aware computing we can apply a technique called demand shifting based on this. Demand shifting can be done in one of two ways, either time or location based. Time-based is particularly applicable when a use case isn’t latency sensitive, such as AI training.
For location the most simple variation of the technique is to just pick lower-carbon regions by default for new, latency-tolerant workloads. More advanced variations might involve moving to different hemispheres seasonally to maximize exposure to sunlight and solar power.
InfoQ: How does demand shaping work?
Humble: Demand shaping means changing how much work your software does, or what kind of work, in response to how clean or constrained the electricity supply is at that moment. One version of this is to give users a choice. For an AI-powered service, you could let users choose to talk to a person instead of the AI up front, or at any point during the process.
You can also apply techniques such as graceful degradation based on higher carbon intensity, for example by serving lower-quality video or images, turning off autoplay, skipping non-essential animations, or reducing refresh rates. You might also use a smaller model.
Tradeoffs include increased complexity, and of course you have to determine if the reduced service is still acceptable.
InfoQ: What can we do to make model training greener?
Humble: Alongside demand shifting for both training and data collection, avoid training from scratch if at all possible. Use a pre-trained model and fine-tune it, or just prompt it and/or use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) if that meets the need.
Shrinking the model size can speed up training and improve efficiency. Distillation, quantization and pruning can all be used for compression. On-device training via Federated learning can be greener in some cases. Keep in mind that for widely used models, inference over the model’s lifetime may cause greater total emissions, so efficiency in serving matters too.
Raghavendra Selvan’s book "Sustainable AI" explores a number of these approaches in considerably greater depth, so if readers want to learn more, this is a great resource.

articles.title: Microsoft va enfin retirer Copilot de votre téléviseur
articles.text:
Microsoft arrête le support de Copilot sur toutes les Smart TV. LG a commencé à en informer ses utilisateurs par un message sur l’écran, sans date précise pour l’instant.
Copilot n’aura donc pas fait long feu sur les téléviseurs. C’est un message affiché sur une TV LG qui a révélé l’info ce mercredi.
Copilot sur TV : installé de force, déjà abandonné
Repéré par Windows Central, la notification en question est apparue sur un téléviseur LG propulsé par WebOS. LG explique que Microsoft a décidé d’arrêter la prise en charge de Copilot sur tous les téléviseurs. La fonction n’est plus disponible et pourrait cesser de fonctionner d’ici peu. Microsoft n’a pas confirmé de date, mais LG s’attend à une fin avant 2027. Fin de support, cela veut dire que Microsoft arrête de faire vivre le service.
Sur ces écrans, Copilot répondait à des questions sur ce qui s’affichait, conseillait des films et des séries, et discutait comme sur les autres appareils. Son arrivée avait fait grincer des dents. En janvier 2025, nous rapportions que LG et Samsung prévoyaient d’ajouter un raccourci vers Copilot sur certains modèles. En fin d'année dernière, les propriétaires de TV LG ont eu la mauvaise surprise de ne pas pouvoir le désinstaller. Quatre jours plus tard, LG déployait un correctif pour éradiquer toute trace de Copilot.
Si le constructeur LG parlait d’un simple raccourci qui ouvre le chatbot dans le navigateur de la TV, pour certains, l’application a été installée de force. Samsung, dont les TV sous Tizen hébergeaient aussi Copilot, est concerné puisque l’arrêt vise toutes les Smart TV. Aucune annonce de sa part n’est mentionnée pour l’instant.
Microsoft a changé de stratégie. Copilot n’est plus présenté comme un compagnon numérique pour le grand public, mais comme un outil de productivité et de travail. L’entreprise a d’ailleurs fusionné Microsoft 365 Copilot et Copilot grand public dans une seule application. Il n’existe plus d’appli personnelle dédiée, et la version TV devient la dernière déclinaison grand public à disparaître.

articles.title: Fujifilm plans 5x production boost of 100TB magnetic storage tapes driven by skyrocketing AI storage demand — $63 million injection is the largest investment in tape for 20 years
articles.text:
Fujifilm plans 5x production boost of 100TB magnetic storage tapes driven by skyrocketing AI storage demand — $63 million injection is the largest investment in tape for 20 years
The move will see the company's largest investment in tape-based data center storage medium in the last two decades.
Fujifilm plans to boost production of magnetic tape by as much as 5x as it works to keep up with demand for the data storage medium that has seen a jump in popularity amid ongoing global AI data center buildouts. The Japanese firm will spend 10 billion yen ($63.3 million) to increase capacity at its Odawara plant throughout its fiscal year 2028. The move will enable it to produce more advanced tapes with capacities of up to 100TB each, Nikkei Asia reports. The expansion of production capacity will mark the company's largest investment in tape-based storage in around 20 years. Fujifilm first began working on magnetic tape technology back in 1954 when it was used for television broadcasting equipment.
Nowadays, magnetic tape is the go-to storage option for data centers everywhere as a form of long-term data backup. While tapes lag behind solid-state drives and traditional spinning hard disks in terms of performance, tapes are hard to beat when it comes to their durability and relatively low cost for storing huge amounts of data. Magnetic tape storage can cost as little as one-quarter that of hard disks, and even less when compared to faster SSDs. That makes them the perfect solution for so-called cold data, information that is rarely accessed but could be considered mission-critical and must be stored safely. Tape storage isn't just cheaper, either, with research showing that it's also less polluting than hard disks and SSDs.
While Fujifilm will produce 100TB tapes, the Linear Tape-Open (LTO) roadmap allows for considerably larger capacities, all the way to 365TB per cartridge. By comparison, SSDs top out at around 256TB and cost considerably more.
Fujifilm is far from the only storage company looking to take advantage of the AI data center boom. Toshiba announced earlier this month its plans to double hard disk production capacity amid shortages, and the company, alongside Seagate and WD, is working towards ever-increasing capacities. Kioxia and SanDisk are also getting in on the act after detailing 332-layer 3D NAND flash in August. The pair hope to bring higher storage capacities to SSDs for data center use.
The demand for AI data center storage is so high that it's at the heart of a global shortage that shows little sign of improving anytime soon. Scarcity has seen prices skyrocket, while manufacturers have chosen to divert resources away from consumer-focused products, instead focusing on the more lucrative enterprise market.

articles.title: Polymarket halts trading after crypto-draining script breach, $2.5M traced
articles.text:
Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading on Thursday after hackers compromised a third-party service to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript, with approximately $2.5 million in assets traced to a suspected attacker wallet.
The company confirmed the security incident, saying it had identified and fixed the issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com, and referred the breach to law enforcement.
"One of our third party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement," Polymarket said.
"Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading and are working to bring the platform back online."
Polymarket initially placed its exchange into cancel-only mode at 2:05 p.m. ET and paused relayer actions while investigating the incident. At 2:37 p.m., the company announced that the issue had been fixed and that trading was temporarily halted out of an abundance of caution.
Trading resumed approximately one hour after the initial suspension, with the incident marked resolved at 3:05 p.m. ET.
"Trading is now fully back online," the company announced on X. "We'll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders."
Polymarket has not disclosed how many users were affected, how much cryptocurrency was stolen, or how the reimbursement process will work.
Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified a suspected attacker-controlled wallet (0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18) embedded in the malicious JavaScript.
BleepingComputer's examination of the wallet's blockchain activity found that it transferred approximately 28.6 million POL, valued at roughly $2.57 million, to three additional wallets.
Blockchain records also show that the wallet conducted numerous transactions involving Polymarket's prediction-market token contract between 1:50 p.m. and 1:56 p.m. ET, shortly before the exchange suspended trading.
Hudson Rock reported that the wallet held approximately $2.19 million in cryptocurrency at the time of its investigation.
Malicious JavaScript used to drain wallets
Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified malicious JavaScript distributed through cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js that was designed to steal cryptocurrency and prediction-market holdings from Polymarket users.
The script was hosted on infrastructure belonging to DebugBear, a website performance-monitoring service that helps organizations track website loading speeds and user experience.
DebugBear's Real User Monitoring (RUM) service uses JavaScript embedded in websites to collect performance metrics from visitors' browsers.
DebugBear has since confirmed that it is investigating an ongoing security incident and warned customers to remove its monitoring JavaScript from their websites.
"We're impacted by an ongoing security incident," DebugBear said in a post on X.
"If you use our RUM product, please remove the embed code from your website."
At the time of writing, DebugBear's website was inaccessible, displaying a Cloudflare error. It is unclear whether the website outage is related to containment efforts or another consequence of the incident.
Hudson Rock's researchers also discovered Polymarket production build metadata containing the commit message, "chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337)," indicating that the platform had removed the DebugBear monitoring integration.
The build was timestamped October 29 at 1:59 p.m. ET, shortly before Polymarket publicly announced the incident.
BleepingComputer analyzed a copy of the malicious JavaScript file (VirusTotal), finding that it was designed to hijack authenticated Polymarket trading sessions, liquidate users' prediction-market positions, and transfer cryptocurrency and other assets to an attacker-controlled wallet.
The malware checks whether a visitor is logged into Polymarket and attempts to use their existing trading session and the platform's trading functionality to carry out unauthorized transactions.
It then checks the user's cryptocurrency balances and prediction-market positions to determine the value of their holdings.
Depending on how the user authenticated to Polymarket, the malware attempts to steal their assets in different ways.
For some users, it tries to automatically sell their prediction-market positions. For others, the malware attempts to transfer their prediction-market tokens directly to an attacker-controlled wallet.
The malware also attempts to convert users' cryptocurrency holdings into assets that can be transferred to an attacker-controlled wallet, using Polymarket's existing transaction functionality.
BleepingComputer found that the malicious script communicated with data.debugbear.com to receive instructions and send data about targeted accounts, wallet addresses, balances, and transaction results.
The use of DebugBear's infrastructure to both distribute the malicious script and serve as a command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration server raises questions about the how much access the attackers had to the company's systems.
BleepingComputer has contacted Polymarket and DebugBear with questions about the incident and will update this article if we receive a response.

articles.title: Harry Potter : la première affiche de la série HBO est là, et elle cache un secret
articles.text:
Harry Potter : la première affiche de la série HBO est là, et elle cache un secret
La très attendue série Harry Potter de HBO vient de s'offrir son tout premier poster officiel, et de confirmer sa date de sortie.
La série Harry Potter est sans conteste l'événement télé de la fin d'année. Et à deux mois de son arrivée sur la plateforme de streaming HBO Max, la nouvelle adaptation des livres de J.K. Rowling vient enfin de dévoiler sa toute première affiche officielle, qui met bien sûr son jeune héros à l'honneur.
Un clin d'œil à Voldemort ?
Et oui, car depuis l'officialisation du projet il y a plusieurs années maintenant, les visuels de la série sont particulièrement rares. Les fans (et nous journalistes) ont dû se contenter jusqu'à présent d'une image d'un Poudlard doré et d'un logo légérement remanié, mais c'était tout.
Et alors que la série est attendue pour Noël, HBO a visiblement décidé de réparer ce manque, et de nous offrir donc cette affiche, sur laquelle on peut voir une partie du visage du jeune Harry Potter (incarné par Dominic McLaughlin), avec sa célèbre cicatrice et le reflet de Poudlard dans ses lunettes.
L'image est accompagnée de la célèbre mention "le garçon qui a survécu", surnom de Harry, ainsi que de la confirmation de la date de diffusion : à partir du 25 décembre 2026. Jusqu'à présent, nous devions nous satisfaire d'un simple et vague "Noël".
Un petit détail a enfin attiré notre attention : le reflet vert sur la lunette de Harry. Celui-ci semble en effet être une référence à la couleur de l'Avada Kedavra, le sortilège utilisé par Voldemort pour tenter de tuer le jeune sorcier, et qui se retournera contre lui.
Une manière d'évoquer subtilement "celui dont on ne doit pas prononcer le nom", qu'on ne devrait qu'entrevoir qu'à la toute fin de la première saison, avant qu'il ne fasse sa véritable apparition complète dans la saison 4 de la série, qui adaptera Harry Potter et la Coupe de feu.
La série Harry Potter est écrite et produite par Francesca Gardiner (Succession). Mark Mylod assure également la production exécutive et réalise plusieurs épisodes. Pour la saison 2, Gardiner partage le poste de showrunner avec Jon Brown (Succession).
Composée de huit épisodes, la première saison de la série adaptera naturellement le premier livre, Harry Potter à l'école des sorciers. La deuxième saison, basée sur La Chambre des secrets, est elle d'ores et déjà en pleine production.

articles.title: FBI leads action to shut down Virtualine bulletproof service linked to major cybercrime activity
articles.text:
FBI leads action to shut down Virtualine bulletproof service linked to major cybercrime activity
Virtualine was hosting multiple illegal forums
- FBI and international partners seized infrastructure tied to Virtualine, a hosting provider allegedly serving cybercriminals
- Authorities say the service facilitated phishing, ransomware operations, illicit crypto activity, and other crimes
- Investigators seized servers and customer data, though no arrests have been announced so far
The FBI has announced it seized the website of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service that allegedly allowed child pornography, laundered stolen and extorted crypto, and facilitated a wide range of other criminal activities.
The operation was carried out in partnership with German and Dutch authorities, as well as multiple private companies, with police raiding a data center in Limburg to seize “dozens of physical servers” that also hosted “hundreds” of virtual servers. As a result, they gained access to information about more than 3,000 of Virtualine’s customers, it was said.
“The police are currently taking follow-up actions towards these users,” the Dutch police said, although it’s difficult to say how valuable the information will be, since most bulletproof hosting providers don’t ask for private data, and criminals are good at hiding it, as well.
Bulletproof hosting
Every website, including hacking forums, criminal service providers, even fraudulent landing pages, needs a server that hosts it. Hosting providers renting out these servers are generally compliant with law enforcement agencies, so when the police requests a takedown or files a complaint, most of them comply. However, there is a subset of hosting providers, colloquially called “bulletproof hosting”, which are unusually resistant to pressure from the authorities.
It doesn’t mean all of them are inherently illegal or malicious. There are cases where such services are necessary - in countries with strong censorship, or where website owners want to protect their identities.
In this case, however, Virtualine was openly criminal, with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) saying it advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums saying, on at least one occasion, “You can use Virtualine for all illegal/black hat activities (including phis[h]ing, carding, email spam, port scanning and all others) except for child contents and terrorism activities.”
The company took it a step further. In March 2026, it introduced an “additional protection plan” that offers customers who receive takedown requests “another shell company not affiliated with Virtualine, after which the server is reactivated.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Interestingly enough, Virtualine said it did not accept child porn or terrorism content, but according to the DOJ - did exactly the opposite.
One of its clients created a forum that allowed users to post and sell access to “nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults,” while also promoting a hack-for-hire service that broke into people’s accounts and stole their explicit photos and videos. Virtualine was even notified about it by law enforcement agencies from Germany, Canada, and Australia, but decided to ignore the warnings and continue hosting the client.
At the same time, Virtualine’s customers were allowed to pay in Bitcoin, offering an unhosted bitcoin address that allowed customers “to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit”. Citing Chainalysis data, BleepingComputer said the company’s wallet was seen receiving funds from ransomware operations, infostealers, Russian-language cybercrime forums, and more.
“Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added.
Piercing the kevlar
Besides confiscating the servers and the data, the main website - virtualine.net - was defaced and now shows the usual FBI “this website has been seized” message. Unfortunately, no arrests have been made, which means the service will most likely continue operating.
According to BleepingComputer, it is “partially online” but its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, which could mean that much of its infrastructure was pulled offline.
Usually, disruptions such as this one are only temporary, and it won’t take long before they are remedied and the service becomes fully operational again.

articles.title: The Canadian legacy of Resident Evil, 30 years later
articles.text:
There are few video game properties as beloved and iconic as Resident Evil. Since its debut way back on the original PlayStation in 1996, Capcom’s survival horror series has left an indelible mark on the medium through its signature mix of haunting atmosphere, tense gunplay, thoughtful resource management systems and ample B-movie charms. With over 200 million copies sold to date, it’s one of gaming’s biggest series, and that success paved the way for numerous high-profile multimedia adaptations, not the least of which being Constantin’s franchise of eight live-action films, including Zach Cregger’s recent eponymous hit.
But despite all of that fame, a lot of people don’t realize just how much of an impact Canadians have had on the Japanese series throughout its entire history. Indeed, from the very first game all the way to its most recent release, actors, directors, models, and other artists hailing from across the Great White North have played pivotal roles in shaping the look, sound, and overall feel of Resident Evil. (That’s to say nothing of the fact that most of the movies were shot in and around Toronto, including multiple from Milla Jovovich’s series and 2021’s oft-forgotten Welcome to Raccoon City, with many Canadian actors featured throughout.)
And so, for the 30th anniversary, we wanted to celebrate Canada’s many contributions to Resident Evil. To do that, we spoke to over a dozen series veterans who worked on everything from the early PS1 games all the way up to the modern photorealistic entries. Along the way, they gave rich insight into the recording and localization processes, the evolution of technology, the vast pool of artistic talent in Canada and much more.
This is the Canadian legacy of Resident Evil.
Wow, what a mansion!
1996’s Resident Evil is one of the most iconic and influential games of all time. It pioneered tense survival horror action. It presented, at the time, incredible 3D graphics. And its setting, the Spencer Mansion, was a masterclass in labyrinthine game design. All of this helped elite S.T.A.R.S. officers Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield’s journey to escape the zombie-filled mansion become an instant classic.
Equally as famous, though, is the voice acting, but not necessarily for the same reasons. In the early days of what would become its biggest series, the company tapped a group of English-speaking expat actors in Japan for both the live-action segments and voice dubbing. But even years later, much of this group would remain in relative obscurity, whether it was due to miscrediting (such as with Jill’s voice, who has often — but never officially — been linked to Alberta actress Una Kavanagh), people not wanting to be associated with the roles, or some having passed away, as was the case of Chris’ actor, Victoria, B.C.-born Scott McCulloch. As a result, this made it difficult to find the right people from this seminal game to include in this feature.
But there is one Canadian who was part of that very first RE who actually openly embraces the project to this day: Pablo Kuntz, who played the villainous S.T.A.R.S. captain Albert Wesker. After graduating from the University of Western Ontario, the Rosemère, Que. native moved to Tokyo at the age of 22 to become an English teacher. However, he soon got bored with that job and tried his hand at modelling and acting, taking on numerous gigs around Tokyo. Along the way, he met Hollywood actor Sergio Alarcon, who was also modelling in Japan, and through him was introduced to a production manager who was casting for a little Capcom game about zombies.
Pablo Kuntz: It was a mixture of wanting to see the world, having a little bit of a glimpse into the culture [from a
childhood friend]. I got a visa, so I could go there legally, and it just seemed like a good fit […] You don’t think too much when you’re like 20. [laughs] You’re like, “Okay, let’s do it, what have I got to lose?” […] Growing up in Quebec, being English first language, I always felt like it was like some sort of handicap. It’s like, if you’re not fluently bilingual, which I’m not […] you learn pretty young that you’re not likely going to get any sort of high position in Quebec if you don’t speak French perfectly. Unless you’re French Canadian, it’s kind of a clique there.
[…] I joined about five or six different modelling agencies [in Tokyo], and I got work right away, pretty much. It was just hustle, hustle, hustle, hustle […] And I remember making friends with this guy named Sergio Alarcon […] Literally at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, I was recording. I remember stealing some line from Q107, actually, when I was doing it, and I put this voice tape together because it was so cheap to rent the studio at that time of the hour, and I gave it to Sergio.
I don’t think they had a pool of 200 people. I really think it was maybe 20, 30 voices. I have no idea the number, exactly, but they knew what I looked like. They knew how old I was. Because Barry [Kjerde] looks like Barry [Burton]. In fact, his name is Barry. He’s Barry! So the Japanese mindset was more like, “Well, if that’s what he looks like, if that’s the height, and then he must sound like that.” They wanted to pair [these attributes]. So when I looked at the picture of Wesker, I was like, “Yeah.” Not that it looked like me, but it wasn’t not me. I started to see [it]. […] It was a small group, and it was hard to get into that voice group. It was tough because they all knew they got paid well, and there wasn’t massive competition. So I was really glad.
While the acting is infamously campy, Kuntz’s recollections of the recording process shed some light on why that came to be.
Kuntz: I remember just being by myself in the recording studio, just one mic. No real direction, that is for sure. I had the mindset of what they needed and what they wanted from TV commercials, which I had done a good year-and-a-half of. A lot of commercials, they’re not long; they’re sometimes eight seconds, and it’s this big emotion, like angry and then sad at the end. You had to overemphasize everything, because when you did that, it translated in a commercial setting. They always said, “More overaction, Pablo, more overaction!” So that was ingrained in us.
That’s just Japan. If you go to Kabuki or you go to see any other live show, they’re always doing that. So we just felt that was the right thing to do. Plus, the dialogue was very obviously just funny translation. Like, why don’t I just say, “Stop, don’t open that door!?” It’s “Stop it!” Why is that “it” there? It’s just totally weird, right? But there was no direction, so it was just, “Stop it, don’t open that door!” And I try to remember that one line why I did it the way I did it. Did I realize that I actually had a couple extra words? “Stop it, don’t open that door!” [laughs] Because the delivery is so corny!
I don’t know what I was thinking. I had the script beforehand, so it wasn’t like I was just going from zero right there. But I didn’t take it that seriously. I’m going to be very honest. I didn’t like read it on, going like, “Okay, I’ve got to get into persona now.” There’s no way. I was just thinking, “Okay, two-day job, I got my lines, see if I can isolate it.” In some situations, I remember doing a couple takes, if it was a long take. You know that last scene in Resident Evil, or close to last scene, where I’m in the hallway and I go [puts on deeper voice] “So, Jill!” That time, I’m kind of getting more warmed up. Because in almost any voice recording, the first few lines are often redone later on. You just get into it, and all of a sudden, “Can we do those first four again? Because it doesn’t sound so good.” But I never had that chance.
[…] It wasn’t like, “Pablo, this time, please….” Nothing like that. It’s nice when a director [does that]. Because in the TV stuff, we often got some direction. “Okay, Pablo, lips a little bit slower this time.” But not [on Resident Evil]. It just felt like one giant experiment. But it was a happy accident. Everything kind of just worked. I think the graphics themselves mimic the voices. They’re all pixelated, and somehow, because the characters are a little bit awkward on screen, the voice being a little bit awkward — it’s somehow a nice marriage there. [laughs] It was so honest.
[…] One person said the reason why your [Wesker] worked […] He didn’t sound necessarily like an evil guy. And I think that’s what was special about Wesker. Because I don’t think I really spent that much time realizing, “Oh shit, I’m actually kind of bad!” [laughs] So that kind of naiveté, the whole thing sort of worked in my favour. There was no hint of me being a bad guy from the onset of Resident Evil. Nobody thought I was a double agent at all […] Because as one person said in the chat, Wesker doesn’t think of himself as being evil. So why do you have to sound evil?
Because it was a brief gig among many, Kuntz never thought much of Resident Evil again and, after a couple of decades, had pretty much forgotten he’d even done it. He would later hold a number of jobs, from building websites for Japanese companies Nissan and Pasona to Unique Japan, his own business that sells certified high-quality Japanese swords. One day, during the COVID-19 pandemic, someone commented on one of his sword videos asking if he was Wesker from the original Resident Evil game, sending him down an internet rabbit hole to rediscover something he had done over 20 years prior. This led him to ultimately embrace the role and the community through interviews, videos and even streamed playthroughs of Resident Evil games with his son on his YouTube channel, Lexonal. But Kuntz admits that he wasn’t always sure if this was the right approach.
Kuntz: My first reaction was like, “Maybe I shouldn’t, because everybody’s making fun of this stuff.” […] I had every reason to just ignore comments and say, “I’m not gonna, what are you talking about?” But there was just a kind of sense of almost taking responsibility. There’s one thing I’ve actually taught my kids, and they know this straight up: if you make a mistake, you fess up to it and don’t run away from that […] That played a role. I think I just said, “Well, I did it!”
Plus, it bothered me a little bit that Sergio was credited. It’s like, “It’s not Sergio!” It still niggles me when I see a video. [laughs] I haven’t seen one in a long time; I think people have come around the fact that it’s me. It’s like, “I could say nothing, and then I’ll live with the fact that it’s always Sergio on here, or just take this time to go and say it’s me.” But I can honestly say I had no idea what that would lead to just by saying it’s me. I really had no clue that people were going to go, “Whoa!” And all of a sudden, I felt this tsunami of interest. I was all of a sudden doing interviews for a while there, Residence of Evil and a few others. But everybody was like, “Yes, we got him! We finally figured out who the guy is!” And some people were still going, “No, no, it’s still Sergio!” And I’m like, “No, it’s not Sergio! Stop with the Sergio crap!” [laughs]
From Tokyo to Toronto
Resident Evil 2 is notable for many reasons. Where the original game focused on the elite S.T.A.R.S. members, this 1998 follow-up stars two scrappy, fresh-faced protagonists: rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield. The sequel also introduced the ingenious “zapping system” in which decisions that players made as one character, such as taking certain guns or defeating specific enemies, would affect how events transpire in another campaign. And if that wasn’t enough, the sequel marked the debut of the classic RE “stalker” enemy that constantly pursues you, realized memorably here with the towering trench-coat-and-fedora-clad Tyrant, affectionately known as Mr. X by fans.
But it wasn’t just the game design that levelled up — so, too, did the voice acting. As it turns out, that was all thanks to a team of marvellous mutants. In the ’90s, X-Men: The Animated Series recorded in Toronto after Fox Kids had great success in the city with Beetlejuice and Dan Hennessey, the late voice director on both shows. Because all of the X-Men vocal talent was already in Toronto, Capcom opted to record X-Men vs. Street Fighter in the city as well. Susan Hart, a local voice director who had already worked with Hennessey on several X-Men episodes, ultimately took on X-Men vs. Street Fighter and, through that, Resident Evil.
Susan Hart (voice director, Resident Evil 2, 3, Code Veronica and many other Capcom games): The scheduler at the studio said, “I’ve got the person for you — just call Susan, she’ll help you.” So when I got the email — “Can you cast this for us?” “Yes.” “Can you produce it?” “Oh, yes!” “Can you voice direct this?” “Of course!” [laughs] It helped because I’d been in the studio before, and I’m comfortable being in the studio, both prior as a performer and being in there working with Dan. It also really helped that I was in casting, so I knew how to direct. I had done many feature films and animated series, so I was very comfortable working with actors. So I knew what a script looked like. I knew the process, and I understood the studio, how that worked, as far as working with the engineer, et cetera, et cetera. So we got started, and I was able to hire a lot of the original cast, and it just kept on coming.
Alyson Court (Claire Redfield, Resident Evil 2, Code Veronica and others, Jubilee in X-Men: The Animated Series): “[Fox] really liked the entire team that they were working with in Toronto, because Dan Hennessey directed Beetlejuice and then went on to direct the X-Men cartoon… They used the same studio, which back then was called Sounds Interchange, and then became D.A.V.E., and then Technicolor. It’s been through a bunch of different names. And it just recently got bulldozed, so that’s very sad. Very similar in a way to Capcom, where they went there for something specific. Beetlejuice was being done there because Nelvana was making it. Nelvana is a Toronto company, but then Fox took it over, and they really liked the team, so they wanted to continue.
And then there’s the fact that the Canadian dollar was lower, and our union fees are cheaper than SAG rates, so it was more economical. And at that time, X-Men and Fox and just the Saturday morning cartoon in terms of superheroes — that was not a thing. It was not popular, and Marvel was in the tank. So doing the X-Men cartoon was a huge leap of faith by the team that put it together and they didn’t really have much of a budget. So economically, I think that played a huge part in the decision to continue in Toronto. And also, the fact that they really loved the talent pool coming off of Beetlejuice. They were like, “No, this is going to be fine.”
They went through several rounds casting for X-Men, and there were a lot of people that were cast in the first place, and then they were replaced. Most of us were replacements, actually — I think after they recorded the initial pilot episode. They were all clearly very passionate about it, and a lot of the replacements were theatre people. They were like, “No, we don’t want people who just have a ton of cartoon experience because that’s not the tone that we’re going for.”
Susan Hart: Toronto has got a plethora of everything. We have film schools. We have theatres. We have improvisational houses. We have so much that the actors can experience and train in all different disciplines. So they’re not just in theatre. They’re also doing some film work. They’re also doing narration. We’ve got Shaw. We’ve got Stratford. We’ve got Soul Pepper. We have production companies from all over the world coming here and shooting. Our actors have got a huge amount of resources to satisfy all their acting itches, and they can perform in a multitude of different disciplines. That is what makes our talent in Toronto, specifically. I know in Vancouver there’s great talent, in Montreal, et cetera, there’s great talent. But right here in Toronto, we’ve got so many platforms for our actors to delve into and grow and become better and better at their craft.
Dawn of the dead
RE2 would be the first of several RE games that were recorded in Toronto. Naturally, this meant that it was a big learning process for all involved. The Canadian and Japanese teams navigated language and cultural barriers. Dealing with the technical limitations of ’90s hardware. Minimal communication about what the project even was. All of that is to say: having this veteran Canadian cast and crew proved invaluable to Capcom.
Susan Hart: They would send out what they needed, cast breakdowns, and so I would do all of that. At that time, when we first started, I think it might have been cassette tapes, not digital audio tapes. We would just do the casting. They’d give me the script. They’d send me the scripts — or sides, pieces of the script — and the character description. And the actors would come in, and they would have the script ahead of time, and I’d audition them, and then we’d send two tapes separately, just in case one got lost. And we sent them via FedEx. So they would get it, they’d listen to it, they’d get back to me if they didn’t hear what they wanted… If they wanted more, I would do it again. And then we would coordinate hours, days, that they would be flying in so I’d book the studio.
The scripts would arrive, but initially, none of the lines were in order. None of the scenes were in order. And initially, the scripts were not allowed out of the studio, so the actors would have to come a day before their booking and sit in the lobby and read the scripts and familiarize themselves with them, just because you didn’t want any of that stuff out there. So we did this for years, and it really was a great system. Initially, we had quite a few people from Capcom come out. I’d say about eight, and there was an interpreter there. And they were just so giving and just so pleased with how organized it was. And the actors coming in were just so kind. There was some broken English going on, but the laughter and the clapping and the camaraderie that was happening — it was really, really nice. And that happened for every game that we did. As the games went on, we started getting to digital audio tapes, less and less people came, and then, for a while, it was just a producer and R&D, probably, that were there at the end of it, when I stopped working there with them.
Alyson Court: They didn’t share really anything about [RE2]. It was the same people that had done the Marvel vs. Capcom game, where I met them to do Jubilee’s voice, but there wasn’t a whole lot beyond that. Even our contracts initially didn’t have the name of the game on them. That was something they did with all of their games. They came here and they came to Toronto and they did a bunch of games, but they were always very secretive on the contracts, which, really, you shouldn’t be. You do have to say what the job is. [laughs]
[…] At the audition, I was told that this character I was reading for, “Think of her as serious, it’s kind of scary, she’s looking for her brother. She doesn’t know anybody, and she’s sort of like Jubilee’s older sister.” [That’s] how it was described to me. “But it’s more adult and serious and that kind of thing.” And what was nice is doing X-Men: The Animated Series definitely gave those of us who had prior animation experience a whole different world to play in in terms of voice acting. Because they didn’t want Saturday morning cartoon characterizations. They didn’t want it for kids, they didn’t want it goofy; they wanted it with some gravitas and serious stories with consequences and people being killed.
