They wanted that drama and that level of performance to come through, so I think that’s a huge part of why Capcom chose to sort of set up shop in Toronto for a number of years for so many AAA titles, because they had been introduced to a talent pool. We were all theatre trained, so we had this huge wealth of different mediums behind us and under our belts. So they had a really good talent pool to pull from.
Sally Cahill (Ada Wong, Resident Evil 2, 4 and Darkside Chronicles: It wasn’t so much that there was a lot of secretiveness regarding Resident Evil; there wasn’t a lot of buzz or talk in general. I think perhaps because it was still sort of in development. Things are likely very different today when actors hear there are auditions for Resident Evil! I was attracted to the project because though I had done cartoons and other voiceover work, this was my first major role in a video game. It was different, too; it was intriguing and fun.
[…] I remember meeting the creative team from Capcom at the initial audition and at the recordings. I think it really helped having Susan Hart there. Since there was usually a Japanese interpreter, it was often Susan I could see behind the glass in the recording studio in animated conversation with them. She was very good at communicating back and forth, and then coming on the mic and giving me short, clear direction. Susan Hart was great at that. She left room for our own interpretation as well. Actors love that kind of director.
Alyson Court: It was all very odd. I certainly had never played a game like what we were making, so I didn’t have that conceptually in my brain as to that’s what it could be. And we were pretty isolated during the recordings. We might pass each other, either [Leon actor] Paul [Haddad] and me, or occasionally [Sherry Birkin actor] Lisa [Jai] — I might see them out in the waiting room at the studio. But we were mostly alone in the booth, and there wasn’t a lot of communication because the bulk of the people who came over from Capcom were all from Japan. They spoke Japanese, not English. They had a translator there, but they were very quiet about things. They didn’t like to share information […]
It felt like this impenetrable wall. There was the language barrier, but there was a translator. But it’s just culturally so different, and the idea of sharing information, or why you don’t need to know, or whatnot — it was sort of like, “Why would we need to give information?” Down the road, I think they learned it’s important; you need to give as much information as possible to help [us] understand the nuances. Because for a lot of it, it felt like we were recording the same sections of script over and over again — or certainly the same scenes and dialogue, even though it would have a different scene number. And Paul and I just couldn’t understand what was going on.
[…] I think it got to a point when I would be like, “Hi, so is there a performance note? What is it that you want here?” And they’re like, “Why are you asking this?” I’m like, “Well, because we’ve done this five times already, so clearly you’re not happy with it!” [laughs] “So tell me what you want done differently.” And that was the one time during Resident Evil 2 where they all sort of chit-chatted and they’re like, “Oh no, this is a different scenario.” That was the most I could get out of them, and I was like, “Okay, whatever you say.” And by the time Code Veronica came around, I was like, “Now I get what you mean by ‘different scenario,'” and there was this level of understanding, and we could kind of joke about things and [be] more forthcoming with information.
Sally Cahill: There was nothing to reference it to. We were creating the people we were playing as we were recording with very little background or history. I had to make up my own secrets and ideas about [Ada] — at least that was what it felt like for me, which, looking back now, was actually a great gift.
Susan Hart: There was a process for a lot of the games. We would do the voices first, just the voices, that would go back to Japan. They would do their motion [capture] and their blocking. Then they would figure out, “Oh, we need that voice louder because we’re going to put the enemy further away, or we need that person softer. We need the voice faster.” So then we would come back with those. They would come back with those notes. So we would record the second time — “pickups,” if you want to call them that, or just change of script. And then that would go back, and then they would start working on their animation, and then in the animation, they would find that they were needing more “panic” because they had more explosives, or they needed more “despair” because they had more killings, or the guns were heavier, the equipment was heavier, so they needed more exertion.
So then they would come back a third time, and we would record those. And then a lot of the time, what we would do is they would come back after the game was completely finished, and we would just record the lips, so they would get the proper lip flaps. That happened a little later on, but I liked, initially, how we used our imagination for those things. And we had the creators there, so we used them to get started. And we had borders, of course, but we had a little bit more self-expression. We weren’t tied down to, “Well, it has to be this way because it’s like this and this and this and this in the picture and in the story.” We had a little bit more girth. We had a little bit more room. Not to say how they do it now is worse. It’s not. It’s just a different way of recording. And I liked that format, how we did that.
And then, as the years went on and the games went on, only some of the games did we do lip flaps. Other times they had it down pat. And in different recording systems than what they do in Japan. Like a lot of times, when they’re doing dubbing or records, they just have a big room with all the actors. They’ve got seven or eight microphones set up, and the director’s sitting there, “Go!” and they run up, do their line, they sit down, they run up and do their line and sit down. That’s a different way of doing things. They do that now here for a lot of dubbing jobs where they get the whole crowd in and they just get up for their line, which is good because then you can hear what the other actors are saying and so you can feed off of that. So it worked for everything. It worked for years. The new [way] works as well, so no sadness. [laughs]
Remembering Paul Haddad (1963-2020)
No conversation about the legacy of Resident Evil would be complete without Leon S. Kennedy. With his hunky good looks, lovably corny one-liners and penchant for riotous, over-the-top acrobatics, he’s easily one of gaming’s most beloved heroes. But while American actor Paul Mercier would provide perhaps the most iconic take on Leon in Capcom’s 2005 magnum opus, Resident Evil 4, the man who first gave voice to everyone’s favourite suave, roundhouse-kicking badass was the late British-born Canadian actor Paul Haddad.
He would only portray Leon in the original RE2, but the vulnerability and earnestness that he brought to the rookie cop proved enduringly popular. In his final years, Haddad fully embraced Leon and the Resident Evil community, who fondly remember him to this day. And when he tragically passed away in April 2020 at the age of 56, countless fans paid their respects, including Nick Apostolides, the main Leon actor since 2019’s Resident Evil 2 remake and a lifelong fan of the series. Decades later, Haddad remains a true RE icon.
Alyson Court: I was working with Paul since I was 14, 15. If people go digging through the “Paul Haddad Files,” there’s lots out there. You should look up a TV series called Road to Avonlea, he was on that. Just a beautiful, beautiful young man. We also did a cartoon together called Free Willy, he was the lead in that. [I had] tons of time in the studio working with Paul. Just a gem of a human — just a very, very sweet guy. I think you can hear it in some of the interviews that he did in the last years of his life. There’s that deep appreciation for the Resident Evil fanbase in particular. He was always lovely to work with. And then, when he got throat cancer, that was actually several years before his passing, and he actually went through it and managed to come out the other side. He went through so much because of what a strong, beautiful voice he had, and the idea of that being taken away from you… He went through a lot. But he was always a very kind and generous person to work with.
Sally Cahill: When I was first introduced to Paul Haddad, it was in a dark recording booth with a single light on my script and blackness all around. And then this very intense and amazing voice filled my headphones. It came very naturally for me to work with his Leon because his voice was very committed and compelling. He was always referred to, while I was working in the booth, as “Leon,” as I assume I was likely always “Ada” for him — not “Paul” or “Sally.” And we never met in person. Years later, we did speak on the phone. It was a strangely sweet moment to be chatting as Sally and Paul, but also a little poignant. He was not well then, but I had no idea we would lose him so soon. That’s why Resident Evil 2, besides being the first game I did, will always have a special place in my heart. Because when you play it, Paul is in the room again. And he always will be.
Susan Hart: Paul was very grateful. Paul was very talented. He researched his character, he felt his character. Paul had a real knack for taking the lines and just bringing them to life. And the energy — I will always remember his energy in the booth. I will always remember how grateful he was, and how humble he was, and how he just wanted to keep on learning. And that’s a good actor. When an actor is always open to learning new things, new ways of approaching and listening — those are all good attributes for an actor to have. And Paul had all of those, all of them. That’s what you’re feeling. You’re feeling his insides. You’re feeling that he cared, and that goes a long way with the character. And look where the character is now.
I’ll give you S.T.A.R.S.
Alongside Code Veronica, Capcom was toiling away at its third and final Resident Evil for the original PlayStation. And like Code Veronica, it directly picked up threads from the original game, with Jill and her fellow S.T.A.R.S. members being hunted by a deadly bio-organic weapon (BOW) known as Nemesis. It led to a more action-oriented premise while presenting a stalker enemy that was significantly more frightening than RE2‘s Mr. X. To bring Jill’s harrowing journey to life, Capcom once again looked to both X-Men and its own fighting games, ultimately casting the voice of Jean Grey.
Catherine Disher (Jill Valentine, Resident Evil 3): They were here in Toronto, Capcom, doing the Marvel vs. Capcom fighting games, and they wanted the original voice actors from X-Men on them. But it’s funny, because when you hire an actor for a principal role, and then you give them a secondary role, you get a big discount on the secondary role. And so, instead of hiring more than one female actor at the time on those fighting games, I did Jean, Jill, Psylocke, Spiral… I did Storm because Alison Sealy-Smith wasn’t on it yet. I did a whole bunch of those, and then obviously, not Jill at the very beginning. So that was their first foray in Toronto doing these games, and they stuck around.
And what they said to me [about Resident Evil] was, “Here, listen to this.” And it was the voice actress from the very first Resident Evil. All I heard was a recording of her voice, and they said, “Look, she was a non-professional actor in Japan at the time.” I think she might have even been in high school or something. And so they said, “Can you voice match this? Because we want to shoot it here.” And weirdly enough, I listened to it, and I was like, “Yeah, we sound enough alike. And I’ve done voice matches before. This is no problem.” And so they said, “Great.” And I gave an example, and they were like, “Perfect.”
And so when we started it, I was so aware that they might want an exact voice match that I kept stopping because when I do those kinds of jobs, they have a reference on file, or I make sure they do. And every once in a while, I go, “Hey, can I hear the reference?” And after like the fourth or fifth time, they were like, “You’re fine. Just do whatever you’re doing. That’s great.” So then I stopped worrying about that and just played the part. Because that intrigued me. Those other video games I’d done had all been fighting games, which are mostly grunts or like a few key phrases being thrown out. And this one [RE3] with the diary entries felt like much more of a fully formed character in an interesting situation, so that really appealed to me. And it sort of continued to appeal to me all through the recording. That character, she really felt real, like there was really something to hang on to and play with.
Disher recalls the direction that Hart and Capcom gave her.
Disher: There was a lot of direction given. I mean, yes and no. It’s not like they micromanaged me, but it was more because I had the script with the cues. But you need to know the circumstances of what’s going on. Like, “What am I doing here? Why is this line [here]? What’s going on?” And I forget what the script itself looked like, but that’s informationally what I want to know, and that’s information they can give. So there’s a real give and take there with the voice director. And so in the room, as I recall, we had Susan Hart, we had obviously the engineer, and there was an assistant, and then there were, I think, as many as three, possibly even four, engineers from Japan, game designers, and their translator. So when I had a question, it would always run through the translator to the game designers and then back. And it was a laborious process.
And also, I would do a line, and they were all on the other side of the glass. It was almost like meerkats. They were waiting for the line, and then as soon as I said it, they’d be on their computers like this [taps keyboard]. I was like, “What are they writing? What are they thinking?” And so often you’d do a line and then wait for feedback, and that would take a while to go through. And I remember laughing at one point because I had asked a question about something, or I was waiting for feedback after a line. And keep in mind, we would do take after take after take after take of lines. And also, every time, it almost felt like Groundhog Day because some of the lines were so similar to each other because, of course, it depended on choices that people made in the game.
But I do remember waiting for feedback on a line. They mute you, so I can’t hear what’s going on the other side of the glass in the booth while they talk. And I prefer that. I don’t want to hear anything anyone’s saying about me or my performance. Everything should come through the director, the voice director. So they would mute me, and then I would see the Japanese game designers talking animatedly to their translator, and it would go on for quite a long time.
And then they’d unmute me, and the translator would go, “Faster,” or something, and I’d be like, “Really? Is that all they said to each other?” [laughs] Or maybe he said that to the director, and then Susan would go, “Faster.” And I’m like, “That’s not everything [they] said!” So it was an interesting process, and it took longer because of the translation aspect of it.
I had no visuals. They had no artwork. I had no idea that she was wearing a miniskirt and tube top, fighting zombies. I only found that out when they came back to do some additional dialogue recording later on. I think I was aware that it was titled Resident Evil, but at some points, it was also referred to as 1.9. So there were layers of inscrutability; I wasn’t quite sure what was going on. Interestingly enough, we recorded it in the same studio that we had been recording X-Men, so it was a very familiar studio to me. In fact, we were recording there up until a few months ago. I don’t know if they’ve torn down the building yet at 49 Ontario, but that’s where we did X-Men all those years ago. That’s where they came back and started with X-Men ’97.
[…] I was in there all the time, and they would bring other actors. Like Carlos [Vince Corazza] would come in for two or three days, and Brad [Evan Sabba] would come. People would come in and out, and I got very lonely. I was really excited when they brought other actors in, because it took a long time. I think the fighting games we knocked off pretty quickly, but this, I’m sure, had at least 14 or 15 recording days that we did over the course of a few weeks. So it was a much more involved project, and I did go a bit squirrelly because there’s no window in that studio. And like I said, I didn’t know anything about it, and so I had all these questions about different lines and what the setting was. […] They were all extremely nice, and it was really fun. And I haven’t done another video game like that since, where I was the lead character and had all that stuff to do.
Susan Hart: One thing that was always so fun to do is when we had to do the zombies. Those were like extras. So if we had actors coming in and doing a role and said, “We’ll have a separate role. We’ll have you do a zombie.” It was just always so much fun because they’d have their tongues out and they’d kind of cock their heads and they’d put their arms up. And I just remember having so much fun doing those zombies, doing those little background sounds, background noises when they’re in the market, or when the soldiers were yelling or screaming for their lives…
Doing the layers of directing was a lot of fun. Even when the incidentals came in, which were the smaller characters, and a lot of times, they were more colourful characters. They would be the store owner, or the shop owner, or the driver, or something like that. Even those, I really enjoyed doing, and I took all of those roles as a director seriously, and did something unique with each one of those layers, so that one was just not hanging out, and then you had some drab at the back end. Everybody stood out.
Redfield reunion
One year after Resident Evil 3, Capcom put out Code Veronica, which, at one point, had actually been considered for the next numbered entry instead. In retrospect, that makes a lot of sense, given that the story follows Claire and Chris Redfield as they deal with a viral outbreak in the Southern Ocean and Antarctica and, in the process, come face to face with Wesker. It was also the first Resident Evil game for next-generation hardware, Sega’s Dreamcast, allowing Capcom to feature significantly upgraded visuals including, most famously, a gloriously over-the-top John Woo-inspired opening cinematic.
Alyson Court: I remember after [RE2] came out, I was actually on tour for The Big Comfy Couch, and it was like November, December 1998. A couple of the guys were part of the crew, so they’d travel on the bus, and they had their PlayStations there, and they played their video games. And the one guy was telling me, “You know that Resident Evil is a big deal, right?” I’m like, “Is it? I’m so clueless.” [laughs] He’s like, “Yeah.” I’m like, “Okay.” And so I went and tried to look it up. The late ’90s wasn’t that great for search engines and stuff. And it was my dad that actually found a review of the game where they’re talking about the voice performances and how they were like leaps and bounds better than the first game.
I actually printed that out and took it when Capcom came back in March of 1999 to do Code Veronica. They had me come in and audition again. [laughs] Whether that was absolutely necessary or some of their staff members were just kind of being jokesters, who knows? But they had a full casting session, I guess, because they had to cast some of the other roles. But I had to come in. And on the breakdown, it describes Claire’s character, and it had my name as voice reference. [laughs] And I’m like, “What?” So I printed out the review of the voice performance from Resident Evil 2 and brought it in. I’m like, “Look, I don’t suck! Okay? The people out there are saying we’re really good, so there!” [laughs] And they’re like,”Yeah, okay, whatever.” I was quite tickled to read some of those reviews. I mean, it’s still campy as all get out. But there’s a kind of “chill vibe” camp to it. It’s not this “over-the-top pushed” camp that some stuff has today. It was just naturally campy in places. Now, I find, sometimes things just try too hard to replicate what we managed to just do naturally back then. There’s a bit of a forced vibe now.
[…] When they came back to do Code Veronica, there was a lot more transparency, a lot more information flow, and understanding about, “Okay, so this scene…” And we were much more comfortable with each other by then. So there would be that, “Yes, it feels like the same scene, but this is if Steve didn’t complete the task in the other room, so you guys don’t have the microchip or something.” Just as an example. Or if a different weapon got left behind. So understanding that and having those little bits of information… It might seem like nothing, but let me tell you, when you’re in the booth by yourself, you feel like you’re going crazy because you’re like, “I swear, I recorded this exact same scene like six times! What is going on?”
[Veronica] was a very different experience. First of all, because I now had a certain familiarity and comfort with the environment and what was going on with the property. I had by that point played Resident Evil 2, so I did have an understanding. I got to work with all of the other actors. So any scenes that I had with other characters, we were in the booth together, which was fantastic because a lot of them didn’t understand what we were making. These were theatre people who were like, “Video game is Pac-Man! I don’t understand what’s going on.” And it can be really trippy if you’re there in the booth by yourself and you’re not getting a lot of communication or feedback from the clients. So one of the things, it was actually the producer, Erik Suzuki, who had said he wanted to have me in the booth with all of the other actors because I was basically grounding them. I was their anchor because I’d been through it before, so I could sort of share my battle stories and tips for survival. [laughs]
So it was great. We had a lot of fun working on that. I love working with other actors. There are some people who prefer to be in the booth on their own. For me, ensemble is the way I would always go, if possible. And during those initial recording sessions for Code Veronica, we didn’t get to see the technology. All I knew was that two of the fellas from Japan were from Sega, and they were there because this was for the Dreamcast. And then you had the two guys from Capcom, which were [localization lead] Tom [Takuya Shiraiwa] and Erik, and every now and then they were alternating days between doing Code Veronica and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
So they were kind of swapping people out with the two different games. It wasn’t until we did the pickups for Code Veronica that I got to see just how much better this game was going to look. And because they had me do it to picture for that opening scene, they wanted the breathing and the running sounds, and as she drops down… We did that a few different ways, but I did all of it to picture. Every time I picture that scene, it’s just instinct now — I always go like this [beats chest with hands] because our engineer, Paul Shubat, and Susan Hart, every time they would watch it, because of the helicopters, they would sit there and do the helicopter sound on their chests. [laughs] So that’s the visual that I have forever burned in my brain, getting ready to dub to pictures and watching the scene. And I look up and I can see the two of them doing their helicopter sounds. That’s when I got to see it.
[…] But I will say seeing those graphics for the first time when we were doing the ADR pickups for Code Veronica, it was unreal — just stunning and so cinematic and, yes, very John Woo. Which was great because in ’97 when I’d been working on Resident Evil 2, I was also doing an episode of John Woo’s Once a Thief. Huge, huge John Woo fan, so when they showed me that scene, it was just stunning, and I was actually very, very excited for the game.
Richard Waugh (Albert Wesker, Code Veronica, 0 and 4 : I actually only have fleeting memories that seem to only surface when people ask about it or fellow cast members talk about it. (It was decades ago). I do remember knowing very little going in to the first recording session, almost nothing other than what was given to us for the auditions… It was a Japanese video game (first time I’d heard the term “anime”). My character was a villain. It was a horror. That was it. It was just one voice job in a handful that week. Never in a million years did I expect to be talking about it or signing autographs almost thirty years later.
I wasn’t directed to go where I did with it. As I said, we were given a bit of information (villain, horror) along with some lines for the audition, and I latched onto the villainy. My kids were little and we had been watching the original Disney Jungle Book. The villain in that is Shere Khan the Tiger, voiced by the amazing George Sanders. I loved his voice and had been crossing my fingers I’d find a place to steal his read for something. So I did my best George for my audition because he was my favourite villain at the time, and they liked it. So, Wesker went from regular North American guy to vaguely bored, vaguely British aristocrat.
I’ve heard Pablo Kuntz was none too pleased that I’d changed it up so much. But in my defence, I had never heard his Wesker, never even heard of Wesker, never even heard of Resident Evil, so… no insult intended, Pablo. […] I placed Wesker’s accent somewhere in the middle of the Atlantic, and American ears sometimes hear that as Canadian. I wanted Wesker to sound like a North American who was educated at Oxford or Cambridge and pretentious enough to come home with the accent.
[…] There was no mo-cap or cameras. At first, there weren’t even illustrations to reference. We recorded alone in a booth with our director, the great Susan Hart, filling us in on everything else, what was physically happening, what the vibe of the scene should be, even the tone of our scene partner who may or may not have had recorded earlier. It was all just using our imagination.
Susan Hart: It was theatre. It was finding those big voices, those moments, those sad moments, those grotesque moments. And so it was a lot like theatre directing and having the actor in the booth. There was a lot of emotion, and a lot of the actors, I would say 99.9 per cent of them, were all extremely experienced actors in theatre, film, and television. And so they brought with them this energy. And the stories were good. The adventure was good. The characters were well-written. It has some great adventures. I had that with other shows and other brands that I had worked on as well. But there was a common thread that I really enjoyed: it felt like theatre.
New gen, new Jill
With video game remakes being all the rage nowadays, it’s fun to consider that one of the earliest and most defining was 2002’s Resident Evil. Thanks to the beefier specs of Nintendo’s GameCube, director Shinji Mikami reimagined his original 1996 game with dramatically overhauled visuals, a rewritten script with new voice actors (including American Heidi Anderson as Jill), and new enemies and weapons. As part of these changes, teenaged Canadian model Julia Voth, who was in Japan at the time on a work contract, was hired to provide the likeness for the updated Jill Valentine. The small-town Saskatchewan native would subsequently be featured as Jill in 2007’s The Umbrella Chronicles and 2009’s Resident Evil 5, but even in the years that followed, she remained the face of Resident Evil’s OG heroine for many fans.
Julia Voth: It helped that I was so young. I was 14 the first time I went to Japan, and 14-year-olds have this beautiful ability to just say yes with no fear. No one leaves the modelling business unscathed, that’s for sure, but I got to start with that fearlessness. The contrast couldn’t have been bigger. The Prairies are vast and open, and I love them. Saskatchewan is my home and always will be. But even as a little girl, I longed for something different.
Then I landed in Japan, and it was the absolute opposite: crowded, loud, people everywhere. It was exactly what I’d been yearning for. My attitude was basically, “Yeah, I can do that.” That naive, green energy really worked to my advantage. After a few years of going back, I’d spent so much time there that I partly grew up in Japan too, and it started to feel normal. Not everyone in my small town understood what I was trying to do, but the important people did: my teachers and my family.
As we’ve now learned was quite common with these auditions, Voth had no idea what she was joining.
Voth: My manager explained what the game was, but I didn’t play video games at the time, so it didn’t mean much to me. When we went to the audition, there was no context at all. But I remember it so clearly. It was a big boardroom with a huge table and maybe 20 businessmen in suits. A bunch of models were brought in and sat in front of them, and one by one we’d stand up, turn around, they’d discuss, and then we’d sit down.
I was 15, and I was chatting with the girl beside me when my manager whispered, “Shh, don’t talk.” I’d been a girl again for about five seconds and had to snap right back into model mode. And when I did, I looked up and saw them all looking at me, talking, going through my book. I sat up straighter, took my turn, and did my thing. I could hear the inflection in their voices, and it sounded like they were excited by what they saw. A couple of days later, my agent sat me down, smiling, and said, “Julia, this is a really big job. This is really amazing.” I think I said, “Oh, that’s cool!” Because at the end of the day, I was still just a kid.
This was before motion capture as we know it now. I didn’t act anything out on a green screen with tracking balls all over me. I was just in regular clothes, and they scanned my hands, feet, ears, face, even my tongue into a computer. Then they had me make different mouth shapes and facial expressions, and scanned those in, too. That was it. It took an afternoon. The facial expressions were the most fun. They’d say, “Imagine you see a scary monster. What do you do?” and I’d go, “Ah!” My first real acting gig, I guess […] Since it was all rendered on a computer, there wasn’t much collaboration. But it has always meant a lot to me, especially after I started acting and people recognized me for something I did when I was 15.
As it turns out, Capcom never needed to re-scan Voth for Jill’s appearance in those later games, even with the more advanced hardware. But the character has continued to stick with her, even as she moved into other acting roles and, in more recent years, her own LA-based real estate business, House of Zonshine. Over the years, she’s embraced RE wholeheartedly, attending conventions around the world and even doing professional cosplay shoots as Jill.
Voth: I couldn’t understand why someone wouldn’t. Yes, it was a job, but very early on I could see the organic love and admiration fans have for Jill. People grew up playing her, and when you spend that much time with someone, real or fictional, you become connected. Because she was based on me, I got to feel that love in return, from all those years and hours of collective playing.
When I started acting, and people found out Jill was based on a real person, I couldn’t not give them what they wanted. My job was already to dress up and play characters, so why wouldn’t I take it one step further, dress up as myself, go to cons, meet people, and do photo shoots? That’s what being young and having fun is supposed to be. It all started at a convention in Bahrain, where a fan gifted me the beret I still wear. I put it on, took a photo, and thought, “Oh my god, I should do this.” I never got the fan’s name and haven’t connected with him since, but if he ever reads this, thank you. That beret was literally the start of my cosplay journey.
Breaking out
Of all the Resident Evil games, 2003’s Outbreak is perhaps the most overlooked. For one, it was the first multiplayer Resident Evil, and for another, it’s long been stranded on PS2 hardware while most of the other games have been ported to modern platforms. (The inability to officially play Outbreak on modern platforms outside of emulation is especially glaring considering that one of the two main characters from this year’s Resident Evil Requiem, Grace Ashcroft, is actually the daughter of one of Outbreak‘s leads, Alyssa Ashcroft.)
Even without Capcom’s support, though, Outbreak has proved to be ahead of its time in many ways, featuring a novel co-op experience centred around everyday people in Raccoon City who must work together to survive while growing infections bring them closer to death. The game was also a big step up for the Toronto-based Resident Evil crew, with none other than Alyson Court taking over as the voice and motion capture director on the local shoots and leading a scrappy band of Canadians into uncharted territory for the series.
Alyson Court: I knew the world, and I was working with Capcom and other stuff as well, helping with localization. We’d done Onimusha 2 and Devil May Cry, and a lot of audition stuff for a bunch of their games, Mega Man, and all of that. But taking on the performances — it was both voice and mo-cap — was exciting for me because I’m a horror fan. I’ve been a horror fan my whole life, so not only did I have experience with understanding the world of Resident Evil, understanding the people at Capcom and their vision, but I had a pretty solid relationship with many people who work at Capcom, so there was that comfort level… Just getting to explore more of the survival horror side and the visual side of it and the storytelling side that, as an actor, you don’t always get to bring into it.
But when you’re directing and you’re doing performance capture, you have to actually do the layout to get the performance, and we were also working on changing the dialogue. So you get the translated dialogue, but localizing is a lot more than that, and it’s trying to find the equivalent of what this character might say in that moment. In Japanese, they’ll say something, and to us, it’s like, “That makes no sense! Well, it’s a little saying, a little colloquialism or whatever. What would our equivalent be?” So [it’s] a lot of that stuff, and making it feel more within a North American audience, which is what they wanted. Really getting to dive deep into all of that. So I was fully immersed in everything Outbreak and those characters, those main characters, the eight of them and all of the storylines. That was my life then.
There’s certainly something to be said to have continuity from people. It’s good to have fresh blood come in if you want to have some new ideas, but I’ve been in this industry long enough to know that there’s a fine line between fresh blood to help bring some new great ideas to the table, and people who just want to put their thumb on something for the sake of putting their thumbprint on it. So we didn’t have that with Outbreak. That was one of the hardest-working teams I’ve ever seen in my life. I feel like we went through war together. [laughs]
Mark Alberts (Outbreak mo-cap engineer): It was actually just by circumstance that I got involved. I was living in Vancouver and I was working at a motion capture facility, and the production was looking for a couple of people to get involved to run the system that they had out here in Toronto […] Myself and another colleague of mine, a good friend of mine named Ray Ng, were working there as the sort of like public liaison, troubleshooter, entertainment industry sort of representatives. And so when the production of Resident Evil was going around putting the team together, they got wind of us. They kind of headhunted us, for lack of a better word, and we ended up coming out here to Toronto to work on the game. So it was really just circumstances and good fortune that I got involved originally. I knew of Resident Evil as an IP. So certainly, finding out that that’s what we were being hired to do was very exciting.
Mark Perceval Maxwell (Outbreak mo-cap engineer): I was employed by the studio before learning it was a Resident Evil game. Although I knew there was an association with Capcom, I didn’t find out about the actual project until a few months after joining and helping set up the studio. It was an incredible surprise, as Resident Evil had always been one of my favourite game series. Being my first job in the industry, it really couldn’t have been better.
Alberts: It was a lot of trial and error along the way and working out the methodology and the workflow, particularly because it was just the three of us, Mark, Ray, and myself, processing enormous amounts of data and mapping the characters at different sizes. And the motion capture workflow was something we were still figuring out. In terms of how that relates today, I think the workflow is still very similar in terms of the steps that you need to take in order to put somebody in a studio space and ultimately get them onto a character. That remains pretty much unchanged. There’s better tools and it’s faster and all that kind of stuff. The technology has advanced so much that you can do photorealistic, real-time facial capture, hand capture, body capture, all simultaneously, which you couldn’t do back in those days, but you can now.
The second advance — which, as a small boutique studio owner myself [at Toronto-based VFX and animation house Electric Square], I feel more passionate about — is that technology has evolved to the point where you can also do motion capture on your phone. Now you can shoot video of somebody standing in a room and moving around, and using that same kind of workflow that I just talked about. Use that video to encode to motion data and then to map to a character, which again, is mind-blowing to me. 20 years ago, you needed 12 cameras all calibrated in a space, having to deal with it like it’s a very fragile system that one little nudge is going to throw everything off and you’re going to lose half a day of work. [Now] you can turn around a quick motion capture test with a phone or even a cheap mo-cap suit and get very high-quality motion in your living room.
Perceval-Maxwell: The mo-cap cleanup process is far better now. Back then, cleaning up data could be incredibly gruelling, whereas these days it’s much less of an issue. Working with real-time engines like Unreal, where you can light your scenes as you build them, is also incredibly satisfying. What’s interesting is how little the fundamental workflow has actually changed. Vicon systems are still among the best and operate more or less the same way they did back then. Even some of the pipeline software hasn’t changed dramatically in over 20 years. I still mainly use MotionBuilder, which back then was called Filmbox.
Court: It was 14 cameras in a big open room. People had to wear the black suits with the silver Mylar little balls all over, and the markers had to have very specific placements, and they were on with Velcro. Our team was amazing. We did a combat scene at one point where there’s soldiers and there’s a mom. They’re wrangling refugees or survivors, and the army’s there trying to get people out. And there’s a mom carrying a boy, and he’s actually a zombie and she’s trying to hide that. And then the soldier comes up to take the kid, and the kid bites him and they fall and then the soldier shoots and all this stuff [happens]. We did that scene with six people, and we captured them. And in this day and age, I think people are like, “Yeah, that’s no big deal.” We had 14 cameras, and all the limitations of, when people would touch, the data would get swapped. It was nuts.
And our team, after we captured it, we had to do it a few times — it would take the whole weekend. The guys would have it rendered just to fully come into existence. And then they’d have to go in and clean up the swapped markers and stuff like that. But we did it. It was pretty amazing. We did some incredible stuff. And then all of that to learn, because you’re capturing 120 frames per second… So you watch the playback, and you’re watching like the dots, T-characters — these little green skeleton dot things doing their interactions. But you can see what’s happening, and it was amazing to watch back. And then you find out that at the end of the day, they have to strip the 120 frames per second down to three frames per second because the engine can’t handle anything more than that.
So the biggest learning curve for all of us working on Outbreak was that ultimately, PS2 — at least, the initial version of it — could not handle all the things that we thought it was going to be able to handle when we first started making the game. So there was a lot of revising and truncating and making smaller and simplifying and all of that stuff. So we went from like 50 scenarios down to — we ended up completing like 19 or something? But I don’t know how many ever got released.
Craig Burnatowski (Outbreak mo-cap actor, Wesker in 2023’s Resident Evil 4 and Zeno in Requiem):
Outbreak is still the only game I’ve worked on that I haven’t played myself. I just didn’t have the hardware at the time, and now it’s only available through emulation. I have often heard that many fans held it in their hearts as one of their favourite titles, but it’s definitely something I hear more often these days. Especially with the ties that Requiem makes to Outbreak‘s characters. I haven’t exactly been silent about my involvement with Outbreak many years ago, but it’s still a thrill when fans find out I did mo-cap for that project as well.
[…] The first thing I notice the upgrade in tech [with modern Resident Evil] affecting is the level of realism and truth I see in performances. Outbreak’s dialogue was done in recording booths, often one actor at a time, and then we would listen to the edited dialogue and try to move as convincingly as we could to those voices. Full performance capture allows for the actors to really connect to each other, listening to the nuances in the other’s delivery, and seeing the micro-emotional looks on their faces. Today, a smirk can change a whole scene. If I could show younger me what cutscenes in video games today were capable of, it would blow my mind!
Alberts: It’s a little hazy now, but I think it was every two to three weeks, these guys from Capcom would come over from Japan, and we would do a session. So it would be like a full week of motion capture where the voices had already been recorded. So we had that as audio cues, and we’d get the talent in, and many of them had never done motion capture before. So there was a bit of a learning curve for them — and for us, too. It was pretty much in its infancy back in those days.
[…] But it was a lot of using your imagination in this big empty space and having to understand that later on in the game, “There’s going to be a monster over there, or don’t go over here because there’s a wall here.” So we’d set up cinder blocks. That was really our only prop that we had in the space, and those would be our placeholders for where objects in the video game space would be. And the guys from Capcom would be there to oversee that because they were the ones who knew the big picture. We were just making these modular little scenes where we would play the audio track that had been recorded, and the actors would sort of act out to the audio track what was supposed to be happening in the game. And it was great — it was so fun.
[…] It wouldn’t have worked without [Alyson] because she not only knew the property, the IP, but she’d had this experience with previous games and doing voice work on other projects as well — just understanding how it all was put together. She was amazing to work with. I’d never collaborated with somebody who’d had this granular understanding of how all the different components went together. And to be honest, I don’t even know if at the time I realized that. But certainly in the years that have passed, and in retrospect, I think back to those times and think she was just masterfully overseeing this whole thing and being able to direct the talent in a really generous and gentle kind of way because she, coming from an acting background, knew how to interact with actors.
[…] I think the highlight of working on the game was actually not specifically the motion capture sessions, but it was when the gentlemen came over from Capcom from Japan and would be here for the motion capture sessions. Because we would be working together during the day, but in the evenings we’d also socialize sometimes, and I really liked that. It was really cool because they were interested in what life in Toronto is like and what you do when you’re not down at the Portland studio space doing motion capture. So we would sometimes go out for dinner or even drinks sometimes and just hang out. And there was a language barrier, so it’s fun to navigate that and try and break through and get to know your client as a person. That, to me, in retrospect, really stands out as being a really special part of the experience, having that time with them.
Hasta luego…
The release of Resident Evil 4 in 2005 was a pivotal moment both for Capcom and the video game industry as a whole. With original director Shinji Mikami back at the helm, RE4 became a full-on action thrill ride that set the gold standard for third-person shooters while cementing Leon, now a U.S. secret agent fighting to save the president’s daughter from an infected cult in Spain, as one of the medium’s most beloved heroes. But RE4 also marked the end of Capcom’s storied run of recording in Toronto. While some of the previous Canadian RE actors returned, and Toronto-born Rino Romano (The Batman) joined the cast as Luis, the bulk of RE4‘s Western production moved to LA, where it’s predominantly been ever since.
Susan Hart: I can’t remember; I think some of the stuff was recorded here. But yes, it did go to the States because I think they may have had an R&D branch there, and budgeting. It had nothing to do with anything we did. It just had to do with the company. They were happy up here. They were grateful up here. Everything was going well. It just moved for whatever reason. But I’m still in touch with a couple of the guys still, so [we’ll say] “Hi, how are you?” and send pictures of kids and stuff like that. If I do get [to the U.S.], which I may be going to next year, I definitely will be knocking on their door and saying, “Hey, how are you?” and have a little reunion. Nothing happened, it was just a shift. I continued to voice direct other games. And I still had my foot in that door. But things were starting to really pick up in animation for me, so it was just a natural segue.
Alyson Court: There were multiple reasons. There was SARS [in 2003], so that was sort of the final nail in the coffin. One of the guys from Capcom wanted to move to LA; he wanted to set up shop in LA. “If I can make the switch and move things to LA, then I get to live here,” and that’s what he wanted. And he wanted to do it on the company dime. So that was a behind-the-scenes thing that was going on.
And then by that point, I believe, the union there did have a video game-specific contract that they’d finally negotiated, whereas in Canada we didn’t. We were all working under animation contracts. So Capcom obviously wanted to move to something that was video game-specific, so that it would be an in-perpetuity buyout and all that. So it’s the usual reasons: it’s finances, and there’s always going to be somebody who has their own personal agenda.
Sally Cahill: The fact that I was involved in one of the greatest games ever made seems wild to me now. I’m glad I didn’t know at the time what was to come, or I may have felt a lot of pressure. It was all recorded in Toronto, and I lived so close to the studio downtown I used to ride my bike to it. I was really happy to be back. I felt connected and at home playing Ada. When they pivoted to the U.S. actors to continue the later games, I think at first we all felt a bit strange, as if something we had nurtured had been taken out from our hands. But then you remember this industry is
transitory; things end — shows, series, plays — and you learn to adjust and move on to the next thing.
I think one of the most exciting parts about Resident Evil 4 OG was having more detail for Ada in her interactions and relationships. Also, the relationship between Leon and Ada continued to have sparks and conflict as well as chemistry. Separate Ways was a different turn for me. Suddenly, instead of saying a little or just enough before leaving the room or jumping out a window, a lot of her inner mind was revealed. I was learning more about Ada myself as I read the script and recorded it, and if memory serves, we did it in one session take […] I’m not sure what the experience was like for the other V.O. actors, but for me the process of recording didn’t seem to change [with the new console technology]. I was still approaching the work as a V.O. actor. The visuals changed, but my voice and my intentions didn’t. It was just great; I had more to work with in the script.
Richard Waugh: By that time, I was invested in [Wesker], and when they moved to LA and I was replaced by D.C. Douglas, I was a little hurt. Someone told me they moved to California because they could use cheaper non-union actors. I repeated that somewhere, and it turned out to be not entirely true. I eventually got the chance to apologize to D.C. for implying he was some random amateur. He and I have communicated a few times. I really like him. We even met up in LA with our mutual friend Adrian Hough [Nightcrawler in X-Men: The Animated Series]. D.C. had the idea of an all-Wesker panel — the voices, models, film actors, everybody. I would love for that to happen.
…Hola de nuevo
It’s no secret what happened with Resident Evil in the late 2000s and early 2010s. 2009’s Resident Evil 5, while generally well-received, marked a radical departure from previous RE games by focusing on West Africa-set co-op action between Chris Redfield and newcomer Sheva Alomar that was widely criticized for being racist. As the first mainline RE game recorded fully in LA, it didn’t star any Canadians. Following that, 2012’s Resident Evil 6, which also didn’t feature any Canucks, was a huge commercial hit but garnered a mixed response from critics and fans for having disjointed and bombastic campaigns featuring Leon, Chris and several other characters that further lost sight of what people loved about the series. It was only after five years that the series would be revived in a big way with Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, returning to classic survival horror and paving the way for the renaissance we’re now in.
From there, Canadian involvement in the games started to return. First, Toronto-based model Jordan McEwen is the likeness of Claire Redfield in 2019’s beloved Resident Evil 2 remake (and seemingly returns in the 2027 Code Veronica remake), while 2020’s reimagining of Resident Evil 3 features Montreal-born actor William Hope (Aliens) as both Captain Mikhail Victor and Dr. Nathaniel Ward.
But it was Capcom’s third modern Resident Evil remake that brought Canada back to the series in a truly significant way. For 2023’s Resident Evil 4, the performance capture was handled at prolific Vancouver-based motion-capture company Beyond Capture Studios. This meant that virtually every actor in the acclaimed game outside of returning Leon star Nick Apostolides was actually Canadian. It was an ironic twist of fate. The original RE4 signalled the end of the series’ time in Canada, while the remake brought it back here in an even bigger way thanks to 20 years of technological advancements.
Genevieve Buechner (Ashley Graham, Resident Evil 4 remake): We were in the full suits. We had the headcams. So all of the characters’ facial expressions and movements and stuff in those cutscenes, we fully, physically, acted them out, and it was an absolute blast. But you definitely have to have a lot of imagination because you’re just in a big empty room and you’re wearing this like silly Velcro suit with these dots all over you, and we’ve got these big camera helmets on, and it’s kind of awkward, and you have to pretend like none of that is happening, and you’re really in those situations.
So I had a great time because I have a super active imagination. It was an absolute blast for me. I got to just play pretend to the maximum, basically, and I loved it. But I think something that a lot of people don’t know is that most of what we did was performance capture. Because a lot of people say, “Oh, they’re voice actors,” but we really were acting everything. We were doing all of it. And then the voice work was really only in certain parts of the game, mostly gameplay, and the rest was performance capture.
[…] My favourite part of fleshing out this character and working on this game was definitely working with the team and seeing everything that they had already worked on. We’re the actors — they’ve put years of work into this game before I even show up. So there was so much care and love already there for these characters. And getting to see all of that and then having them, in the studio, hand us the reins was just incredible. And the people that I got to work with were amazing. And I think we all just kind of clicked into place really easily.
André Peña (Luis Serra, Resident Evil 4 remake): I’d just gotten [to West Edmonton Mall]. Funny enough, I was looking at a Mauser C96 in the shooting range because they have a shooting range because it’s so big. That’s when I got the audition, and my agent says, “You know what? You have to get your butt back home right now to do this audition.” And I was like, “Okay!” So I didn’t even get a chance to get lost [in the mall]. I was literally there, I set my foot in there, and then I stepped right back out, and then the 13-hour drive back [to Vancouver]. It’s crazy that I was looking at Luis’ gun while I had the audition for Resident Evil 4. It was wild. Almost feels like it was meant to be.
[…] The fun I had portraying Luis! I took a lot of inspiration from Rino Romano, the original Luis, but at the same time, I wanted it to be my own. I wanted it to be different. So there was a lot of the original Luis, but I do feel like he’s a little bit more quirky this time around, which made him that much more fun because I feel like he doesn’t take things too seriously. That’s what makes him even more charismatic in a way. Even in the face of fear, in this place where everything is just falling apart, he’s able to say, “Hey, relax!” So that was really, really cool, to put myself in that situation. Because as an actor, that’s what we have to do, we have to fully feel like we’re there — and then, at the same time, be free, in a way, by being so charismatic or carefree or quirky or whatever it is. I love doing that.
I studied acting for film and television, and you’re able to act very subtly, depending on where the camera is placed. If it’s a close-up, you can be as subtle as you want. But in high school, I was a little bit of a theatre kid. And with that experience, you have to project everything. You have to exaggerate everything a little bit, you have to really make yourself believe that you’re in that situation. In a film set, you might have an actual prop that you can work with, whereas here, on the soundstage where we film, you have a stick with a weird ball at the end that is the marker. That’s supposed to be your lance or something. So I was able to use both skills there, where I can act as subtly as possible, because there’s over 80 cameras pointed at you at once, but at the same time, you have to pretend that everything is real because everything is skeleton-ized, everything is bare bones.
So I was really able to use my imagination, if you will, and it was a ton of fun to be able to do that. So it’s kind of this weird mix of theatre and film acting, where you can act in both ways, or you need to have both of those experiences to be able to act well in this. And I had a ton of fun doing that, and I loved it. Being able to use my imagination to say, “Oh yeah, that door is really there, that wall is really there, or that’s gonna be a barrel that I’m gonna lean against where it’s nothing there,” that was really cool.
[Craig Burnatowski is in the unique situation of having played Wesker and Zeno, two intrinsically connected yet nonetheless separate characters, so we asked him about the process of working on them both.]
Craig Burnatowski: Bringing a character, or in my case two characters, like this to life takes an entire team. The original story writers, localization team, interpreters, directors, character and costume designers, motion capture team, animation team, stunt team, and every other person involved in the production deserve just as much credit as the performance capture artists. I’m often told just enough of the story necessary to capture the scenes I’m working on. So there is a great deal of trust shared by the entire team. I think Kate Saxon, Requiem’s director, deserves a great deal of the credit for helping me differentiate Zeno from how we had established Wesker in RE4R. Zeno is most definitely a person that uses a different set of tactics to achieve his goals.
REflection
August 28, 2026. Huge crowds of Redfields, Kennedys, Valentines and merchants are gathered in the Metro Toronto Convention Centre. They’re eagerly awaiting a Fan Expo Canada panel featuring a slew of (predominantly Canadian) Resident Evil stars in what’s being billed as the largest RE reunion to date. There’s so much interest in the panel, in fact, that the room had reached full capacity and Fan Expo had to turn away some hopeful attendees.
Many of the actors had never even met, and some of them had done few, if any, convention appearances before, making the day particularly special for all. It was the perfect example of the powerful relationship that all of the Resident Evil talent, including those who weren’t at the panel, have had with the franchise and its fans over the past 30 years.
Alyson Court: The inspiration [for the panel] was the amazing people who have worked on [Resident Evil] over the years. All of those actors, and the mo-cap crew — all of those guys that haven’t been out going to these cons. And you see all of the other actors, and they’re out there, and they’re doing lots of signings and stuff, which is great. And I, myself, have been able to go to these events all over and do signings and really get to see just how much Resident Evil love is out there […] Initially, they were skeptical, and they’re like, “Oh, no one’s gonna want to come see me.” I’m like, “You have no idea. Trust me.”
Even my lovely Outbreak cast — they had no idea. That was the one, more than anything. Because there is such a die-hard fanbase for that game because of the lack of support from PlayStation and Capcom. The fact that they took the servers down, so fans built their own and did the whole mirroring to run it for the servers. […] Laura Thorne, who plays Yoko — she’s just such a sweet, lovely soul. I remember when I was explaining to the whole group, I had all of the different actors on [Zoom] and saying, “Here’s my plan. Here’s what I want to do with you guys.” Laura’s just laughing and shaking her head when I’m explaining. “Yeah, people will bring their games or a poster or if you have a table print, they’ll pay you to autograph.” And she’s just like, “Alyson, no one is gonna pay me to sign something!” [laughs] And I’m like, “Laura, just come — trust me.” And sure enough…
View this post on Instagram
[…] Those cast members who got to get announced and walk out on stage and hear those cheers — that was the thing that I wanted more than anything. I was like, “I want you all to experience what I’ve been getting to taste and what I know is out there and how much love that these people want to give you. You need to get here and you need to experience it.” I was feeling more like an audience member than a cast member because I was just so giddy seeing it all come to life and watching my friends get that love from the audience and just watching their faces. I was like, “This is the best thing ever.”
Craig Burnatowski: Meeting Richard Waugh was a bucket list item for me, and he’s a riot. I hope we get to do more of these together. Alyson Court has been a friend since she directed me in Outbreak, and years later I brought her in for a project I was directing. She is a force to be reckoned with, and I will always have an immediate yes to anything she asks me to be involved with. I had a wonderful time chatting with Riva Di Paola Lombardi, who played Rebecca in RE0, and it was great to meet the Outbreak actors that I did motion capture for.
[…] I consider Toronto fortunate that Capcom decided to make the first few games here. I honestly don’t know what went into that decision, but I’m grateful that it happened. I am so proud of this city and it is absolutely stuffed with incredibly talented people! There are so many productions of shows, films, and video games that most people don’t know are shot in Toronto. I’ve made a game out of spotting my friend’s neighbourhoods or condos in some of my favourite shows! And yes, I feel very proud to be part of the Canadian contingent of Resident Evil cast members.
Mark Alberts: Just to be included in that [panel] was really special to me. And it was wonderful to see Alyson again. It was also really cool to see Craig Burnatowski, because he was our main guy for Outbreak. He did numerous roles. Everyone was great, but he was very much the predominant talent that we had in the motion-capture space, and again, just to see him and to see that he’s still involved in the franchise too is amazing. It’s so cool. He’s really made a good go of it with Resident Evil, and he’s still as gung-ho and enthusiastic about it as I remember him being 20 years ago, which is fantastic. And the other cool thing about being there was being up on that stage, knowing that my 15-year-old son was in the audience. He was at Fan Expo, and he’s a big gamer now. So that was pretty meaningful to me to be up there on stage and to know he was out there in the audience and is interested now in getting into Resident Evil.
Genevieve Buechner: That [panel] was so special and lovely, and I’m so glad [Alyson] did that. There were tons of people up there that I had never had an opportunity to meet yet. Getting to meet some of these OG characters from this absolutely iconic franchise was so special, and I had a blast. And I’m so glad that everybody who was there got to see everybody and meet everybody, and we could all chat. And it’s definitely something I’ll always remember. I was really excited to meet OG Leon [Paul Mercier] as Ashley. That was really, really special to me. I got a photo. That was pretty peak for me. That’s special. Such an iconic character […] I also didn’t know how many people [in Resident Evil] were from Canada before. I had no idea that it was such a legacy. And I can’t tell you how grateful and lucky I feel that I got to be one of those Canadians that got to be a part of it. I didn’t know it was such a thing, and I’m honoured to be a part of that.
André Peña: I feel absolutely honoured to have been cast in Resident Evil 4 Remake. Being [in the con] booths, you hear all the time, “Your game has inspired me. Your game has changed my life.” I said that to Paul [Mercier], because without him, I wouldn’t have a career. So it really changed my life. And I am honoured to have been blessed with this opportunity and to be able to interact with so many people — fans and other creators and other actors, like the rest of the Resident Evil cast that I got to meet. It’s just been an honour.
Richard Waugh: I had a great time seeing old friends like Sally Cahill and meeting hopefully new friends like the Outbreak cast. Craig is great. I like him so much I felt entirely comfortable teasing him on a podcast we were both part of recently. We have every hope of crossing paths again. It was also a highlight seeing Alyson again after several years. I adore her. RE abounds with cool people. […] I can’t say there is one particular moment or scene that jumps to mind, but I can say that there are several fan interactions that I have found quite moving. That my voice became so important to someone, got them through a bad time or is a thing these smart, funny people turn to for fun and comfort, it’s humbling. I don’t feel worthy.
Sally Cahill: When we reunited at Fan Expo, even when we did a group chat, new memories kept coming back and still
do. I think perhaps the most interesting thing is that my memories were of something fledgling and new. We were all just trying our best to make it work all while having no idea of what it was to become and how many people all over the world would connect and be brought together by it and how long it would continue and develop in so many way. It’s been almost 30 years and it’s still going on. More movies. New games. Hundreds of fan sites dedicated to it. And it all started for us in a little basement studio in the east end of Toronto in the ’90s. I could still ride my bike there.
Pablo Kuntz: People were saying, “I want you to play the game!” And I’m not a big gamer myself. But my son, Lennon, likes to play games, and this was around COVID time […] And so I embraced the game by having my son play it, and then we both really enjoyed it. It was very fun to watch the first Resident Evil, just to see it in action, the dogs coming through the window and scaring the life out of him. He was only 12, so we recorded that. We put it on his channel and put it on my channel, and then that really took off, and I got a couple thousand subscribers pretty quickly just from that. But then I wanted to support Lennon, and so we ended up continuing to play Resident Evil on his channel, and we continue to play every week pretty much. We’ve gone through all the games, all the remakes, and I just sit there. It’s been a great father-son thing. We don’t get a ton of people, maybe 30, 40, 50 people join on a livestream, and we just chat. But they’re so genuine, the fanbase. They’re so gracious and funny.
[…] I just watched the Resident Evil movie with my son. We went to see it. I thought it was great. It was a lot of fun. I was tickled to see everybody in there. It was a fairly packed cinema, and it’s a nice feeling — I didn’t say to anybody my experience of Resident Evil. I was just with other fans, and it’s nice just to think that this little germination in Tokyo led to so many years of this thing. It’s managed to survive; it’s amazing. And also, the fact that I was the first one. Even though the voice might be kind of funny and all that — the fact that it’s the first is a nice feeling. It’s been nothing but positive.
Mark Perceval-Maxwell: That whole year in Toronto was pretty surreal. We were a small, newly formed crew figuring things out as we went, and sometimes we’d improvise shots we probably had no business attempting, like a Licker whipping someone across the room. There was a fair bit of chaos, but it was all part of the fun. Still one of the most unconventional experiences of my career […] Mark Alberts told me about the reunion, and I really wish I could have been there. I wasn’t actually aware of the recent renewed interest in Outbreak, but I’m not surprised it still has its fans. It’s always been a big part of my career.
In fact, when I joined Rocksteady back in 2008 [to become a cinematics artist on the Batman: Arkham series], the cinematic director was a huge Resident Evil fan and told me that my work on Outbreak was one of the reasons they wanted to hire me. So the game has stayed with me in more ways than one!
Catherine Disher: It was interesting to see how many people came out specifically for Resident Evil that day and all through the weekend. Sometimes, over half of the people that come to me at those cons are for Resident Evil. It’s that big, and it seems to be getting bigger, weirdly enough. And more and more people pay attention. So it’s an honour to be around. I feel very connected to Jill. I feel very proud of being a part of it. She’s really a kind of feminist icon. I got corrected on Reddit once. I had been told that she was the first playable female character in a survival horror game, and I was roundly corrected that there was one that preceded her, I believe. [Ed. note: There’s a 1995 survival horror game called Clock Tower that stars a woman named Jennifer Simpson.] And now I love the miniskirt and the tube top; it’s iconic. And I love the boots — the sound that the boots make. [taps table in footsteps rhythm] That’s my favourite part of it.
Julia Voth: It’s a little removed from my life now, so people don’t really come up to me anymore. But it comes up in conversation a lot, and the reaction is always amazing. Sometimes people get a little awkward, and I feel the need to crack a joke to break the ice, because I get it, it really is unexpected and kind of random. I did that job at 15, and I’m 41 now. The fact that something from that long ago still lives with me and is still recognizable is mind-blowing. It’s the job that keeps on giving. The fan interactions, hands down [are my favourite]. Not everyone gets to meet their hero, and Jill is a hero to a lot of people. I felt a real responsibility to show up as the person they hoped I’d be, and that’s what I carry with me. The best part was getting to be that for everyone who cared.
Susan Hart: I’m very proud of it, and I’m very grateful that I happened to be sitting on the couch that day when a call came through. I’m very, very grateful that I can be a part of something that moves people, that entertains people, that makes people talk, that makes people meet together, that makes people share. I’ve been directing for 30 years, so it’s where I’ve chosen to spend my time, and it’s my passion. And very, very grateful that I was on the couch that day. I could have been somewhere else, and that wouldn’t have happened. So I’m happy for it. And each game had special memories, each of them had special experiences. And Capcom — gracious, good, thoughtful, talented individuals. There were no egos. We were all in there to work on one thing and one thing only: make it the best that we can. And I love that camaraderie.
These interviews were edited for language, clarity and length.
A big thank you to everyone for taking part, and a shout-out to the many other Canadian artists who aren’t featured here. And, of course, endless gratitude goes out to the amazing Capcom developers for making these beloved games in the first place!
Header image credit: Capcom

articles.title: Why the Office Printer Still Generates So Many Support Calls, and How to Tame It - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Persistent Problem of Office Printers
Despite the rise of digital documentation and paperless workflows, office printers remain a critical component of business operations. Yet, they are notoriously prone to issues that frustrate employees and IT departments alike. From paper jams and connectivity glitches to driver errors and unexpected maintenance alerts, printers continue to be a major source of support calls in many organizations.
The paradox is clear: even with advances in printer technology, the average office printer still generates an estimated 20-25% of all IT support tickets related to hardware malfunctions. According to a 2023 survey by Spiceworks, 22% of IT professionals identified printers as one of the top three hardware devices causing the most support challenges in the workplace. This ongoing issue impacts productivity, delays important document handling, and increases operational costs.
Given that printers are so essential yet so troublesome, it’s no wonder they remain a perennial headache for IT teams. Understanding the root causes behind these frequent support calls is the first step toward taming the problem and restoring workplace efficiency.
Common Causes Behind Printer Support Calls
Printers are complex devices that combine mechanical, electronic, and software components. This complexity creates multiple points of failure. Some of the most frequent reasons for support requests include:
– Paper jams and misfeeds: These mechanical issues can arise from poor quality paper, improper loading, worn rollers, or internal debris.
– Connectivity issues: Wireless or network printers can lose connection due to IP conflicts, expired credentials, router problems, or firewall restrictions.
– Driver and firmware problems: Outdated or incompatible drivers cause print jobs to fail or produce errors.
– Low toner or ink alerts: Unexpected depletion of supplies halts printing until replacements arrive.
– Configuration errors: Incorrect default settings, permissions, or print queue problems can prevent users from printing.
– User errors: Simple mistakes like selecting the wrong printer, printing to an offline device, or misunderstanding printer functions often trigger support calls.
Each of these issues can frustrate end-users and lead them to seek help from IT support teams, diverting resources from higher-value tasks. In fact, a report by IDC found that printer-related issues contribute to roughly 23% of all hardware-related help desk tickets in medium to large enterprises.
Leveraging Expert Help to Streamline Printer Support
One effective way to reduce printer support calls is to partner with specialized service providers who offer quick, reliable assistance. For instance, businesses can benefit from on-demand tech support by OSG, which provides fast response times and expert troubleshooting to resolve printer issues before they impact operations.
With on-demand tech support, companies gain access to technicians who understand the nuances of printer technology and can diagnose problems remotely or onsite. This approach expedites resolution and prevents minor glitches from escalating into major disruptions. By outsourcing printer support, IT departments can focus on strategic initiatives instead of firefighting printer errors.
The Role of Preventative Maintenance
Beyond reactive support, organizations should invest in preventative maintenance and user education to tame printer-related headaches. Regular servicing of printers such as cleaning, replacing worn components, and updating firmware-extends device lifespan and reduces malfunctions.
Preventative maintenance can drastically reduce the frequency of common issues like paper jams and connectivity failures. A 2022 study by Brother International showed that companies that implemented regular printer maintenance saw a 30% decline in support calls related to hardware problems.
Empowering Users Through Training
Additionally, training employees on proper printer use, including how to load paper correctly, clear minor jams, manage print queues, and understand printer status indicators, empowers them to handle small issues independently. This reduces unnecessary support calls and fosters a more efficient workplace culture.
In addition to maintenance, having a reliable local partner can make a significant difference. Companies looking to improve their printer reliability can contact IT Force in Mississauga, where experienced IT professionals can help implement best practices and tailored support solutions.
Data-Driven Insights on Printer Support Impact
The financial and operational toll of printer support calls is notable. A 2022 IDC report revealed that businesses spend an average of $120 per printer annually on support and maintenance, with hidden costs related to lost productivity bringing the total closer to $400 per printer. For enterprises with dozens or hundreds of printers, these expenses quickly accumulate into significant budget items.
Moreover, a study by Brother International found that 65% of employees experience frustration due to printing issues, with delays in printing documents negatively affecting deadlines and customer interactions. Printing delays can lead to missed deadlines, poor customer service, and a general decline in workplace morale.
Understanding these statistics reinforces why tackling printer support calls is vital for business efficiency and employee satisfaction. It also highlights the importance of investing in solutions that reduce downtime and streamline printer management.
Practical Steps to Reduce Printer-Related Support Calls
To minimize printer support tickets, businesses can adopt a multi-faceted strategy:
- Standardize printer models: Limiting the variety of printers in the office simplifies driver management, reduces compatibility issues, and streamlines support processes.
- Implement centralized print management: Using software tools to monitor printer status, toner levels, and usage patterns allows IT to proactively address potential problems before users are affected.
- Automate driver and firmware updates: Ensuring printers are running the latest software decreases errors, enhances security, and improves overall reliability.
- Provide clear user guidelines: Distributing quick reference guides or digital tutorials helps employees troubleshoot basic printer issues, such as clearing paper jams or selecting the correct printer.
- Schedule routine maintenance: Regular checkups by qualified technicians prevent hardware degradation and unexpected failures, extending printer life and reducing support calls.
- Encourage proper printer etiquette: Educate users on batching print jobs, avoiding unnecessary prints, and reporting issues promptly to prevent escalation.
By combining these measures with professional support options, organizations can dramatically decrease the frequency and severity of printer support calls. This integrated approach not only improves printer uptime but also enhances overall IT service quality.
The Future of Office Printing Support
As office technology evolves, so too will the ways businesses manage printer support. Emerging solutions such as AI-driven diagnostics, cloud-based print management platforms, and remote troubleshooting tools are set to further reduce printer downtime and simplify maintenance. These innovations enable predictive maintenance, real-time monitoring, and faster issue resolution.
For example, AI-powered systems can analyze printer usage patterns and detect anomalies before they result in failures, allowing IT teams to intervene proactively. Cloud-based print management also provides centralized control over distributed printer fleets, simplifying updates and access control.
Early adopters of these innovations will enjoy smoother operations, lower IT costs, and enhanced user experience. However, until printers become entirely foolproof, human expertise remains indispensable. Investing in skilled IT support-whether internal or through trusted partners- continues to be a vital part of taming the office printer’s reputation as a frequent troublemaker.
Conclusion
