articles.title: Meta perdió su apelación en París y deberá negociar con la prensa francesa y revelar sus ingresos
articles.text:
La corte de apelaciones de París rechazó este 29 de octubre los recursos de Meta contra las medidas provisionales que le impuso la autoridad de competencia de Francia. La empresa deberá seguir negociando con los medios franceses el pago por sus contenidos y entregarles datos sobre los ingresos de sus redes sociales.
El tribunal dijo en un comunicado que las prácticas de Meta para fijar los montos que debe pagar a los editores de prensa pueden constituir un abuso de posición dominante, algo que prohíben las leyes europea y francesa.
Un vocero de Meta dijo que la empresa está decepcionada con el fallo. Agregó que evalúa los próximos pasos, pero que seguirá cumpliendo las medidas y negociando de buena fe, y que espera que los editores hagan lo mismo.
Las medidas son provisionales: la autoridad de competencia todavía no decidió si Meta infringió la ley. Se mantienen vigentes hasta que resuelva el fondo del caso.
Qué debe hacer Meta mientras dura la investigación
La autoridad adoptó las dos medidas el 8 de julio. Ordenó a Meta negociar de buena fe con agencias y editores, con criterios transparentes, objetivos y no discriminatorios, y por el uso de contenidos desde el comienzo de 2025.
También le exigió entregar en 15 días la información necesaria para evaluar sus ofertas de pago. Y le prohibió modificar la forma en que se muestran los contenidos de los medios durante la negociación. Meta debe además enviar informes periódicos sobre el cumplimiento.
La autoridad no fijó un monto provisional. Según su comunicado, hacerlo podía influir en las conversaciones entre las partes.
Los reclamos llegaron de dos organizaciones. La Alianza de la Prensa de Información General (APIG) agrupa a más de 300 diarios. La Sociedad de Derechos Vecinos de la Prensa (DVP) administra los derechos de agencias y editores y, según el medio especializado PPC Land, representa a 920 publicaciones y más de 60 agencias.
Quién debe probar el valor de las noticias
PPC Land, que citó una traducción no oficial del comunicado de la corte, informó que el tribunal consideró justa una remuneración solo si toma en cuenta la naturaleza y el alcance del uso de los contenidos y el valor económico que ese uso genera. Según esa traducción, corresponde a las redes sociales demostrar ambos factores.
El tribunal también concluyó, según esa misma fuente, que las condiciones de transparencia necesarias para fijar un precio justo no parecían cumplirse. Sostuvo que la conducta de Meta causa un daño grave e inmediato al sector de la prensa, distinto de las dificultades económicas estructurales que atraviesa.
Dos acuerdos vencidos y sin renovar
La ley francesa de 2019 reconoce a agencias y editores un derecho a cobrar cuando una plataforma reproduce su trabajo. Meta firmó acuerdos con APIG en diciembre de 2021 y con DVP en junio de 2024. Vencieron el 31 de enero de 2025 y el 31 de diciembre de 2024, respectivamente.
Las negociaciones posteriores no lograron acuerdo sobre el monto, los usos cubiertos ni los servicios de Meta incluidos. Desde el vencimiento, los miembros de ambas organizaciones no recibieron pago alguno, según la autoridad.
Meta apelación presentó el 6 de agosto. La autoridad de competencia debe aún pronunciarse sobre el fondo del caso, y las medidas provisionales seguirán vigentes hasta entonces.
La decisión mantiene abierta una discusión central para el ecosistema informativo: si las plataformas obtienen valor económico de las noticias, la negociación requiere datos que permitan medirlo. Hasta que la autoridad francesa resuelva el caso, las medidas preservan un marco de diálogo y obligan a Meta a justificar cómo calcula una remuneración que los editores consideran insuficiente en la actualidad.

articles.title: Reflex raises $14M to help enterprises replace generic third-party software with custom business apps - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Reflex raises $14M to help enterprises replace generic third-party software with custom business apps
Reflex, a startup that uses artificial intelligence agents to build, deploy and maintain custom business software for enterprises, said today it has closed on a $14 million Series A round of funding.
Standard Capital led the round, which saw participation from Databricks Ventures, Y Combinator, Lux Capital and Abstract Ventures.
The startup, which has now raised $19 million in total, is taking aim at what has long been one of the most widely accepted inefficiencies of enterprise software. Most businesses today have little option but to rely on generic, third-party software platforms that contain dozens of features they never actually use. But worse than that, they lack many of the specific, niche capabilities they do require.
Businesses generally get around this problem by purchasing overlapping subscriptions to multiple software platforms, so they can patch their capabilities together. If there are any gaps, these are usually filled with messy manual spreadsheets and repetitive manual workflows. Most companies have little choice but to do this, because it’s far beyond their capabilities to create bespoke, mission-critical software themselves. Such endeavors require access to teams of specialized and expensive software engineers that only the biggest companies can afford.
But the arrival of generative AI means that reality has changed. By pairing AI-assisted development with a unique “software factory” workflow, Reflex can help much smaller companies to identify, assemble, deploy and maintain highly customized business applications that are designed specifically for their unique operational processes.
What customers end up with is software that’s precisely optimized for their workflows, with all of the functionality required to get their work done in a single package. Companies no longer need to rely on expensive pre-packaged software with superfluous functionality that means nothing to them.
The biggest advantage of building custom business software is that companies get to fully own the applications they build. When they design their apps with Reflex, they can avoid getting locked into an expensive third-party ecosystem. Whenever new functions are needed, teams can describe the capability they want in natural language, iterate, tweak the design and so on until they get it just right.
Customers also get plenty of flexibility too, with Reflex’s software able to run in the public cloud, on-premises data centers or in highly secure air-gapped environments. This makes them more attractive to enterprises in tightly regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare and government, the startup says.
Reflex is led by its co-founder and Chief Executive Nikhil Rao (pictured, right), who previously served as one of the first engineers at the autonomous driving startup Drive.ai Inc. When that company was acquired by Apple Inc., he joined the iPhone maker’s Special Projects Group, where he helped to create many AI innovations. The startup’s other co-founder is Chief Technology Officer Alek Petuskey (left), who formerly worked as a machine learning engineer at Ancestry.com Inc. and a researcher at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
Rao and Petuskey originally developed Reflex as an open-source Python framework and only decided to build a company around it after seeing it explode in popularity. Within months, Reflex had built up a loyal developer community, racking up almost 30,000 GitHub stars and reaching 400,000 monthly downloads. To date, Reflex has been used to build over a million deployed applications globally, with its users including some of the world’s biggest organizations, including Amazon.com Inc., Walmart Inc., The World Bank and Dell Technologies Inc.
Dell used Reflex’s platform to design and build a dedicated server monitoring system that’s now being used by more than 6,000 of its staff. Meanwhile, an unnamed aerospace company used Reflex to rip out and replace its legacy manufacturing resource planning platform. With massive customers like these, it’s little wonder that Reflex has managed to grow its revenue more than 10 times in the past year.
Standard Capital’s Dalton Caldwell the popularity of AI coding has made many companies realize that there is an alternative to buying traditional software-as-a-service applications. “Most companies still run on software that was built for someone else’s business,” he said. “Nikhil and Alek built a platform companies already trust and an elite team that helps create production software for non-software companies.”
Reflex said the next thing on the agenda is to expand its engineering and sales operations teams to support the growing demand for its custom software platform in the traditional corporate and government sectors. It’s also putting the final touches on a new product called Workflows, which will use AI agents to automate multistep business operations.

articles.title: Google ärgert Anthropic mit Gemini 4 Carbon
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Carbon: Google kündigt nur 2 Wochen nach Argon noch besseres KI-Modell an
Kurz vor dem Börsengang des KI-Rivalen Anthropic hat Google mit Gemini 4 Carbon sein bisher leistungsstärkstes KI-Modell präsentiert. Und das nur zwei Wochen nach der Veröffentlichung seines bis dato führenden Frontier-Modells Gemini 4 Argon.
Gemini 4 Carbon überholt Anthropic-KI
Im Intelligence-Index des unabhängigen Testdiensts Artificial Analysis springt Carbon am bisherigen Spitzenreiter Claude Opus 5.5 von Anthropic vorbei an die Spitzenposition, wie Google mitteilt. Argon hatte in dem Ranking zuvor nur auf dem sechsten Platz gelegen.
Dabei handelt es sich bei Gemini 4 Carbon um eine Weiterentwicklung von Argon. Google zufolge zeige das, „mit welcher Geschwindigkeit wir die Grenzen des Machbaren weiter hinausschieben“. Die Forscher:innen und Modelle des Konzerns arbeiteten „Hand in Hand“, um die Leistungsfähigkeit schneller zu steigern. Gleichzeitig baue das Unternehmen aber die Schutzmaßnahmen aus, wie Google versichert.
Programmieren und Cybersicherheit im Fokus
Carbon selbst soll seinen Vorgänger vor allem bei anspruchsvollen Programmieraufgaben und in puncto Cybersicherheit übertrumpfen. Google zufolge sei das neue Spitzenmodell imstande, komplexe Fehler in großen Codebasen zu finden und zu beheben. Außerdem könne die KI länger an entsprechenden Aufgaben arbeiten.
Im Cybersecurity-Ranking SEC-bench Pro, das auf das Finden von Sicherheitslücken abzielt, hat Carbon einen Wert von 88,2 Prozent erhalten. Zum Vergleich: Argon kam auf 83,4 Prozent, OpenAIs GPT-6 Astra auf 85,4 Prozent. Auch bei den populären Cybersecurity-Benchmarks Exploitgym (Ausnutzen) und CWE-bench (Beheben von Lücken) liegt Googles neues Topmodell zum Teil deutlich vor der Konkurrenz.
Derweil muss Gemini 4 Carbon Anthropics Claude Opus 5.5 den Vortritt lassen, wenn es um agentische Programmierfähigkeiten geht (Coding Agent Index). Und auch in den Benchmarks Terminal-Bench und Frontiercode hat Anthropic die Nase vorn.
Start zunächst nur für ausgewählte Nutzer
Zudem ist Carbon derzeit nur für ausgewählte Nutzer:innen wie Cyberabwehr-Expert:innen verfügbar, wie Trendingtopics schreibt. Erst nach dem Absolvieren des freiwilligen Vorabprüfverfahrens der US-Regierung soll die neue Gemini-KI auch Entwickler:innen, Unternehmen und Verbraucher:innen zur Verfügung stehen.
Für eines hat Google mit der Veröffentlichung von Gemini 4 Carbon jedenfalls sicher gesorgt: für Unruhe bei Anthropic vor dessen geplanten Börsengang. Möglich, so Beobachter:innen, dass der KI-Anbieter im IPO-Vorfeld jetzt noch ein eigenes, besseres KI-Modell, etwa Claude Opus 6, ins Rennen schickt.

articles.title: Breet Makes the Case for Simpler Crypto Payments at Moonshot
articles.text:
Making cryptocurrency payments easier to use is as much a challenge as building the infrastructure behind them, Breet chief operating officer Vivian Mbene told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos on Wednesday.
Mbene said the company’s biggest task was making a complicated product appear simple to customers, allowing businesses to accept digital assets without taking on the operational demands of managing them.
Breet, founded in 2019, converts cryptocurrency into cash for individuals in Nigeria and Ghana. It also offers an application programming interface that allows businesses to accept crypto payments and receive settlement in local currency.
The proposition separates the payment method from the currency a merchant ultimately wants to hold. Customers can pay with digital assets, while businesses receive local money without having to build a crypto operation of their own.
For Mbene, the objective is to reduce the work required to complete that transaction. “We’re just obsessed with simplicity,” she said.
That approach places much of the complexity behind the scenes. Functions such as monitoring transactions, routing deposits and converting currencies need to work together without requiring merchants to manage each step themselves.
But making the process look straightforward can create a different problem: convincing customers and business partners to trust it.
“Sometimes simplicity brings suspicion, and when it’s powered by crypto, the suspicion kind of doubles,” Mbene said.
Her remarks highlighted a tension for crypto payment providers. A simpler interface can reduce the effort involved in using a service, but it does not necessarily remove doubts about the technology underneath it.
Breet’s pitch is that businesses should be able to use crypto as a payment channel while continuing to manage their finances in familiar currencies. For providers pursuing that model, the commercial test is whether they can make accepting digital assets both straightforward and credible to merchants.

articles.title: Anthropic Says Nobody Needs a Mental Model of Claude Code. Practitioners Are Testing That
articles.text:
Anthropic has published how the Claude Code team runs code review now that Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code itself. The claim drawing the most scrutiny is not the percentage but what the team says it no longer needs.
The post, by Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang, is the companion to Anthropic’s account of replacing git with an in-house system after its monorepo went from roughly 2,500 merged changes a day in May to more than 30,000 in September. Review was the next thing to break. The target is that most pull requests "merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents."
On comprehension, the team is explicit:
Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don’t think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
That passage dominated the Hacker News discussion, where commenter jonahx set out what it trades away:
There is no longer anyone to turn to if this system breaks by, eg, having a critical bug that no one can figure out. No causal model in anyone’s head that can be appealed to, to slowly and methodically debug. The new trust model is: We trust Claude to always understand the system enough to debug anything or make any reasonable change we could want.
He also noted that many large legacy systems already work this way.
One documented case tests the explainer claim on Anthropic’s own repository. In August, Claude Code collaborator Boris Cherny answered a long-running complaint about issue auto-closure in a comment carrying the "Generated with Claude Code" footer. It said issues are closed when they have "had no activity for a while and are missing information needed to reproduce," and that "nothing is triaged solely by counting."
The repository’s issue-lifecycle.ts sets fourteen days to stale and fourteen more to closure, exempting only issues with ten or more upvotes. Developer marcindulak counted more than 6,000 issues labelled as carrying reproduction steps that were closed anyway as "inactive for too long." The remedy the comment offered, commenting to have an issue reopened, is blocked by a workflow that locks closed issues after seven days. That meta-issue is now locked.
The answer that started this issue, and misdiagnosed how issues in this repo are managed, was generated by a world-class model.
The failures the post documents are specific. The first appears only when both sides are machines:
Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.
"One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it," the team writes. Running more rounds by default made things worse, so they capped them. On r/ClaudeCode, commenter ChemicalExcellent463 reported reaching the same control independently, stopping after two failed fixes because repeated failure means the agent’s picture of the code is wrong rather than the line it keeps editing.
The second failure is what those rounds were finding:
When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer’s first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.
What gates a merge is a risk tier picked by a classifier, where "the change sets the tier, not the author." Low risk covers docs, copy, and additive changes behind a flag, and clears with no human approval. Medium risk, including caching, the auto-updater, and system prompts, needs one person. Two rules hold the line: "an agent’s approval never counts as a person’s," and the person who prompted a change "counts as one of the required reviewers."
That boundary drew a question the post does not answer. Reddit commenter Oximy-Naman asked whether low risk covers agent instruction changes shipped as documentation, since those "could change what an agent does without touching application code," and got no reply. The post assigns no tier to CLAUDE.md, the file its own reviewer loads on every review. On compliance, Hacker News commenter gaal_dornick reported that their own SOC 2 reviewer required every change to be seen by a second human before production; the post does not discuss audit requirements.
One control is missing, and the team says so:
We don’t yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.
Not everyone reads this as reckless. Commenter cheema33 argued that large organizations have never had anyone holding a complete model, making this an upgrade on the status quo, and commenter markbao reported spending a few thousand dollars a month on AI review against human review that consumes up to a third of an engineer’s time.
Parts of the system ship publicly. Code Review for Claude Code is generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and the security review runs as an open-source GitHub Action whose README states that it "is not hardened against prompt injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs."

articles.title: Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next
articles.text:
Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next
Many MCP servers do one thing. An agent asks for data, and the server hands it back. AWS’s James Ward thinks that leaves a lot on the table. The protocol works best, he told me, when the server acts less like a database and more like another voice in the conversation.
Ward is a principal developer advocate at AWS and sits on the technical committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, the Linux Foundation group that now houses MCP. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose the day before he and co-presenter Alexander Ioffe were set to give a session on moving MCP from a basic API to an agent integration interface.
“Many times our MCP servers are just these APIs, like ‘get me the customers,’ and that is a good place to start,” Ward said. “I imagine MCP as the third person in this conversation, or a fourth or a fifth, depending on how many MCP servers you have.”
In practice, that means a tool response carries guidance with the data. It tells the agent what it just did, what it might want to do next, and where to find more.
The other half of his pitch is visibility. Web developers can trace a click on a page all the way down to the database. “MCP by default doesn’t have any way to do trace ID,” Ward said.
The workaround AWS uses is rather low-tech. Add a session ID parameter to the tools and tell the agent to pass it on every call, so individual calls can be stitched into one journey. A second parameter can carry the user’s prompt or a summary of their goal. Teams can then compare what the user wanted with the path the agent took, build an eval around it, adjust a tool description or parameter, and measure whether more tasks get completed. Ward said AWS built much of this for the MCP servers its own developers use.
In May, AWS opened its MCP Server to everyone and added Lambda diagnostics in September. In an Agentic AI Foundation profile published before the conference, Ward described an agent fetching customer records one at a time because the server only offered a one-record tool. Watching the full journey is how teams spot that pattern and build a batch tool to fix it.
Ward didn’t present MCP as the only solution. AWS also ships a CLI and skills, he said, partly because MCP’s OAuth model can’t toggle between AWS user profiles the way the CLI can. Which works best depends on the model, the tool descriptions, and how the agent discovers tools, so AWS tests them against each other with evals.
None of this is exotic, and Ward knows it. “There’s nothing new under the sun,” he said. Observe the journey, reproduce it, measure it, and improve it. The difference is that teams now have to understand the path a human and an agent take together, and test whether changes to their tools actually help them finish the task.

articles.title: Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
Intel is reportedly preparing two new processor SKUs focused on extremely low-power computing. The first, called "Moon Lake," is designed as a pure low-power efficiency (LPE) core SoC. The "Moon Lake" generation features no P-Cores and up to 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores on the Intel 18A die. Unlike "Wildcat Lake," which includes at least 2 P-Cores, "Moon Lake" is intended to be a much smaller design for embedded devices like NAS. The base power of "Moon Lake" is reportedly rated at 6 W, similar to an SoC typically used in smartphones. The number of Xe3 cores in this SKU is unknown, but since "Wildcat Lake" has up to 2 Xe3 cores, we expect "Moon Lake" to have half of that to maintain its 6 W TDP. Intel has manufactured "Moon Lake" on its 18A node and placed it on the BGA1516 package, the same platform used by "Wildcat Lake." The official moniker for "Moon Lake" is MNL, and it could be a successor to the N-Series, like the previous "Alder Lake-N" series of low-power processors.
Additionally, Intel is preparing an overhaul of "Wildcat Lake" with the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh." When Intel launched the Core 300 Series "Wildcat Lake" earlier this year, these processors came with up to 2 P-Cores, 4 E-Cores, and up to 2 Xe3 GPU cores, with a package reaching up to 35 W. However, the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh" is expected to increase the number of P-Cores to 4 while keeping the same base microarchitecture of "Cougar Cove" and maintaining 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores. The integrated graphics remain similar, with up to 2 Xe3 cores. Importantly, this refresh adds support for Intel's vPro technology, meaning that enterprise customers are in for a surprise with a new low-cost option for their PCs.All three platforms—"Wildcat Lake," "Wildcat Lake Refresh," and "Moon Lake"—are reportedly well-received in the low-power computing space, as Intel is actively pushing their development. All three are based on the 18A node for manufacturing, with Intel Foundry handling the work, and they share the BGA1516 package.

So it's a fine product that will be made more or less interesting by pricing, and could be a good replacement for Alder Lake-N devices. You lose the P-core single-threaded performance from Wildcat Lake, but save some money and power.
Still, it's a shame (given how much money was invested in 18A) TSMC gets to make big chips and 18A is left for producing crumbs.
Now if there were cheap PCIe 4.0 switches/bridges things would be different because MNL/WCL with 6 PCIe 4.0 lanes has a third more bandwidth than ADL-N with 9 PCIe 3.0.
Lunarlake/Wildcatlake/Pantherlake are same battery life and power wise. XPS 13 on Pantherlake does 27 hours without VRR and 41 with while web browsing, not idle. That's actually lot better than Lunarlake XPS 13 as it has similar efficiency to the Pantherlake without VRR, and Wildcatlake has same basic advances.No Wildcatlake has 8 LPE cores. They all have 4.It'll be faster than quad core from those gens as these chips can actually hold their clocks, whereas Sky to Comet can only do for a short time.
1 Xe3 core is 2-2.5x the performance of UHD 630, nevermind having support for XeSS, meaning you can adjust for further gains.
www.notebookcheck.net/HD-Graphics-620-vs-Intel-Graphics-1-Xe3-WCL_7435_13536.247598.0.html
It's over 3x the performance in GTA V, with Core 3 304 on Med 768p settings getting 70 fps and outperforming HD 620 1024x768 Low getting miserly 27.8 fps. Also you'll get much better compatibility and less errors.If 3.6GHz Darkmont cores are shitty, so are 3.6GHz Zen 5 or 3.6GHz Lion Cove(Arrowlake) cores.

articles.title: Tool that identifies AI-generated material helps Pixel Systems raise €2.7 million | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Swedish AI startup Pixel Systems has raised €2.7 million ($3.1 million) in a Seed round to accelerate their commercial initiatives and continue building the technology that helps identify AI-generated and manipulated images, documents, and other digital material.
The round was led by Unconventional Ventures, at a pre-money valuation of approximately €18 million ($21 million).
“Generative AI has made it extremely cheap to fabricate evidence. The problem is that almost every digital process still rests on the assumption that what people submit is authentic. That assumption is disappearing,” says Robel Efrem, co-founder and CEO of Pixel.
Pixel’s funding follows other European investments in digital trust and fraud-prevention technology reported by EU-Startups in 2026, including Sweden’s Bits (€12 million), Denmark’s Flare (€3.6 million), France’s Marble (€6.5 million) and MokN (€12.9 million), Spain’s Zepo Intelligence (€12.8 million), and UK/Germany-based Diligent AI (€2.1 million).
Together, these rounds represent approximately €49.9 million in funding, excluding Pixel’s €2.7 million Seed round, across companies addressing different aspects of verification, fraud prevention and financial crime.
EU-Startups previously covered Efrem as co-founder and CEO of Swedish esports platform Challengermode, which raised €10.1 million in 2020.
“We believe the ability to verify digital information will become as natural a part of tomorrow’s infrastructure as cybersecurity is today. That a Swedish company has the opportunity to take a leading position in this field is exactly the kind of development we want to help make possible,” adds Nora Bavey, General Partner at Unconventional Ventures.
Founded in 2026 in Stockholm, Pixel develops proprietary technology to detect AI-generated and manipulated digital content. By combining several independent forensic analysis methods, Pixel helps companies verify images, documents, and other digital material before it is used as the basis for decisions, payouts, or other critical processes.
The team behind Pixel consists of senior engineers, AI specialists, and competitive programmers.
In Pixel’s internal tests, the platform has achieved a detection rate of 99.98 percent for AI-generated and manipulated material, reportedly placing the technology at a world-leading level.
Pixel is used today in businesses where digital material forms the basis for financial decisions, including insurance, FinTech, e-commerce, and professional services.
Use cases include manipulated damage photos in insurance claims, fabricated receipts and invoices, AI-generated product images in refund fraud, and manipulated material in financial or legal processes.
“The internet was built for a world where an image could largely be treated as proof. That world no longer exists. Now every company that receives images, receipts, and documents from its customers needs to be able to check that material before money is paid out,” says Robel Efrem.
The funding comes just months after the company was founded. Three weeks after its commercial launch, Pixel has reached its first €89k ($100k) in contracted recurring revenue.

articles.title: Microsoft spent $6.5 billion less than expected on AI infrastructure, but it wasn't by choice
articles.text:
In brief: It's a rare sight these days to see a tech giant admit it spent less money on capital expenditures than expected. But the $6.5 billion less that Microsoft spent than Wall Street forecast wasn't a sudden outbreak of unexpected restraint. It was delayed data centers that pushed some of its spending back.
Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures, including finance leases, in the September quarter, compared with the $51.7 billion expected by analysts cited by the Financial Times. That's still around 30% more than a year earlier, illustrating just how expensive the AI infrastructure race has become.
Redmond has now cut its calendar 2026 spending forecast from $175 billion to $170 billion, which is still an astronomical figure, admittedly.
CFO Amy Hood blamed delayed capacity deliveries from third parties, with those facilities now expected online in the second half of Microsoft's fiscal year. Spending will accelerate during that period, primarily because of all-too-familiar rising memory hardware costs.
Microsoft added 24 data centers during the quarter, but it also relies on smaller cloud operators. It's signed more than $80 billion in contracts with CoreWeave, Nebius and Nscale since 2023, according to the FT.
Some projects are struggling. Microsoft recently abandoned an Nscale capacity deal because of power constraints, while a Nebius facility in New Jersey is progressing more slowly than expected.
This sort of problem isn't exclusive to Microsoft. Amazon is stockpiling billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia racks because some facilities lack the electricity to run them. Its roughly $220 billion capital spending budget for this year is $50 billion higher than Microsoft's revised forecast.
Alphabet, meanwhile, is maintaining its $195 billion to $205 billion annual budget. It spent $51.4 billion in the September quarter, also below expectations, and expects spending to increase significantly next year. Its quarterly free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, continuing a trend from when Google reported its first negative quarterly free cash flow in July.
Azure provides some justification for Microsoft's enormous bills. Revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion, while the company's free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion.
The spending push comes as Microsoft continues to reduce staff costs, including making buyout offers to as many as 60,000 employees.

articles.title: Google Touts Powerful Cybersecurity Capabilities in Gemini 4 Carbon Model
articles.text:
Google on Wednesday announced Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier AI model that, according to the company, beats rival models on benchmarks for detecting, exploiting and patching vulnerabilities.
The model is not broadly available yet. This week, Google is opening access to a select group of cyber defenders, then expanding it in stages to a wider pool of approved partners via its Fairwind Program.
Fairwind offers governments, critical infrastructure operators and major technology platforms early access to advanced models for cyber defense. The company says more than 650 organizations currently participate.
Carbon follows Gemini 4 Argon, which Google launched two weeks ago. Some Fairwind partners already have exclusive access to Argon’s cybersecurity defense capabilities.
Google said Carbon scored 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, which tests a model’s ability to uncover flaws in real-world software. It also achieved 54.8% on the ExploitGym exploitation benchmark and 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench patching benchmark, topping OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 in the company’s comparison.
These results were obtained with no guardrails in place, the company noted.
Google frames exploitation as a defensive step that helps teams decide what to fix. “To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable,” the company said.
Based on Google’s internal benchmarks, Carbon is more than twice as successful as Argon at writing secure code. When it came to generating high-quality patches, Google’s Chrome team found Carbon outperformed a large frontier model from a rival lab by more than 10 times.
Wiz, the Google-owned cloud security firm, has observed Carbon taking the top spot on web penetration testing benchmarks.
On the safety front, no attack succeeded against Carbon in Gray Swan’s indirect prompt injection benchmark, compared with a 0.7% success rate for Argon. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, none of Carbon’s cheating attempts succeeded, and those attempts fell to 0.4%.
Compared with Argon, the new model made about half as many unsupported claims. Google’s internal teams, using Carbon in real coding environments, saw a nearly 80% decrease in high-severity misalignment alerts.
Google says it is involved in the US government’s voluntary effort to test models before they are released. “We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible,” the company said.
Carbon will launch at Argon’s introductory rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. When the introductory period ends, the price goes up to $4 and $20, respectively.

articles.title: Ofcom reveals age-check methods for UK social media ban — facial scans and photo ID spark privacy pushback as 40% of teens plan workarounds
articles.text:
'The risks aren’t hypothetical': Ofcom reveals age-check plans for UK social media ban — but privacy experts aren't convinced
Take your pick
- Ofcom has assessed the best ways of enforcing age checks online
- The regulator also identifies methods that aren't effective
- Around 4 in 10 under-16s plan to try to get around the ban in the UK
Back in June, the UK government ruled that under-16s should be banned from social media platforms, with enforcement scheduled to start during the first half of 2027. Now the communications regulator Ofcom has set out the ways it expects tech companies to abide by the law.
In its new announcement (via the BBC), Ofcom highlights four "highly effective" methods for keeping under-16s out of apps and off sites they shouldn't be accessing — and they're all going to be familiar to anyone who's used age-gated services online in recent times.
The four methods are photo ID matching (using something like a passport or driving license), bank-based checks (Ofcom says 90% of UK 16-17 year-olds have a bank account), digital ID services (a third-party service like EasyID or Yoti), and facial age estimation via a webcam (which Ofcom says is best deployed as a secondary check).
This is a "rapid assessment" from Ofcom, and none of these approaches are confirmed yet — UK lawmakers will take the suggestions on board, and decide the best way to enforce the rules at a later date, most probably before the end of the year. All of these methods can be delivered "in a way that protects users' privacy" according to Ofcom.
Ultimately though, it will be down to tech companies to decide how to implement age checks that fulfil the requirements set down by the government. "Here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you," Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes told the BBC.
Challenges ahead
Ofcom also lists checks that it thinks are ineffective: self-declaration, general contractual agreements, and verifiable parental consent. The regulator also acknowledges that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", but says that correctly implemented safeguards should "significantly reduce the likelihood" of unauthorized access.
In its rapid assessment announcement, Ofcom also encourages app stores to take more responsibility over age checks. Right now, self-declarations are most commonly used to unlock downloads for age-restricted content.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
These are going to be tough rules to enforce, whatever the approach is: recent research from EE suggests that 42% of 11-15 year-olds are planning to try and get around whatever restrictions are put in place. This could be by switching to apps or platforms not covered by the new laws, including messaging services and gaming sites.
Last week Ofcom also admitted that the Online Safety Act introduced in July 2025 had so far made "no significant change" to the harmful content children had been exposed to online. The act was intended to ensure protection from content involving pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny, and bullying.
"This finding is concerning and shows that further progress is needed to protect children online," says Ofcom. The regulator also recommended adding material around body stigma and depression to the primary content categories that children should be protected from online.
Analysis: What do privacy experts think?
Ofcom's proposals are likely to spark some familiar privacy concerns — and security experts told us they aren't without foundation.
“The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check," said Pieter Arntz, Senior Malware Intelligence Analyst at Malwarebytes. "Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, potentially creating another attractive target for criminals. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year, a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users," he said.
Even if facial estimation techniques are more secure, there are are still downsides. "Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction," Pieter Arntz added. "Ofcom itself acknowledges that some technologies have a margin of error of a few years at 16, meaning people near the threshold may face an additional verification check," he said.
"My preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement but doesn’t learn which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you are old enough should not mean revealing who you are," he said.
Others feel the risks are more around teenagers finding workarounds.“The challenge for social media platforms is that teenagers don’t like to be told ‘no’. Many will conform, but tech-savvy young people are going to search for an open window on the ground floor," said Olli Krebs, SVP EMEA at the identity verification software provider Incode. "If the process is clunky, users of all ages will actively seek ways around it," he added.
Those workarounds could unintentionally make the problem worse. "The experience of countries such as Australia is that there will be a real risk of an increasingly technologically sophisticated population of young people will resort to a variety of circumvention techniques (primarily, but not exclusively VPNs) to access content hosted outside of the UK," said Will Richmond-Coggan, Partner specialising in Data and Privacy Disputes at Freeths.
"Such content is liable to be less well regulated generally, and to pose further risks of users gaining unsupervised access to progressively more dangerous and problematic content in relation to which the UK online safety legislation is largely powerless to take action," he added.
“None of this will be perfect. Young people will always push boundaries, and anyone promising a hundred per cent online safety is being unrealistic," concluded Olli Krebs from Incode. Exactly how successful it is depends very much on how the social media giants implement Ofcom's suggested age-check methods.
What you think of the social media ban, and Ofcom's new proposals? Let us know in the comments below.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Dave is a freelance tech journalist who has been writing about gadgets, apps and the web for more than two decades. Based out of Stockport, England, on TechRadar you'll find him covering news, features and reviews, particularly for phones, tablets and wearables. Working to ensure our breaking news coverage is the best in the business over weekends, David also has bylines at Gizmodo, T3, PopSci and a few other places besides, as well as being many years editing the likes of PC Explorer and The Hardware Handbook.
