articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing shows most of its compute goes to R&D, not serving customers
articles.text:
Anthropic’s IPO filing shows most of its compute goes to R&D, not serving customers — company details massive $800 billion in TPU and GPU contracts
Claude covers what it costs to serve, but the racks on order are another matter.
Anthropic spent less than a third of its $8.9 billion first-half compute bill on serving customers, with most of the rest going into training, research, and running Claude internally, its S-1 filing shows. It has meanwhile signed up for hundreds of billions of dollars more in TPU and GPU capacity. By our math, it has meanwhile signed up for roughly $800 billion more in TPU and GPU capacity, and revenue per compute dollar jumped from $0.40 in Q1 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026, which the company links to capacity purchased 12–18 months ahead.
Anthropic’s IPO is likely to beat that of rival OpenAI, which filed confidentially before CEO Sam Altman said its own won’t come this year, amid widespread doubts about an AI bubble. Whether AI labs can cover what it costs to serve their models is an open question.
Anthropic appears to do so easily: it spent $2.4 billion serving customers in the first half of the year, versus $16.3 billion in revenue. Paying for what it has on order is more difficult. Its five compute deals with the biggest stated amounts would cost an estimated $103 billion a year on average once delivered, more than twice its revenue at Q2’s pace of about $46 billion a year. The company also warns that margins may compress as new hardware lands ahead of the revenue it will support.
The company has three main costs: the cost of revenue, which is the inference cost of running Claude for paying customers; R&D, which is mostly compute for training and research into new models plus any internal use; and sales and marketing, which covers the cut taken by channel partners and cloud platform resellers.
Comparing the first half of last year to this year’s, cost of revenue is up about 2.3x, but with revenue up 14x, that means Anthropic keeps an estimated 85 cents for every dollar after serving costs, up from just 12 cents. R&D is up about 5 times, with 66% or more of the compute going to it, and that’s the main source of its operating loss. Sales and marketing is up 16x, and doesn’t show up in cost of revenue, but its partner fees and marketing would lower what it keeps to 66 cents a dollar. The trend here is that serving Claude now more than covers its costs.
| Where Anthropic’s Compute Goes |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | First half of 2025 | First half of 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $1.16 billion | $16.29 billion | 
| Compute and infrastructure, all workloads | $2.33 billion | $8.95 billion | 
| Serving customers (cost of revenue) | $1.02 billion | $2.38 billion | 
| Free access to Claude, at most (est.) | $119 million | $640 million | 
| Training, research and internal use, at least (est.) | $1.20 billion | $5.93 billion | 
| Serving share of compute, at most | 44% | 27% | 
| Revenue left after serving costs | 12% | 85% | 
| Revenue left after serving costs, partner fees and marketing | 2% | 66% | 
Serving has kept getting cheaper for customers since June: in September, Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 model cut costs per task by about 40% versus Opus 5, says the company, and Fable 5.1 cut the cost of typical workloads by about 25% against Fable 5; each came from “a combination of a lower price and improved efficiency,” made “while preserving our margins.”
As for compute, which runs through all three costs, Anthropic runs it as “a single, shared resource across all workloads” and doesn’t disclose how it decides the split between training, research, and serving. Serving was limited, as the company has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute,” which suggests serving costs were muted by a lack of supply, not just efficiency.
Anthropic runs a “multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs,” without giving any percentage splits or GW measurements. For TPUs, it has five-year equipment leases with Broadcom for “TPU-based compute capacity,” with rent of “approximately $161.2 billion excluding interest”; some of that capacity came online this year, with more from 2027. Another $114.5 billion or more is with Google “between April 2026 and July 2033,” with more from Google and other TPU providers from 2028 to 2031, estimated to be in the $125–$150 billion range.
Trainium comes through Amazon, with a deal for “at least $110.0 billion between May 2026 and April 2036,” though the filing doesn’t split AWS spend by chip. Nvidia GPUs come through a series of deals, including “up to $120.5 billion … extending into 2029” with SpaceXAI, “at least $44.9 billion” extending into 2033 with Microsoft, “up to approximately $44.6 billion” also into 2033 with Nscale, and about $41.3 billion into 2034 with Lambda. There is also an AMD hardware supply agreement which, in aggregate, may “exceed $20.0 billion” if Anthropic takes the full initial capacity. These deals each have their own conditions for termination.
| Anthropic’s Compute Contracts |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Partner | Hardware | Amount | Term | Can Anthropic walk away? | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Broadcom | Google TPUs (equipment leases) | About $161.2 billion in rent | Five-year leases; some capacity online in 2026, more from 2027 | No, except on default | 
|  | Google TPUs | At least $114.5 billion | April 2026–July 2033 | No, except on Google’s uncured material breach; minimum owed regardless of use | 
| TPU providers, including Google | Google TPUs | $125–150 billion (estimated) | Delivered 2028–2031 | Not stated; payments depend on capacity made available and deployment conditions | 
| Amazon | AWS (Trainium among its chips) | At least $110 billion | May 2026–April 2036 | No, except on Amazon’s uncured material breach; minimum owed regardless of use | 
| SpaceXAI | Nvidia GPUs | Up to $120.5 billion; about $3.1 billion a month at full delivery | Into 2029; full capacity expected December 2026 | Yes, on 90 days’ notice once the initial periods end in January and March 2027 | 
| Microsoft | Azure (Nvidia GPUs) | At least $44.9 billion | November 2026–May 2033 | No, except on Microsoft’s uncured material breach or for undelivered tranches | 
| Nscale | Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 | Up to $44.6 billion | Into 2033 | No, except in limited cases (missed delivery or availability targets, uncured material breach); billed only as capacity is delivered and accepted | 
| Lambda | Nvidia GPUs | About $41.3 billion | Into 2034 | Partly: either side can end $34.9 billion of it if Lambda doesn’t secure the facility lease in time; otherwise only on Lambda’s uncured material breach or missed delivery milestones | 
| AMD | Instinct MI450 (Helios) | Expected to exceed $20 billion; no fixed dollar commitment | First capacity in 2027 | No, except on AMD’s uncured material breach | 
| Total, deals named in the S-1 (our sum) | All of the above | About $782–807 billion | 2026–2036 | Mix of minimums, caps and estimates; the S-1 leaves its own total blank and mentions other deals it doesn’t describe | 
Anthropic’s minimum purchase commitments, which exclude equipment leases such as Broadcom’s, have gone from about $55 billion at the end of last year to about $265.6 billion by the end of Q2 this year. Since then, it has signed about $245 billion in new minimums, leases included, and TPUs are the biggest line overall. The Nvidia capacity, Microsoft’s aside, is also the easiest for Anthropic to walk away from.
With all these multi-year commitments, bought well ahead of delivery, expenses are paid and recognized “as compute becomes available to us,” the company says. That compute base “did not fluctuate with in-period demand,” so revenue per compute dollar increased as demand surged. When demand outruns that capacity, Anthropic buys short-term compute, which “typically carries a higher cost per unit.”
Our $103 billion estimate is straight-line, spreading each deal evenly over its term except SpaceXAI, which is at its full monthly rate, while payments ramp up as capacity is delivered. Also not included in the estimate is interest on the Broadcom leases. Compute also does not necessarily have to earn revenue, especially in R&D.
The filing has many blanks, such as the total commitment figure, the contractual obligations table, Q3 revenue, and Run-Rate Revenue, which an amended S-1 would normally fill in before pricing. No date for that has been given. Microsoft’s minimum starts in November, and SpaceXAI’s full delivery is expected in December, with non-cancelable periods ending in January and March 2027, after which either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice. More Broadcom TPU capacity and AMD’s first tranche follow next year, by which point most of these deals will be billing.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: As search traffic dries up, Reddit announces it's shifting to a logged-in experience | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Reddit has long attracted millions of users to its site through Google, with many even appending the word “Reddit” to their search queries for better answers. But as search traffic dries up amid the shift to AI-powered search, Reddit is rethinking its relationship with the open internet. In its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, the company announced it’s transitioning to a primarily “logged-in experience.”
The move is designed to protect its data from AI scraping, allowing the company to instead forge lucrative licensing deals with model providers. But just as important, such a shift could help Reddit to increase its revenue even as it faces daily active user declines in its largest market, the U.S.
Overall, Reddit’s global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in Q3 and were down 2% year-over-year.
The company is not alone in seeing such declines; the shift to an AI-centered web has impacted most websites and publishers by now, leading to fewer click-throughs, as AI summaries provide answers that don’t require website visits and Google’s traditional “ten blue links” have reduced relevance. (The change is now even impacting Google’s bottom line, its earnings revealed.)
But at Reddit’s scale, the numbers associated with such a decline are enormous. The company said search traffic referrals dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October. It warned that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low-double-digit percentage by next quarter. (To play that out: a hypothetical 10% to 12% decline could bring Reddit to roughly 115 million to 117 million daily actives, down from 130.3 million in Q3. That’s a huge drop!)
At the same time, Reddit has gotten significantly better at monetizing its audience even as its growth weakens. Revenue increased 53% year-over-year to $895 million, ahead of Wall Street’s expectations of about $875 million. Net income rose 74% to $283 million. Advertising revenue grew 54% to $847 million while nonadvertising revenue, which includes its AI data-licensing business, grew 35% year-over-year to $48 million.
And despite a 2% year-over-year decline in U.S. daily users, Reddit’s average revenue per daily active user in the U.S. rose 53% to $13.82. Globally, average revenue per daily active user increased 36% year-over-year to $6.87.
Shifting to a logged-in experience could boost those numbers even higher because logged-in users are typically worth more to advertisers.
Unlike the logged-out users who often find their way to the site via search, logged-in users provide more signals about their interests and behaviors, which helps to better target and personalize ads.
Those same signals would also help Reddit provide a more personalized experience to its users, which includes personalized feeds, recommendations of new communities to subscribe to, and pushes to vote, comment, participate, and more. (This also includes pushing recommendations to its new algorithmic “For You” feed, announced yesterday, which will combine posts from communities users belong to alongside other recommendations based on their interests.)
Still, a change of this magnitude could be the canary in the coal mine for the open web.
“I don’t know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it’s a big change for me,” wrote Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman in a post published on Reddit’s site. “But I’ve come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business,” he said.
The company notes that the shift to the logged-in experience will not be an overnight change; it will first run tests in select markets outside the U.S. in the fourth quarter. It doesn’t yet have a timeline for when the change will be rolled out to all its users worldwide. It also acknowledged that access to a logged-out front page is important.
Plus, Reddit pointed out that being logged in doesn’t mean having to give up anonymity, nor will it remove its option to browse anonymously through its “incognito mode” experience, which is being rebuilt.
“There are still plenty of questions that are unanswered, particularly around where the boundaries should be between logged-in and logged-out experiences,” Hoffman wrote. “This is a big evolution for Reddit, and not one we’re taking lightly. But I believe it’s the right next step for the platform and for our future.”

articles.title: Estados Unidos cree que el CEO de NVIDIA fue blanco de una espía china
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, el CEO de NVIDIA, está siendo noticia y no por los avances de su compañía en materia de hardware para inteligencia artificial o gaming. Un reporte de The New York Times afirma que el líder de la tecnológica desarrolló una "relación cercana" con una supuesta espía china.
Puntualmente, la publicación habla del caso de una mujer identificada como Alice Huang o Huang Le, ejecutiva de la empresa Megaspeed. Dicha firma tiene sede en Singapur y se desempeña en la industria de los centros de datos, siendo cliente de NVIDIA.
El citado medio indica que la administración de Joe Biden puso en marcha una investigación para determinar si Megaspeed estaba violando el bloqueo que Estados Unidos le impuso a la compra de chips de IA avanzados por parte de China. Como parte del procedimiento, la inteligencia americana descubrió que Alice Huang habría estado enviando información hacia el gigante asiático.
De acuerdo con NYT, Jensen Huang no habría tenido conocimiento de la aparente conexión entre Alice Huang y las autoridades chinas. No se sabe si la ejecutiva en cuestión habría accedido a algún tipo de información confidencial de NVIDIA, aunque la empresa ha salido a aclarar que nunca comparte datos secretos con clientes.
John Rizzio, vocero de NVIDIA, le dijo a la publicación que Jensen Huang se reúne con miles de clientes todos los años y que no hay nada raro en su vínculo con la presunta espía china. "Las interacciones de Jensen con la señora Huang no son inusuales ni inesperadas. Reunirse con clientes es parte del trabajo del CEO", sostuvo.
Una supuesta espía china se habría acercado a Jensen Huang, CEO de NVIDIA
Si bien la investigación sobre Megaspeed se puso en marcha durante la parte final del gobierno de Biden, continuó cuando Donald Trump asumió su segundo mandato presidencial. The New York Times dice que se informó al actual mandatario estadounidense sobre la situación de Jensen Huang y Alice Huang hace más de un año. No obstante, optó por no tomar ningún tipo de acción.
El reporte incluso menciona que no se alertó al CEO de NVIDIA sobre el acercamiento de la aparente espía china. El medio indica que esto muchas veces sucede para que los blancos bajo vigilancia no adviertan que están siendo monitoreados. De todos modos, no se sabe si la falta de aviso a Jensen Huang fue para evitar que Alice Huang se espantara o sospechara.
Las acusaciones sobre posible contrabando de chips de IA hacia China por parte de Megaspeed ha sido investigado previamente por NVIDIA. La empresa sostiene que no ha encontrado pruebas de que esto realmente sucediera, mientras que la firma con sede en Singapur se ha mostrado dispuesta a colaborar con la Casa Blanca.
Pase lo que pase con el caso de Jensen Huang y Alice Huang o Huang Le, los casos de espionaje contra las principales tecnológicas estadounidenses no son nuevos. Poco tiempo atrás se descubrió que un empleado de OpenAI había escondido una grabadora en una sala de reuniones y que aparentemente tenía vínculos con la familia real saudí.
La preocupación más grande en el caso de Jensen Huang no es solo por la información de NVIDIA que podría exfiltrarse, sino por cómo China estaría logrando acceso cercano a los principales líderes tecnológicos globales. No olvidemos que el gigante verde hoy es la principal empresa mundial en términos de valor de mercado con 5,17 billones de dólares.

articles.title: Intel says it’s selling every affordable laptop chip it can make
articles.text:
During Intel’s latest earnings call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said that demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply.” According to CFO David Zinsner, the chips are now sold out. Zinsner said Intel has “seen significant growth in Wildcat Lake. It’s coming exactly at the right time because it’s cost-optimized and we’re seeing a lot of focus in that regard.”
Intel says it’s selling every affordable laptop chip it can make
Intel’s CFO says it’s ‘not optimistic about next year in terms of memory.’
As shortages of RAM and other components have driven up PC prices over recent months, Intel’s Wildcat Lake chips have been appearing in new lower-cost Windows laptops on par with the MacBook Neo, like the new Dell XPS 13 or the HP Omnibook 5 14. Wildcat Lake laptops like these have budget-friendly starting prices, but often with just 8GB of RAM, which Windows laptops can struggle to get by on.
Intel doesn’t expect the memory shortage to improve any time soon. Zinsner responded to a question about memory supply, saying, “Make no mistake, we are not optimistic about next year in terms of memory.” He added, “we’ll, you know, have to see in ‘28 whether things improve, but our expectation is that it does not improve in ‘27.” That’s more optimistic than SK Hynix’s prediction that the RAM shortage will drag on through 2030.
Tan also acknowledged the PC demand slowdown, saying, “The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in the [sic] history, driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence,” referring to AI. Zinsner went on to respond to a question during the earnings call, saying, “We do think the PC is going to go through a renaissance despite this.”

articles.title: Auto-Generation Of Properties: Methodology Insertion
articles.text:
Technology is only useful if it improves an existing methodology. Property generation is still refining that goal, but in the long term it could be very useful.
Key Takeaways:
A top-down semiconductor development flow has long been a goal for chip design, and shift left is certainly making that increasingly possible. The problem is that the starting point — the specification — is often incomplete or nonexistent, because the chip industry has been notoriously bad at writing specifications.
There are several ways to insert AI into existing flows. But just because something can be done doesn’t mean it should be. This is one of the big challenges facing AI adoption. Many existing tasks could be done more efficiently using an agentic flow, but it’s not clear whether that is the right thing to do.
This limitation becomes especially apparent when AI starts to help with something that has been woefully inadequate in the past — the creation of good, complete specifications. The big question is whether AI can enable designs, or verification environments, to be automatically derived from a specification. Perhaps a more correct goal is whether AI can help create better specifications. With better specifications, downstream design becomes a lot easier.
“AI can generate a SystemVerilog assertion in seconds,” says Ben Cohen, verification technologist and book author. “Whether that assertion means anything depends entirely on what it was generated from, and in practice that source is rarely a single, clean, natural-language specification. It is just as often an ambiguous paragraph that needs clarifying before it can be trusted.”
Solving this problem should be considered a high priority. “The increasing complexity of modern SoC designs is making AI-assisted artefact generation and verification closure a practical requirement rather than a research option,” says Simon Davidmann, AI and EDA researcher at the University of Southampton. “The verification problem is, in practice, already at the scale where it cannot be addressed without AI assistance. The 5-to-1 ratio of verification engineers to designers in processor development is not a workforce planning anomaly, but a signal that the complexity has outgrown the methods.”
Going from specification to anything is not a reality today. “If we are actually going to make this reality, we need more discipline in terms of writing the spec,” says Ravindra Aneja, director of applications engineering at Synopsys. “If we really want to make it a reality, we have to work on it. As an industry, are we there? No, we are not there. I don’t think we are at a place where, either starting a new design or doing a derivative design, you can say the spec is good enough.”
Are we even thinking about it in the right way? “A prose specification document is not something a formal tool can reason over directly, because formal engines operate on precise, unambiguous, machine-checkable statements, not natural language,” says Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “What AI can help with is narrowing that gap, translating prose into candidate formal statements faster, which is really what deriving properties from specification means in practice. The properties are the formalization of the spec, not a separate step after it. So rather than thinking of it as spec first, then properties, then formal proof, it is more accurate to say the property set is the machine-readable spec, and formal is working on the spec once that translation has happened.”
Sometimes, specifications are purposely ambiguous. “Human designers interpret them with domain knowledge, prior experience, and the ability to ask clarifying questions,” says Southampton’s Davidmann. “AI models receive the specification text and generate output without the ability to flag ambiguity or identify inconsistency. Specification ambiguity is likely a significant contributor to LLM-generated code failures, but the current research literature does not yet systematically characterize how often this is the root cause, as distinct from model capability limits. The next step is developing methods for automated specification analysis that can identify ambiguity before it enters the generation pipeline.”
Should the problem be looked at the other way around? “Rather than having formal work on specs directly, there is a strong argument that modern spec authorship should be formal and machine-readable by construction,” says Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer at Normal Computing. “This is the only way to solve the inherent problems of trust, coverage, and drift. This is structurally impossible using only existing formal methodologies, but is achievable if you can use novel solvers and languages like Lean.”
That can feed the long-term goal. “I want to give a spec to my large language model, and I want it to generate code,” says Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at Cadence. “But how do you capture the true intent of what a spec is, and make sure that is what you’re using as your single source of truth? There are a lot of things that must be explored, things that existing specifications just take for granted.”
There is probably room for an iterative approach. “When you read RTL, it can give you some abstract information about what your RTL is trying to do,” says Synopsys’ Aneja. “It may not be perfect, but it can give you a good starting point, and then you can modify that spec in an incremental manner. You can go from there. It’s not perfect, but at least it gives you a reasonable starting point.”
Skills migration
One of the supposed advantages of auto-generated properties is that it would reduce the need for specialized verification people. This may not be the case.
“For teams without internal formal expertise, complex AI-generated formal properties can be a boondoggle to review and maintain, and there are well-understood boundaries to the utility of SystemVerilog assertion-based methodologies,” says Normal’s Srinivasan. “The key principle is internal consistency. How can heavily AI-driven design processes leverage formal as both a check against other AI-driven design and verification collateral, but also utilize other collateral as a check against spurious or incorrect formal properties? Users that place stable systems of record and internal consistency at the heart of their processes will be better placed to utilize these systems in a zero-trust fashion.”
Someone still must read each generated SVA property. “They need to judge whether the antecedent is too weak or too tight, whether the consequent captures the actual requirement, whether clocking and reset conditions are handled correctly, and whether the property could pass vacuously,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “That requires fluency in temporal logic and assertion semantics, as well as deep understanding of micro-architecture. Without that skill, a team has no way to tell a strong property from a weak one that happens to look similar, and they will not know how to interpret a formal tool’s counterexample or a ‘proven’ result correctly either. So the practical requirement is that AI lowers the writing burden but raises the importance of having formal-literate engineers in the loop to interpret and validate the output. Organizations adopting this should budget for that expertise rather than assuming the tooling removes the need for it.”
There are some roles where formal properties may be more beneficial than others. “Formal verification is becoming a more important part of the solution,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “It is particularly strong for architectural compliance — ensuring ISA properties hold for all legal instruction sequences — and for enforcing correctness of hardware protocols in implementation verification. But formal is not a replacement for dynamic verification or system-level validation, especially when full SoC behavior and real workloads are involved. In practice, formal methods play a complementary role, proving deep corner-case correctness, while simulation and emulation establish end-to-end completeness.”
Problem areas
Vacuous assertions are a specific accuracy risk that deserves direct attention. “A vacuous assertion is an SVA that compiles correctly, passes the formal tool, and covers exactly nothing, because it is always true regardless of what the design does,” says Davidmann. “Vacuous assertions are not the same as correct assertions. A model that produces plausible-looking but vacuous SVAs provides false confidence while consuming formal tool capacity. A version of this technology that looks accurate on paper and is genuinely dangerous in practice is the one where the model is confident and wrong, the testbench was also generated by the model, and no one in the loop had the domain knowledge to notice. This is not a hypothetical failure mode. It is a workflow that is easy to construct inadvertently.”
There are significant costs associated with them. “In a formal verification flow, these errors are expensive,” says Cohen. “They consume tool runtime, engineer debug time, and — most critically — erode confidence in the verification results themselves.”
Formal verification involves multiple types of solvers, one of which is satisfiability modulo theories (SMTs). These look at determining whether a mathematical formula is satisfiable. “For agentic systems that put formal tools in the loop, there is a non-trivial cost from SMT solver runs,” says Srinivasan. “In addition, these scale with the complexity of the design and number of properties.”
Getting started
Deciding how to start using properties as part of a methodology is not obvious, and there are several issues that must be considered. There is also no single methodology that has been well tested, and it is likely that every company may need to work out what gives them the best balance of skills, time, and compute commitment, and the highest degree of verification closure.
AI needs to learn how generated properties are going to be used. “There are assertions for simulation and assertion for formal,” says Aneja. “There are techniques where you can write formal friendly properties, and that helps you with scaling in terms of, ‘Can you get a definite answer depending on how you’re writing the property?’ When you’re trying to write these properties, rather than writing a very long property, you want to divide that function into multiple smaller parts. That gives you scalability. Then you’re not getting stuck on a behavior that takes 200 cycles to do anything meaningful because it won’t work in formal.”
“Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a principled solution,” says Cohen. “Rather than relying solely on what an LLM learned during training, a RAG-enhanced system queries a curated knowledge base at generation time — retrieving the specific rules, patterns, and lessons that apply to the task at hand. RAG rules represent years of accumulated application knowledge — rules derived from real projects, real tool behaviors, and real failures. They encode not just what is syntactically correct, but what is verifiably sound; the difference between an assumption that constrains the environment appropriately and one that makes the formal proof space unreachable; between a property that checks the right behavior and one that passes vacuously; between timing diagrams that match the generated code and ones that silently diverge.”
There are stepped approaches that could be tried. “There is an intermediate step called formal test plan, where if you have a perfect spec, it talks about what your design does, not what you want to verify,” says Aneja. “The idea is that with all these LLMs and agents, you have the ability to read text, look at timing diagrams, look at FSM diagrams, other pictures you may have, and then you can extract certain features based on the designs you are doing. And you can train your system to say, is it a CPU design? Is it a GPU design? Is it an AI accelerator? Go one level down, is it a memory controller? Is it an interrupt controller? Is it a bus bridge? Or is it some interconnect across different managers and subordinates? Depending on what that is, it can extract certain features that you may want to test.”
The same considerations go for choosing an LLM. “Domain boundary awareness needs to become a first-class engineering discipline,” says Davidmann. “Before adopting any AI model into a production flow, the right question is not only how accurate the model is, but what it was trained on, what that distribution does not cover, and how close the actual design is to that boundary. Every team deploying these tools should run a deliberate boundary-probing exercise on a representative sample of their most complex and novel design patterns, verifying the outputs independently against what a domain expert would produce. That exercise identifies where the distribution ends and the model uncertainty begins. Without it, deployment is proceeding without the information needed to manage the risk.”
Start small and build confidence. “Pilot on a bounded, well-understood block first, compare the AI output against an existing hand-written property set, and measure the gap before rolling this out broadly,” says Darbari. “Finally, this only works well alongside engineers who already understand formal methods. It is not a way to skip that expertise. It is a way to make expert engineers faster. This is one area where I’m seeing an interesting demand from bigger design houses. Management wants engineers trained in formal so they can drive the entire ecosystem of tools and apply methodology properly.”
It is also important that you consider the domain in which you are working. “Tooling is currently ahead of the governance,” says Davidmann. “Most teams do not yet have a standard for documenting which assertions are human-authored, and which are AI-generated, or what that distinction means for sign-off confidence. In addition, most vendor documentation does not specify the training scope, failure modes, or domain boundaries of the models being deployed. Both gaps need to close before AI-generated content scales into safety-critical designs.”
Leave a Reply

articles.title: How Ghana’s TrustCheck helps shoppers vet online sellers before they pay - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ghanaian startup TrustCheck has built a review and trust platform that allows consumers to check out businesses, especially social media sellers, before they part with their money.
Launched in January of this year by Elliot Brenya, Tema-based TrustCheck lets users look up a business, read verified customer reviews, and see a trust score out of 100. The score combines a business’s rating, review volume, how responsive it is to customers, verification status and any open disputes.
“A lot of buying in Ghana now happens on Instagram, TikTok, X and WhatsApp. You see a product, message the seller, send money by Mobile Money and hope it arrives,” Brenya told Disrupt Africa. “Most of the time it does, but when it doesn’t, there is usually no way to get your money back and no record that warns the next person. TrustCheck is meant to be that record.”
Brenya was inspired to build the platform after being scammed while buying a mobile device, having relied on fake ratings for the vendor.
All reviews on TrustCheck are moderated before going live, and reviewers can attach proof of purchase, such as MoMo receipts or order chats, which only moderators can see. Businesses cannot pay to have reviews removed, but can claim their pages for free, respond to reviews and apply for verification. This month the startup also launched a scam check for phone numbers, MoMo numbers, social media handles and websites, as well as a public API that returns a business’s trust score.
“There are global review sites, but they were built around formal businesses with websites and card payments. The sellers people in Ghana worry about most are an Instagram page, a TikTok shop or a WhatsApp number,” Brenya said. “Nothing gives you one searchable place, built for how people here actually buy and pay, that you can check in a minute before sending money.”
The platform is free for shoppers, and makes money by charging businesses for verification and premium tools. It also runs display advertising. Bootstrapped so far, TrustCheck has around 300 registered reviewers and over 50 businesses listed, 20 of which have signed up to manage their pages. It has secured its first paying business customers, though Brenya said revenue remains small.
“Encouraging on the consumer side and slower on the business side, which is what we expected,” he said. “A page they don’t control, with reviews they can’t delete, feels like a risk at first. The ones who have engaged see it the other way round: a page with real reviews and replies is the best proof a small online seller can show a new customer.”
TrustCheck is focused on Ghana for now, but sees West Africa as the obvious next step.
“The problem is the same in Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Kenya and anywhere else where social commerce and mobile money have grown faster than ways to check who you are paying,” Brenya said.

articles.title: Before Your Small Business Buys an AI Assistant: The Data Groundwork Nobody Mentions - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Understanding the AI Assistant Landscape for Small Businesses
Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants have moved beyond sci-fi concepts and are now practical tools that small businesses can use to improve efficiency, customer engagement, and decision-making. From automating repetitive tasks like scheduling and inventory management to providing personalized customer interactions via chatbots, AI assistants promise transformative benefits. According to a recent report, 45% of small businesses plan to adopt AI technologies within the next two years, underscoring the growing interest in leveraging AI to stay competitive.
However, before your business invests in an AI assistant, there is a critical aspect often overlooked: the data groundwork required to ensure your AI solution works effectively and securely. Without a solid data foundation, even the most sophisticated AI assistant can fail to deliver value or, worse, generate inaccurate or biased outcomes that harm your business reputation.
Small businesses, in particular, face unique challenges when integrating AI assistants into their operations. Limited resources and expertise can make it difficult to prepare and manage the data that fuels AI systems. Unlike large enterprises with dedicated data science teams, small businesses often struggle with fragmented data stored across multiple platforms such as CRM systems, spreadsheets, and cloud services. This fragmentation can create blind spots in AI training and decision-making processes.
Many businesses trust 24×7 IT Solutions help streamline data management processes, ensuring systems provide reliable and secure data that AI assistants require. Proper data cleansing, integration, and management reduce errors and improve AI performance, directly impacting customer satisfaction and operational efficiency.
The Essential Role of Data Preparation
Data is the lifeblood of AI assistants. These systems rely on large volumes of high-quality, well-structured data to learn and perform tasks accurately. For small businesses, assembling this data isn’t as simple as plugging in an AI tool and watching it work. Raw data may be inconsistent, incomplete, or stored in disparate locations, making it unsuitable for AI consumption.
Studies show that 60% of AI project failures can be attributed to poor data quality or insufficient data preparation, highlighting the critical need for upfront data groundwork.
Building a Robust Data Infrastructure
Before deploying an AI assistant, small businesses need to invest time in establishing a data infrastructure that supports real-time data processing, storage, and security. This infrastructure should be scalable and adaptable to evolving business needs and AI capabilities. For instance, as your business grows, the volume and variety of data will increase, requiring flexible pipelines and storage solutions.
Data engineering plays a pivotal role here. Engaging with experts such as Atmosera for AI data engineering can help small businesses design and implement data pipelines tailored for AI workloads. This ensures that data flows smoothly from source systems to AI models, enabling timely and accurate insights. A well-designed data pipeline minimizes bottlenecks and prevents data loss or corruption, which are common pitfalls in AI projects.
According to a recent survey, 87% of businesses report that poor data quality negatively impacts their AI initiatives, highlighting the urgency of addressing data groundwork before AI adoption.
Data Privacy and Compliance: Non-Negotiable Foundations
Data privacy is a critical consideration when working with AI assistants. Small businesses must ensure their data handling complies with relevant regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), or industry-specific standards like HIPAA for healthcare. Failure to do so can lead to severe financial penalties and damage to customer trust.
Implementing robust data governance frameworks is essential. This includes defining who can access data, how it is stored and processed, and establishing protocols for data anonymization and encryption. For example, encrypting sensitive customer information both at rest and in transit helps mitigate the risk of data breaches.
Managed IT service providers can assist in creating these frameworks, providing peace of mind that your AI assistant operates within legal and ethical boundaries. Moreover, these providers can help implement continuous monitoring and auditing mechanisms to detect and respond to potential compliance issues proactively.
Measuring ROI Through Data Readiness
Investing in an AI assistant without proper data readiness can lead to suboptimal returns. Conversely, businesses that prioritize data groundwork often see faster deployment times, higher AI accuracy, and better decision-making capabilities. According to McKinsey, companies with mature data engineering practices report a 35% increase in AI project success rates compared to those without.
Furthermore, a well-prepared data foundation reduces the time and cost associated with troubleshooting AI errors or retraining models, accelerating the time to value. Small businesses should view data preparation not as a cost but as an investment that multiplies the value of their AI assistant over time.
Practical Steps for Small Businesses to Prepare Data
- Conduct a Data Audit: Identify all data sources, formats, and storage locations. Understanding your existing data landscape is the first step in preparing for AI integration. This includes structured data like sales records and unstructured data such as customer emails or social media comments.
- Cleanse and Normalize Data: Remove duplicates, correct errors, and standardize formats to create a consistent dataset. Data cleansing tools or services can automate much of this process, but human oversight is crucial to catch context-specific anomalies.
- Engage Data Engineering Experts: Partnering with specialists can accelerate building scalable data pipelines tailored to your AI needs. Experts can also advise on best practices for data storage, metadata management, and performance optimization.
- Implement Data Security and Governance: Ensure compliance with privacy regulations by setting up access controls, encryption, and auditing mechanisms. Define clear policies on data retention, sharing, and disposal to minimize legal risks.
- Leverage Managed IT Services: Collaborate with trusted providers such as to maintain the ongoing health and security of your data infrastructure. They can offer 24/7 monitoring, incident response, and continuous improvement strategies to keep your AI systems running smoothly.
Overcoming Common Data Challenges in Small Businesses
Many small businesses encounter specific hurdles when preparing data for AI assistants. Legacy systems may store data in outdated formats or lack APIs for easy integration. Additionally, limited staff expertise can hinder effective data management.
To overcome these challenges, consider incremental data modernization. Start by consolidating critical datasets into a centralized repository such as a cloud data warehouse. Cloud platforms offer scalable storage and built-in security features, reducing upfront infrastructure costs.
Training your team on data literacy and AI fundamentals is equally important. Understanding how AI uses data helps align data preparation efforts with business goals, ensuring that the AI assistant addresses real operational needs.
Future-Proofing Your AI Investment
AI technologies evolve rapidly. What works today may become obsolete as new models and data types emerge. Building a flexible and well-governed data foundation ensures your small business can adapt to these changes without costly overhauls.
Regularly revisiting your data strategy is advisable. Schedule periodic audits to assess data quality, compliance adherence, and infrastructure performance. Engage with managed IT and data engineering partners to stay informed about emerging tools and best practices.
Conclusion: The Hidden Investment in AI Success
Small businesses eager to adopt AI assistants often focus on the technology’s capabilities and overlook the foundational data work required. Proper data preparation, infrastructure, and governance are essential to unlocking the full potential of AI assistants. By investing time and resources in these areas, businesses not only improve the accuracy and reliability of AI but also safeguard their operations against compliance risks.
Partnering with experienced managed IT services and data engineering providers can bridge the expertise gap, making AI adoption smoother and more effective. Remember, the smartest AI assistant is only as good as the data it learns from. Prioritize your data groundwork today to ensure your AI assistant becomes a true asset for your business growth.

articles.title: Ace Blend bags $9.91M as it looks to scale science-led nutrition
articles.text:
Ace Blend bags $9.91M as it looks to scale science-led nutrition
The nutrition company will use the funding to advance research-led product development and launch patented nutrition formats.
Ace Blend, a science-led nutrition company, has raised $9.91 million in a Series A2 funding round led by 3one4 Capital, a venture capital firm whose portfolio includes Licious, Darwinbox and Kapiva.
Existing investor Fireside Ventures, an early-stage investor in consumer brands, has increased its backing after leading Ace Blend’s $3.3 million pre-Series A round.
The new funds will support research-led product development and the commercial launch of patented nutrition formats, with the first expected in the fourth quarter of FY27.
Founded in 2018 following more than a decade of research, Ace Blend develops supplements targeting heart health, immunity, sleep, recovery and brain health.
Co-founder Saif Mehkri joined in 2022, bringing nearly three decades of experience in the nutrition industry.
The company said its approach starts with clinical evidence, using research to determine a nutrient’s form, dose and delivery rather than building products around popular ingredients. It also controls sourcing, formulation and manufacturing, while clinical validation and automated testing are conducted by accredited laboratories in Europe.
Partnerships with ingredient suppliers DSM and TCI give it exclusive rights in India to certain technologies, according to the company.
Ace Blend claims 300% growth in FY26, with more than 46% of its customers returning to purchase.
Fireside Ventures principal Ankita Balotia cited repeat purchases and word of mouth as evidence of consumer trust. However, repeat buying alone does not independently establish a supplement’s clinical effectiveness.
3one4 Capital managing partner Pranav Pai said the company was “tackling the hardest problems in nutrition”, including developing formulations suited to Indian needs and maintaining consistent quality.
The funding comes amid wider investment activity in Indian nutrition. TruNativ raised $30 million in June, led by healthcare investment firm OrbiMed. In July, daily supplement brand Supply6 secured Rs 48 crore from Unilever Ventures and Zeropearl VC. More recently, The Stack raised Rs 21.5 crore in October to expand research and its product portfolio.
These investments point to growing investor interest in differentiated formulations, product innovation and repeat demand in a crowded market.
Regulation remains important as brands make increasingly specific health claims. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has regulations covering health supplements and nutraceuticals, alongside separate rules governing advertising and claims.
In February, the government said there was no dedicated Ministry of Food Processing Industries scheme for nutraceuticals, although broader food-processing programmes support infrastructure development.

articles.title: Chrome extensions with 13.4 million installs caught hijacking searches
articles.text:
A massive search-hijacking campaign involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations redirected users' searches through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo.
A new report by Socket's John Tuckner expands on the researcher's April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with 6 million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users.
"These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," explained Tuckner.
The extensions, with the full list shared at the bottom of Socket's report, pretend to be PDF converters, manual finders, safe search, and AI search tools. However, for the most part, the extensions simply redirect users' searches through a series of sites until they land on Bing or Yahoo.
Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, Google's official portal for Chrome add-ons, Socket says they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store.
Instead, the extensions are promoted through shady advertisements found on websites.
Tuckner explains that many of these extensions need almost no code to achieve their goal, as Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_overrides' setting allows them to replace the default search provider.
One example analyzed in the report includes only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, content scripts, or requested permissions.
Browser-hijacking extensions like these have long blurred the line between potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) and malware, with BleepingComputer reporting on hundreds of similar extensions over the years.
Risk extends beyond ad fraud
The extensions currently focus on revenue generation through search referrals, passing user searches through an operator-controlled server before they reach Yahoo or Bing.
However, Tuckner warns that the final destination can change at any time without updating the extension, including redirecting users to phishing sites or malicious downloads.
"The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," explains Tuckner.
An example of this is the Predator Search extension, which redirected Tuckner to four different sites when performing six identical searches.
"Six identical searches sent through its proxy search server ended in four different places: straight to Yahoo with partner tags (hspart=sz&hsimp=yhs-026), a landing page on searchlio.net, a hop through searchtosearch.com to a second results domain (mcftink.com) before Yahoo, and a Cloudflare non-responsive error page," Tuckner reported.
"The extension never changed; the proxy chose each destination as the search came in."
The largest recently active cluster of extensions is "Bing-Search," with 37 extensions and 2.2 million users, often promoted through Bidbrain ads. Another one is the "SecuryBrowse" wave, with 58 extensions and 4.9 million users, promoting security-themed add-ons like Fire Shield, Securify, and WatchTower.
The researcher said most of these extensions had been removed from the Chrome Web Store when the report was published. However, new ones are constantly being added.
Users should uninstall the extensions listed in Socket's report from their web browsers, run a full AV scan on their systems, and avoid downloading unnecessary tools and browser add-ons from unknown publishers.
BleepingComputer has contacted Google for a comment on Socket's findings, but we have not received a response by publication.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Fin du démarchage téléphonique : 43 000 signalements recensés en deux mois, malgré l’interdiction
articles.text:
Fin du démarchage téléphonique : 43 000 signalements recensés en deux mois, malgré l’interdiction
Depuis l’interdiction du démarchage téléphonique non consenti cet été, 43 000 signalements ont déjà été déposés. Un nombre moins important qu’auparavant, mais qui témoigne de la persistance d’une pratique pourtant hors la loi.
Les appels commerciaux indésirables continuent de perturber le quotidien des Français malgré le durcissement récent de la législation. Depuis le 11 août 2026, tout démarchage non sollicité nécessite pourtant le consentement explicite, préalable et traçable du consommateur. Mais entre début août et fin septembre, la répression des fraudes (DGCCRF) a tout de même recensé quelques dizaines de milliers de signalements, preuve que certains professionnels du secteur contournent ouvertement la loi.
Un volume d’alertes encore difficile à interpréter selon la répression des fraudes
Au total, ce sont 43 000 signalements de démarchage téléphonique non sollicité qui ont été déposés de début août à fin septembre sur la plateforme SignalConso et sur feu Bloctel durant ses derniers jours d’activité. Plusieurs acteurs continuent donc de passer outre la loi, alors que la nouvelle réglementation leur impose désormais d'obtenir l'accord explicite des particuliers avant tout appel. À noter, de nombreuses plaintes enregistrées concernent des appels liés à la rénovation énergétique, un secteur où le démarchage téléphonique est pourtant proscrit depuis 2020.
Pour la répression des fraudes, il reste néanmoins “trop tôt pour tirer des conclusions” sur l’évolution réelle du nombre d’appels reçus. L’administration souligne d’ailleurs que le suivi des plateformes ne montre pas d’augmentation marquée des plaintes par rapport aux années précédentes. À titre de comparaison, plus de 150 000 signalements avaient été enregistrés sur les premiers mois de 2026. Sur l’ensemble de l’année 2025, la DGCCRF avait comptabilisé 287 000 alertes, contre 266 000 en 2024, tout en infligeant plus de 11 millions d’euros d’amendes aux entreprises en infraction.
Avec cette réforme, l’exécutif espère endiguer les sollicitations abusives, massivement rejetées par les consommateurs et qui débouchent régulièrement sur des escroqueries. Selon une enquête publiée en février par l’association Que Choisir Ensemble, 97 % des Français se disaient “agacés” par ces appels incessants. Reste donc à patienter encore quelques mois pour avoir les premiers rapports jugeant de l’efficacité ou non du dispositif, qui devrait se concrétiser via de futurs contrôles et sanctions appliquées aux sociétés récalcitrantes.

articles.title: Hay juntas presionando a vecinos morosos negándoles la llave del ascensor. La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal tiene algo que decirles
articles.text:
Si formas parte del 65% de españoles que vivimos en pisos sabrás que la convivencia dentro de un mismo edificio no siempre resulta sencilla. Toca tomar decisiones conjuntas, limar diferencias y (en ocasiones) afrontar situaciones espinosas. Por ejemplo, cómo responder ante un vecino moroso. ¿Qué margen deja la ley para presionarlo y que se ponga al día con sus cuotas o derramas? ¿Podemos privarle del uso de una piscina, gimnasio o pistas de pádel comunitarias, si las hubiera? ¿Y el ascensor? ¿Puede la junta de propietarios instalar un cierre y negarle la llave al vecino moroso?
La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal es clara al respecto.
¿Hay deuda? No hay ascensor. Suena tentador. Cuando una comunidad de propietarios se encuentra con un vecino que no paga sus cuotas o derramas (y no es algo tan extraño) puede surgir la tentación de aplicarle un castigo. Por ejemplo, privarle del uso de instalaciones comunes. Al fin y al cabo… ¿Tiene derecho a disfrutar de la piscina, los jardines o un ascensor alguien que no contribuye a su mantenimiento? Llega una búsqueda rápida en Google para comprobar que es una idea que se le ha pasado por la cabeza a más de una comunidad.
La ‘Biblia’ de la convivencia. Como es habitual cuando hablamos de bloques de viviendas, las respuestas debemos buscarlas en la ‘Biblia’ de la convivencia: la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal (LPH). En ella se dedica todo un artículo (el 21) a aclarar cómo debe proceder una comunidad cuando se encuentra con un vecino que acumula deudas.
“La junta de propietarios podrá acordar medidas disuasorias frente a la morosidad por el tiempo en que se permanezca en dicha situación, tales como el establecimiento de intereses superiores al interés legal o la privación temporal del uso de servicios o instalaciones, siempre que no puedan reputarse abusivas o desproporcionadas o que afecten a la habitabilidad de los inmuebles. Estas medidas no podrán tener en ningún caso carácter retroactivo y podrán incluirse en los estatutos. En todo caso, los créditos a favor de la comunidad devengarán intereses desde el momento en que deba efectuarse el pago correspondiente y éste no se haga efectivo”.
¿Es un artículo importante? Mucho, porque en él se desliza una advertencia fundamental: las comunidades tienen cierto margen para reclamar deudas, pero en ningún caso pueden saltarse las líneas rojas que marca la ley. Y una de ellas (esencial) es que la “privación temporal del uso de servicios e instalaciones” no puede ser “abusiva o desproporcionada”. Tampoco afectará a “la habitabilidad de los inmuebles”.
Por lo general, los expertos consideran que vetar el acceso a zonas comunes resulta “controvertido”, pero una cosa es debatir si se puede o no restringir el uso de una piscina o un gimnasio (zonas recreativas) y otra muy distinta un ascensor. La LPH le otorga de hecho tanta importancia a los elevadores que prevé que si un edificio carece de él y un anciano lo reclama, la junta de vecinos deberá instalarlo sin necesidad de acuerdo. Eso sí, deben darse una serie de requisitos legales.
“Jurídicamente muy discutible”. Por si la LPH no fuera lo suficientemente clara, los expertos insisten en que las comunidades deben ser cautas a la hora de restringir el acceso a sus instalaciones. “Limitar el uso del ascensor solo a los propietarios que se encuentren al corriente de pago de las derramas o cuotas aprobadas resulta jurídicamente muy discutible y, en nuestra opinión, claramente impugnable ante los tribunales”, advierte Legálitas en El País.
“El ascensor forma parte de los elementos comunes del edificio y su utilización afecta directamente a las condiciones de habitabilidad y uso normal de las viviendas, por lo que la comunidad no puede privar a un propietario de su utilización como medida de presión frente a situaciones de morosidad”, recalca. No importa que la decisión tenga el aval de la junta. Que esté consensuada entre los vecinos no significa que “automáticamente” sea legal. “Cualquier propietario que se considere afectado podrá impugnar”.
¿No puede haber llaves entonces? Son cosas distintas. Como recuerdan los portales especializados Idealista y Fotocasa, no es extraño que haya comunidades de vecinos que decidan poner llaves a sus ascensores. De hecho, hay casos en los que hasta resulta comprensible. La clave es la accesibilidad del elevador y si la cerradura restringe o limita su uso a los vecinos del bloque, algo que puede resultar conflictivo.
Instalar una cerradura en el ascensor implica alterar un elemento común, con lo que de entrada la decisión de hacerlo o no deberá pasar por la junta de propietarios. Allí tendrá que lograr además un respaldo suficiente (tres quintas partes). Otro aspecto importante es para qué se instala la cerradura y, sobre todo, qué uso se hará de ella. Al fin y al cabo, la LPH aclara que no podemos dificultar el acceso de un vecino a su casa, con independencia de sus deudas.
La clave: la seguridad. Ese es el quid del asunto. No todos los edificios son iguales. Tampoco sus ascensores. Y hay ciertos casos en los que el uso de un sistema con llaves puede ser crucial para garantizar la seguridad de los propietarios y las viviendas. Por ejemplo, si hablamos de ascensores instalados en las fachadas y que por lo tanto son accesibles desde el exterior (algo no tan infrecuente) o que comunican con zonas privadas, como garajes y trasteros.
Incluso hay elevadores que conectan con balcones o el interior de viviendas, con lo que la instalación de un cierre con llave refuerza su privacidad. Es un matiz importante. LPH establece como actuación “obligatoria” las "obras que resulten necesarias" para “satisfacer requisitos básicos”, incluida la seguridad.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft va moderniser son application Windows Sécurité
articles.text:
L’application Sécurité Windows, qui intègre entre autres Windows Defender, le Pare-feu Windows ou encore Smart App Control, a pour objectif d’assurer toute la sécurité de votre PC. Mais jusqu’à présent, son interface utilisateur reposait sur les codes graphiques hérités d’anciennes versions de Windows. C’est sans doute l’une des raisons pour laquelle vous évitez soigneusement de l’utiliser quotidiennement. La bonne nouvelle, c’est que son interface devrait rapidement évoluer. Microsoft vient d’annoncer une refonte complète de son application.
Une interface modernisée en accord avec le design de Windows 11
Microsoft ayant récemment fait la promesse d’améliorer son système d’exploitation, une refonte globale de l’application Sécurité Windows était donc inévitable. Et la prochaine mise à jour du module, qui est pour l’heure testé auprès des Insiders, devrait s’articuler autour de quatre évolutions majeures.
La firme de Redmond explique ainsi s’être penchée sur la navigation de celle-ci. Les différentes pages de l’application vont être revues pour adopter une structure et une navigation plus cohérentes avec une meilleure adaptation visuelle lorsque la fenêtre est maximisée.
Les différentes commandes et éléments visuels vont par ailleurs être modernisés. Microsoft explique que les commandes, l’indicateur d’état, les typographies utilisées, mais aussi les espacements et les couleurs vont profiter d’une remise à niveau pour que l’expérience utilisateur soit enfin harmonisée avec le reste de Windows 11.
L’interface devrait également proposer une meilleure lisibilité des différents statuts et actions à prendre. La présentation des différentes informations de sécurité va ainsi être entièrement revue dans l’ensemble de l’application.
Microsoft a également indiqué qu’elle planchait sur un chargement optimisé des informations sur les appareils gérés. Concrètement, sur les machines professionnelles ou gérées au sein d’un parc informatique, les détails de sécurité vont se charger progressivement pour que les données soient affichées plus rapidement.
Le déploiement de cette nouvelle interface est pour l’heure testé dans la version 1000.29680.0.1000 de l’application auprès des membres du programme Insider. Il faudra donc patienter encore quelques semaines avant que cette nouvelle interface soit déployée à grande échelle auprès du public, sans doute dans une prochaine mise à jour du système d’exploitation.

articles.title: Police, procès, dossier vide au ministère : le FSD de Tesla tourne au vaudeville en Corée du Sud
articles.text:
Il n’y a pas qu’en Europe que le FSD de Tesla, son aide à la conduite supervisée, anime l’actualité. En l’espace de 72 heures, en Corée du Sud, plusieurs affaires ont attiré l’attention des médias locaux sur la technologie FSD de Tesla. Mais pas toujours pour les bonnes raisons.
D’un côté, la police de Séoul a transmis au parquet, ce mardi 27 octobre 2026, les dossiers de 80 automobilistes accusés d’avoir débridé illégalement leur voiture. De l’autre, le tribunal du district central de Séoul a rejeté ce jeudi 29 octobre la demande de remboursement de 88 clients de la marque. Entre les deux, Tesla tente d’obtenir une dérogation du gouvernement pour sauver les meubles.
Deux Tesla identiques, mais une seule a le droit d’utiliser le FSD
Selon les chiffres transmis par Tesla Korea au député Chang Jong-tae et publiés par le Korea JoongAng Daily, sur les 239 000 Tesla immatriculées en Corée du Sud fin septembre, seules 53 000 environ ont légalement le droit d’activer le FSD. Ces quelque 183 000 Tesla fabriquées en Chine (des Model 3 et Model Y), soit plus des trois quarts du parc, ne peuvent pas activer officiellement le FSD, alors même que leurs propriétaires ont parfois payé l’option jusqu’à 9 millions de wons (environ 5 800 dollars, soit près de 5 000 euros). Tout dépend de l’usine d’où sort la voiture.
En Corée du Sud, les modèles Tesla importés des États-Unis (Model S, Model X et les premières Model 3) profitent de l’accord de libre-échange américano-coréen (FTA). Leurs aides à la conduite sont homologuées selon les normes fédérales américaines (FMVSS), ce qui les dispense de l’homologation coréenne et permet à Tesla d’y activer le FSD par simple mise à jour.
Mais depuis que Tesla approvisionne massivement le pays depuis sa Gigafactory de Shanghai, la machine s’est grippée. Les Model 3 et Model Y « made in China » doivent répondre aux standards de sécurité coréens, qui suivent dans les grandes lignes les règlements de l’ONU, sans avoir encore adopté celui qui encadre les aides à la conduite supervisées (UN R171). Les normes coréennes sur les systèmes de direction imposent de garder les mains sur le volant et d’actionner soi-même le clignotant avant de changer de voie. Le FSD change de voie seul, sous la surveillance du conducteur : il est donc interdit sur ces voitures. Une situation que les clients de la marque peinent à comprendre.
Certains conducteurs débrident leur Tesla pour accéder au FSD
Face à ce blocage, certains propriétaires coréens ont décidé de se faire justice eux-mêmes. Un marché parallèle de boîtiers de débridage s’est développé.
Ce mardi 27 octobre, la police métropolitaine de Séoul a annoncé avoir transmis au parquet les dossiers de 80 conducteurs de Tesla et saisi 21 boîtiers non autorisés, achetés en Europe ou en Chine, ou fabriqués par leurs utilisateurs. Ces modules, branchés directement sur le bus CAN du véhicule, trompent les calculateurs pour contourner le blocage géographique et forcer l’activation du FSD.
La police invoque de graves risques d’accidents et de mauvaise interprétation de la route (ou de réactions inadaptées du véhicule). De son côté, Tesla menace depuis avril de faire sauter les garanties et a déjà banni à distance certains utilisateurs indélicats, se retrouvant dans la posture inconfortable de devoir traquer ses propres clients qui essaient juste d’utiliser ce qu’ils lui ont acheté. Une situation qui existe également en Europe et en Chine.
La justice a débouté les clients qui se plaignaient
En 2024, un groupe de 88 clients a attaqué Tesla Korea en justice, réclamant l’annulation pure et simple de leur contrat et le remboursement intégral de l’option FSD. Ils reprochaient à la marque de leur avoir vendu au prix fort, depuis 2017, des fonctions avancées de conduite assistée qu’elle n’a toujours pas pu déployer entièrement en Corée.
Selon Reuters, le tribunal du district central de Séoul a rejeté la plainte en bloc. Selon les juges, Tesla n’a pas commis de rupture de contrat dans la mesure où les acheteurs bénéficient déjà d’une partie des fonctionnalités promises (Autopilot de base et Autopilot Amélioré) et conservent leur droit aux futures mises à jour. Pour le tribunal, les clients « savaient » que le déploiement de telles technologies prendrait du temps et dépendait des évolutions réglementaires. Les juges estiment aussi que l’option FSD ne promettait pas une conduite entièrement autonome, sans intervention humaine.
Tesla Korea a déposé le 22 octobre une demande de dérogation auprès du ministère du Territoire, des Infrastructures et des Transports pour autoriser le FSD sur ses voitures fabriquées en Chine. Mais l’article du règlement invoqué (114-2) n’a jusqu’ici servi qu’à des équipements physiques, comme des systèmes d’éclairage ou des dispositifs qui évitent de se tromper de pédale. Le ministère reconnaît qu’il n’a jamais été appliqué à une mise à jour logicielle. Selon le Korea JoongAng Daily, le dossier de Tesla ne comporterait pas non plus les données techniques nécessaires à l’examen de sécurité, et le ministère prévoit de nouvelles discussions avec la marque.
Les clients coréens de Tesla gardent un œil sur l’Europe. Les Pays-Bas ont autorisé le FSD en avril, une dizaine de pays européens l’acceptent aujourd’hui, et les États membres de l’UE pourraient voter dès décembre sur une autorisation dans toute l’Union. Un responsable du ministère coréen dit suivre ces discussions internationales, même si elles ne le concernent pas directement.
