articles.title: Le pistage en ligne vous fait peur ? CyberGhost VPN est à -82 % pour Halloween, avec 2 mois offerts — Frandroid
articles.text:
Si des publicités pour des produits que vous avez déjà consultés sur internet vous suivent de site en site, ce n’est pas un hasard. Les pages web que vous consultez, les régies publicitaires et même votre fournisseur d’accès récoltent des données vous concernant. Mais lesquelles précisément ?
Pour mieux protéger votre connexion, CyberGhost chiffre le trafic sortant de vos appareils et masque leur adresse IP auprès des sites visités. Pour Halloween, son prix passe à 2,62 euros TTC par mois pendant deux ans avec deux mois offerts.
Qui se cache derrière le pistage en ligne ?
Les premiers observateurs de vos activités en ligne sont les services que vous utilisez. Un site marchand connaît les produits que vous consultez chez lui. Un réseau social sait sur quels types de contenus vous arrêtez de scroller. Dans ces situations, vous êtes déjà identifiable grâce aux cookies de navigation, même si vous visitez ces sites sans y être connecté, car ils sont stockés directement dans le navigateur web.
À cela s’ajoutent les partenaires publicitaires et data broker qui récoltent des données vous concernant sur de nombreux sites web afin d’établir un profil. Si vous faites des recherches sur des poussettes, vous serez tout de suite identifié comme un futur parent, et donc ciblé avec des publicités concernant la petite enfance.
Votre fournisseur d’accès récolte lui aussi un certain nombre d’informations vous concernant. Grâce au HTTPS, il ne peut pas lire le contenu des pages que vous visitez ni vos échanges, mais il voit les noms de domaine des sites consultés, notamment grâce aux requêtes DNS. Enfin, les FAI mesurent les horaires de connexion et le volume de données échangé. La loi française prévoit la conservation de ces données de connexion pendant un an.
Ce qu’un VPN change pour votre vie privée
Le rôle d’un VPN est justement de limiter votre exposition à ces pistages. Une fois activé, il établit un tunnel chiffré entre votre appareil et un serveur VPN distant. Le fournisseur d’accès voit ainsi que le trafic passe par un serveur VPN, mais il ne voit plus ni les sites consultés ni le contenu des échanges.
Les sites consultés, eux, ne peuvent lire que l’adresse IP du serveur VPN par lequel le réseau transite. Ils ne peuvent plus vous relier à l’adresse IP de votre smartphone ou de votre ordinateur.
Cette protection s’applique aussi lorsque vous utilisez le Wi-Fi public d’un hôtel ou d’un café dont vous ne pouvez pas vérifier la sécurité. Si quelqu’un s’infiltre dans le réseau, il ne peut pas lire les données qui transitent par le tunnel chiffré du VPN.
Il faut en revanche garder une limite en tête : changer d’IP n’efface ni les cookies ni les comptes connectés. Si vous ouvrez Instagram avec un VPN, le réseau social peut toujours vous identifier grâce à votre compte. Un VPN ne neutralise donc pas tous les pistages sur le web, c’est aussi à l’utilisateur de faire attention pour parfaire sa protection.
Les bons réflexes pour laisser moins de traces
Le premier réflexe consiste à refuser les cookies proposés à l’arrivée sur un site. Ce sont eux qui permettent de vous suivre de site en site, même si vous utilisez un VPN. Certains navigateurs ou extensions permettent de bloquer systématiquement les cookies tiers depuis les paramètres. Il faut toutefois noter que supprimer tous les cookies peuvent dégrader l’expérience de navigation web.
Pour compléter ces précautions d’usage, CyberGhost permet de protéger votre connexion en chiffrant le trafic entre votre appareil et ses serveurs, tout en masquant votre adresse IP et votre localisation exacte auprès des sites visités. Votre fournisseur d’accès et les sites consultés en apprennent ainsi moins sur vous, en complément des réglages contre le pistage.
Le service couvre aussi la plupart des appareils du quotidien : ordinateurs Windows, macOS et Linux, smartphones et tablettes Android et iOS, mais aussi Android TV et Fire TV. Un même abonnement protège jusqu’à sept appareils en même temps, et le service peut même être configuré sur un routeur compatible. CyberGhost s’appuie enfin sur un réseau de plus de 9 500 serveurs répartis dans 100 pays, pour choisir une connexion en France ou à l’étranger en fonction de vos besoins.
À l’occasion de la fête d’Halloween, le VPN de CyberGhost est en promotion au tarif de 2,62 euros TTC par mois pendant deux ans avec deux mois offerts.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : Samsung bientôt détrôné sur le marché des smartphones pliants ?
articles.text:
Samsung règne depuis des années sur le marché des smartphones pliants, mais l’arrivée d’Apple pourrait changer la donne plus vite que prévu. TrendForce estime que l’iPhone Duo pourrait déjà représenter près de 30 % du marché mondial en 2027, à quelques points seulement de son rival sud-coréen.
Apple n’aura peut-être pas à attendre plusieurs générations pour se faire une place sur le marché des smartphones pliants. Selon les dernières projections de TrendForce, l’iPhone Duo pourrait capter 29,8 % du marché mondial en 2027. Le cabinet tablait déjà sur 24,8 % en 2026, avec environ 5 millions d’appareils expédiés, alors même que le marché devrait quasiment stagner cette année-là.
L’iPhone Duo pourrait capter près de 30 % du marché en 2027
En 2027, le marché des smartphones pliants pourrait subir quelques perturbations avec l’arrivée d’Apple. TrendForce anticipe 23,5 millions de smartphones pliants expédiés dans le monde, soit une progression de 16,3 % sur un an. L’arrivée d’Apple pourrait contribuer à relancer la demande, alors que les fabricants Android devraient, quant à eux, traverser une période moins favorable.
Les délais de livraison donnent, selon le cabinet, une première indication de l’accueil réservé à l’iPhone Duo. Quelques heures après l’ouverture des précommandes, le site d’Apple annonçait des livraisons pouvant être repoussées jusqu’en janvier 2027 pour certaines commandes. Ce seul constat ne suffit évidemment pas à mesurer les ventes réelles (tout dépend aussi des stocks disponibles et des capacités de production d’Apple), mais va dans le sens des prévisions relativement ambitieuses de TrendForce.
Samsung conserverait la première place, mais son avance se réduirait
Sans réelle surprise, Samsung resterait en tête du classement en 2027, mais sa part de marché passerait de 35,1 % en 2026 à 31,9 %. Dans le même temps, Apple grimperait déjà à la deuxième marche du podium avec 29,8 %. L’écart entre les deux marques concurrentes ne serait alors plus que de 2,1 points. À la troisième place, Huawei, qui reculerait également de 24,8 % à 21,3 %.
On le rappelle : ces chiffres restent des estimations. Samsung conserverait donc potentiellement la première place dans le scénario de TrendForce, mais son avance serait malgré tout nettement réduite.
Pour le cabinet, l’atout d’Apple tient notamment à sa maîtrise conjointe des puces, du système d’exploitation et de l’écosystème d’applications. L’enjeu ne se limite pas à proposer un écran qui se plie, encore faut-il que les applications exploitent correctement la surface supplémentaire offerte par ce format et que le matériel résiste à une utilisation prolongée.
Force est de constater que sur ces deux aspects, l’iPhone Duo n’est pas encore totalement au point. Certaines applications affichent encore des bandes noires ou n’utilisent pas pleinement l’écran déplié. Des signalements de dalles fissurées ont par ailleurs remis sur la table la question de la fiabilité et du coût des réparations, surtout pour un appareil facturé au minimum 2 339 euros.
Une chose est certaine, la course au smartphone pliant ne se jouera pas uniquement sur les parts de marché. Pour Apple, il faudra transformer l’intérêt suscité par son premier modèle en demande durable. Pour Samsung, l’enjeu sera de préserver une avance qui, selon TrendForce, pourrait déjà se réduire à presque rien en 2027.
Sources : TrendForce, 9to5Mac

articles.title: Grey targets dollar-free payments for African businesses
articles.text:
Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, says it has built direct currency conversion routes to help African businesses pay suppliers across borders without first converting their money into US dollars, as it expands its services for businesses trading across the continent.
Speaking at a media briefing with journalists on the sidelines of Moonshot by TechCabal 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, on Thursday, Idorenyin Obong, Grey’s co-founder and chief executive officer, identified payment reliability and foreign exchange (FX) liquidity as two major challenges businesses face when making international transactions.
Payments between African countries can involve multiple currency conversions. For instance, a Nigerian business paying a supplier in Kenya may need to convert naira into US dollars before exchanging it for Kenyan shillings, adding another step to an already complicated transaction.
“Most times, if you’re trading within Africa, there’s always some form of intermediary currency,” Obong said. “We’ve built out these currency pairs, these exotic currency pairs, such that you never have to go in between to the USD.”
Obong said Grey has invested in payment infrastructure that allows customers in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana to collect and send money, supported by liquidity arrangements across multiple currencies.
The company said the infrastructure enables real-time settlement in several supported currencies, reducing the need for businesses to source FX through multiple intermediaries.
The problem extends beyond Grey’s customers. In October, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the global bank for central banks, said that many payments between African countries still pass through correspondent banking networks outside the continent, increasing costs and exposing businesses to operational risks.
Other payment providers are also trying to address the problem. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), developed by Afreximbank in partnership with African institutions, has been expanding local currency payment infrastructure.
In February, it partnered with Kenya’s Pesalink network to connect regional payments with Kenyan banks and mobile money providers.
Reducing currency conversion steps is only one part of the problem for Grey. Businesses also need assurance that payments will reach suppliers within an expected timeframe, particularly when delays can disrupt procurement and trading relationships.
Obong said customers moving amounts as little as $50, and larger amounts reaching $1 million, can experience uncertainty over whether funds will reach their destination when needed. To address this, Grey provides estimated payment delivery times and says it has invested in infrastructure to improve the reliability of its international payouts.
“We spent the last six years building the infrastructure to ensure that we’re delivering at the last mile at 99.99% to our customers,” Obong said.
In February, Grey expanded into payments and settlement for businesses, as its consumer transaction volumes grew. During the briefing, Obong disclosed that the company had processed more than 40 million transactions and nearly $5 billion in payments since inception.
Grey Business, its multi-currency platform for startups and small businesses, has processed nearly $100 million since launching in February, according to the company. By June, the company said that the platform had processed $61.4 million in its first four months, partly driven by demand for stablecoin-based payments.
The company has also expanded payouts to China, allowing businesses to pay overseas suppliers in Chinese yuan.
Beyond business payments, Grey is trying to solve another problem: what happens after individuals receive money from abroad.
Obong said the company initially launched in 2020 as a currency exchange service but expanded into foreign currency accounts after discovering that customers struggled to receive international payments in the first place.
Remote work accelerated demand for those services, especially among professionals earning foreign currencies while living in African markets.
“Most of our customers were using Grey to receive their foreign salary. And so we decided to build what I would call simply a salary account for these customers,” he said.
That insight led the company to build Paycheck, the salary product Grey launched on Wednesday. The service allows professionals earning in dollars, pounds, and euros to receive and manage their salaries, with features designed to separate money intended for spending and saving.
Obong said Paycheck also integrates with Pouch, Grey’s savings feature, which allows customers to set aside money for goals such as education, travel, or major purchases. The company is exploring additional benefits, including credit and lifestyle rewards.
The push reflects Grey’s ambition to build services around customers’ financial activities rather than simply helping them receive or transfer money.
Grey also faced questions at the briefing about difficulties some customers encounter when accessing foreign currency accounts and obtaining support.
The company said it offers round-the-clock digital assistance and has a physical office, although it considers online support more effective for routing customer issues to its distributed teams.
Grey’s next challenge is proving that its expanding range of services can solve these problems consistently.

articles.title: SecurityScorecard benchmark tests AI on third-party risk work and resistance to attack - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SecurityScorecard benchmark tests AI on third-party risk work and resistance to attack
Security ratings company SecurityScorecard Inc. today released an open benchmark for testing whether artificial intelligence models can handle third-party risk management work without being turned against the companies using them.
The TPRM Benchmark is built for vendor risk programs, where a model may need to interpret security telemetry and decide which exposures matter. A lot of what the model reads comes from questionnaires and documents that vendors filled out themselves, and parts of that may be incomplete or manipulated on purpose. SecurityScorecard says generic benchmarks built around static or academic tasks were not designed with that in mind.
On the capability side, tasks cover disciplines such as exposure triage and fourth-party technology risk, and each one starts as a snapshot of SecurityScorecard’s own vendor-risk telemetry that domain experts check before any model is scored. The answer keys are protected. Inputs rotate too, so a model that memorizes the test has less to gain.
Scores are measured against a baseline with confidence intervals attached, and each model gets an autonomy readiness level from L0 to L4 based on its performance across repeated trials. SecurityScorecard says the rating is meant to show how far a model can be trusted to work without human oversight.
Attack resistance is tested separately in the Model Security suite, which hits each model with prompt injection, jailbreaks and other techniques. Grades run from A to F. Some of the capability tasks are also seeded with deceptive vendor self-attestations that contradict the underlying telemetry, and scoring on those tasks shows how far the false claims pull down a model’s accuracy.
Performance in the early runs, which covered closed frontier, open-weight and international models, depended heavily on the discipline being tested. Open-weight models are closing the gap with leading frontier models on supply chain security tasks, according to Mike Mylrea, chief information security officer and chief AI officer at SecurityScorecard. Several of the open-weight models are “highly susceptible to adversarial attacks,” he said. The announcement did not identify the models tested or give their scores.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at developer security company Snyk Ltd., said the benchmark gives security teams “a shared, transparent way to evaluate models on capability and attack resistance together.” Snyk’s own research across 3,000 enterprise environments found that 74.5% of those with a detected model reference at least one that scores “high” on an attacker goal under adversarial testing.
Aleksandr Yampolskiy, co-founder and chief executive of SecurityScorecard, likened putting an untested AI agent into a vendor risk program to “giving a new employee privileged access on day one and hoping for the best.” A company that can’t say whether its model can do the work, or whether the model can be turned against it, has “a new attack surface,” he said.
SecurityScorecard has open-sourced the framework. Participants who download it can run their own models or agents and submit the results to a public leaderboard. A limited group of AI labs, security vendors and researchers is also being invited to help decide what the benchmark tests and how.
Version 2026.09 of the public release is available now with documentation, the Model Security suite and registration for the leaderboard. Official expert-verified scores come from SecurityScorecard’s live internal tier. A security team running its own tests on the public tier will get results marked synthetic-calibrated, which the company says are directly comparable for research and self-assessment. For a certified evaluation of a candidate model or agent, enterprises have to go to SecurityScorecard directly.

articles.title: La nostalgia llega a PlayStation 5: así son los nuevos mandos y carcasas inspirados en los años 90
articles.text:
Sony presentó una nueva colección de mandos DualSense para PS5 que recupera uno de los diseños más reconocibles de los años 90: las carcasas translúcidas que permiten ver parte de los componentes internos de los dispositivos.
La línea, denominada Prism, incluye tres versiones en naranja brillante, verde esmeralda y gris grafito, con un acabado transparente que busca recuperar la estética de una época en la que este estilo se popularizó en consolas, controles y otros aparatos electrónicos.
Los nuevos mandos estarán disponibles a partir del 4 de febrero de 2027, mientras que las reservas comenzarán el 10 de noviembre de 2026. La propuesta forma parte de la estrategia de Sony para ampliar las opciones de personalización de su consola de actual generación mediante accesorios con diseños diferenciados.
La colección Prism mantiene las características habituales del DualSense, el mando de PlayStation 5, pero introduce cambios en su apariencia exterior. El principal atractivo está en el acabado de la carcasa, que deja ver parcialmente el interior del dispositivo y combina ese efecto con colores intensos.
La compañía también difundió imágenes y un video promocional para mostrar los tres modelos. Por ahora, la información disponible se centra en el diseño y las fechas de lanzamiento de estos accesorios.
Así son los nuevos mandos DualSense Prism para PS5
Los tres modelos comparten la misma idea visual: recuperar la transparencia que caracterizó a numerosos dispositivos electrónicos durante los años 90. A diferencia de las carcasas convencionales, este acabado permite observar parte de la estructura interna del mando, aunque no significa que todos sus componentes queden expuestos.
Sony apuesta así por una tendencia que vuelve periódicamente al mercado tecnológico: recuperar elementos de diseño del pasado para ofrecer productos que se distingan de las versiones tradicionales.
Cuándo se podrán comprar los nuevos mandos de PlayStation 5
La colección Prism tiene previsto su lanzamiento para el 4 de febrero de 2027. Los usuarios interesados podrán reservar los mandos desde el 10 de noviembre de 2026, de acuerdo con las fechas anunciadas.
Por el momento, los datos proporcionados no incluyen los precios oficiales de cada modelo ni precisan si habrá diferencias de disponibilidad entre países. Estos detalles serán importantes para quienes quieran adquirir alguno de los accesorios desde el día de su lanzamiento.
Los mandos DualSense son uno de los principales accesorios de PS5 y se caracterizan por funciones como la respuesta háptica, que transmite sensaciones mediante vibraciones más precisas, y los gatillos adaptativos, capaces de modificar la resistencia de los botones según las acciones de cada videojuego.
La nueva colección se concentra en el aspecto exterior, por lo que no se ha anunciado que los modelos Prism incorporen cambios técnicos frente a los mandos DualSense convencionales.
La estética de los años 90 vuelve al diseño tecnológico
Las carcasas translúcidas fueron populares en distintos productos electrónicos durante los años 90 y principios de los 2000. Este estilo permitía observar parte de los circuitos y mecanismos internos, algo que contrastaba con los diseños opacos que predominaban en muchos dispositivos.
Con el paso del tiempo, la industria adoptó acabados más uniformes y minimalistas. Sin embargo, la estética transparente ha regresado en distintos accesorios y productos tecnológicos, impulsada por el interés en diseños retro.
En el caso de PlayStation, la colección Prism traslada esa tendencia a uno de sus accesorios más reconocibles. La propuesta combina el recuerdo de los dispositivos de décadas anteriores con el diseño actual del DualSense.
Una consola portátil de PlayStation también aparece en los rumores
Mientras Sony amplía las opciones de personalización de PS5, también circulan especulaciones sobre sus próximos dispositivos. Una de ellas apunta a una posible consola portátil vinculada a la futura generación de PlayStation.
El medio especializado Digital Foundry comentó la posibilidad de que Sony tenga algún tipo de exclusividad relacionada con AMD y la arquitectura gráfica RDNA 5 para un dispositivo portátil futuro. Sin embargo, esta información no constituye un anuncio oficial de la compañía.
Por ahora, tampoco se conocen especificaciones confirmadas, fecha de lanzamiento ni detalles sobre el funcionamiento de esa supuesta consola. La posibilidad permanece en el terreno de los rumores y no debe confundirse con las novedades anunciadas para los mandos DualSense Prism.
La colección translúcida, en cambio, sí tiene fechas previstas de reserva y lanzamiento. Con ella, PlayStation recupera una estética asociada a los años 90 y la incorpora a los accesorios de su consola actual, sin anunciar cambios en sus prestaciones técnicas.

articles.title: How Secure Are US Elections? Voting Machine Risks and the Growing Threat of AI
articles.text:
The integrity of the US voting system is a continuing concern, involving machine tampering, ballot counting, and voter influence. These all have some cybersecurity relevance. Other concerns include accurate voter registration, differing voter ID requirements across states, and the potential for voter fraud where identity verification measures are considered insufficient. Those are a different kettle of issues that are largely although not necessarily outside the scope of cybersecurity and not discussed here.
The Process
Voting: casting and counting
The US voting process is a state-run multi-stage operation. Processes vary by state and county. Most voters mark paper ballots by hand, but here we focus on jurisdictions that use ballot-marking devices for in-person voting, which carry the most cybersecurity relevance.
Furthermore, although voters may have the option for mail-in voting, we’ll focus on Election Day in-person voting via voting machines. Here, the voter indicates the candidate of choice on the voting machine. This machine is pre-certified by the Election Assistance Commission (EAC), and air-gapped for additional security.
The machine prints a paper ballot with the elector’s choice of candidate. This includes a human-readable element that allows the voter to visually check the accuracy of the vote. It usually includes a barcode or QR code containing the same information. The paper ballot is then scanned into the vote-counting part of the voting process. The paper ballot itself remains intact as an ongoing form of verification.
The scanned votes are counted by machine and delivered to the election officials. Further statistical manual checks may be used: does, for example, a small manual count of a portion of the paper ballots statistically conform with the overall machine-counted result?
This sounds straightforward and secure.
Influencing the vote
Received wisdom is that foreign nations attempt to disrupt US elections with influence campaigns targeting the voters. It is believed the primary motivation is to undermine confidence in democratic institutions. This is a valid concern, because lower public trust can lead voters on either side to question the legitimacy of an outcome.
Influence campaigns are particularly relevant to the US. The country is extremely partisan and almost exactly split between just two parties. Throughout this discussion it is worth remembering that small changes to the vote can lead to big changes in the result.
Hard proof of foreign influence campaigns is difficult. Nevertheless, the possibility for and potential effect of influence campaigns remains a serious concern.
Securing the integrity of elections
Voting and counting
US election voting machines are certified by the EAC. This certification is designed to ensure their security and applies to both the voting and counting machines.
Shai Bargil, co-founder and CEO at Sequent, is doubtful. There is no direct correlation of the certification process to the four-year election cycle and certification can occur in any of the four years. The certification process may take a year, but probably less than two years. In the worst case scenario, a voting machine whose certification began in the first year of the electoral cycle will have been sitting, untouched, for two years.
“That’s pretty ridiculous,” comments Bargil. “Software needs to be updated and patched pretty much continuously. In the commercial world we patch our systems every month, but for elections we are trusting software that hasn’t been patched for two years or more. In the final analysis, this EAC certification is pretty much meaningless.”
Additional security is theoretically applied by keeping the machines air-gapped. Air gaps can be bridged by someone who can get close to the target. So, now consider this scenario, which is implausible but possible. Certified machines are often taken to the Voting Village, a hands-on election‑security lab run at DEF CON. It gives security researchers, election officials, and the public legal access to real voting equipment so they can test the security (or insecurity) of them. Some of these machines are still in use in the current election cycle when they are delivered to the Voting Village.
“Basically,” continues Bargil, “every voting machine that has been delivered to a Voting Village has been successfully hacked once the hackers have hands-on access.” Going back to the length of the certification process and the fixed four-year election cycle, it is distinctly possible that the machine used to produce the ballot papers in an election is the same unpatched machine that has already been hacked.
It is equally possible to imagine that the same successful hacker could turn up to vote with everything necessary to repeat his successful hack installed on a USB stick. If this is done early in the morning, every subsequent voter at that machine may be using a compromised system doing who knows what. Implausible? Yes. Possible? Well…
Modern cybersecurity professionals would hesitate to claim voting machines are secure. But the problems don’t end there. The ballots (the slip of paper generated by the voting machine, designed to allow voters to visually verify the accuracy of their votes) are scanned into other machines and totaled before the result emerges at the other end. It’s effectively a black box process certified, possibly a year or more ago, by a third party that hasn’t patched the software for the same period of time.
Worse, while the ballot may provide human-readable confirmation of the voter’s selected candidate, the data scanned by the counting process is usually delivered by a barcode or QR code on the ballot paper. The voter cannot visually verify what is counted by examining a ballot paper produced by a voting machine that may have been hacked.
Bargil says this results in two primary problems. “One is that the voting machines are not to be trusted. The second is that the counting process takes too long and is also not to be trusted.”
The mistake, suggests Christiaan Beek, VP of cyber intelligence at Rapid7, is treating voting machines as the ultimate source of truth. “Treat them as one component in a broader, potentially hostile system,” he says. “Assume that the software may contain vulnerabilities, the firmware may be insecure, the supply chain may be targeted, an administrator account may be compromised, and a determined adversary may eventually gain access.”
His recommendation is to make any compromise as difficult as possible, to limit any blast radius and expose any manipulation, and to provide a way to reconstruct and verify the outcome.
Bargil has his own recommendations to improve security without radically changing the process. The first is to make all software used by the machines open source. “It can still be certified by the EAC, but if it’s open source, it basically means all the academics and security experts that typically review elections can see any potential problems.”
It’s not a 100% guarantee of the security and integrity of the software in use, but, he adds, “If you have open source software, I can use tools to check the code and do my own pentesting. I can use AI to speed the process, and confirm that the EAC and the vendor have done their job properly.”
His second recommendation would ensure the validity of the vote count. The voting machine software should be amended to generate an encrypted voting record sent directly to the counting system and used to count the individual votes.
“It provides evidence that every vote was correctly cast, recorded by the system and counted according to the voter intent: and this is mathematical proof that can be independently verified,” says Bargil, whose company develops verifiable voting software. This would be in addition to the paper ballot rather than simply instead of it.
Interestingly, the Microsoft ElectionGuard project, designed to help governments run secure, auditable and trustworthy elections, also proposes homomorphic encryption of the votes. This could ensure that all votes are counted, not altered, and that no votes were removed nor added to the process. ElectionGuard does not, however, suggest open sourcing the software, even though ElectionGuard itself is open-sourced by Microsoft.
In short, current US voting cannot be considered secure in strict cybersecurity terms, but there are options that would make it more trustworthy. This, however, still leaves the problem of third-party election influence campaigns unresolved. “The harder problems are on the perimeter – voter registration databases, county websites, the email accounts of campaign staff and election workers. Based on what we’ve seen, starting in 2016, this is where the adversaries focus. While the machines get the headlines, the operational layer around them is what actually protects the vote,” says Dave Gerry, CEO at Bugcrowd.
Election influence campaigns
Adam Marrè, former FBI special agent and now CISO at Arctic Wolf, explains the concern. “Elections have long been attractive targets for geopolitical actors because they provide an opportunity to influence public trust, shape political narratives, create division, and undermine confidence in democratic institutions.”
He suggests, “Most election-related activity today is not focused on changing votes. Instead, adversaries often seek to influence perceptions around the election itself,” citing “disinformation campaigns, social media manipulation, cyber espionage, phishing attacks targeting election officials, or attempts to disrupt election-related services.”
Bobby Ford, chief strategy and experience officer at Doppel, agrees with this view. “Today, attackers don’t need to infiltrate election infrastructure to have an impact. They can influence public perception through impersonation, fake websites, and AI-generated misinformation designed to create confusion, evoke urgency, or erode confidence in the process.”
Multiple sources claimed that Russia ran a pro-Trump multi-faceted influence campaign prior to the 2016 election. In 2017, the US intelligence community (CIA, NSA and FBI) said so. In 2019, special counsel Robert Mueller said so. And in 2020, the Senate Intelligence Committee said so.
More recently, in 2024, US intelligence agencies attributed a hack-and-leak operation targeting the Trump campaign to Iran.
Now AI is opening a new potential. “The simplest way to influence an election is to get voters to stay home. The simplest way to do that is with targeted robocalls and robotexts,” comments Alex Quilici, CEO at YouMail. On a relatively small scale, this has already happened with the 2024 Biden impersonation robocall in New Hampshire.
This was a deepfake Biden voice-impersonating automated robocall urging Democrats to stay at home and preserve their vote until the November election. It falsely suggested that their vote would only matter in November, not in the primary. This attack failed (the perpetrator said it was not a serious attack, but an attempt to open people’s eyes to the possibilities of AI), but is widely considered to be a landmark event suggesting an increased use of AI in future influence campaigns, where targeted suppression of one candidate could potentially elevate a different candidate into a winning position.
AI has become the joker in the pack of tools available to any third party wishing to influence the outcome of an election. Always bear in mind the finely balanced US electorate between the two major parties. Any attempt to change the outcome of an election would only require successful influence targeted at a few well-chosen voters.
Throughout this article we have discussed implausible but technically possible attacks on the voting process. We won’t stop now. Consider this hypothesis. On August 12, 2026, Google Search briefly reported that Sam Altman was dead. This was because it had found a ‘vandalized’ Wikipedia entry, and this much of our hypothesis is true.
Now imagine how a nation-state could use such an approach against a few selected candidates across the US. ‘Dead’ might be a bit extreme and too easily checked since it is a pure binary fact. Behavior, however, is associated with analog belief – so a campaign promoting a false rumor of insalubrious behavior prior to the vote could affect wide and negative attitudes toward a single candidate. With nation-state resources, this could include large-scale and amplified X tweets, and Facebook and LinkedIn posts. Carefully timed, it could succeed and effectively promote a different preferred candidate before being discovered – and changing a vote is difficult.
Even if an appeal is successful and a complete redo is initiated with the false rumor successfully countered (is that even possible since rumors tend to linger in the mind?), Marrè’s initial suggestion that the purpose of influence campaigns is to ‘undermine confidence in democratic institutions’ is successful.
As Ford suggests, “As AI makes these attacks more scalable and personalized, election security has become just as much about protecting trust as it is about protecting technology. That means defending election officials, campaigns, and trusted information sources alongside the infrastructure itself.”
Casey Erikson, director of penetration testing at NRLabs, adds, “In the end, every architectural decision carries a tradeoff. The objective is not to eliminate risk but to constrain it. It becomes about access control. Verifiable backups are essential, redundancy at multiple layers is best.”
Summary
The purpose of this discussion is not to criticize the US voting system, but to examine it through a cybersecurity lens. Looking at implausible but technically possible attacks shows that, in strict cybersecurity terms, no part of the process can be considered beyond compromise.
That does not mean US elections have been compromised. Election officials rely on layered safeguards, including pre-election testing, chain-of-custody controls, bipartisan poll workers, and post-election audits of paper ballots, and there is no evidence that machine tampering has changed the outcome of a US election.
A similar examination of voting systems elsewhere would likely reach the same conclusion. In the current digital and geopolitical climate, an absolutely secure election is essentially impossible – which is why verifiability, auditing, and public trust matter as much as the technology itself.

articles.title: Data breach at Sony ISP subsidiary exposes 2.5 million customer records as Japan hit with another major cyberattack
articles.text:
Data breach at Sony ISP subsidiary exposes 2.5 million customer records as Japan hit with another major cyberattack
Hackers are gunning for Japan's ISPs
- Sony Network Communications discloses breach affecting roughly 2.5 million ISP customers and former users
- Exposed data included personal details, while some email service users also lost email passwords
- Company contained the intrusion, notified authorities, and warned customers about phishing and fraud risks
A subsidiary of Sony Network Communications, the Japanese tech giant’s Internet Service Provider (ISP) arm, has confirmed suffering a data breach which saw it lose sensitive data on roughly 2.5 million people.
Among the stolen files were people’s phone numbers, email addresses, and in some cases - email passwords.
The company confirmed the news in an apology and notice letter in which it said threat actors accessed So-net, the company’s consumer-facing ISP service brand. The identity of the attackers was not disclosed, and nor was the method they used to break in. The breach happened on Monday, October 19 2026, and was spotted four days later, on October 23.
“Immediately after confirming the incident, we shut down the affected server and blocked communications from the source of the unauthorized access,” the machine-translated letter reads. A day later, the investigation determined that the attackers exfiltrated a total of 2,141,986 sensitive records belonging to both current and former members.
Trickling down to NTT Docomo
Of that number, roughly 1.8 million belong to current members, who had their names, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, genders, and internet connection IDs exposed to the hackers. Passwords were not leaked, Sony said.
There were also more than 440,000 records taken from plala (S Course), and this part also affects NTT Docomo, a separate internet service provider that uses Sony Network Communications’ underlying infrastructure as part of its service.
NTT Docomo issued a separate statement, notifying its customers of the incident, and urging them to stay vigilant with incoming emails and other communications:
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“There is a risk of suspicious communications from those who misuse potentially leaked information in the future,” the machine-translated notice reads. “Please pay attention to the following points:
・Do not respond to emails, SMS, or phone calls
・Do not open links in the body
・Do not open attached files.”
The company added that the incident affects all Hikari service clients, as well as those that cancelled from May 2026, onwards.
Some So-net members’ email addresses and email passwords were, indeed, taken. A separate set of data affecting Email Service (G), A-Box (an additional mailbox service), So-net VAIO Mail, and PostPet Mail Account Service was nabbed, and the company reported 24,655 affected addresses for Email Service (G), 17,672 for A-Box, 7,005 for So-net VAIO Mail, and 5,069 for PostPet Mail Account Service. The breach affects both current So-net customers, and those that cancelled their subscriptions in March 2026 or later. Those that cancelled by the end of February were not affected, according to the announcement.
Banking data struck, too
Some customers also had their banking data exposed - but not many. “We confirmed the leakage of 16 records containing bank account information, including financial institution name, bank code, branch name, branch code, deposit account type, account number, and account holder's name,” the company said.
It stressed that it does not hold bank account PINs and therefore, they could not have been compromised. “We will individually contact the affected customers to apologize,” the notice reads.
Sony Network Communications said it notified the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission and other relevant government and law enforcement organizations and is currently investigating the attack.
So far, no hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the attack, and the data has not yet appeared anywhere on the dark web. There is also no word of this being an extortion attempt.
The attack comes less than a week after Japanese internet giant GMO Group told its customers to scan their computers for viruses, back up all of their data, disconnect the devices from the internet and then shut them down.

articles.title: Fake PS5 emulators are being used to steal gamers' passwords — two well-known GitHub repos, including popular AnyPS5, get hit, infecting gamers' computers with password-scraping malware
articles.text:
Fake PS5 emulators are being used to steal gamers' passwords — two well-known GitHub repos, including popular AnyPS5, get hit, infecting gamers' computers with password-scraping malware
Emulators downloaded via GitHub may be stealing your passwords, with two well-known projects being exploited.
Malicious GitHub repositories masquerading as two well-known and legitimate PS5 game emulation tools have been identified as spreading malware that steals gamers' passwords. The malware uses self-signed certificates, created using fake company names and on the same day the malware was built — suggesting that the malware campaign may be automated. Just two minutes after infection, a cleanup script scrubs the affected computer of the malware's files, leaving no trace that it was ever present, according to a report shared with Tom's Hardware by NordVPN's Threat Intelligence research team.
The campaign trades on the back of the popularity of two projects that have become popular within the PS5 emulation community. AnyPS5 is a portability layer that allows PS5 games to run as native applications on both Windows and Linux. Kyttyps5 is an emulator for running PS5 games on PCs, and both projects are freely available for download via their respective GitHub repositories. However, users who visit one of the malicious repositories posing as these tools are directed to download a zip file containing a Windows executable. Notably, the GitHub repositories used as part of the malware campaign rapidly rotate, and it's possible that GitHub is not the only source.
The malicious executable unpacks a hidden application before launching its own multi-stage loader. It first checks whether the PC is a legitimate machine or a security researcher's sandbox by checking if less than 2GB of RAM is available, if it's a virtual machine, if it's running on a cloud-based server, or if it doesn't have a physical GPU installed. If any of those criteria are met, the loader exits silently. If the machine is deemed to be a legitimate target, the malware adds exclusion rules to Microsoft Defender to ensure that it will never be scanned and identified during an antivirus scan. Finally, the payload is decrypted and executed.
That payload, we're told, is an executable protected by a commercial packer that is believed to be an infostealer — a type of malware whose job it is to steal passwords as well as any other sensitive data that it comes across.
While this appears to be a relatively new malware attack, there are some steps that you can take to avoid falling foul of it. If you're trying to download tools like AnyPS5 and Kyttyps5, it's vital to ensure that the repository belongs to the official project team. Double-check the owner of the project, look for download links that use third-party destinations, and check metadata like the project and files' creation dates.
If you do find yourself in a position where you have accessed a suspected malicious download, disconnect your computer from the internet and run a full antivirus scan. It's also recommended that you change your passwords from a separate device where possible.
PS5 emulation is likely to become more popular than ever once GTA 6 is released on November 19, 2026. The game will be a console exclusive at launch, with a PC version expected to arrive in early 2027.

articles.title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together.
Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI.
Why Amazon Quick user groups matter
The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can:
- Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results.
- Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity.
- Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts.
- Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts.
- Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context.
Event overview
Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate, while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper.
What a typical event looks like
All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins.
From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience.
The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule.
What customers shared
Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments.
At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization.
By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa, a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5.
Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab, a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows.
        “What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.”
— Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab
The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story.
From presentations to participation
Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute.
Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges.
Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement.
Collective impact in action
A huge thank you to our dedicated AWS Partner, Data Reply, whose consistent contributions and thought leadership have been instrumental in making every UK user group meetup a success.
Our UK leadership team led us to reach every milestone:
Liam Yusuph, AI and Data Delivery Lead, Data Reply
Priyanka Bettaswamygowda, Solutions Architect, AWS
Sahar Shahbaz, Data Analyst, Data Reply
Sofia Bourika, Lead BI Developer, Arriva
Tobi Daramola, Senior Data and Analytics Lead, Carsa
Ali Hayat, AV Support Associate, Amazon
Lam Phan, BI Developer, AWS
Rikhi Singh, ADC Engineer, AWS
Amazon Quick Community resources
The Amazon Quick Community website has tens of thousands of members and thousands of searchable questions. It also offers over 600 learning resources on accelerating your productivity with agentic AI and Amazon Quick.
        “The Quick Community is about learning together and building connections. It’s where users at any skill level can find help, learn something new, and meet others. What I love most about the Quick Community is how genuinely helpful everyone is. It’s a place that reveals possibilities you wouldn’t have thought to explore on your own, where you stumble into people working on projects and use cases, you’d never even think to ask about, and suddenly your world gets a whole lot bigger.”
— Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, AWS
Learning opportunities include approximately two free live online sessions per week, monthly feature update detailed and advanced automation sessions, and 4-hour Immersion Day workshops. AWS Solutions Architects, Product Managers, and subject matter experts are active on the platform and available for direct messaging. Kristin continues, “People jump in to help solve tricky problems, share their clever workarounds, and experiment with new ways to use Quick together.”
Key takeaways
A few themes came up consistently across the three events.
The format keeps changing because we listen
The Amazon Quick User Group UK runs on a set structure: an introduction, a product update, customer stories, a hands-on workshop, and a feedback session. But we’ve been adjusting it every quarter. Early on, we had the “What’s New with Quick” segment right after customer stories, and it broke the flow. People were engaged with how a real company was using the product, then we’d switch to feature announcements. We moved “What’s New” so the customer stories lead straight into the workshop, and the difference was noticeable. For Q3, we added an interactive quiz to get more back-and-forth going in the room. Attendees also called out the overall format and pacing, and the chance to meet new people. As one first-time attendee put it, “the networking opportunities were excellent… I thoroughly enjoyed the day!”.
Customers present, not us
At least one customer shares how they use Amazon Quick at each event. Across three events, we’ve had Carsa, Arriva, Propulse Lab, and a few other customers on stage. After the very first event, one of the clearest pieces of feedback was that people wanted more customer speakers. That told us we were on the right track. The sessions work because the audience is hearing from peers who face similar problems, not from someone trying to sell them something. The impact goes beyond the event itself. Attendees said the customer stories showed them new ways to use the tools and started useful discussions about return on investment (ROI). One attendee told us a customer session “has already prompted a lot of conversation internally” at their organization.
The workshop is where it clicks
Every event has a hands-on workshop, and people consistently tell us it’s the part they get the most out of. There’s a gap between watching someone demo a product and sitting down with it yourself. That gap is where most attendees say Amazon Quick starts to make sense for what they’re trying to do. We know it lands because the most common question afterwards is whether they can keep access to the workshop environment so they can carry on experimenting on their own.
Conclusion
The success of this year’s meetups is a testament to every single member who showed up, shared their knowledge, and contributed to making this community what it is today. As we look ahead, we’re more energized than ever to keep this momentum going and continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with Amazon Quick.
Get involved
To learn more about Amazon Quick and connect with the community:
- Join the UK Amazon Quick User Group on LinkedIn.
- Join the Amazon Quick Community to learn agentic AI together and access over 600 learning resources.
- Explore Amazon Bedrock for additional generative AI capabilities.
- Register for the next UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup: January 28, 2027.
- Not in the UK? Attend a meetup in Austin, Phoenix, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, New York City, or Munich/DACH.
- Complete the leadership interest form to start an Amazon Quick User Group in your city.
For questions about the event or the Amazon Quick Community, Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, Amazon Quick Community and User Group program, at kmandia@amazon.com.

articles.title: Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: "There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors."
articles.text:
Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: “There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors.”
On Thursday, Mistral released the weights for its frontier open model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), on Hugging Face.
Made available for preview just three weeks ago, the French AI company says ML4 has significantly improved since then, thanks to reinforcement learning and testing with customers and partners. Now, it claims, ML4 is the “best open agentic coding model in the world,” beating GLM-5.3 on cybersecurity and coding benchmarks (though only barely on the latter), at a fraction of the cost, Mistral says.
“We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.”
From here, the AI company promises continued growth. In an embargoed press briefing attended by The New Stack, Pierre Stock, Mistral’s VP of Science, calls ML4 merely “a stepping stone,” saying, “We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.”
Mistral’s VP of Science doesn’t want to live in a world without open weights
Stock told reporters that Mistral fully supports “the power of open weight,” calling it essential to ensure business continuity, transparency, and auditability for everyone: “I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said.
“I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said.
Recalling when OpenAI announced plans to cut off Cursor’s direct access to its models or when the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals, Stock’s case for open weights bears weight — perhaps why he says the philosophy is in the French company’s DNA.
“Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity.”
“Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor or an oligopoly can cut off electricity from one day to another.”
Mistral puts open weights at the center of its approach. Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei has argued that open weights alone cannot resolve the concentration of AI power because access to computing infrastructure remains concentrated.
As Stock points out, this way, “nobody can switch it off because it can run either on your infrastructure or on an infrastructure that you can trust.”
Coding + cyber = the biggest impact
An open-weight model, though, does need the goods to back it up, and Mistral says ML4 is there, calling it “the best open model built in the West.”
To back those claims, the company points to Terminal-Bench 4.0, one component of Artificial Analysis’s Coding Agent Index, where, by Mistral’s numbers, Le Chonk — Mistral’s official nickname for ML4 — ranks as the top open model in the world for agentic coding, scoring 41% to Muse Spark Open’s 6%, Kimi K3’s 21%, and just eking past GLM 5.3’s 40%.
“What the graph doesn’t tell you,” Stock said, “is that it’s more efficient than the competitors,” adding that Le Chonk uses 47% fewer tokens per task on average than GLM 5.3. “It means that you can get things done way faster and at a lower cost,” he explained.
Coding prowess, however, wasn’t the startup’s only focus when training its model.
“We identified, really, coding and cyber as the two main areas that impact and that can benefit our customers and help them transform their entire business with AI,” Stock said in the briefing.
So Mistral backed investments to advance the model’s cyber capabilities. In CyberGym E2E from the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which tests defensive cybersecurity capabilities, the French model once again pulls ahead of much of the competition, scoring 79% to GLM-5.3’s 29% (though Z.ai’s smaller GLM-5.3 Flash scored 74% in the same chart). In Mistral’s comparison, ML4 exceeded DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 1017’s 76% and tied MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s 79%.
To that point, Stock explains how some Mistral customers are already putting the model to work, using it to support automated pen testing, where specialized agents analyze an application’s logs and test for potential entry points.
Breakneck improvements, at a fraction of the cost
When Mistral launched ML4 in public preview at the start of October, it came after about two months of training on about 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in its European data centers. In the last three weeks, Stock says the model has undergone “significant improvement,” which he chalked up to the team’s reinforcement learning. Mistral’s own Terminal-Bench 4.0 score rose from 28% at preview to 41%.
“I have no information about someone being able to do it with this amount of resources.”
More notably, he claims, the French company ran that reinforcement learning on only 10 megawatts of power, “a fraction of what all the competitors have.”
When pressed on how Mistral can know with certainty that it’s more cost-efficient than its competitors, Stock told reporters, “I have no information about someone being able to do it with this amount of resources.”
He also said Mistral’s resource efficiency means the French startup could advance further with the right investments: “If you give us 10 times more capital, then we’ll factor in these efficiency gains.”
Mistral wants to lead the frontier
Throughout the embargoed briefing, Stock consistently referred to ML4 as “a stepping stone,” hinting at Mistral’s plans for what’s next.
One certainty? Developers can expect smaller versions of Le Chonk to ship in the coming months, with Stock confirming, “There’s going to be a family of models, and one of them is going to be on a laptop.”
Mistral says ML4 can help software engineers modernize legacy codebases (where OpenAI has recently made a striking leap for COBOL migration), as well as in finance, manufacturing, industrial engineering, and geospatial applications. Looking ahead, the French company seems to have its sights set on playing an even bigger role:
“We think the only way forward [is] to own the entire stack.”
Learning Path

articles.title: Datadog Builds a Specialist AI Model for SRE Investigations
articles.text:
Datadog has released Scout, a model trained to investigate production problems. It runs inside Bits Investigation, the company's AI SRE product, where it can pick up an alert, look through telemetry and suggest what caused the problem. Datadog engineers and a small number of customers are using it in a closed preview.
Most of the work described in the announcement concerns cost. An investigation may require many model calls as Bits tries a query, studies the result and decides what to check next. General-purpose models can do this, but Datadog says the bill makes it difficult to run them against every alert. The authors of the announcement want Bits to begin work while an engineer is still responding to the page.
"Our goal is for Bits to serve as an always-on first responder, gathering evidence and identifying likely causes before an engineer steps in."
Othmane Abou-Amal, Ben Cohen, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar, Omri Sass and Daniel Shan
On Datadog's AlertEval benchmark, Scout medium received a similar score to GPT-6.1 Sol high and Claude Opus 5.5 high. Its estimated inference cost was between three and eight times lower. At the xhigh setting, Datadog says Scout matched Claude Fable 5.1 xhigh for one quarter of the cost. No prices are published, so these figures are relative to the cost of a Scout medium investigation.
AlertEval uses real alerts, archived telemetry and explanations written by Datadog engineers. An LLM judge compares Scout's account with an expert account, rewarding matches at both the immediate and underlying cause level. Contradictions and claims without evidence lose marks. The resulting score runs from zero to 100, but Datadog warns that it is not a percentage of incidents solved.
Scout is based on GLM-5.3 Flash. Datadog post-trained the model with reinforcement learning, using incident simulations made from patterns found in historical cases. The simulations contain an alert, telemetry that can be queried and a known cause. They do not contain customer data, according to the company. Scout practises with tools modelled on the ones in Bits, including searches across logs, metrics and traces, as well as code, deployment and feature flag inspection.
"Its training rewards finding the cause and supporting its conclusions with evidence."
Othmane Abou-Amal, Ben Cohen, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar, Omri Sass and Daniel Shan
The technical report gives a useful account of what went wrong during training. A reward based on the final answer prompted Scout to make fewer claims and stop investigating early. That made it less likely to be penalised, without making it a better investigator. The team changed the reward to take account of correctness, exploration and supporting evidence. They also removed tools from some training runs, or shortened the time available, to stop the model learning one fixed route through an incident.
Datadog ran a second evaluation on SREGym, a public set of 90 faults. Scout resolved 71 cases at medium effort, 79 at high and 80 at xhigh. GPT-6.1 Sol xhigh completed 82. Datadog carried out these tests itself, including the runs for newer comparison models, so independent results would be useful.
Scout arrives as observability suppliers work out how much of an incident an agent should handle. AWS DevOps Agent combines telemetry from several monitoring products with source code, deployment records and runbooks. AWS is joining information across tools, whereas Datadog is training a cheaper model for repeated use inside its own product.
Honeycomb's Canvas Agent is closer to the way many engineers investigate by hand. It opens a shared Canvas when an alert fires or an SLO burns, runs queries, tests ideas and leaves the evidence visible for an engineer to examine. Teams can capture familiar debugging procedures as Canvas Skills. Honeycomb also provides an MCP server, which allows external agents to query its telemetry. Honeycomb has not announced a dedicated SRE model; its focus is on the query engine and the record of how the investigation progressed.
Splunk and New Relic have gone further into the repair stage. Splunk AI SRE groups alerts and produces a probable cause with an evidence chain. A connected Claude agent can prepare a code change in a sandbox and open a pull request. New Relic's SRE Agent brings runbooks, incident reviews and previous resolutions into its analysis, while Autopilot can suggest remedial action. Both keep an approval step before a production change.
A ClickHouse study reported by InfoQ found that general-purpose models could produce summaries, but needed human guidance to find root causes consistently. Instacart takes a similar approach with Blueberry: agents collect context before an engineer assesses the proposed cause in Slack.
The benchmark evidence for Scout remains largely Datadog's own. In a response to the launch, the independent AI news account AGTP pointed out that AlertEval has not been independently tested. It also asked for an audit trail showing which evidence Scout considered and discarded. Honeycomb's visible Canvas and Splunk's evidence chain indicate that other vendors see the same requirement. A short answer may help during an incident, but engineers also need to see how the model reached it.
Datadog has not given a date for general availability. The company plans to add more types of failure to its simulations and eventually allow Bits to carry out repairs. The preview stops before that point: Scout investigates, gives its diagnosis and proposes recovery actions, while an engineer remains responsible for the change.

articles.title: Mausstudio Announced As Custom Gaming Mouse Designer for 3D Printing
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
Mausstudio Announced As Custom Gaming Mouse Designer for 3D Printing
It seems as though the mouse modding scene has been on a winning streak lately, with brands like Keychron publishing a catalogue of free 3D models of its mouse shells, and projects like Openmouse providing brand-agnostic, open-source mouse customization and remapping. The latest eye-catching project comes from a small 3D printing outfit called Unskilled Design, who recently introduced Mausstudio. Mausstudio is a work-in-progress custom mouse design tool that helps users design custom mouse shells for 3D printing. 
As described in a recent demo on X, Mausstudio allows users to import an STL of an existing mouse PCB, define the positions of core features, like screw holes, switches, the scroll wheel, and sensor position, and then generate a shell around it using custom parameters. Currently, it supports custom dimensions for the basics, like width, length, and height, as well as more niche customizations, like left-handed side button placements, base structure (lightweight or solid), hump position, honeycomb cutouts for lightweight shells, and battery positioning.After the shell is created, Mausstudio can automatically add screw holes for the PCB and create a cutout for the scroll wheel to fit through. The developer has a neat walkthrough of the available features in the demo reel on X, although it's unclear when exactly the project will be ready for launch or whether it will be a paid project or something like a browser-based utility. The creator behind the project, Bastian, is also careful to note that the actual shell being created is based on maths, with no generative AI involved in the 3D model's creation. It's unclear if generative AI was used to create the project itself, however.
Source:
				@UnskilledCast on X
