articles.title: Cisco Open Sources Quarry to Catch AI Agent Attacks Hidden in Harmless Steps
articles.text:
Detecting an AI agent attack isn’t simply finding multiple small needles scattered in a large haystack; it is recognizing whether and for what purpose the needles are connected.
Traditional security controls evaluate single actions to classify whether an intent is bad or benign. This approach fails on AI agent activity when the bad intent only emerges over a series of benign actions. It only becomes apparent if and when the overall sequence of actions is viewed or actioned.
Fraud detection is an example. A bank analyzes each purchase on its own. That’s largely how traditional security operates. Fraud detection, however, needs to see patterns of apparently benign single purchases across multiple purchases, possibly in multiple locations with unlikely timing (potentially employing agent capability). “Agent security needs the same combination of pattern detection and evidence, applied to the steps an agent takes rather than to purchases,” writes Cisco in announcing the open sourcing of its Project Quarry.
Cisco describes Quarry as a neurosymbolic rule language, combining machine learning judgment with rule-based checks. “It covers single-turn and multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.”
Each defined rule draws on neural evidence from ML classifiers and LLM judges, and symbolic rules that check exact conditions, sequences, string matches, and tool relationships. It is designed to provide a shared policy layer rather than be a replacement for every detector or every enforcement control.
Quarry can be used to provide runtime guardrails on agents, post-hoc rule set security analytics, and incident response. It integrates with Cisco’s existing Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework. It expands the framework from describing AI risk toward detecting it in agent activity, and is positioned as the policy and evaluation layer for the framework. The framework defines AI risks while Quarry provides detection of the risks in agent activity – the framework categories also offer a roadmap for the further development of new rules.
Quarry’s detection purpose is to identify suspicious patterns that span individual permitted actions. Such patterns may only become suspicious over a period of time. In 2025, Claude Code was used by bad actors in two campaigns: one against around 30 organizations, and a second against Mexican government institutions. The former attack was split into small routine-looking tasks that told the existing defense it was part of new defense testing. It looked like an authorized pentest from its parts, but the true intent (theft of data) only became apparent when the requests came together in the right sequence.
It is the ability of AI to separate an attack into multiple individually benign steps that defeats traditional defenses and requires this new form of neurosymbolic threat detection. But it is not a ‘write once and move on’ requirement. Attackers are constantly developing new approaches to their attacks. So, whenever a new attack technique is recognized, defenders must respond immediately by writing a new Quarry rule that can be used by all organizations everywhere.
But writing new rules by hand does not scale against the attackers’ use of AI to develop new malicious agents. “We want agents, as well as security and AI engineers, to be able to write Quarry rules,” declares Cisco. A Quarry Plugin allows a coding agent to compose, compile, and refine rules from a plain-English description of an organization’s risk, and then test those rules against real conversations. A rule that passes in a coding agent should behave the same way at runtime.
By open sourcing the project, the traditional cybersecurity asymmetry of attack and defense (multiple attackers against individual defenders) is equalized (multiple global attackers now face multiple global defenders). Allowing the use of AI for development also balances the speed advantage that bad actors have enjoyed in AI-assisted attacks.
“The open-source project,” says Cisco, “gives practitioners a working foundation for detection engineering.” The Quarry starter pack includes:
- a readable DSL for conversations, tool use, and event relationships;
- an evaluation runtime with configurable safety and resource limits, which compiles each rule when it loads;
- a command-line scanner for individual traces, directories, and datasets;
- a Python SDK for application integration;
- optional configured model operations for semantic signals;
- the Quarry plugin for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents;
- rule metadata, examples, documentation, and message-format guidance; and
- a workflow for validating rules against positive and benign datasets.
Project Quarry is intended to become a common, open standard for expressing and sharing detections for AI-agent attacks, much as Snort, YARA, and Sigma became standards in other areas of cybersecurity. “Hugging Face reconstructed roughly 17,600 agent actions after the fact,” says Cisco. “Our aim with Project Quarry is to help defenders recognize sequences like that one while they are still in progress, and to preserve the evidence behind each finding for the people who have to act on it.”

articles.title: Cloudflare Introduces Web Search API for AI Applications
articles.text:
Cloudflare has recently launched a beta Web Search API through AI Gateway. Available through REST APIs and Cloudflare Workers, it provides unified logging, access controls, and billing, and supports bring-your-own-provider keys.
The API enables AI agents to retrieve live web results from Ceramic.ai, Exa, and Linkup. It provides a unified interface, integrates search billing with AI Gateway, logs search requests alongside model inference, and requires providers to follow verified-bot requirements and return source links.
Cloudflare’s Web Search API allows AI applications to retrieve current web content, including recent news, API changes, and technical documentation, and provide the results as context to language models during inference. Michelle Chen, group product manager at Cloudflare, Sam Else, senior director at Cloudflare, and Gabriel Massadas, senior systems engineer at Cloudflare, explain the challenge that the company is trying to address:
When you use an agent and it needs to fetch a live web page, the agent usually just guesses the URL of the page and then makes a tool call to curl it. This is why you’ll sometimes see web fetches come back with a 404 Not Found, which happens if the agent incorrectly guesses the URL of that information. As you can imagine, it’s not super efficient to randomly guess URLs all the time.
Applications and external services can access web search through a REST endpoint by providing an AI Gateway authentication token and specifying a search provider in the request payload, with the endpoint returning the search results. Chen, Else, and Massadas add:
The crawler used by the web search provider must comply with Cloudflare’s publicly stated requirements for "Verified bots" as defined in our developer documentation, and web search responses must include a link to the location of crawled content. These rules are net-positive for a fair Internet, and allow creators to decide what they want to do with their data.
In a popular Hacker News thread, the community discusses search quality, data-retention restrictions, and whether a unified API offers meaningful advantages over existing alternatives. Simon Willison writes:
My number one question about search APIs is always if they allow you to store and resyndicate results you get from them. If I'm running an agent system but I'm not allowed to store the responses - or provide a "share transcript" button - that's a pretty significant limitation. The answer to that question is inevitably buried deep in the terms.
Maximilian Goisser, CTO and co-founder of Erato Labs, notes:
I think Cloudflare is (for companies already using it) approaching the status of trusted main cloud supplier (which usually would be AWS, GCP, Azure) via which the majority of cloud costs are billed (so you don't have to go through a fresh procurement process).
Cloudflare states it will identify providers that support Zero Data Retention and offers search at providers’ list prices without additional markup. The company plans to add native server tools to AI Gateway, starting with web search. Until then, developers can integrate web search into their workflows using Cloudflare Workers.

articles.title: Mass Effect Fan Group Buys Times Square Ad, Crowdfunds Billboards Aimed at EA
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
Mass Effect Fan Group Buys Times Square Ad, Crowdfunds Billboards Aimed at EA
A fan group backing the #SaveMassEffect campaign has taken it offline. We Are Mass Effect, a fan community founded by Ariel Pena Aguilar, teamed up with illustrator and YouTuber Kala Elizabeth to buy a slot on a Times Square billboard in New York on October 26. The ad read "Keelah Si'yah #SaveMassEffect" and apparently ran for 15 seconds once an hour, costing just $250. This comes about a week after EA shut down BioWare and cancelled the next Mass Effect game, part of around 400 job cuts across the company.
Elizabeth, Ariel and Mer of We Are Mass Effect then started a GoFundMe for three mobile billboards: one outside EA's Redwood City headquarters, one outside its Edmonton office, and one at The Game Awards in Los Angeles on December 10. The $5,274 goal was reportedly hit in under 15 minutes, and donations are now paused at $5,715 from 89 donors. Any leftover money was meant for the Game Workers' Hardship Fund, though that fund can't take direct donations right now.The Change.org petition is a separate effort under the same hashtag. A fan named Joe Smith (possibly a placeholder) started it on October 21, and it was nearing 180,000 signatures last week before climbing to about 267,000 now. Smith reportedly reached out to Elizabeth about working together, and the GoFundMe asks donors to sign the petition, though neither side has described a formal partnership. The petition asks EA to keep funding the series or license it to another studio. EA doesn't seem to have responded, while former BioWare producer Mark Darrah thinks EA could sell its BioWare IPs or just shelve them.
Sources:
				We Are Mass Effect on X, 				GoFundMe, 				via Kotaku

articles.title: Alphabet shares plunge over 10% as Google's AI search struggles to make money
articles.text:
What just happened? Alphabet has given investors another reason to worry about whether the AI spending frenzy will ever pay off. Shares in Google's parent fell more than 10% in after-hours trading as disappointing earnings and slower search growth overshadowed its cloud business. In even worse news for its AI ambitions, Google's AI Search mode is struggling to turn extra queries into equivalent advertising dollars.
Alphabet reported quarterly revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25% year over year, but earnings of $2.12 per share missed expectations of around $3.01. Its net income fell to $26.2 billion, though an $8.7 billion loss on equity investments contributed to the decline.
In what has become a familiar sight among tech giants, the spending figures are eye-watering. Capital expenditure reached $51.4 billion during the quarter, more than double the $24 billion spent a year earlier. Alphabet maintained its full-year forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion, while free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. Google reported its first negative quarterly free cash flow in July.
Despite that obscene amount of money, Alphabet expects capital expenditure to increase significantly again in 2027.
"I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise," said CEO Sundar Pichai.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler identified AI Mode's lower monetization as one reason search revenue growth slowed. AI Mode currently earns less from its queries than Google's old-school search engine, despite the company's overly aggressive enthusiasm for getting everyone to use it. Exactly how much less AI Mode is earning compared to traditional search wasn't revealed.
Schindler also cited currency movements and changes in advertiser spending, while Pichai said query growth was the strongest in five years. More searches don't automatically translate into more money, of course.
Schindler still believes that AI search will become a big earner.
"On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent," he said. "In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time."
Search revenue grew 12%, compared with 17% in the previous quarter. Google is expanding AI Mode advertising into additional countries, though it remains to be seen whether that helps close the gap.
There was a familiar bright spot. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, beating the $29.57 billion analysts expected.
Ultimately, though, the results add more fuel to the AI bubble fears. Citadel founder Ken Griffin recently warned that investors are probably in a bubble as businesses struggle to extract consistent value from AI. Meanwhile, Meta is planning a $95 billion stock offering to help finance its own AI ambitions.

articles.title: ‘The most entertaining durability test video I've ever seen’: this Trump phone teardown proves it’s American in name only
articles.text:
Teardown reveals the Trump phone to be an HTC U24 Pro in almost all but name — but at least it’s fairly durable
Proudly American, but mostly Taiwanese
- JerryRigEverything has performed a teardown and durability test on the Trump phone
- This revealed that it's so similar to an HTC phone you can even swap their motherboards
- The Trump phone did at least survive the durability tests
It was starting to feel like we wouldn’t have to hear any more about the Trump Mobile T1, but a new durability test has confirmed what we already largely knew — namely that it's little more than a rebranded HTC.
A previous teardown from iFixit revealed that the Trump phone had essentially identical specs and components to the HTC U24 Pro — a mid-range Taiwanese phone from 2024. The design is ever so slightly different, with the Trump phone having a different camera housing and a gold paint job, but the dimensions are the same too.
Now, though, JerryRigEverything has gone a step further, revealing that not only is the internal layout the same, right down to the number of screws, but if you swap the Trump phone’s motherboard with the HTC U24 Pro’s, both phones still work.
So the Trump phone really is almost a carbon copy of that HTC handset — rather calling into question its claims of being “proudly American.”
Passes the durability test
The only upside to all this is that, by essentially being an HTC U24 Pro, the Trump phone matches that device for durability. It survived being bent in multiple directions, seemingly has effective water resistance, and has a screen that’s just as scratch-resistant as most modern smartphones.
So if you have bought one of these devices, then at least it might last you a while — but that’s likely more down to designers and engineers in Taiwan than anyone in the US.
And even if you haven’t bought one, the video is worth a watch, targeting as it does not just the phone but the entire Trump administration, to the point where one Reddit commenter described it as “the most entertaining durability test video I've ever seen”.

articles.title: Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work — Humanist argues that offloading his thinking to LLMs violates his beliefs, Title VII accommodation protects employee
articles.text:
Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work — Humanist argues that offloading his thinking to LLMs violates his beliefs, Title VII accommodation protects employee
David Durman says that he's unwilling to outsource his thinking to AI tools.
David Durman, a research administrator at the University of Kentucky (UK), has successfully argued that using AI violates his beliefs as a humanist and has received Title VII religious accommodation from university officials not to use the technology. According to the Religion News Service (RNS), Durman believes in "the human part of life," which includes making his own decisions. However, he says that when the UK asked its employees to use AI, he felt that doing so would mean outsourcing his thinking to tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, thus violating his deeply held beliefs.
“The process and work involved in thinking through situations, through my work, through my ethics, through the way I handle other people, is a key component in being able to develop myself as a moral person,” Durman told RNS in an interview. “And offloading that labor, regardless of whether it’s taxing or not, is undercutting my ability to be a moral actor.” Because of this, the research administrator was granted a Title VII exemption under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. While humanism is often a non-religious philosophy or a worldview, federal courts have ruled that it qualifies as a religion.
The American Humanist Association (AHA) assisted Durman with his request for the accommodation. “This is the first of its kind at the AHA and for humanism generally to exempt those who see AI use as flying in the face of their freedom of conscience,” AHA staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens said to RNS. She also added, “For us, humanism is a comprehensive way of life. It’s built on inherent worth and dignity, and everyone should have room to exercise this comprehensive way of life at work the same way Christians do, or Muslims do.”
It should be noted that while anyone can request a Title VII exemption, it will only be granted if the applicant has a deep moral conviction that could count as an article of faith. Aside from that, the law also states that the request should not place an “undue hardship on the employer’s business.” So, even though Durman is no longer personally required to use AI tools for his tasks, he is still expected to attend meetings and cooperate with colleagues who use AI or to submit materials to AI tools, as needed.
AI use in corporate settings has been one of the biggest questions ever since LLMs exploded in popularity with ChatGPT. While AI proponents have said that the technology would increase productivity multiple times, reports say that corporate America, except for Big Tech, is not seeing any financial returns. Even so, about half of all U.S. employees now use AI one way or another at work, even as many executives remain uncertain about AI’s return on investment. But as for Durman, he says that the fact that Americans are already thinking about the impact of AI is a good thing, and that he hopes that his story would help others who’d rather not be forced to use the technology.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.text:
We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
Right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. Here’s what we need to do instead.
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.
The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.
AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.
No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.
Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

articles.title: Patrick Stewart has died at age 86
articles.text:
Patrick Stewart, best known for his roles in Star Trek and X-Men, has died at age 86. A message posted to Stewart’s Instagram account says the actor died in his Los Angeles home on Wednesday “following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.”
Patrick Stewart has died at age 86
Stewart was best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek.
Born in 1940 in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, Stewart began his acting career in theater. He eventually landed the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran from 1987 to 1994. Stewart returned as the Star Trek captain in subsequent films, including Star Trek: Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998), and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002). Stewart also starred as Professor Charles Xavier in several X-Men movies. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010.
“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the message on Instagram says. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”

articles.title: Souveränes ChatGPT? Mistral Large 4 soll China-Konkurrenz bei Coding- und Cyber-Aufgaben schlagen
articles.text:
Souveränes ChatGPT? Mistral Large 4 soll China-Konkurrenz bei Coding- und Cyber-Aufgaben schlagen
Nach einer dreiwöchigen Preview-Phase hat die französische KI-Firma Mistral AI die Gewichte für ihr neuestes Modell Mistral Large 4 auf Hugging Face zur Verfügung gestellt. Das multimodale Modell wurde auf 3.800 Nvidia-Beschleunigern trainiert und kommt mit einer Billion Parametern. Damit ist das Modell momentan noch zu groß für die Nutzung durch Hobbyist:innen mit Gaming-PCs oder einzelnen Nvidia-KI-Beschleunigern. Seit dem Ausrollen der Vorschauversion an „Mitglieder eines Early-Access-Kundenprogramms und spezialisierte Cybersecurity-Partner“, darunter ASML, Cisco, Crowdstrike, Microsoft und die European Space Agency, habe sich die Qualität des Sprachmodells durch Reinforcement Learning, also durch die „Belohnung“ des Modells bei der Ausgabe erwünschter Ergebnisse und das daraus resultierende Finetuning, nochmal deutlich verbessert.
Mistral galt ein Stück weit abgeschrieben, wenn es um das Rennen um die leistungsfähigsten Open-Weight-Modelle ging. Vor Mistral Large 4 veröffentlichte das KI-Startup das mittelgroße Modell Mistral Medium 3.5. Das wurde zwar als Flaggschiff verkauft. Laut der Analyseplattform Artificial Analysis blieb es in Benchmarks aber teilweise deutlich hinter der Konkurrenz aus China zurück. Auch die Öffnung der eigenen Compute-Infrastruktur für die Konkurrenz deutete an, dass die Nutzung der eigenen Modelle hinter den Erwartungen lag.
Mistral Large 4: Besser als die Konkurrenz von Qwen, Kimi und Co. aber genauso intransparent?
Genau diese Konkurrenz schlägt Mistral Large 4 laut eigener Angabe bei zwei Benchmarks. Auf dem Cybersicherheits-Benchmark CyberGym-E2E liegt es vor der China-Konkurrenz GLM-5.3 und Kimi K3. Beim agentischen Coding-Benchmark Terminal Bench 4.0 zieht es mit GLM-5.3 gleich. Zudem schneidet es mutmaßlich deutlich besser ab als Kimi K3 oder Metas offenes Modell Muse Spark Open. Eine unabhängige Evaluierung von Mistral Large 4 fehlt bislang allerdings. Vor Veröffentlichung der Gewichte lag die Preview-Version von Mistral Large 4 kostentechnisch bei 1,4 US-Dollar für eine Million Input- und 4,2 Dollar für eine Million Output-Tokens. Das ist deutlich günstiger als Kimi K3.1 Pro mit zwei respektive zehn Dollar und auf ungefähr dem selben Niveau wie GLM-5.3 über die offizielle API von Z.ai.
Leistung und Effizienz ist das eine, Vertrauen in generative KI, gerade hinsichtlich aktueller Cyber-Vorfälle rund um KI-Agenten, die von Wissenschaftler:innen zu bedenklichem Verhalten gepromptet werden, das andere. Im Rahmen eines Pressebriefings hat t3n Mistral mit diesem Problem konfrontiert. Auf die Nachfrage, ob die Firma sich vorstellen kann, deswegen statt Open Weight auf voll transparente Open Source zu setzen wie die Konkurrenz von Soofi oder Apertus, weicht Pierre Stock, Wissenschaftsvize des Startups, aus. „Ich denke nicht, dass KI eine derartige Blackbox ist, wie die Leute glauben. Seit es Reasoning-Modelle gibt, wird sichtbar, was die Modelle denken.“ Außerdem nutze man Überwachungs- und Entscheidungsmodelle. Damit wolle man die „Interpretierbarkeit und Transparenz“ seiner größeren Modelle erhöhen. Die Überprüfbarkeit von Reasoning-Schritten könnte allerdings in Zukunft deutlich schwieriger werden.
In den kommenden Wochen will Mistral auch kleinere, sogenannte quantifizierte Versionen von Mistral Large 4 verfügbar machen. Dazu sollen auch Modelle zählen, die auf Laptops oder Gaming-PCs nutzbar sein sollen. Um die Weiterentwicklung seiner Modelle und den Zubau von Rechenkapazität zu finanzieren, hatte die französische Firma erst im September 2026 drei Milliarden Euro frisches Kapital eingesammelt.

articles.title: How AI Redefines Semiconductor Manufacturing, From Materials Up - EE Times
articles.text:
Demand for more powerful AI chips is pushing semiconductor design forward, but commercializing those designs depends on whether chip manufacturing and packaging technologies can keep up.
A far less visible part of the semiconductor ecosystem is therefore coming into focus: the equipment, components, and materials used to manufacture and package advanced chips. As semiconductor processes become more precise and performance requirements rise, materials must operate reliably under more demanding conditions. Materials engineering helps bridge the gap between advanced chip designs and what manufacturers can produce reliably at scale.
Advanced chips raise the bar for materials
Semiconductor manufacturing already requires materials that perform in highly specialized environments. Components used in semiconductor processing equipment must withstand extreme operating conditions, resist mechanical wear, and maintain process stability and precision.
Producing higher-performance devices requires even greater precision in all phases of manufacturing. Even small changes in a component’s dimensions, surface condition, or performance can impair precise semiconductor manufacturing processes. Advanced ceramics can help equipment maintain tight tolerances and consistent performance.
Importantly, materials selection involves more than choosing the material with the greatest strength or heat resistance. Depending on the application, engineers must consider chemical resistance, plasma resistance, wear resistance, and thermal stability, among other characteristics. The relative priority of each property can vary significantly depending on where and how a component is used.
Materials engineering is a balancing act
No single material can maximize every characteristic required by every semiconductor manufacturing application.
Instead, engineers determine which combination of properties is most important for a particular operating environment. A component designed to withstand plasma exposure will have different material priorities than one intended to withstand mechanical wear or significant thermal demands. Performance must also be considered alongside practical factors such as manufacturability, geometry, and cost.
Advanced ceramics illustrate how materials can be engineered to meet these increasingly complex requirements. Unlike traditional ceramics, advanced ceramics are formulated using specialized raw material powders, additives, and binders to optimize a specific set of mechanical, thermal, electrical, or optical characteristics. Their properties can therefore be tailored to provide chemical resistance, plasma resistance, wear resistance, and thermal stability.
Advances in manufacturing methods also expand the role ceramic materials can fulfill. Beyond traditional pressing and injection molding, newer ceramic forming approaches can enable more complex geometries while addressing manufacturing considerations such as cost. As semiconductor equipment becomes more specialized, the ability to pair material properties with complex component designs is an increasingly important part of the engineering equation.
Packaging as a performance driver
The same development can be seen further along the semiconductor manufacturing chain. Semiconductor packaging was historically viewed as a means of protecting an integrated circuit. Today, packaging plays a key role in optimizing performance.
Higher-performing devices now integrate multiple ICs, chiplets, and functions within a single package. Each component can introduce different requirements for heat dissipation, protection, isolation, and electrical connectivity. Rather than simply fitting an IC inside a package, engineers have to consider the interactions among multiple ICs, the package, and the board to maximize the performance of the complete device.
This represents a significant change from earlier generations of semiconductor technology. As recently as 10 to 15 years ago, package design could be driven largely by the mechanical requirements of fitting and protecting a device. As functions have become more integrated and IC architectures more complex, connections among components have become increasingly consequential to overall performance. Packaging is therefore becoming part of the system-level design challenge rather than a consideration that begins after the chip has been designed.
AI infrastructure makes those pressures particularly visible. In optical communications, for example, signal speeds at the device level have risen from approximately 10 Gbps two decades ago to around 200 Gbps per lane today. This requires packages capable of transmitting signals faster while minimizing loss, even as package structures and signal routing become more miniaturized and complex.
At the same time, greater integration creates additional thermal and structural challenges. Ceramic materials can provide advantages in areas such as heat dissipation, design flexibility, and rigidity, but the broader engineering challenge remains the same: Package materials and designs must evolve alongside the semiconductor devices they support.
AI innovation extends beyond the chip
These challenges will intensify as AI infrastructure evolves. Higher semiconductor processing speeds and greater functionality are expected to continue increasing demand for heat dissipation, while the integration of additional functions can result in larger and more complex packages. Engineers may increasingly need to achieve high-speed performance, thermal management, and low warpage simultaneously as package dimensions and complexity grow.
The same principle applies upstream in semiconductor production equipment. As semiconductor features become smaller and more precise, the equipment used to manufacture and inspect them must likewise support rising levels of performance. Materials that were adequate for previous generations of semiconductor manufacturing may not provide the combination of characteristics required by future processes.
For the semiconductor industry, this points to a broader lesson about the AI era. Progress will not depend exclusively on designing faster or more efficient chips. Every improvement at the chip level creates new requirements elsewhere in the manufacturing ecosystem, from semiconductor fabrication and processing equipment to the materials and packages enabling chips to reach previously unattainable levels of performance.
As AI chip designs become more capable, advances across the manufacturing chain will be essential to turning those designs into reliable, scalable devices.

articles.title: Rethinking Shift Left In Chip Design
articles.text:
Is it better to do everything earlier in the flow, or should design be more flexible and iterative?
Key Takeaways:
Experts at the Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the good and bad of shifting left amid ongoing changes in how chips are designed, used, and updated throughout the flow, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise. What follows are excerpts of that conversation.
L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv.
SE: We’ve been talking about shifting left in the design-through-manufacturing flow for more than a decade, but more and more capabilities are being added to improve reliability and yield, and produce silicon faster. What changes are you seeing?
Schirrmeister: We’re now adding digital twins, which are shifting very left.
Berg: That’s correct. And the issue now is working with multi-physics models. Using that data to assemble surrogate models is important. As we go further into different technologies with different materials, you have to go back to the materials science solvers and physics solvers to get models that designers can use. This is happening in areas that are not typically digital design, but as we get down to the CFET level, it’s starting to be used there, as well.
Schirrmeister: There are three changes. Number one, now we have the technical ability with compute, with agents, to shift much further left than we ever hoped we would get to in our lifetimes. The problem there is whether shift left is trustworthy. Is the surrogate model a reliable representation of what’s happening? You can’t have the agent decide that. In the past, for virtual prototyping, you would get a human being who is responsible for ensuring that the model represents what’s happening, and that it’s accurate. That’s number one. So the trust is changing. Number two, you need to trust the shift-left model to be predictive of what you’re doing. Otherwise, you’ll regret you’re shifting left because you’ll need another spin. In a Qualcomm keynote, the speaker talked about the new reasoning gap. He said we used to have a productivity gap, but now we have a reasoning gap. They want engineers to reason about the product and make that product better. But the tools can’t deal with reasoning yet. The third one is the rapid pace of shift-left options. If I get to the point where I can trust the models, then I have new things I can do. At the architectural level, I can decide something and kick off ‘n’ options to try it out if the models are predictive enough.
Darbari: The shift-left discourse started at least 15 years ago. What has changed is AI and the agentic use model. What has not happened yet is the trust element in today’s AI agents. There are all these excellent use models for the agents, which we use and our customers use, to go through the specifications. A lot of discussion has now moved into spec-to-silicon, because people believe you can extract requirements from specification documents — if you have them. But most of the time you don’t have them, and that is one of the problems. Another big change I’m seeing in the work we do with formal verification is that functional verification is now seen as a problem, at the same level as security, functional safety, and power, with all of the hardware feeding into the AI ecosystem, which is the largest investment pool. A lot of companies are investing in PPA analysis on the first day. For example, I know of customers that are taking their designs, even the older generation, and saying, ‘Let an AI agent rewrite it for optimized PPA.’ But how do I know it is correct? Can I prove it to be equivalent to something else? So the big 10 companies in the semiconductor space, which have big budgets and big teams of people, are adopting agentic AI flows, and they’re heavily leaning on whether they can trust it or not trust it. That trust gap is often being solved through early adoption of formal through proofs. The know-how is not necessarily the biggest blocker. It’s mostly whether tools can integrate more seamlessly into the system.
But if you look at what is enabling more shift left, it’s the time spent on debug. When you’re bringing up an architectural analysis and you have a failure, you can feed it to an agent. There’s a lot of data coming out of the agents, and we need to do more work on insights. Are you spending your time wisely? Even if it is correct or incorrect, if a manual review has to happen, that could be a massive blocker in the early phases of adoption of shift left. With agents being adopted earlier, will this lead to better designs with fewer bug escapes? That remains to be seen, and I don’t believe that shift left alone will be able to fix it.
Laviv: Shift left is identifying the bottlenecks in our industry and looking at what you can do in order to pull in work and schedule as much as you can earlier in the design and verification cycle. Nowadays, the agents are leaping forward to help, but everything that happens gets us into bottlenecks — new bottlenecks or old bottlenecks — that we have to solve.
SE: We have so much that has to be looked at and verified concurrently that it becomes a problem to shift that much stuff left, and it gets more complicated with multi-die assemblies and lifecycle management. How do all the pieces go together and stay together?
Schirrmeister: Is shift left even the right thing? Shift left assumes that I have a solid knowledge of what I’m actually going to do, and it assumes I can specify what I want six or nine months or a year from now. Maybe we’re thinking about this wrong. Perhaps what we need is a general direction, and then the ability to make adjustments based on the information we gain as we go toward implementation choices. Shift left implies that you can get to zero in some magic future world by having something spec’d, and you get all the way there. What I hear people doing is different. They say, ‘Okay, I’m building something, and with agentic AI I can now build this model that potentially represents most of it. So now I make the decision, ‘This one is fairly straightforward and it doesn’t need that much effort on an Arm processor, or I can make a RISC-V processor for it.’ Now I reset my spec, which is kind of messed up because I did not have the correct hardware spec, so now I’m making adjustments. The cool part is we are approaching a time when we can shift left to this new refinement. It’s almost like an agile shift left. In an agile way, you make adjustments to your implementation for micro choices that happen later based on what you’re doing now.
SE: That addresses a big problem with these designs, because you don’t know what the workload will be by the time this chip is deployed in the market. This is a more generic approach that focuses on adaptability, right?
Schirrmeister: Exactly, and we didn’t dare do this in the past because this was all sequential. Now it becomes more circular. So there was a product manager who knew the market and said, ‘I’m building this, and then 18 months later you found out it didn’t work.’ Right now you have new data all the time, so there can be this agility in refining what you’re doing.
Darbari: I agree that there are lots of choices in agility and lots of changes, and not everything is known up front, which is the reality in building anything. However, I do not see that things are so fuzzy. If you’re building a new machine learning chip, or a GPU or a CPU, you have some idea of what the derivative design was before. What is the general architecture you’re going to play with? What you don’t know is what the implementation choices are going to be for power, for functionality, and with AI bringing lots of challenges on training or inference. Those are quite novel. So you need to make multiple choices at every step along the way, with or without agents. But agents can help you do that more efficiently. What I don’t know is whether the outcomes of these agile agents can be reconciled very quickly and trusted.
Schirrmeister: You don’t let AI actually make the decision for you, and you don’t trust the AI. You then need to go down into a verified model.
Berg: That’s a really important point. The AI agents don’t replace humans. They are effectively junior engineers, and they need to have their work reviewed by somebody who knows it. The notion that it’s agile, and is growing agile, is very real. There’s this notion that a flow does an inverse design. But what happens if that inverse design could be based on multi-physics solvers. You put together a surrogate model, digital twins, and then you say, ‘Okay, give me a transistor or give me a chip — or even so far as a chip through RTL at this point — that works with these constraints and these things that are going on. And all of a sudden you have an empty set. It’s over-constrained. Now what do you do? This is why the notion that you have to be agile is very valid.
Laviv: If we take the example of the digital flow, you have virtual platforms today, formal, software simulation, emulation, FPGA, and you have engineers and AI engines. You will need to make adjustments. And if you’re designing a CPU, or something that’s tangible, and you can do it better with formal and bring it to the table sooner with a more stable design, then emulation and FPGA can run sooner in the pipeline of doing the verification stuff, and the same thing with simulation. If you have done something to solve the bottlenecks in formal, in simulation, virtual prototyping, or even the flow itself, this would help shift everything left and allow you to make better decisions earlier in the game. That way if you need to change stuff, you can change it.
Darbari: The validation problem is significant. I’m seeing real evidence with some customers, who literally are going back to the drawing board to build a ground-up architecture that can address different phases of their chips being used. So they could build a CPU, a GPU, a machine learning chip, and they really need to scope out whether what they intend to build would cover all kinds of use models. That’s not easy, especially when you bring software into the loop, and the software isn’t what used to run 20 years ago. There is training, inference, power coming into the chain all the way back to the architecture level, and then you’ve got to make these choices.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: How Uganda’s School Monitor Technologies is helping schools function more efficiently - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ugandan startup School Monitor Technologies operates a cloud-based school management platform designed specifically for how schools in Uganda and East Africa actually function.
Founded in 2022 by Annet Nuwayo and Vincent Matsiko, School Monitor Technologies simplifies student record management, academic results entry and analysis, automated report card generation, staff attendance and leave management, asset and inventory tracking, fee collection and tracking, accounting, library management, and a parent communication portal.
Nuwayo trained as a teacher, and that background helped her develop a solution to a problem she understood well.
“From my experience, I understand how schools actually function, where the pressure points are, and what schools genuinely need from a digital tool,” she said.
School software with a difference
So what makes School Monitor different from generic school software?
“It has an accounting module that helps schools manage revenues, expenses, budgeting, payroll, among others. School Monitor provides real-time financial reporting, including trial balance, balance sheet, and profit and loss statements, so school leadership always has an accurate picture of their institution’s financial health. It also uses SMS to reach parents on basic phones rather than requiring smartphone access,” said Nuwayo.
The system uses role-based access, meaning each user—head teacher, bursar, teacher, or parent—sees only what is relevant to their role, keeping data secure and operations clean.
“Uganda has over 30,000 schools – primary, secondary, and institutions. The overwhelming majority of them still run entirely on paper. They record fee collection in handwritten ledgers. Report cards are produced each term manually, consuming weeks of teacher time,” said Nuwayo.
“School directors who own multiple campuses have no way to see what is happening across their institutions without physically being present. Parents have no reliable channel to track what their child owes or how they have performed.”
Priced for local, but seeking funding
School Monitor provides just this, and was built by people who understand Ugandan schools – and priced for them. Built largely through bootstrapping and client subscription revenue, the company has not taken external equity investment to date, but recently secured a catalytic grant of US$10,000 from the Standard Chartered Foundation’s Women in Tech Accelerator, implemented in Uganda by Innovation Village, with support from Village Capital.
“This provided critical working capital at a stage when cash flow constraints were the primary limiter on growth. The grant was deployed directly into the development of School Monitor Version 2, which has since launched,” said Nuwayo.
“I also received mentorship, and learned a lot from the programme’s structured curriculum. I would indeed recommend others to apply.”
150 schools, with regional expansion ahead
School Monitor Version 2 is a major product upgrade with significantly enhanced modules, a WhatsApp integration, improved financial reporting, and a redesigned interface, and it is a landmark in itself.
“It represents the most significant product investment the company has made and has already driven new school enrolments,” said Nuwayo.
School Monitor is now deployed in around 150 schools across Uganda, serving more than 30,000 users on the platform. Nuwayo said there are many more schools in the pipeline that are ready to take up the system, but have not made the final decision yet.
“The platform saves schools an average of 40 hours per term in manual report card processing alone — a concrete, visible benefit that makes the value proposition easy for school leaders to understand and justify,” she said.
“Retention has been strong. Schools that adopt the platform continue using it because it solves real, daily problems rather than being a tool adopted for compliance or novelty and then abandoned. Parent-facing SMS delivery of results has been a particularly well-received feature, extending the platform’s reach beyond administrators to the wider school community.”
The company is now positioned to pursue deliberate regional expansion. South Sudan is a near-term target, alongside other East and Central African markets like Malawi and Tanzania, and others facing the same challenges: paper-dependent school administration, curricula that imported tools do not support, and a growing private school sector that needs affordable digital infrastructure.

articles.title: The GEO Playbook: How Australian brands can optimise for Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT search - Tech Guide
articles.text:
For more than two decades, the standard playbook for Australian businesses online was straightforward: identify target keywords, optimize metadata, acquire authoritative backlinks, and compete for a spot in Google’s “ten blue links.”
That paradigm has fundamentally fractured.
With the rollout of Google AI Overviews and the rise of conversational answer engines like ChatGPT Search and Perplexity, search engines are shifting from navigational directories to synthesis engines. Instead of presenting users with a list of external destinations to evaluate, large language models (LLMs) parse the web in real time, extract key facts, and deliver direct, conversational answers.
For digital marketers and business leaders across Australia, this shift presents a new challenge: Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO). To remain visible, brands must learn how to earn recommendations and citations directly inside AI-synthesized answers.
What is Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO)?
Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) is the practice of structuring, writing, and technically delivering website content so that it can be accurately crawled, ingested, and cited by generative AI engines.
While traditional SEO focuses on maximizing organic rank positions and direct page clicks, GEO focuses on information gain and citation share. It’s structuring and adding information to a webpage that improves the chances that an AI agent selects your brand (or page) as a primary source when answering user queries.
The Princeton GEO benchmark
Optimizing for generative engines is not guesswork. The foundational rules were empirically established in a landmark study led by researchers from Princeton University, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI, and IIT Delhi, titled, GEO: Generative Engine Optimization.
The researchers evaluated approximately 10,000 queries across multiple domains to measure which on-page adjustments caused generative engines to cite and attribute sources most frequently.
The study revealed two vital insights:
- Specific GEO tactics increased content visibility inside AI responses by up to 40%.
- Traditional keyword stuffing failed completely, actually decreasing visibility inside conversational engines by 10% below the baseline.
The strategies that yielded the highest attribution gains were:
- Statistics Addition: enriching content with verified quantitative data)
- Cite Sources: adding direct citations to credible third-party benchmarks
- Quotation Addition: including authoritative expert commentary.
The 4 pillars of a GEO strategy that works
To capitalize on these dynamics, Australian companies need to modernize their search architecture across four distinct technical areas.
1. Inverted pyramid / Direct answer formatting
Generative crawlers read web pages under strict latency budgets. If a scraper must read through 800 words of introductory preamble to find an answer, the LLM will skip the page in favor of a more direct competitor.
- The Fix: Place a direct, declarative answer of 40 to 60 words immediately beneath your <h2> or <h3> headers. Follow that summary with bulleted specifics, practical criteria, and data points. This provides the AI scraper with a clean, pre-packaged snippet ready for extraction.
2. Entity-based semantic structuring
Traditional crawlers establish trust by understanding index strings of text. In contrast, LLMs assess a brand’s reputation by evaluating entities and the semantic relationships between them. Entities refer to distinct people, places, organizations, and concepts. It assesses a brand’s reputation.
- The Fix: Move beyond basic schema. Implement comprehensive JSON-LD markup that maps your organization to clear entities. Use AboutPage, ItemPage, FAQPage, and sameAs schema linking directly to verified databases, which includes your Australian Business Number register, LinkedIn profile, and industry bodies. This helps language models disambiguate your brand from global namesakes.
3. Machine-readable data tables
LLMs process structured HTML far more efficiently than long paragraphs of text. When benchmarking products, listing pricing, or presenting operational workflows, plain HTML tables consistently outperform narrative prose.
| Feature / Metric | Traditional SEO Focus | Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) | 
| Primary goal | Top 3 organic ranking on Google SERP | Inclusion & citation within LLM synthesis | 
| Optimization focus | Keyword frequency, backlink volume | Reputation and associations, information gain, statistics, entity clarity | 
| Content structure | Long-form, conversational prose | Direct answers, semantic HTML, structured tables | 
| Primary metric | Organic impressions, click sessions | Citation frequency, qualified conversion rate | 
4. Technical crawl access for modern AI agents
Many businesses inadvertently block generative engines from reading their content. When companies update their robots.txt files to safeguard data against AI model training, they often accidentally block the real-time search crawlers that generate live search citations.
- The Fix: Audit your server logs and robots.txt directives. Ensure your site allows real-time retrieval bots, including Google-Extended, GPTBot, and PerplexityBot, access to public-facing informational guides, while keeping sensitive proprietary data protected behind authentication walls.
Winning brand citations in Australia
The implications of AI search are particularly pronounced for Australian mid-market companies and service providers.
When a user in Melbourne or Sydney asks ChatGPT or Gemini, “Which cybersecurity consultancy complies with the Australian Essential Eight framework?”, the engine does not output a directory of 50 links. It synthesizes a short list of two or three validated providers.
To be chosen, a business must demonstrate local consensus. LLMs verify corporate entities through third-party mentions, including regional media outlets, local industry directories, and authenticated customer reviews. If an AI model cannot triangulate your brand across external sources, it will default to citing established competitors.
Implementing comprehensive AI search optimisation is no longer a forward-looking experiment. It is the baseline required to preserve brand discovery in an ecosystem dominated by zero-click interfaces.
The 5-point GEO audit checklist
Before publishing your next digital asset, run it through this operational checklist:
- Clear header-to-answer hierarchy: Does every sub-header answer the search intent within the first two sentences?
- Proprietary data: Does the page contain original statistics, survey findings, or benchmarks that cannot be scraped elsewhere on the web?
- Verified attribution: Are technical assertions backed by outbound references to academic papers, regulatory standards, or recognized industry benchmarks?
- Valid schema implementation: Has the page been validated using Google’s Rich Results Test for appropriate JSON-LD structured data?
- Clean HTML Markup: Are key comparisons housed in standard HTML tables rather than complex JavaScript accordions or embedded images that scrapers cannot parse?
Citations over clicks
The transition toward generative search engines does not mean the end of organic traffic, but it fundamentally redefines its value.
While top-of-funnel, casual informational queries will increasingly be resolved directly within the search interface, users who follow source citations out of an AI summary do so with significantly higher commercial intent. They have already evaluated the synthesis; they are clicking through to verify credentials, request quotes, or initiate transactions.
Australian businesses that adapt their content architecture to the principles of GEO today will secure the institutional citations that define market leadership for years to come.

articles.title: 480 milliards de dollars volatilisés : la bulle de l'IA vient-elle d'éclater en Chine ?
articles.text:
Entre effondrement boursier et investissements pharaoniques, le secteur technologique chinois traverse une zone de fortes turbulences. Porté par une euphorie boursière que certains qualifient de folie spéculative, l’indice STAR50 de la bourse de Shanghai, qui regroupe des acteurs de l’intelligence artificielle et des semi-conducteurs, a chuté de 40 % en l’espace de quatre mois, faisant disparaître 480 milliards de dollars de valeur boursière selon des informations relayées par Reuters.
La dégringolade boursière des fleurons de l’IA
Après une forte dynamique haussière, le marché de la bourse de Shanghai a finalement dégonflé. Parmi les exemples les plus marquants, on retrouve la société de robotique Unitree qui a perdu 50 % de sa valorisation depuis son introduction en bourse en août dernier. De son côté, le fabricant de puces CXMT a perdu plus d’un quart de sa valeur au cours du dernier mois.
À lire : Du jamais-vu pour la police : un robot saisi après une agression sexuelle
Malgré cette correction sévère, certains géants continuent de lever beaucoup de fonds. C’est notamment le cas de DeepSeek qui a récemment bouclé une levée de fonds de 15 milliards de dollars pour rivaliser avec les concurrents américains OpenAI et Anthropic, pour ne citer qu’eux. De son côté, Huawei a décroché un prêt de 2,3 milliards de dollars auprès de banques chinoises pour financer ses achats de puces dédiées à l’intelligence artificielle.
Des pressions géopolitiques et une absence de rentabilité
Autre élément qui n’a pas aidé le marché chinois : les restrictions imposées par les États-Unis qui cherchent à isoler l’industrie chinoise de la concurrence à travers des barrières douanières et des projets de sanctions ciblant les équipements pour data centers. Ces barrières à l’exportation et l’interdiction de commercialiser les produits à l’étranger pèsent donc aussi beaucoup sur le ralentissement du marché autour de l’IA dans le pays.
À lire : Le gouvernement américain banni DeepSeek : l’IA chinoise est accusée de surveillance de masse
Mais comme aux États-Unis, où la bulle n’a pas encore éclaté, les entreprises chinoises de l’IA peinent encore à être rentables. Les investissements sont massifs, un petit groupe d’entreprises s’auto-alimentent, mais les débouchés commerciaux se font encore attendre. Oui, les entreprises et les particuliers utilisent massivement l’IA, mais le prix des abonnements ne suffit pas à couvrir les investissements colossaux du secteur. En Chine, les investisseurs soutenus par l’État ont tenté de réguler la volatilité en vendant lors des rebonds de la bourse. Mais ces symptômes montrent la grande fragilité du modèle économique autour de l’IA.
