articles.title: French startup Bleu Robotics secures €5 million to teach humanoid robots new tasks with fewer demonstrations | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Bleu Robotics, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.
The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.
Benoît Berkoukchi, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less.”
The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.
In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.
Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.
Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.
Thomas Poitrineau, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years.”
Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.
Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.
According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.
Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.
Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.
As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.
Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

articles.title: Canada’s new national security strategy puts tech front and centre
articles.text:
Canada’s first national security strategy in more than two decades highlights the country’s technological strengths and vulnerabilities in an effort to sketch out a path to “true sovereignty.”
The 13-page strategy, titled The Plan for a Stronger Canada, released on Thursday, contained a broad summary of the government’s national security intentions rather than detailed guidance. A foreword from Prime Minister Mark Carney promises that leading Canadian technologies will be part of the “bedrock” of relationships that “promote a sovereign Canada and contribute to a more secure and prosperous world.”
The strategy lists frontier AI as a challenge that must be weathered, in the same way as “great power rivalries,” authoritarian aggression, climate change, and pandemics. To withstand those challenges, the strategy places emerging technologies as the first on a list of eight critical sectors Canada needs to build on. It states that those emerging technologies include cloud and AI compute, quantum computing, space-based communications and navigation, semiconductors, and telecommunications.
“Candidly, an investment like this today makes sure Canadians have control of our sovereign destiny, and sovereignty is a form of safety.”
AI Minister Evan Solomon
The strategy’s other strategic sectors are critical minerals, defence, energy, transportation, pharmaceuticals and biotech, food security, and financial systems.
“Building these capabilities underpins our economic, foreign policy, and defence strategies,” Carney said in Montréal on Thursday. The national security strategy says that, where it can, Canada will build these strengths at home, and otherwise will partner with reliable, complementary allies to bring strength and scale.
To further this, the strategy pledges that the government will produce plans on nearly 40 policy points, many of which the government has already announced. Those include a buy Canadian policy, improving defence procurement, as well as a plan to “cement Canada as a major player in developing and commercializing advanced technologies,” including in AI, quantum computing, and space technology.
The strategy says Canada wants to strengthen its intelligence and security agencies like Communications Security Establishment Canada and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), and increase its contributions to the international Five Eyes intelligence partnership. It outlines plans to modernize Canada’s intelligence authorities to “reflect current threats and technologies,” improve its capability to detect foreign information manipulation, and invest in technologies like AI and secure cloud to improve intelligence processing.
Daniel Perry, the director of federal affairs at industry lobby group the Council of Canadian Innovators, said in a statement that the federal government has identified the right priorities, but raised concerns about the strategy’s lack of detail on intellectual property ownership or standards for the firms that would build the critical technologies outlined in the strategy.
RELATED: Feds to buy stake in Cohere via planned $7-billion Series E at $36-billion valuation
“Strategic autonomy depends on Canadian ownership,” Perry said. “If the technology and IP behind these capabilities are owned elsewhere, Canada’s dependence has simply moved onshore.”
The national security strategy continues the Carney government’s focus on improving Canada’s technological autonomy. Carney has remarked about pulling away from United States-controlled technologies like Starlink and, in 2026 alone, has rolled out a Defence Industrial Strategy and a refreshed AI strategy which both heavily emphasize sovereign technological capabilities.
Just as the national security strategy was revealed on Thursday, Carney also announced his government’s $1.6-billion investment in homegrown frontier AI developer Cohere, remarking that, “we are choosing to grow Canada’s technology future instead of someone else’s.”
“The new threat environment with cyber and AI is real,” AI minister Evan Solomon told BetaKit of the new national security strategy following the Cohere investment announcement. “Candidly, an investment like this today makes sure Canadians have control of our sovereign destiny, and sovereignty is a form of safety.”
As next steps, the prime minister plans to convene a First Ministers meeting on national security, and said that the federal government plans to bring forward a proposal to modernize national security legislation in the next year.
Feature image courtesy Mark Carney via X.
With files from Madison McLauchlan.

articles.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy
articles.text:
AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy
For more than a decade, the managed application platform industry has optimized around a compelling promise: get code running as quickly as possible.
Five-minute deployments. Git-based workflows. Minimal configuration. Infrastructure abstracted away from developers. That simplicity changed how software gets built, and for good reason. Application teams should spend more time building software and less time assembling infrastructure. But for organizations in regulated industries, getting an application running is only the beginning.
A patient scheduling system, financial application, government service, or aerospace workload may remain in production for years. During that time, operating systems need patching. Runtimes reach end of support. Security requirements evolve. Applications scale. Teams change. Auditors ask for evidence. Regulatory frameworks expand.
For these organizations, the question is no longer simply: How quickly can we deploy? It is: How easily can we deploy, and keep that application secure, supported, observable, auditable, and operational for years?
“The services built for fast starts also need to support long stays.”
That is why platform selection for regulated workloads runs on three axes rather than one. Developer simplicity still matters. But compliance posture and service continuity decide whether that simplicity survives an audit or a roadmap change.
The missing middle in regulated industries
Large enterprises often address this challenge by building specialized organizations around their applications: platform engineering teams, SRE organizations, cloud centers of excellence, security engineering teams, FinOps practices, and dedicated compliance functions.
Many mid-size organizations operate under similar regulatory expectations without comparable specialization. A healthcare software company still needs to satisfy HIPAA requirements. A financial services company still operates within PCI DSS or SOX controls. Government contractors encounter FedRAMP requirements.
Data residency, security reviews, vulnerability remediation, access controls, and audit evidence don’t disappear just because an organization has fewer engineers. Regulatory obligations do not scale down with the size of the engineering organization.
That creates a difficult operating equation. These teams need production-grade infrastructure and strong governance. But every hour their application developers spend maintaining deployment infrastructure, investigating platform issues, patching underlying systems, or reconciling configuration is an hour not spent improving the applications the business depends on. Workforce shortages in specialized IT roles compound the problem: the team keeping a patient scheduling application running is frequently the same team preparing audit evidence. This is not a question of technical maturity. It is an operating-model problem.
The applications already exist
Modernization discussions often begin with the destination: containers, cloud-native architectures, microservices, and increasingly sophisticated infrastructure platforms. Regulated organizations rarely have the luxury of beginning with a blank sheet of paper.
A mid-size healthcare organization might operate patient portal front-ends on Java and Tomcat, HL7 integration services on .NET and IIS, patient intake workflows in PHP, and lab data pipelines in Python. All in audit scope, all maintained by the same small team that also manages network security and prepares evidence for the next compliance review. Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient.
“Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient.”
That creates an important test for any application platform intended for this market: Can it improve how organizations operate the applications they have today, not only the applications they hope to build tomorrow?
A Java Spring Boot application packaged as a JAR file should deploy without containerization, without a Dockerfile, without a container registry. A .NET Framework application running on IIS should deploy to Windows Server environments.
That workload has no equivalent managed path on most modern platforms that focus exclusively on Linux containers. A Python service processing regulatory reports should deploy alongside a Java integration service in the same portfolio, managed through the same interface, with the same operational model applying to both. Modernization should not require transformation before organizations can realize operational benefits.
From an application problem to a portfolio problem
Managing one production application is an engineering problem. Managing dozens of independently operated applications becomes an operating-model problem. Consider an organization with 30 applications, each provisioned and managed independently. Each application brings its own deployment configuration, scaling model, monitoring setup, patching cadence, security controls, runtime lifecycle, and operational procedures.
For regulated organizations, that fragmentation carries another cost: evidence. Controls have to be understood. Exceptions have to be documented. Patching needs to be demonstrated. Security findings need to be remediated. Operational practices need to be defensible.
“Compliance programs rarely fail because of a single application. They fail because of drift.”
As the application portfolio grows, operational inconsistency becomes the largest source of complexity. The problem is not infrastructure cost. It is the multiplication of operational responsibility, and the enemy has a name: drift. Five applications deployed five different ways, each with its own conventions, gaps, and undocumented exceptions. Compliance programs rarely fail because of a single application. They fail because of drift.
The application platform therefore has a second job beyond making deployment easier: help create a repeatable operational model across applications, and make drift visible before it becomes an audit finding.
So what kind of platform addresses drift without removing the visibility regulated teams require?
Managed simplicity, visible control
The answer is not to hide infrastructure completely. For regulated workloads, abstraction without sufficient visibility creates a different problem. A service that abstracts infrastructure without providing audit visibility creates a compliance gap that no amount of developer experience can close.
The people accountable for the workload need to understand where it runs, how access is controlled, how networking is configured, how security policies apply, what gets patched, what changed, and what evidence is available to auditors. The more useful model is managed operational responsibility with appropriate customer visibility and control.
The application team provides its application and configuration. The platform automates the repetitive infrastructure work required to run it: provisioning, deployment, capacity management, load balancing, health monitoring, scaling, and platform maintenance. At the same time, the workload stays within the organization’s cloud environment, where its identity, networking, monitoring, security, and governance models still apply.
The right model delivers simplicity and account-level visibility, because the people accountable for the workload need both.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk has operated this model since 2011. A team provides application source code or a Dockerfile and configuration. The service orchestrates the AWS resources needed to run it: compute capacity, load balancing, auto-scaling, health monitoring, and deployment workflows. Environments run in the team’s own AWS account, not behind an opaque abstraction.
“A service that abstracts infrastructure without providing audit visibility creates a compliance gap that no amount of developer experience can close.”
That transparency distinction matters for compliance. Elastic Beanstalk is HIPAA-eligible and appears among AWS services in scope of SOC, PCI, ISO, and FedRAMP. Regulated industries ask about these frameworks by name. The claim is verifiable: organizations can download third-party audit reports through AWS Artifact and hand them directly to their own assessors.
From individual environments to a shared operational baseline
Over more than a decade of operating this model, AWS has spoken with more than 10,000 customers about how they build, deploy, and operate applications. Those conversations reinforced something important: customers were not asking us to choose between simplicity and production readiness. They wanted both. They wanted application developers to deploy without becoming infrastructure specialists. They wanted existing applications to benefit from managed operations without rewriting every workload first.
They wanted AWS to take on more repetitive operational work while retaining the visibility, security boundaries, and controls their organizations require. And as their application portfolios grew, they wanted the operational model to grow with them.
The portfolio dimension matters most in this evolution. When each environment operates independently (its own deployment pipeline, scaling configuration, and patching schedule), the operational surface area grows linearly with the portfolio.
Elastic Beanstalk’s new Cluster Mode addresses this directly: multiple applications share managed infrastructure with a consistent operational baseline.
The implication for regulated teams is structural. The difference between twelve isolated environments and one shared operational baseline is not incremental cost savings. It reduces duplicated infrastructure controls, provides a consistent platform-maintenance model, and gives assessors one operational baseline to evaluate. Application code and dependency patching remain workload-specific. One operational model, applied across the portfolio, turns consistency from an aspiration into evidence an assessor can verify.
Production readiness is about time
What happens six months after deployment? What happens when a runtime reaches end of support? What happens when the security organization introduces a new requirement? What happens when an auditor asks for evidence? What happens when the organization grows from five applications to fifty? And what happens when the platform itself changes direction?
These are not edge cases for regulated industries. They are part of the expected lifecycle of production software. Among engineering leaders in healthcare, aerospace, defense, and finance, service continuity now ranks as the top evaluation criterion, ahead of developer experience and pricing. The industry spent a decade optimizing for developer onboarding speed. Regulated teams need platforms built for long-term operations.

articles.title: Gemini agora permite editar PDFs, documentos e planilhas dentro do chat
articles.text:
O Google ampliou as ferramentas do Gemini e passou a permitir que usuários criem, visualizem e editem documentos diretamente nas conversas com a inteligência artificial (IA). A novidade elimina a necessidade de baixar arquivos para fazer alterações em outro aplicativo e depois enviá-los novamente ao chatbot.
O recurso foi anunciado nesta quinta-feira (29) e está disponível para todos os usuários do Gemini, em todos os idiomas e regiões onde o aplicativo funciona. Entre os formatos compatíveis estão PDFs, documentos do Google Docs, planilhas do Sheets, apresentações de slides, arquivos Markdown, TXT e códigos de programação.
A ferramenta permite abrir os arquivos em visualização ampliada, fazer alterações manualmente ou selecionar trechos específicos para pedir que a IA os modifique. Também é possível destacar partes de um documento e fazer perguntas sobre o conteúdo.
Na prática, o usuário pode, por exemplo, solicitar a criação de um documento, conferir o resultado na própria conversa e pedir ajustes sem precisar alternar entre diferentes programas.
Como funciona a edição de arquivos no Gemini
- A atualização amplia uma capacidade que o Google já oferecia: a geração e o download de arquivos a partir de comandos enviados ao Gemini. A diferença é que, agora, o conteúdo pode ser refinado diretamente na interface do chatbot;
- O usuário pode expandir o arquivo para ocupar a tela inteira e editar o texto por conta própria. Outra opção é selecionar uma parte do conteúdo e pedir ao Gemini que faça uma alteração específica;
- Também é possível combinar essas funções. Uma pessoa pode gerar uma apresentação, revisar sua estrutura, selecionar um trecho e solicitar mudanças no texto ou nos elementos visuais. Em planilhas, por exemplo, o usuário pode destacar uma tabela e pedir que o Gemini a transforme em um gráfico;
- Depois da edição, os arquivos podem ser abertos em ferramentas do Google ou baixados em formatos compatíveis.
Leia mais:
- Google cria IA que trabalha por você e faz tarefas em 1 clique
- Gemini 4 Argon finalmente chega ao app e à busca do Google; saiba mais
- ChatGPT e outras IAs mudam resultados de testes de personalidade conforme o idioma
Recurso tem limitações entre celular e computador
Apesar da disponibilidade ampla, nem todos os formatos funcionam em todos os dispositivos. A edição e a visualização de PDFs estão disponíveis tanto na versão web quanto nos aplicativos móveis do Gemini.
Já documentos, planilhas, apresentações, arquivos Markdown, TXT e códigos podem ser editados diretamente apenas na versão para navegador, pelo menos neste primeiro momento.
A novidade também não significa que o Gemini substitua completamente os programas tradicionais de edição. O recurso oferece uma maneira de criar e ajustar arquivos dentro da conversa, mas os usuários ainda podem recorrer a aplicativos especializados para tarefas mais complexas.
Google acompanha movimento no mercado de IA
A atualização aproxima o Gemini de experiência que outras empresas de IA também estão desenvolvendo. A Anthropic, por exemplo, lançou anteriormente ferramenta semelhante no Claude, permitindo criar e editar documentos e apresentações dentro das conversas.
A disputa entre os chatbots passa, assim, por oferecer mais do que respostas em texto. Ao incorporar ferramentas de criação e edição, as empresas tentam transformar seus assistentes em ambientes nos quais os usuários consigam executar tarefas completas, sem precisar alternar constantemente entre aplicativos.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Amazon tells engineers to stop tokenmaxxing and judge AI tools by what they ship
articles.text:
Big quote: Amazon is telling its engineering teams to judge AI coding tools by the software they help deliver, not the volume of tokens they consume. The updated engineering guidelines warn against treating AI adoption, token consumption, code changes and code reviews as performance targets. "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," Amazon wrote.
Amazon is not abandoning usage data. It is asking managers to examine those figures alongside other indicators.
The company recommends examining teams at both ends of AI adoption. Low usage may suggest engineers are missing opportunities to improve their work. Heavy usage should prompt a different question: whether delivery is improving enough to justify it. Neither figure settles the question on its own.
The guidance targets tokenmaxxing – deliberately inflating AI consumption to appear productive on internal dashboards.
Earlier this year, Amazon employees were using MeshClaw, an internal AI agent that can deploy code and interact with Slack, to increase their token counts. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard in May after employees gamed the rankings. Amazon says it has not imposed employee token caps.
Amazon's guidance leaves room for engineers to conclude that a particular task does not benefit from the available tools. It describes that conclusion as "a finding, not a failing," treating an explanation of a tool's limitations as evidence of judgment rather than resistance to adoption.
"We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice," the company wrote.
Other companies are confronting similar gaps between AI consumption and useful output. Uber president and COO Andrew Macdonald said in May that higher token usage had not yet translated into useful consumer features. His comments followed the company's disclosure that it had exhausted its 2026 Claude Code budget by April.
At Accenture, leaked audio obtained by 404 Media in June captured executives discussing rising token spending as clients moved from chatbots to agentic workflows. Executives discussed uncertainty about both the cost of individual tasks and whether the spending was worthwhile. The firm was reportedly developing an advisory tool called Token IQ to help clients manage those expenses.

articles.title: The R2 SUV is already Rivian's best-selling vehicle | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rivian’s new R2 SUV was its best-selling vehicle in the third quarter, the company said Thursday, marking an auspicious start for the all-important EV.
While Rivian didn’t say exactly how many R2s it sold over the three-month period, the company is confident enough in the pace of sales that it raised its delivery guidance for Wall Street. Rivian had previously expected to deliver between 65,000 and 70,000 EVs this year. On Thursday, it bumped up that floor to 67,000.
It’s the second time Rivian has raised its delivery guidance this year, and the company is now on track to break a three-year stalemate during which it struggled to ship more than 50,000 vehicles annually. The company launched the R2 just in June, but it has made a major bet on scaling production of the lower-cost SUV at a historically quick rate.
The early success of the R2 is also a sign that Rivian is finding new customers despite last year’s loss of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit. The death of that tax credit, along with changes made by the Trump administration to U.S. regulations that supported the growth of EVs, has caused many major automakers to shift their attention back to internal combustion and hybrid vehicles — leaving room in the market for pure-EV companies like Tesla and Rivian.
“In a U.S. automotive marketplace starved for high-quality EV choice, R2 is an attractively priced option for everyday adventures that is resonating with a broad set of consumers and we expect will be a game changer for Rivian’s long-term growth and profitability,” the company said in a letter to shareholders released Thursday.
Rivian revealed earlier this month that it built 19,751 vehicles in the third quarter and delivered 19,248. That was roughly 45% more than it delivered in the same period last year and a big jump from the 12,613 vehicles built and 12,194 delivered in the second quarter of 2026. The increase was driven in large part by the company launching a second production shift at its factory in Normal, Illinois.
Rivian said Thursday that the R2 was responsible for “much of the gain quarter-over-quarter,” but didn’t go into specifics. The company generated $2.2 billion in revenue in the third quarter and suffered a net loss of $913 million — down from $1.2 billion in the same period last year.
Rivian launched the R2 at a starting price of just under $60,000. A more affordable “premium” trim is supposed to be available later this year that starts at $53,990. Even cheaper versions are slated for 2027, which will be available for as low as $44,990.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. Real-time observation of topological defect dynamics mediating two-dimensional skyrmion lattice melting. Nature Nanotechnology, 2025; 20 (10): 1405 DOI: 10.1038/s41565-025-01977-2

articles.title: GitHub says massive influx of AI-generated code required extra 4 million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of storage to manage — a sixfold increase to 7.4 billion monthly commits in one year
articles.text:
GitHub says massive influx of AI-generated code required extra 4 million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of storage to manage — a sixfold increase to 7.4 billion monthly commits in one year
Everyone knew the rise was sharp, but the figures are staggering.
Is most programming code now made by AI? That's not hard to believe given the number of testimonies, but we now have exact figures behind that statement. GitHub, the world's largest code repository, says that over the course of this year, it added 4 million CPU cores, 160PB of storage, and 50 Tb/s of networking capacity to keep up with the influx of AI-generated code.
Raw repository activity saw a massive year-over-year increase, as per GitHub's technical report. Code commits (adding/removing code) grew sixfold, while merged pull requests (finalizing a feature or bugfix) jumped 4x.
The multipliers sound impressive enough, but the exponential growth pattern is even more so: half a year ago in April, there were already 1.4 billion commits per month — a figure that rose to 2.9 billion in August, and now sits at 7.4 billion for September. GitHub saw 17.9 billion code pushes in the past 12 months, which is more than all of 2024 and 2025 put together.
Predictably, the company says that agentic AI is behind the dizzying rise in the amount of code, and the need for it to both upgrade and rethink its technological infrastructure. By last September, over 40% of pull requests were started by an agent, up from 17% in March 2026. Moreover, repositories that kick off using AI generally see eight times the activity compared to handcrafted operations.
All this code activity puts disproportionate strain on CI/CD pipelines. In modern development, whenever someone commits code or merges a pending pull request, many actions are triggered: for example, checking for leftover "to-do" items, visually arranging code for consistency (linting), and running code and integration tests to check that the new code doesn't break existing functionality within the application and works correctly with associated programs, services, and APIs.
Triggering all of the above for each commit and/or pull request means that GitHub's hardware requirements have ballooned, now requiring massive amounts of computing power and I/O. The rise was so intense that the firm even had to reengineer its backend to try to decouple storage from compute as much as possible. Given how quickly demand is rising, GitHub is likely to have to upgrade sooner rather than later.

articles.title: Denza trae a España el BAO 5: su enorme SUV de 544 CV, hibridación DMO y 835 km de autonomía
articles.text:
El Bao 5, uno de los SUVs más interesantes de Denza, aterriza en España para sumarse al catálogo de SUVs premium disponibles. Se trata del primer SUV de la marca y lo hace con la tecnología de hibridación enchufable DMO con diversas propuestas de motorización y con una autonomía que se dispara hasta los 835 km en autonomía conjunta.
En este sentido, el Denza Bao 5 combina un motor de gasolina turboalimentado de 1,5 litros y dos motores eléctricos, uno delantero y otro trasero, para ofrecer una potencia máxima de 544 CV (400 kW) y 760 Nm de par.
Por separado, el motor de gasolina del Denza Bao 5 desarrolla 150 CV y 240 Nm de par, pero su función principal es suministrar electricidad tanto a la Blade Battery de 31,8 kWh como a los motores eléctricos en el eje delantero y trasero que desarrollan 272 CV y 388 CV respectivamente. Una potencia increíble, teniendo en cuenta que estamos hablando de UN SUV de cinco plazas y 4,9 metros.
Este sistema híbrido supone que el Denza Bao 5 acelere de 0 a 100km/h en tan solo 4,8 segundos en la versión Elegance y en 5,0 segundos en la versión Ultimate. Este SUV de Denza combina un chasis de largueros y travesaños con una serie de sistemas de control propios del DMO.
Además, monta un sistema de suspensión hidráulica inteligente DiSus-P, que analiza constantemente los datos de más de 20 sensores: desde el ángulo de giro del volante y la posición de los pedales del acelerador y del freno, hasta la velocidad y la orientación de las ruedas, e incluso la presión y la temperatura. Cierran el conjunto dos diferenciales electrónicos y un sistema de bloqueo central. Todo ello para ofrecer una enorme versatilidad tanto en caminos como en carretera. Un pack bastante potente para aquellos que quieran un SUV híbrido de gama alta.
Respecto a su interior del Bao 5, el conductor tiene acceso a una instrumentación completamente digital de 12,3 pulgadas y a un Head-Up Display, a la que se suma en la consola central una pantalla táctil de 15,6” (39,6 cm) y una pantalla panorámica para el acompañante, situada justo delante de su asiento. El coche tiene su propio asistente de voz con cuatro zonas distintas de detección y un sistema de audio de alta fidelidad firmado por Devialet y equipado con hasta 18 altavoces en la versión Ultimate.
Sobre el precio, estamos hablando de un SUV premium, por lo que tiene un precio de venta recomendado de 76.290 euros para la versión Elegance y de 86.420 euros para la Ultimate. Esta última incluye una garantía oficial para el vehículo de 6 años o 150.000 km, de 8 años o 150.000 km para el sistema de propulsión y de 8 años o 250.000 km para la Blade Battery. Ambas versiones en una buena selección de colores, tanto exterior como interior.

articles.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
articles.text:
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
A powerful feedback loop could drive more warming than predicted.
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.
A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.
None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.
A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.
At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.
So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.
Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

articles.title: Reddit will force everyone to log in
articles.text:
Reddit is announcing a huge shift: It’s going to start requiring users to log in.
Reddit will force everyone to log in
Reddit is becoming a ‘logged-in-only experience,’ says CEO Steve Huffman.
Right now, you can browse Reddit without having an account, and the site is generally a great resource for crowdsourced information on a whole range of topics. I know I’m not the only person who appends “reddit” to a lot of Google searches to find answers to things written by actual humans instead of robots. But that openness has made it a target for scraping and automated traffic, leading Reddit to file lawsuits over alleged unauthorized access of its data and make product changes like limiting access to “Old Reddit.”
There’s no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you’re logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren’t logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in “select markets outside the US” in the “coming months,” according to CEO Steve Huffman. “We’ll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there.” Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app’s incognito mode.
Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit’s user experience and its ads business and is “more protective of Reddit data.” The “vast majority” of unauthorized Reddit access happens “through our logged-out experiences,” though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user’s identity — “Honestly, we don’t want to know” — just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver “more relevant ads.”
“This is a big change for Reddit, where we’ve allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades,” Huffman says. “And I don’t know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it’s a big change for me. But I’ve come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business.”
Reddit is making this announcement alongside its Q3 2026 earnings, which were released today. Search traffic was “down meaningfully” in Q3, Huffman says in the company’s shareholder letter, with logged-out traffic and web traffic being the most heavily impacted. “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week,” Huffman says.
However, Huffman notes that app and logged-in daily active unique users make up “over 80% of the monetization on Reddit,” which he says “speaks to the strength of Reddit as a destination and the impact of our ongoing product work.”

articles.title: China und E-Autos: Das sind die Gründe für den Milliardenverlust bei Volkswagen
articles.text:
China und E-Autos: Das sind die Gründe für den Milliardenverlust bei Volkswagen
Volkswagen steuert auf das erste Verlustjahr seit dem Diesel-Skandal zu. Im dritten Quartal stand unter dem Strich ein Verlust von rund 5,82 Milliarden Euro, wie der Konzern in Wolfsburg mitteilte. Damit ändern sich auch die Vorzeichen für das bisherige Jahr: Für die ersten neun Monate steht ein Ergebnis nach Steuern von minus 2,72 Milliarden Euro. Ein großer Teil davon sind zwar Buchverluste – aber nicht nur.
Das sind die wichtigsten Gründe für die tiefroten Zahle bei Europas größtem Autobauer:
Mehr Stromer, weniger Geld: das E-Auto-Paradox
Volkswagen verliert bei den Verkaufszahlen deutlich an Boden. Im laufenden Jahr steuert der Konzern weltweit auf ungefähr acht Millionen Auslieferungen zu. Einen Lichtblick gibt es aber: das Geschäft mit E-Autos in Europa. Jedes fünfte bis Ende September ausgelieferte Auto auf dem Kontinent war ein reiner Stromer – und rund 40 Prozent des Auftragsbestands entfallen auf E-Modelle. Für den Boom verantwortlich macht VW unter anderem die hohen Spritpreise und die bessere Verfügbarkeit von Einstiegsmodellen. Allein für die Kleinwagen-Familie um den ID. Polo lagen zuletzt 150.000 Bestellungen vor.
Nach Angaben von VW-Finanzchef Arno Antlitz liegt die Nachfrage auf einem Niveau, das der Konzern erst für 2029 erwartet hatte. Doch mit Blick auf den Gewinn hilft das nicht: «Der Markterfolg unserer Elektrofahrzeuge setzt unser Ergebnis zusätzlich unter Druck», sagte der Manager. Denn ein E-Auto bringt dem Konzern derzeit weniger Gewinn als ein vergleichbarer Verbrenner.
Wächst der Anteil der Stromer, sinkt also der Ertrag. Der schnelle Hochlauf bei E-Autos verwässere die Gewinnmarge, sagte Antlitz. Die Marge des Modells ID. Cross liege bei 70 bis 80 Prozent eines vergleichbaren Verbrennermodells. Bei anderem Modellen sei der Wert niedriger. Antlitz ging davon aus, dass sich der Effekt in den nächsten Monaten verstärken wird. Man müsse daher die Kosten senken. Immerhin: Antlitz gab sich zuversichtlich, dass VW durch den Boom die CO2-Flottengrenzwerte der EU zunächst einhalten und Strafzahlungen vermeiden kann.
China: vom Gewinnbringer zum Problemfall
China ist der weltgrößte Automarkt und immens wichtig für Volkswagen. Die Geschäfte in der Volksrepublik laufen aber seit einiger Zeit schlecht. Neben der Konkurrenz lokaler Hersteller macht dem Konzern ein Nachfrageeinbruch zu schaffen. VW-China-Chef Ralf Brandstätter sprach zuletzt von einem Markt «im freien Fall». 2025 wurden mehr als 24 Millionen Autos dort verkauft. Für 2026 werden demnach weniger als 19 Millionen erwartet.
In den ersten neun Monaten sanken die Verkäufe um gut 30 Prozent auf 1,38 Millionen. Die Entwicklung nahm zuletzt auch an Fahrt auf. In Spitzenzeiten verkaufte das Unternehmen jährlich mehr als vier Millionen Autos in China.
Die Erwartungen sind entsprechend niedrig: Für 2026 rechnet VW in China vor Abschreibungen mit einem Abschneiden um die Gewinnschwelle. Nach dem ersten Halbjahr war VW für das einstige Wachstumsgeschäft noch von 200 bis 600 Millionen Euro positivem anteiligem Beitrag ausgegangen. Antlitz zufolge besteht aber ein erhebliches Risiko, dass das vierte Quartal das Ergebnis vor Abschreibungen in den Negativbereich drückt. Zum Vergleich: In Spitzenjahren verdiente VW in China mehr als 4 Milliarden Euro.
Außerdem hat VW den Wert von chinesischen Tochterfirmen, die der Konzern komplett kontrolliert, um rund eine Milliarde Euro nach unten korrigiert.
Abschreibung auf Porsche-Firmenwert
Für das laufende Jahr rechnete der VW-Konzern zuletzt mit Sonderkosten von rund 10 Milliarden Euro. Davon wurden 8,7 Milliarden bereits verbucht. Größter Einzelposten ist eine Abschreibung auf den Firmenwert des Stuttgarter Sport- und Geländewagenbauers Porsche. Er beläuft sich auf rund 6,4 Milliarden Euro. Die Wertberichtigung ist nicht zahlungswirksam, drückt aber den Gewinn. Hintergrund sind niedrigere Erwartungen an die Entwicklung der Tochter.
Bereits ein Jahr zuvor war die Lage bei Porsche einer der Hauptgründe für den Quartalsverlust. Die Luxusmarke, einst eine Gewinnperle des Konzerns, steckt bereits länger in der Krise. Belastend wirkten insbesondere der Einbruch beim China-Geschäft, die US-Zölle und Kurskorrekturen bei der Elektro-Strategie. Zuletzt hatten sich die Geschäftszahlen von Porsche stabilisiert.
Umbau kostet: Was noch auf der Rechnung steht
Die VW-Führung um Chef Oliver Blume baut den Konzern gerade um. Und das kostet massig Geld. So wirkt sich demnach im dritten Quartal der angestrebte Verkauf des Werks Osnabrück an den Finanzinvestor Aurelius sowie an das Land Niedersachsen belastend aus. Beide wollen den Standort auf Rüstung trimmen. Eine genaue Summe nannte Volkswagen nicht.
Ohne die Sondereffekte hätte VW im Tagesgeschäft einen Gewinn von 8,8 Milliarden Euro verbuchen können. Der Konzernumsatz lag nach neun Monaten bei 233,4 Milliarden Euro (minus 2,2 Prozent).
Und jetzt?
Ob Volkswagen das Jahr tatsächlich mit Verlust abschließen wird, muss sich zeigen. Doch viel deutet darauf hin. Der E-Auto-Hochlauf dürfte den Gewinn weiter drücken. Außerdem laufen im vierten Quartal voraussichtlich weitere Sonderkosten auf, zum Beispiel für zusätzliche Vorruhestandsregelungen.
Auch eine Einigung mit den Arbeitnehmern über die weiteren Sparpläne des Vorstands könnte zusätzliche Kosten verursachen, etwa für Abfindungen. Auch wenn das vor Jahresende als unwahrscheinlich gilt. Das Management selbst rechnet im Tagesgeschäft höchstens mit einem Mini-Gewinn.

articles.title: AI Raises The Bar For Tomorrow’s Engineers
articles.text:
Universities are redesigning curricula and assessments around judgment, validation, and technical depth.
Key Takeaways:
Today’s science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) students will be entering the workforce at a pivotal moment. They grew up on iPads, attended high school classes on Zoom during the COVID pandemic, and are navigating college amid an AI revolution. Now, with generative and agentic tools able to accelerate many tasks, a burning question remains: How can universities adapt to this new era and help students harness AI’s advantages without weakening the foundational knowledge and judgment they will need as engineers?
Academic institutions are working to help students get the most out of AI tools while ensuring the next generation of engineers doesn’t cut corners on foundational knowledge. One trend is universities placing greater emphasis on critical-thinking tasks so students don’t swallow GenAI slop in totality. Just as large language models need guardrails, universities are developing tests and quizzes to ensure students learn properly and to minimize cheating. [See Table of University Approaches below.]
“We are seeing people who skate through or miss something fundamental that was important for a particular job, and they have to go back and relearn it,” said Alexandra Werth, assistant professor in biomedical engineering at Cornell University. “Higher ed is in trouble if we don’t work hard to make sure that doesn’t happen. I just went to an American Society of Engineering Education conference, where there were thousands of engineering educators, and this was what everyone wanted to talk about and figure out because this is what makes education relevant. People are trying a lot of different things, and we’re still in a weird place where AI technology is constantly changing. Saying, ‘This is the right approach,’ or ‘This is the wrong approach,’ is still in flux.”
Students are adopting AI tools faster than industry and academia can determine the right balance. “Everybody’s kind of struggling with it, to be honest,” said Matthew Ozalas, master application development engineer, scientist at Keysight. “I’ve talked to professors and heard a lot of different perspectives across the gamut. Some professors are saying, ‘No technology in my class — just blue books back to the old days.’ Others say, ‘Use whatever you want, but you have a time limit.’ I’ve been really impressed with how AI-savvy young people are. At the same time, there’s this idea about how much they need to know in the engineering field. People have asked, ‘Do they even need to know everything anymore? Can’t they just ask their large language model?'”
That means validation of AI responses is key. “The biggest shift we’re seeing is that next-generation engineers need to be good at defining problems, providing the right context to AI, validating its output, and understanding tradeoffs,” said William Wang, founder and CEO of ChipAgents. “Engineering judgment has become even more important, not less, because engineers are now responsible for validating AI-generated work, recognizing incorrect assumptions, and knowing when deeper investigation is required.”
That uncertainty only raises the stakes for mastering the fundamentals, especially when AI can produce answers that sound convincing but are wrong. “From an industry perspective, it is strongly recommended that universities should teach students how to combine fundamentals with AI-assisted workflows,” said Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris. “Specify the problem clearly, generate alternatives, validate assumptions, test results, and document decisions. The graduates who will stand out are not those who use AI, but those who can use it safely, critically, and productively.”
Students also must be able to defend their findings orally, without AI help. “Graduates need soft skills tailored for a generation who have grown up on screens,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “In industry, engineers have to explain their reasoning on the spot — in design reviews, with customers, and when something goes wrong. Clear, confident verbal communication matters more in the AI era because it shows thinking that AI can’t produce for you. Universities should make it a deliberate part of the curriculum.”
In short, students still need the knowledge and judgment to evaluate what an LLM tells them.
Experience makes the risks clear. “If you work with AI and you’re experienced, you can see how confidently it gives you completely wrong answers or will hallucinate its way through,” said Ozalas. “It’s the balancing act that we have to strike. I can imagine it’s really hard right now to be a student or a young person trying to get into this.”
One professor, who spoke on condition he not be named, pointed to a potentially more disturbing issue. “AI is a resource that has been helping facilitate student research and learning over the past several years,” he said. “However, over this period, I have observed an overall decline in student retention and performance in the same type of curriculum, suggesting that the benefits of AI may be outweighed by increased reliance on this tool. The overall trend has appeared to be that students are having decreasing attention spans as AI becomes more integrated into education and knowledge transfer.”
Another professor, speaking on condition of anonymity, declined to discuss students’ use of AI. Her reason: “Because then I’ll be bitter.”
Universities must address such concerns. “It is essential for university curricula to target GenAI weaknesses,” said Tamara Popovic, educational developer for IT and electrical engineering at ETH Zurich. “One of the biggest challenges we face is what’s called the illusion of competence. When a student prompts an LLM to explain a concept like heterojunction formation, the tool generates a beautifully structured, highly confident response. The student reads it, feels an immediate sense of clarity, and mistakes that passive clarity for actual mastery. They skip the difficult mental strain required to truly internalize the physics behind the phenomena. To break that illusion of competence, we started to design learning activities that target the specific cognitive blind spots of GenAI, namely, complex spatial relationships and non-standard visual abstractions.”
For example, the university introduced exercises based on multi-variable graphic shifting. “We present a standard plot, like a MOSFET C-V curve, but introduce a unique physical anomaly,” said Popovic. “Text-based LLMs, for now, cannot accurately map these multi-layered physical transformations onto new visual representations without making fatal logical leaps. Forcing students to navigate these visual-spatial shifts ensures they are relying on their own internal mental models rather than an external algorithm.”
If AI can mimic understanding, universities must decide how to teach the real thing.
Developing curricula in the AI era
Universities are figuring out how to allow AI tools while preserving academic rigor and integrity.
“Faculty is uncomfortable,” said Stanley Chan, professor of electrical and computer engineering and director of engineering AI education at Purdue University. “It’s the first time that we are navigating this path, and I tell administration and faculty members that we don’t have a crystal ball.”
The Purdue board recently approved a plan to integrate more AI into each successive year of a four-year degree. “We have to make the transformation because otherwise we will be outpaced by AI,” said Chan. “It’s a matter of time that higher education will be fundamentally reshaped because a new technology is here.”
To avoid loss of learning, professors have to ask students tough questions, and students need to learn how to ask AI tough questions, noted Chan. “Why are you doing this? Can you give me the evidence? Can you show me that this is working? Have you considered other design options? Why is this design done in this way, and have you thought about approaching the problem in another way? Maybe you should think about the other direction.”
Syllabi also need to strike the right balance. “There is that question of how to even write a good syllabus nowadays,” said David Janes, professor of electrical and computer engineering and the director of the semiconductor degrees program at Purdue. “In your syllabus you need to define what is and is not appropriate use of AI, and the answer is usually that you can’t use AI. If you use AI, you are still responsible for verifying and checking it. You are responsible for independently learning and understanding these concepts.”
Fig. 1: A student and professor working in Purdue University’s Birck Nanotechnology Center. Source: Purdue
Given this complex semiconductor work, AI fluency must be grounded in engineering fundamentals, whether students are tackling network-on-chip congestion or semiconductor test.
“AI can propose a fabric configuration in seconds, but knowing whether it will hold up under real traffic patterns, achieve physical implementation, and survive routing and other tradeoffs requires that underlying domain depth,” noted Nandan Nayampally, chief commercial officer at Baya Systems. “That combination — AI plus real expertise — is where you get the actual productivity boost, not from AI alone. Without the fundamentals to validate it, AI-driven design accelerates disasters as fast as it accelerates progress.”
For semiconductor testing, students need deep, domain-specific knowledge that takes time to develop, observed Ryan Moran, head of talent acquisition at the Center of Excellence at Teradyne. “Universities that treat AI literacy as complementary to rigorous foundational training are producing the graduates we most want to hire. The more forward-thinking programs are redesigning assignments so that AI tool use is assumed. New graduates who arrive having used tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or similar assistants can produce working code drafts faster than earlier cohorts. The challenge is to maintain technical knowledge to both understand and verify what the code actually does.”
Foundational skills and deep disciplines such as physics and mathematics bring many job opportunities. “You can go very deep in linear algebra or calculus,” said Pradheepa Raman, chief people officer at GlobalFoundries. “If you go into the linear algebra side, you become a data scientist or AI engineer. If you go into the calculus side, you can become a quant in financial institutions. These old types of deep skills are in many curricula to help students become deep experts. I would prioritize that first because it’s hard for companies to teach students unless you have the basics.”
Ideally, graduates will know both science and AI. “The strongest candidates are those who know how to use AI as a productivity tool while also demonstrating solid engineering judgment, a problem-solving mindset, and a strong grasp of first principles,” said Gabriela Cruz Thompson, director of university research collaboration at Intel. “In other words, we are not looking for graduates who simply know how to prompt an AI model. We’re looking for graduates who understand the underlying science and engineering well enough to know when an AI-generated answer is correct, incomplete, or wrong.”
Producing those graduates requires assessments that reveal genuine understanding, not merely polished AI output.
AI-proof assessments
While students can enter prompts for just about anything, from emails and job applications all the way to semiconductor designs, the most valuable new skill is not prompt writing by itself. “It is the ability to use AI as an engineering assistant while maintaining technical ownership of the result,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “The challenge for universities is to move beyond policing AI use and toward teaching responsible, verifiable engineering with AI in the loop.”
However, no universal silver bullet can prevent students from using AI to cheat. Assessments must be AI-proof, and professors need teaching assistants to help them adapt the curriculum course by course, Purdue’s Chan noted. “We need to ask the question, ‘Can AI solve all the homework problems by itself?’ If the answer is yes, then the class itself has to be rethought. Otherwise, no matter how many countermeasures you put in, it’s going to be ineffective.”
That need for course-by-course redesign is widely shared. “AI can now answer most of the questions we used to set in exams and coursework, and universities are under pressure to make assessments AI-proof,” said Axiomise’s Darbari. “That isn’t only an assessment problem. It changes how students learn and what they are equipped with when they graduate. The risk is that we produce graduates who can get answers but can’t stand behind them.”
At the same time, students must still memorize some math and physics. “Some of the higher-level concepts they have to learn by heart,” said Chan. “We still want to keep some of the paper and pencil exams so that when they go to the design stage, they will know what questions to ask. That cannot come in a day.”
Creative assessments are also key, and some faculty hold in-class competitions. “There is an engineering design goal such as building a robot, and then there are targets, and you see who performs better,” he said. “You cannot cheat by just using AI. The robot has to physically run on the road.”
Students lose out if they take shortcuts. “At the Bachelor level, mastering a course such as semiconductor devices requires a massive amount of mental effort,” said ETH Zurich’s Popovic. “When students use generative AI as a cognitive shortcut, they bypass the very struggle that builds deep engineering intuition.”
Students using AI to cheat is not viewed differently from students copying others’ code or written work. Purdue has used plagiarism checkers on graduate theses for quite some time to ensure students write their own work and cite appropriate sources, Purdue’s Janes says. “It’s a very parallel thing with AI, though we would go about it differently if it’s an engineering analysis than writing. We all struggle with the same problem.”
Physics cannot be traded for AI. “When engineers don’t know physics, they don’t know reality,” Keysight’s Ozalas said. “It’s the same with coding. If you don’t know coding and you just prompt everything, you lose the connection with the real world, and that’s a concern.”
Ultimately, traditional tests may still be best for fundamental knowledge. “Then provide more workshops, more projects, more labs, but definitely allow them to use the AI tools,” said GF’s Raman. “If you don’t, it’s like saying, ‘Hey, I have all these tools, but I want you to go the traditional way even though it will take enormous time.’ Time is also of the essence. They can learn more if they are allowed to use the tools.”
All the company’s summer interns had access to AI tools, Raman noted. “They were amazing using these tokens. They were happy to get access and build things. It was awesome to see.”
Conclusion
Like all new technology, AI in education brings pros and cons.
“AI has the potential to make both teaching and learning more effective, but only when it is designed and used thoughtfully,” said Ying Zhang, professor at Georgia Institute of Technology. “Like any educational technology, its impact depends on how educators and students use it. For instructors, AI can reduce time spent on repetitive tasks, such as generating practice problems or answering routine questions, allowing them to devote more time to mentoring students and designing engaging learning experiences. For students, AI can provide personalized explanations, timely feedback, and on-demand learning support, particularly outside of class and office hours.”
At the same time, there are legitimate challenges. “General-purpose AI systems can generate inaccurate or misleading information, often referred to as hallucinations,” said Zhang. “There is also a risk that students may become overly reliant on AI if it simply provides answers, reducing the cognitive effort that is essential for developing deep understanding and independent problem-solving abilities.”
Given the direction the industry is heading, denying students access to AI tools is pointless, even though the industry still hasn’t decided on the best approach to manage access. “From the AI perspective, you do need to build AI,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Everything will have AI built in as a technology eventually, so you need AI security specialists to make sure that they build secure solutions for AI. AI tools might change the job landscape, but I don’t think positions will go away. It’s just that they’re going to change in their nature. To keep up with the technology, you’ll have to use AI tools and rely on AI assistance. I’ve heard from academia that there is a need for having specialized skill sets.” However, she added that the exact nature of these skills is still evolving.
This also means students need both hard knowledge and soft communication skills. “The graduates who do well in the AI era will be the ones who can use the tools, defend their reasoning, and communicate it clearly in the moment,” said Darbari. “Universities that build all of that into their curriculum will produce the engineers the semiconductor industry most needs.”
Darbari’s tips for universities:
The pace and depth of change in university curricula vary considerably across institutions. Both academia and industry benefit from open discussions about navigating the AI era.
| University | Directive | Hard skills | Soft skills | Innovations | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cornell | Each discipline needs to wrestle with what AI literacy means to them. | Math; mathematical graphical intuition; programming; prompting; weigh up pros/cons of various AI algos (see biomedical examples). | Critical thinking; professional behavior; how to email and find contacts; human networking to get past AI bots on resumes; lifelong learning skills. | Completely oral exams; small quizzes in class; flipping the class with recorded lectures and in-person workshops. | 
| ETH Zurich | Does not integrate AI into its formal degree curriculum; focuses on building a profound physical understanding of underlying phenomena, preserving the integrity of the learning process. | Understand abstract concepts such as carrier transport and quantum tunnelling taught in physics courses; connect concepts to real-world electronic devices. | Critical evaluation; treat AI not as an authority, but as a flawed draft that requires expert auditing. | Classroom activities where they flip the script by providing students with AI-generated solutions to complex problems, then task them with identifying structural flaws, false assumptions, and hallucinations in the text. | 
| Georgia Tech | Per its AI policy and guidance, encourages responsible, ethical use of AI to support teaching and learning; instructors encouraged to establish clear expectations for AI use and help students develop skills to use AI responsibly, ethically, and effectively. | Strong engineering fundamentals and AI competency; focus on defining problems; evaluating and validating AI-generated results; integrating information from multiple sources; how to use AI tools effectively; when to trust AI vs. when to question outputs. | Deeper learning, critical thinking, and responsible AI use; accountability for own understanding and work; exercise sound engineering judgment; communicate and collaborate effectively across multidisciplinary teams; critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and professional judgment central to engineering practice. | In the school of ECE, developed SMART Tutor, a course-specific AI tutor that combines RAG with principles of self-regulated learning; guides students through the problem-solving process; encourages them to develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. | 
| Purdue | Every graduate will need to have AI competency; each college and department determines what that means; each year to have progressively more AI integration; students must get the fundamentals right, per industry stakeholders. | Physics, math; fundamentals of AI technology; statistical thinking, probabilistic reasoning to make sense of data; algorithmic reasoning; programming; data analysis; Python for data science class to look at data and programming together; verification. | Human perspectives, creativity, originality, and ability to make judgment; understanding how AI works and what it can and can’t do; utilizing AI in projects; how to be a manager of AI; building intuition and knowledge to keep moving forward without AI doing everything for them. | Launched summer bootcamp for graduating class, including how to do an interview in the AI era according to recent grads; how to prepare a portfolio or resume; 4+1 program for extra training; semiconductor degrees program, advised by a 40- member semiconductor degrees leadership board; semiconductor career fair. |

articles.title: Solink raises more than $100M to pull business data from security cameras with AI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Solink raises more than $100M to pull business data from security cameras with AI
Video intelligence company Solink Corp. revealed today that it has raised more than $100 million in new funding.
Solink started out in Ottawa in 2009 selling cloud video surveillance, and its software now uses artificial intelligence to pull information out of the security cameras retailers, restaurants and warehouse operators already have installed. The company said the new money will fund its roadmap for what it calls AI vision intelligence. By its own count, about 500,000 cameras at more than 35,000 customer locations in 65 countries now feed into the platform.
The company added AI agents for perimeter security and loss prevention work in February. Those agents run on edge devices and do not need proprietary cameras. The VerifEye command center that Solink sells to security operations centers gained vision language models a month later, with the aim of filtering out false alarms before an operator ever sees them.
Nobody should need to watch footage to know what is happening inside a business, in the view of co-founder and Chief Executive Mike Matta. He called the present a “watershed moment” for physical businesses. With the new money, Matta said, Solink wants to help customers reduce loss and uncover revenue from their existing cameras.
Toronto-based private equity firm Vertu Capital led the round. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. also put in a material amount through Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, according to Solink. The bank’s asset management arm led the company’s $60 million Series C round in July 2023. Golub Growth and Comcast Ventures came in as new investors.
Eric Kafka, a partner at Vertu, called AI vision intelligence “one of the most significant opportunities in software today.” Solink, he said, has shown the foresight and execution needed to define the category. Customer adoption and the product roadmap made coming back “a natural decision,” said Mike Reilly, a managing director in Goldman’s growth equity group.
Solink did not disclose a valuation, and it gave no detail on the strategic opportunities it also plans to fund with part of the round. Including the new funding, investors have now put more than $198 million into the company.
