articles.title: L'écran de l'iPhone Duo est-il lisible en plein soleil ? Nos mesures — Frandroid
articles.text:
Apple entre enfin dans la danse du pliant avec son iPhone Duo. Pour équiper son nouveau format hybride, la firme de Cupertino aligne deux dalles OLED Super Retina XDR ProMotion : un écran externe de 5,4 pouces et un grand affichage pliant de 7,6 pouces.
Pour chasser les reflets sur cette dalle souple et supprimer visuellement la pliure induite par les écrans pliables, Apple a eu l’idée d’y coller en usine un film nanotexturé mat. Une trouvaille séduisante sur le papier, mais qu’en est-il sous un soleil de plomb ?
Armé de ma sonde colorimétrique et du logiciel Calman de Portrait Displays, j’ai passé les deux dalles sur notre banc d’essai pour vérifier si ce grand écran reste lisible en extérieur et passer au crible l’ensemble de nos mesures de laboratoire.
    Pour aller plus loin
Quel est le meilleur smartphone pliable en 2026 ?
            
Spécificités des deux écrans
L’iPhone Duo repose sur une cohabitation asymétrique. En façade fermée, on dispose d’un écran rigide de 5,4 pouces au format plus carré qu’à l’accoutumée, ce qui donne cet aspect passeport au Duo. Sa définition atteint 1398 x 2034 pixels pour une résolution de 460 ppp. Il est protégé par un verre Ceramic Shield 2 avec traitement anti-reflet, dans la droite lignée des finitions réservées aux modèles Pro.
Une fois le terminal ouvert, on change d’univers avec une dalle pliable de 7,6 pouces. Elle dégage une surface utile de 175,4 cm², soit un ratio écran/corps d’environ 90,4 %. Sa définition grimpe à 1878 x 2670 pixels, maintenant une densité confortable de 430 ppp. C’est sur cette surface que prend place le revêtement nanotexturé mat appliqué en usine.
Les deux dalles profitent de la technologie LTPO avec rafraîchissement adaptatif ProMotion de 1 à 120 Hz. Côté plage dynamique, la compatibilité avec les flux HDR10 et Dolby Vision répond présent.
| Caractéristiques techniques | Écran externe | Écran interne (pliable) | 
| Technologie de dalle | LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED | LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED | 
| Diagonale | 5,4 pouces | 7,6 pouces | 
| Définition | 1398 x 2034 pixels | 1878 x 2670 pixels | 
| Résolution | 460 ppp | 430 ppp | 
| Taux de rafraîchissement | ProMotion adaptatif (1 à 120 Hz) | ProMotion adaptatif (1 à 120 Hz) | 
| Protection / Finition | Ceramic Shield 2 + Anti-reflective coating | Nano Texture finish + Anti-reflective coating | 
| Luminosité standard (typ) | 1 000 nits | 1 000 nits | 
| Luminosité pic HDR (peak) | 3 000 nits | 3 000 nits | 
| Normes HDR | HDR10, Dolby Vision | HDR10, Dolby Vision | 
Pour la partie logicielle, pas de surprise chez Apple. iOS confie l’intégralité du rendu au moteur ColorSync. Le système bascule automatiquement entre le Rec.709/sRGB et l’espace étendu Display P3 selon la nature des photos ou des vidéos consultées. Il n’y a aucun réglage manuel de profil « Vif » ou « Naturel » à activer dans les sous-menus.
Réflectance et lisibilité en plein soleil : le piège du film mat
Passons au nœud du problème : la lisibilité en extérieur. Je me permets ici de citer nos confrères de 01net. Ils ont mis à profit un outil de mesure de la réflectance. Leurs mesures relèvent 72 GU (Gloss Units) pour l’écran externe et seulement 2 GU pour l’écran mat de l’iPhone Duo. C’est ridiculement peu. Cela signifie que les reflets sont annihilés sur cette surface. Un très beau travail. Concernant l’écran externe, en revanche, Samsung semble faire mieux sur son Galaxy Z Fold 8 avec seulement 60 GU. Néanmoins, dans les deux cas, on est sur de très belles performances, plus que les smartphones traditionnels, même les plus haut de gamme.
Ça, ce sont les mesures labo. Sur le terrain, la réalité est nettement moins rose. Ce film mat ne fait pas disparaître les photons, il les diffuse. Plutôt que de subir un reflet net et localisé que l’on esquive d’un léger mouvement de poignet, toute la dalle interne transforme les rayons du soleil en un voile blanc un peu laiteux. Le contraste infini de l’OLED en prend un coup immédiat. Pas sous la sonde, mais au niveau du rendu qu’il renvoie à nos yeux. Les noirs infinis virent au gris délavé en plein jour.
Sous un soleil direct, l’écran déplié n’est pas des plus flatteurs. Ça peut même être compliqué de le consulter surtout si comme moi vous utilisez le mode sombre d’iOS.
Durant mon test, j’ai rapidement pris une habitude : en extérieur, dès que le soleil tape trop fort, je referme l’iPhone Duo pour repasser sur l’écran externe de 5,4 pouces. Dépourvu de cette texture mate, il se montre bien plus lisible en plein jour. En revanche, de nuit ou en intérieur, ce désagrément disparaît totalement et j’ai même un contraste parfait quand je me regarde une série au fond du lit, à la nuit tombée.
Cela ne concerne que le film mat. Parce que la luminosité, elle, est excellente sur les deux écrans :
- Écran externe (5,4 pouces) : 1 313 nits au maximum en SDR et un pic à 2 800 nits en HDR.
- Écran interne (7,6 pouces) : 1 300 nits au maximum en SDR et un pic mesuré à 2 770 nits en HDR.
Apple annonce 3000 nits en pic et on s’en approche vraiment. En revanche, comme je l’ai dit, si les 1 313 nits suffisent à l’écran externe en plein soleil, les 1 300 nits de l’écran interne s’épuisent à compenser le voile laiteux créé par la nanotexture.
À noter que le film mat n’est pas fait pour être retiré à la main, mais il peut être remplacé en Apple Store en cas d’usure prématurée contre 55 euros (alors que chez Samsung, c’est offert la première fois). Et Apple ne propose pas d’alternative brillante si vous vous posiez la question.
Mesures de l’écran externe
J’ai installé l’iPhone Duo sous notre sonde Calibrite couplée au logiciel CalMAN Ultimate de Portrait Displays pour disséquer les performances de la dalle externe de 5,4 pouces. Les résultats confirment l’excellente maîtrise technique d’Apple sur ses écrans rigides.
| Critère | Conséquences concrètes | 
| Luminosité | Parfaite lisibilité en plein soleil ; aucun éblouissement dans le noir absolu (1 nit). Les reflets en HDR offrent un éclat saisissant. | 
| Contraste | Noirs parfaits et infinis grâce à l’OLED. Textes nets sans halo de lumière (blooming) et scènes sombres très immersives. | 
| Fidélité des couleurs – Usage standard | Rendu très naturel sur le Web et les applications du quotidien. Écart moyen imperceptible à l’œil nu, avec un blanc à peine frais. | 
| Fidélité des couleurs – Usage vidéo | Respect fidèle de l’étalonnage des films et séries. Les tons chair et les paysages restent naturels sans saturation excessive. | 
| Température des couleurs | Équilibre général neutre et propre. Aucune dérive jaunâtre gênante, avec une nuance bleutée quasi indétectable]. | 
| Capacité à reproduire les nuances | Dégradés fluides et sans banding. Couverture sRGB/P3 quasi intégrale adaptée à la retouche photo sans aplats disgracieux. | 
Pour la fidélité des couleurs, c’est un carton plein. Notre sonde relève un DeltaE moyen de 1,82 en sRGB et de 1,78 en Display P3. Pour faire simple, l’œil humain ne fait plus la différence. Les visages ont une teinte naturelle, les paysages ne sont pas fluo et les couleurs que vous voyez à l’écran sont exactement celles de la réalité. L’écran couvre d’ailleurs 99,4 % du sRGB et 99,1 % du P3. Il affiche tout le spectre sans manquer une seule nuance.
Le seul vrai défaut concerne l’affichage des blancs et des niveaux de gris. Avec un DeltaE moyen qui monte à 3,4 sur les gris et un pic à 5,7 sur le blanc pur, la dalle triche un peu. Dès que l’image devient très claire (au-delà de 70 % de luminosité), l’écran force sur le bleu et retire une pincée de vert. Mesurée à 6 643 K pour une cible parfaite à 6 500 K, la température des couleurs trahit ce choix : le blanc tire très légèrement vers le froid, avec un très discret voile bleuté. Rien de méchant à l’œil, mais ce n’est pas un blanc parfaitement neutre.
La courbe gamma moyenne (2,226) fait du très bon travail. La gradation entre les zones sombres et claires reste fluide jusqu’à 85 % de luminosité. Passé ce cap, l’écran freine un peu l’intensité pour ne pas abîmer ses diodes OLED. Enfin, la dalle est capable de descendre à seulement 1 nit en luminosité SDR. C’est un vrai bonheur pour lire dans le noir complet sans se faire agresser les yeux.
Mesures de l’écran interne pliable
Ouvrons l’iPhone Duo pour ausculter sa grande dalle pliable de 7,6 pouces. L’exercice est complexe pour Apple en raison de la structure souple.
| Critère | Conséquences concrètes | 
| Luminosité | Lisibilité totale en plein soleil grâce aux 1 300 nits en SDR et aux pics à 2 770 nits en HDR. Confort absolu la nuit sans éblouir grâce au plancher de 1 nit en SDR (3 nits en HDR). | 
| Contraste | Noirs parfaits et profondeur d’image maximale propres à l’OLED (ratio virtuellement infini), sans aucun effet de halo autour des éléments lumineux. | 
| Fidélité des couleurs – Usage standard | Rendu très juste et naturel au quotidien (DeltaE 2000 moyen de 1,81 en sRGB et 1,85 en P3) : les tons chair, les photos et les interfaces ne souffrent d’aucune distorsion chromatique perceptible. | 
| Fidélité des couleurs – Usage vidéo | Excellente précision sur les films et séries (DeltaE moyen de 1,76 en P3 BT.1886). Le gamma initial un peu ferme (2,275 en moyenne) donne du relief mais peut légèrement assombrir les détails dans les très basses lumières. | 
| Température des couleurs | Blancs légèrement froids (6 625 K à 6 659 K mesurés contre 6 500 K visés), tirant discrètement sur le bleu dans les hautes lumières, sans virer au bleu franc criard. | 
| Capacité à reproduire les nuances | Restitution intégrale et riche de la palette colorimétrique avec 99,7 % du gamut sRGB et 99,2 % du DCI-P3 couverts, assurant des dégradés propres sans perte de teintes. | 
Sur le grand écran de l’iPhone Duo, la précision d’affichage fait pratiquement jeu égal avec la dalle externe. Le DeltaE moyen descend à 1,81 en sRGB et tourne autour de 1,80 en Display P3. Pour une dalle souple, c’est une excellente performance, on a un affichage très juste. Les couleurs sont très naturelles, sans dérive visible. La régularité est remarquable sur tout le spectre et les deux espaces de référence sont couverts sans le moindre manque : 99,7 % pour le sRGB et 99,2 % pour le DCI-P3.
Le constat sur le blanc est identique à celui de l’écran externe. L’écart maximal se concentre sur le blanc pur. Quand on regarde les niveaux de couleurs de plus près, la dalle manque un peu de vert et pousse le bleu dès que la luminosité dépasse les 30 %. Avec une température moyenne relevée à 6 625 K pour une cible à 6 500 K, le blanc est très propre, mais garde une pointe de fraîcheur.
La courbe gamma moyenne, quant à elle, est un peu raide sur les premiers paliers de gris. En clair : dans les scènes très sombres, l’écran a tendance à boucher les ombres sous les 20 % de luminosité en avalant quelques petits détails, avant de s’éclaircir sur les hautes lumières. Enfin, comme pour l’écran interne, celui-ci descend à 1 nit en luminosité. Idéal pour lire la nuit, surtout que l’écran mat se prête à merveille à dévorer des bouquins, BD ou mangas plutôt que de ressortir sa liseuse.
Verdict
Sur le plan de l’étalonnage pur, Apple réussit une copie remarquable avec l’iPhone Duo. Les deux écrans OLED Super Retina XDR délivrent une colorimétrie exemplaire, avec des DeltaE moyens systématiquement sous la barre des 1,9 et une couvertures quasi intégrale des gamuts sRGB et Display P3. La puissance lumineuse est aussi un atout que je leur trouve avec plus de 1 300 nits en SDR et des pics HDR frôlant les 2 800 nits.
Le bémol ne vient pas de la sonde, mais du ressenti utilisateur. Sous la lumière du jour, la dalle interne montre un autre visage. Si le film nanotexturé mat fait chuter la brillance à 2 GU sur le papier, il diffuse les rayons solaires sur toute la surface de l’écran. Ce voile blanchâtre dégrade le contraste et complique sérieusement la lisibilité en plein soleil, particulièrement avec le mode sombre. En extérieur lumineux, c’est à mon sens l’écran externe de 5,4 pouces qui offre la meilleure expérience de lecture.

articles.title: The Complexity Between The Bits
articles.text:
What biological reasoning can teach us about verifying silicon systems.
By Vidya Chandran Darbari and Ashish Darbari
A recent conversation about carbon intelligence and silicon intelligence stayed with me. What interested me was not which one wins, but the complexity we take on as we ask silicon to sense, interpret, decide and act.
My work as an experimental structural biologist taught me to ask what a structure could explain, and what it could not. Solving a molecular structure was not the same as explaining the behaviour of the system to which it belonged. The next question was always about mechanism: what happens when the parts interact? That question shaped my perspective as a deep generalist in life sciences, connecting molecular mechanisms, biological networks and system behaviour.
Now, as Chief Strategy and Operations Officer at Axiomise, I return to that question in a different setting.
A chip is not a cell. But investigating biological complexity can sharpen how we investigate engineered systems—provided the comparison changes a question we ask, an observation we make or an obligation we verify. Otherwise, it remains an interesting analogy.
In life sciences, a protein interaction map is where questions begin. A connection identifies a possible interaction; it does not establish when that interaction matters. Concentration, localization, binding affinity, feedback and timing influence the outcome.
The same messenger can stimulate or suppress an immune response depending on the receptor and the receiving cell’s state. The molecule has not become inconsistent. Our description was incomplete without its context.
Silicon engineers already understand dependencies. The useful transfer is not simply to think in networks, but to distinguish connectivity from the conditions under which connected components produce a particular behaviour.
A link can transport packets correctly, a controller can enter its power states correctly, and an interconnect can arbitrate correctly under its assumptions. Their combination can still violate a requirement if those assumptions cease to hold.
The engineering consequence is to make context explicit: which neighbouring states, available resources and event orderings does each guarantee depend on? Those conditions belong in verification, not just in integration notes.
Our senses make context tangible. Combining cues helps only when their timing supports treating them as evidence of the same event. More signals do not automatically resolve ambiguity.
Consider an illustrative edge controller combining camera and distance-sensor data. Both measurements could be accurately encoded, transported without corruption and individually plausible. If they describe different moments but are treated as simultaneous, the fused estimate can represent a situation that never existed.
The bits arrive intact while the interpretation is wrong.
The biological perspective directs attention to the signal’s relationship with the state in which it is received. The engineering response is concrete: timestamp association, freshness, allowable skew and missing observations belong in the requirements.
Similar questions arise during reset, link retraining and power transitions. What happens to a transaction accepted before the transition? Which state survives recovery? When can a receiver safely treat new data as valid?
An interface is a relationship over time, not merely a set of wires. Verification must capture that relationship, particularly when the resulting interpretation controls an action.
It is tempting to describe biology as grey and silicon as black and white. That contrast obscures more than it explains.
Biological models can combine continuous quantities, discrete events, deterministic equations and stochastic processes. These are separate distinctions. A graded response need not be random.
A digital block can have a uniquely defined next state for a given state and input while leaving a system question unresolved: which input sequences and environmental behaviours must we consider? Formal verification can examine behaviours admitted by a model under stated assumptions. That is not physical randomness.
Beneath the abstraction sits physics. Metastability is not digital logic becoming analog because an architecture grew complicated. It is physical behaviour the design must accommodate.
The differences matter because a physical measurement, statistical association and logical proof answer different questions. Learning from biology should make us more precise about where uncertainty resides—not less demanding about correctness.
My life-sciences training made me wary of assuming that a symptom identifies its cause.
Consider an illustrative chiplet system, not a customer incident. A transaction times out. A power controller has gated a clock before outstanding traffic drained. It will restore the clock after receiving a wake request, but that request is queued behind the stalled traffic.
Each side waits for the other. The timeout is the symptom; the mechanism is a circular dependency. Extending the timeout would not remove it.
Other mechanisms could produce the same symptom: a lost credit, inconsistent reset state or starvation. Reproducing a trace does not distinguish those explanations.
Here, experimental reasoning suggests a useful question: which intervention would separate the hypotheses? What happens if the clock remains running? What if wake delivery is independent of normal traffic? Does the failure persist when downstream service changes?
These are familiar verification activities. Their explanatory purpose matters: choose an investigation because its outcome challenges a mechanism, not merely because it produces another passing run.
A counterexample also needs interpretation. It may expose a defect, an unrealistic environment or behaviour introduced by abstraction. A passing result needs equal scrutiny: did the assumptions exclude the situation we needed to examine?
Life sciences investigates activity at different levels: genome sequence, gene expression, protein machinery and metabolism. These measurements are not interchangeable. Discrepancies can reveal regulation, compensation or an incomplete explanation.
There is no exact mapping from these layers to a chip. The transferable principle is to connect evidence across levels rather than expect one measurement to explain everything.
RTL and configuration describe one view. Workload activity, transaction traces and physical telemetry provide others. Imagine a workload increasing power demand, a thermal policy reducing frequency and a controller approaching its deadline. Neither the transaction trace nor the temperature reading alone establishes whether the complete sequence was permitted.
I see an opportunity for tools that organize observations around shared events and competing explanations. AI-assisted analysis could help propose relationships, but correlation should lead to a testable hypothesis, not be labeled a root cause.
Observability should follow the same reasoning. For the clock-gating example, we need to relate outstanding traffic, clock decisions, wake generation and wake delivery. More logs are not necessarily better evidence if those relationships remain invisible.
Once we understand a mechanism, we should not leave it in a debug report.
What must prevent the circular dependency? Must traffic drain before clock gating? Must wake delivery remain independent? What happens if the normal sequence is interrupted?
These questions turn explanation into architectural obligations. This is the connection I see between biological reasoning and formal-first engineering: one directs attention towards context and competing mechanisms; the other helps express and check precise requirements in a design model.
At Axiomise, formal-first means asking those questions while the architecture can still change. Credits must not be lost or double-counted. Ordering must be preserved where required. Reset and recovery must restore compatible endpoint states.
Progress needs its own argument. Nothing being corrupted does not establish that an accepted request eventually completes. Service and fairness assumptions must be justified by the architecture.
Local proofs need the same treatment. If one component assumes a neighbour responds, where is that response established? Individually successful checks cannot establish a system claim when their assumptions are incompatible or circular.
Formal-first is not formal-only. Simulation, emulation, physical analysis and system validation contribute different evidence. The task is to connect them around identifiable questions.
If a failure mechanism crosses power management, traffic control and recovery, preventing it cannot depend solely on each team completing local checks.
Someone must own the cross-system obligation: what must remain true, which components contribute, which assumptions are required and which changes trigger reassessment. A revised power policy should reopen the progress argument if it changes its conditions.
This does not diminish specialist expertise. It gives the relationships between specialisms the same standing as the components they produce.
Other fields will not hand silicon engineering a ready-made solution. They can help us recognize incomplete descriptions and design better investigations. Biology’s contribution is not permission to accept ambiguity, but a discipline for challenging explanations.
Looking back at structural biology, I recognize the temptation to let a beautifully resolved model feel like the end of the investigation. The important question was what it helped explain—and what should follow.
The bits can be binary. Our understanding of the system is not automatically complete.
Ashish Darbari is the founder and CEO of Axiomise.

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – Acecore wins $10,000 at Moonshot - TechCabal
articles.text:
Good morning, and cheers to an unforgettable Moonshot! ☀️
Moonshot 2026 is over, and what an eventful, blockbuster two days it has been. Thousands of founders, investors, operators, policymakers, and builders packed the National Theatre in Lagos, Nigeria, for conversations that stretched from AI and fintech to capital markets, commerce, cybersecurity, and the future of African technology. Packed stages, hurried hallway conversations, familiar faces, new connections, and ideas kept us talking long after the lights went out. If you were there, thank you for being part of it. If you missed it, we’ve got plenty of stories, interviews, and takeaways coming your way.
Thank you, Lagos!
—Emmanuel
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Moonshot
Acecore wins $10,000 at Moonshot 2026’s TC Battlefield
If you thought African startups were running out of problems to solve, you only needed to spend some time at Moonshot 2026’s Startup stage in Lagos to reconsider.
Fertitude, a healthtech startup, pitched its digital platform that combines reproductive health tracking, AI-powered guidance, and access to healthcare specialists. Lena, an edtech startup, showed how it uses AI-powered games to help children learn subjects such as mathematics and science. Qiqi Farms pitched its technology-driven food distribution business, which connects farmers to markets and uses cold-chain infrastructure to deliver fresh produce.
These startups, alongside seven others, made the final ten of TC Battlefield 2026, TechCabal’s annual startup pitching competition, sponsored this year by Yango Group, the Russian-founded mobility company operating in Africa. The competition allowed founders to pitch their businesses to investors and compete for $17,500 in equity-free funding.
After the pitches, Acecore won, taking home the $10,000 grand prize. The Nigerian climate-tech startup is building locally manufactured, AI-powered solar battery systems through its Powercell product. Paired with its Powercore app, the system allows users to monitor energy performance and manage their power supply, offering an alternative to unreliable electricity.
Supplya, a Nigerian startup that helps small retailers source inventory from manufacturers and access interest-free buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) financing, was first runner-up, winning $5,000. Navidyn Limited finished third, taking home $2,500.
TC Battlefield is an annual startup pitching competition, held as part of the Moonshot conference. It gives early-stage African startups a platform to showcase their products and compete for equity-free funding and other growth opportunities. The competition has become a recurring feature of Moonshot, with Ulé Homes, a Nigerian proptech startup that helps people finance rent payments, winning last year’s edition.
Founders who missed out this year have an opportunity for redemption. TC Battlefield will return at next year’s Moonshot.

It’s a wrap. Moonshot 2026, the biggest gathering in African tech, ended after two packed days at the National Theatre. You got it all. Over 7,500 people came through the doors, two large exhibition halls ran out of space, and the tweets did not stop coming.
If you weren’t there, you probably felt like you were missing out. I was there, and I can confirm you were.

I ran into my friend Kwadwo, who flew in from Ghana, only twice all day. Both times, he told me he had never expected anything like this from us. That means something coming from him: Kwadwo works at the Bank of Ghana, which runs its own big tech event next door.

Herotel must open its fibre network to rivals
Herotel built its fibre business like a private road. If you wanted to use the road, you also had to buy Internet from Herotel. South Africa’s competition regulator is now making it open the gates to rivals.
What happened? Herotel, South Africa’s third-largest fibre network operator, will begin selling wholesale access to its network to other Internet service providers (ISPs). The change was imposed as a condition of Vumatel’s takeover, completed in June. Vumatel now indirectly owns 99.9% of Herotel.
Third-party ISPs must also receive the same pricing, service quality, and delivery terms offered to companies inside Vumatel’s parent group.
Explain like I’m new here: Herotel started by connecting smaller towns and underserved communities using fixed wireless Internet, before expanding aggressively into fibre in 2019. Unlike most large South African fibre operators, it kept the entire customer relationship to itself. Herotel built and owned the fibre, then sold Internet directly over it.
Vumatel works differently. It builds fibre networks and lets dozens of ISPs compete to sell internet over those lines.
Between the lines: Open access changes Herotel’s economics. It no longer gets every retail customer connected to its infrastructure, because another ISP can now win that customer. But every rival that sells a package over Herotel fibre also becomes a wholesale customer.
That trade-off becomes more important as Herotel expands. It wants to reach another 800,000 homes, taking its footprint beyond 1.4 million, largely in places bigger fibre operators have historically overlooked.
Why it matters: Fibre is expensive to build and cheap to leave idle. Opening Herotel’s network gives more ISPs an incentive to sell connections over existing infrastructure, potentially increasing how many homes actually take up fibre.
Herotel is losing exclusivity over its roads. The bet is that more traffic can make up for it.
Capital markets
Banque du Caire’s IPO is 27x oversubscribed
For weeks, we’ve been talking about Banque du Caire’s imminent initial public offering (IPO), and the listing is now gaining momentum. Apparently, Egypt’s sixth-largest bank is popular with retail investors. The lender hasn’t gone public yet, but investors are asking for more shares than it has to give—a lot more.
What happened? Retail investors ordered about 9.29 billion shares in the Egyptian state-owned bank, even though only 343.1 million shares were available to them. That made the retail portion of the IPO about 27 times oversubscribed.
At the final price of EGP 5.30 ($0.10) per share, roughly EGP 49.2 billion ($921 million) was chasing just EGP 1.8 billion ($34 million) worth of stock. Investors will receive about 3.7% of the shares they requested.
Explain like I’m new here: The IPO was due to “execute” on October 29, while normal trading begins on November 2. Those are two different things.
Execution does not mean investors are already trading Banque du Caire shares with one another. It is the step where the IPO orders are finalised, shares are allocated to successful investors, and Banque Misr, Banque du Caire’s owner, completes the sale. Once those shares sit in investors’ accounts, regular trading can begin on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX).
Think of it as buying a concert ticket before the doors open. You already own your ticket, but the event has not started.
Between the lines: Retail demand looks huge, but oversubscription only tells us investors wanted the shares at EGP 5.30 ($0.095). The bigger test begins when trading opens, and buyers and sellers can set the market price.
Retail investors also have some protection. During the first 30 days of trading, they can submit shares for sale at the IPO price under a stabilisation arrangement.
If Banque du Caire trades comfortably above EGP 5.30 ($0.095), Egypt will have something more useful than a heavily oversubscribed IPO: evidence that demand survived the jump from the order book to the open market.

articles.title: Fuite de données : les informations de 230 000 Français compromises lors d'une nouvelle cyberattaque
articles.text:
Une nouvelle fuite de données secoue la France. La Compagnie des transports strasbourgeois (CTS), qui gère les bus et les trams de l’agglomération, annonce avoir été victime d’une cyberattaque. Dans un communiqué, l’entreprise explique avoir « récemment identifié une exfiltration de données concernant environ 230 000 comptes clients, rendue possible par une utilisation illicite de son site internet ».
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque contre Engie – une fuite de données touche des clients en France
Les données compromises
Les données dérobées comprennent le nom, le prénom, la date de naissance, l’adresse postale et l’identifiant client. Bonne nouvelle, « les données bancaires et les mots de passe ne sont pas concernés par cette exfiltration », précise la CTS. Il n’y avait aucune raison que ces données, plus sensibles, soient stockées aux côtés des autres.
L’attaque remonte à la nuit du dimanche 18 au lundi 19 octobre. Emmanuel Auneau, le directeur de la CTS, révèle à nos confrères des Dernières Nouvelles d’Alsace que ses équipes ont remarqué « une sollicitation anormalement élevée de notre base de données ». Les pirates se sont servis d’une faille pour arriver à leurs fins, mais les « serveurs ne sont pas altérés », et « les hackeurs ne se sont pas infiltrés dans notre système informatique ». En fait, les truands ont exploité une interface de programmation d’application vulnérable, qui permet à des logiciels de dialoguer avec le site de la CTS.
La compagnie assure avoir réagi dès que la cyberattaque a été détectée. Le communiqué indique que « l’exfiltration a été stoppée et la sécurité autour du site a été intensifiée ». La Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés (CNIL) a été prévenue, et une plainte va être déposée auprès du tribunal de Strasbourg. Ce n’est pas la première fois que la CTS se retrouve dans le viseur des cybercriminels. En 2024, l’entreprise avait déjà enregistré un accès frauduleux à certains comptes clients.
A lire aussi : Les failles PHP à nouveau exploitées – une vaste cyberattaque chinoise fait des ravages avec l’IA
Gare aux faux e-mails et SMS
Les 230 000 clients concernés ont été prévenus par courriel cette semaine. Comme l’explique la compagnie des transports, « le principal risque associé à cette exfiltration est celui de tentatives de phishing, les données recueillies pouvant être utilisées pour donner davantage de crédibilité à des messages frauduleux ». La CTS rappelle qu’elle ne demande jamais à ses clients d’effectuer un paiement ni de communiquer des coordonnées bancaires par e-mail. Au moindre doute, ne cliquez sur aucun lien et passez directement par le site, ou encore mieux, par l’application officielle sur votre smartphone.
Le piratage de la CTS s’ajoute à la très longue liste des entités françaises victimes d’une fuite de données, qui comprend déjà les impôts, plusieurs opérateurs, et des dizaines de fédérations sportives. Selon une étude de Cybermalveillance, la plateforme de cybersécurité de la France, près de la moitié des Français ont été piratés cette année.

articles.title: Top 6 subscription billing platforms for MSPs and IT distributors in 2026 - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Managed service providers used to sell hours and hardware. Now a growing share of their revenue is recurring cloud subscriptions from Microsoft, Adobe, Acronis and a long tail of other vendors.
The catch is that every vendor and distributor sends its own invoice, in its own format, on its own schedule.
Market analysts don’t agree on the exact size of the managed services market in 2026. Mordor Intelligence puts it at about US$430 billion, while MarketsandMarkets is closer to US$380 billion. Either way, the money is real, and so is the admin. Flexera’s 2025 State of the Cloud Report found 84% of organisations call managing cloud spend a top challenge, and billing teams feel that first. Here are six platforms worth a look, each with one verdict.
1. Infiterra
Infiterra is a strong contender for the best subscription billing platform for MSPs and IT distributors that resell other people’s subscriptions and need one accurate invoice at the end of it. It handles prepaid, postpaid, usage-based and hybrid billing, with proration and multi-currency support, and it can consolidate several subscriptions onto a single customer invoice.
Around that core sits a product catalogue, a white-label cloud marketplace, reseller management with multi-tenant controls, and credit risk management. It connects to ERP, CRM, accounting and PSA systems, supports payment gateways, and exposes open APIs. Pre-built vendor connectors cover names like Microsoft, Adobe, Acronis and Dropbox, which is the part that matters most if Microsoft CSP automation is your pain point.
One customer, the DACH-region MSP Cosmo Consult, reports 95% automation of its billing on Infiterra’s own case page. That’s a testimonial, not independent testing, so treat it as a signal rather than proof.
Best for: distributors and larger MSPs with multi-vendor portfolios.
2. RackNap
RackNap covers subscription management, billing and a cloud marketplace for MSPs, CSPs and cloud distributors. It handles resale of Microsoft 365, Azure, AWS, Google Workspace and Acronis, plus usage-based and hybrid models.
It’s feature-rich, and it’s priced like it. RackNap’s own 2026 comparison lists its Standard plan from US$10,000 a month plus setup and transaction fees, a figure the vendor reports itself.
Best for: cloud-heavy providers with the budget to match.
3. Pax8
Pax8 is a distributor marketplace first and a billing tool second. Its integrations with PSAs such as Autotask, ConnectWise, Kaseya, Syncro and SuperOps mean invoices from Pax8 flow straight into your billing, which is genuinely convenient.
The limit is obvious. It reconciles Pax8 purchases, not everything else you buy.
Best for: MSPs sourcing mostly through Pax8.
4. ZaveIT
ZaveIT targets MSPs that want ordering and billing in one place. It offers a centralised product and service catalogue and branded self-service ordering portals, so customers can order without emailing your service desk. That ties in with what managed IT support covers for a small business day to day.
Public detail on pricing and integrations is thin, so confirm connector coverage on a demo before committing.
Best for: small MSPs wanting ordering plus billing.
5. Chargebee
Chargebee is a well-established recurring billing platform, and RackNap’s comparison names it a top pick for SaaS companies. Plans, coupons, trials and dunning are all handled well. It wasn’t designed around distributor reconciliation, so expect custom connectors if you resell lots of third-party licences.
Best for: MSPs selling their own SaaS products.
6. Zuora
Zuora is the heavyweight of subscription billing, and RackNap’s comparison lists it as the pick for large enterprises. Complex pricing models are its strength. Implementation is its weakness: projects are long and costly, and a typical MSP won’t use most of what it offers.
Best for: large organisations with dedicated finance systems teams.
What to look for in a subscription billing platform
Billing for managed services is not the same as billing for a single SaaS product. A good platform has to cope with the messy middle between what you buy and what you resell.
- Vendor and distributor reconciliation. Can it ingest usage and licence data from Microsoft CSP and distributors, then match it to what you charge?
- Proration and mid-term changes. Customers add and drop seats all month. Manual credit notes get old fast.
- Hybrid pricing. Flat fees, per-seat, usage-based and bundles, sometimes on one invoice.
- Multi-currency and tax. Australian buyers need AUD handling and GST done properly, especially when vendors bill in USD. As our look at financial infrastructure for growing tech businesses explains, exchange rates can eat into margins when software is sold across borders.
- PSA, ERP and accounting integrations decide how much re-keying your team does.
- Reseller and multi-tenant controls. Essential for distributors billing through channel partners.
A caveat: no tool nails all six. Be honest about which two or three cost you the most time today, and weigh the list against those.
How to choose
Match the platform to your revenue mix, not the longest feature list.
- Distributor or large reseller with many vendors: a dedicated platform like Infiterra or RackNap.
- Mid-size MSP buying mostly from one distributor: Pax8’s marketplace may be enough.
- Small MSP: ZaveIT keeps things light.
- Own-SaaS vendor: Chargebee, or Zuora at enterprise scale.
Whichever you shortlist, ask about security early. Billing platforms hold customer and vendor data, and the Australian Signals Directorate publishes ACSC guidance on engaging MSPs that’s a sensible checklist for supplier questions.
Conclusion
If cloud resale and multi-vendor invoicing dominate your revenue, a dedicated billing platform will beat PSA billing every time. If you mostly sell your own product, a general SaaS tool is fine. Many businesses are rethinking in-house IT, which only adds to the number of subscriptions MSPs need to bill. Request demos from two or three vendors and test them with your messiest real invoice.

articles.title: StrollMe bags €22 million to put more bikes, strollers and car seats into European homes | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Strollme, a German provider of children’s mobility on subscription, has secured €22 million in equity and debt financing to support their growth in its existing markets and lay the foundation for future expansion into other European countries.
Existing investors including Hanse Ventures, HGDF, JOSS and business angel Kristina Schreiner from the better ventures network are participating again, alongside new investor BMH Beteiligungs-Managementgesellschaft Hessen mbH (BMH), investing through its managed fund Hessen Kapital I. The credit facility is provided by Growth Credit Partners (GCP).
Sebastian Reichelt, co-founder and Managing Director of StrollMe, says: “This financing is a milestone for StrollMe. The equity from our existing and new investors and the credit facility from Growth Credit Partners enable us to significantly expand our fleet and offer families even more choice on subscription. We have also laid the foundation to strengthen our position in Europe step by step and in a capital-efficient way.”
StrollMe’s financing comes amid further investment in European subscription and asset-backed business models in 2026.
In the UK, London-based Raylo secured €34.5 million in equity and debt to expand its electronics subscription offering, while GIN e-bikes received €215k in fleet-backed debt to grow its bicycle rental service. In Germany, Berlin-based Everphone obtained €15 million in refinancing for its leased device fleet, while London’s equipal announced €18.84 million in equipment financing and equity.
Together with StrollMe, these announcements represent approximately €90.6 million in combined financing, including debt and refinancing facilities.
Lena Lang, Senior Investment Manager at BMH, adds: “A circular economy needs business models that scale. StrollMe shows that using rather than owning works for children’s products, and we are delighted to continue supporting the growth of the Hesse-based team.”
StrollMe was founded in 2020 by Timon Beutel and Sebastian Reichelt and is headquartered in Frankfurt. The company offers children’s mobility on flexible subscription in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands: kids’ bikes, balance bikes, strollers, car seats and accessories from brands such as Woom, Bugaboo, Doona, Nuna and Thule, matched to the child’s age.
After each subscription, products are professionally refurbished and rented out again; at the end of their rental life, sister brand Kiddly sells them on as refurbished products.
The company’s model is built on circularity, with more than 100,000 rentals completed since its founding.
Luke Wilson, Growth Credit Partners, says: “StrollMe offers families a compelling alternative to buying children’s products outright and has built a strong subscription business around a high-quality fleet. We’re delighted to support Sebastian, Timon and the team as they expand the fleet and grow the business in Germany and across Europe.”
According to the company, revenue increased by around 70% in 2025, but limited availability of popular models meant the company could not fully meet demand.
The additional funding will therefore support the expansion of the rental fleet, broadening the range and increasing the availability of kids’ bikes, balance bikes, strollers, car seats and accessories, and making high-quality children’s products accessible to even more families.
EU-Startups previously listed StrollMe in its November 2023 funding round-up.

articles.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.
Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.
As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.
Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.
AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.
Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company.

articles.title: Aus 90 Kilometern im All fotografiert – dieses Bild enttarnt Chinas geheimen Raumgleiter Shenlong
articles.text:
Chinas Raumgleiter Shenlong: Satellitenfoto zeigt erstmals Details im Orbit
Der US-Militärgeheimdienst Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) mit Sitz in Washington, D.C. hat in seinem Bericht „Challenges to Security in Space 2026“ (PDF) erstmals eine im All entstandene Aufnahme des chinesischen Raumgleiters Shenlong veröffentlicht. Das Foto zeigt das wiederverwendbare Raumfahrzeug während eines Flugs in der Erdumlaufbahn und stammt von einem kommerziellen Überwachungssatelliten.
Während die Staatsführung in Peking bislang keine technischen Daten oder Bilder des Raumgleiters freigegeben hat, absolviert das System seit Februar 2026 bereits seine vierte Langzeitmission. Nach Einschätzung der Geheimdienstanalyst:innen verfügen derzeit neben den USA lediglich die chinesischen Streitkräfte über ein solches Raumfahrzeug, das auf einer Rakete ins All startet und nach Monaten im Orbit wie ein Flugzeug auf einer Landebahn landet.
Vantor-Satellit Worldview-3 fotografiert Shenlong mit geöffneter Nutzlastbucht
Obwohl der Sicherheitsbericht der US-Behörde erst Ende Oktober 2026 erschienen ist, entstand die darin enthaltene Aufnahme bereits am 28. Mai 2024 während des dritten Testflugs von Shenlong. Wie das US-Fachportal The War Zone unter Berufung auf den Satellitenbetreiber Vantor, ehemals Maxar Technologies, aus Westminster im US-Bundesstaat Colorado berichtet, fotografierte der Erdbeobachtungssatellit Worldview-3 den Gleiter aus einer Entfernung von rund 90 Kilometern.
Für solche Aufnahmen nutzen Betreiber:innen das sogenannte Non-Earth-Imaging-Verfahren, bei dem Satelliten ihre sonst auf die Erdoberfläche gerichteten Kameras im Flug drehen, um andere Objekte im Weltraum abzubilden. Auf dem so entstandenen Bild ist der chinesische Raumgleiter von schräg unten zu erkennen, wobei die beiden Tore seiner zentralen Nutzlastbucht nach außen aufgeklappt sind.
Darüber hinaus bestätigten Sprecher:innen von Vantor gegenüber Space.com, dass am Heck des Raumfahrzeugs ein separater Satellit mit ausgeklappten Solarzellenflächen angedockt ist. Laut einer Bildanalyse des italienischen Luftfahrtportals The Aviationist deutet ein Vergleich verschiedener Dateiversionen allerdings darauf hin, dass US-Behörden einzelne Partien am Rumpf vor der Veröffentlichung im Bericht geschwärzt haben.
Mit seinem dunklen Hitzeschild an der Unterseite, den kurzen Deltaflügeln und dem V-förmigen Leitwerk ähnelt Shenlong äußerlich dem US-Raumgleiter X-37B, den der Luft- und Raumfahrtkonzern Boeing für das US-Militär gebaut hat. Vor der Freigabe des Satellitenfotos existierten in der Öffentlichkeit lediglich unscharfe Aufnahmen durch ein Bodenteleskop, die der österreichische Amateurastronom Felix Schöfbänker im Sommer 2024 angefertigt hatte.
Vier Shenlong-Missionen seit 2020: Annäherungsmanöver im niedrigen Erdorbit
Wie aus einem Faktenblatt der Secure World Foundation hervorgeht, schickte China den ersten Prototyp des offiziell nur als „wiederverwendbares experimentelles Raumfahrzeug“ bezeichneten Gleiters im September 2020 für zwei Tage ins All. Beim zweiten Flug ab August 2022 blieb Shenlong bereits 276 Tage im Orbit und führte sogenannte Rendezvous-Manöver durch, bei denen sich der Gleiter einem ausgesetzten Begleitsatelliten wiederholt auf weniger als 100 Meter annäherte.
Nach einem dritten Testflug über 268 Tage, der im September 2024 endete, hob der Raumgleiter am 7. Februar 2026 auf einer Trägerrakete vom Typ Langer Marsch 2F vom Weltraumbahnhof Jiuquan in der nordwestchinesischen Wüste Gobi zu seiner vierten Mission ab. Auch während dieses seit über 260 Tagen andauernden Flugs registrierten Mitarbeiter:innen des US-Weltraumüberwachungsunternehmens Leolabs im Juni 2026 wieder ein unidentifiziertes Objekt in unmittelbarer Nähe des Raumfahrzeugs.
Neben Shenlong führt der US-Bericht mit dem Modell Tengyun noch ein zweites staatliches Raumgleiter-Projekt auf, das als zweistufiges System mit einem Trägerflugzeug konzipiert ist. Zudem arbeitet China seit Ende 2024 an dem kommerziellen Frachtgleiter Haolong-1, der künftig Versorgungsgüter zur chinesischen Raumstation Tiangong transportieren und wieder zur Erde zurückkehren soll.
Dual-Use-Technik im All: Zwischen Satellitenwartung und Weltraumwaffen
Aus Sicht von Militärexpert:innen besitzen Technologien zum Aussetzen, Ansteuern und Greifen von Objekten im Orbit einen sogenannten Dual-Use-Charakter. Dieselbe Mechanik, mit der sich defekte Satelliten betanken, reparieren oder als Weltraumschrott entsorgen lassen, kann im Konfliktfall auch dazu dienen, gegnerische Aufklärungs- oder Kommunikationssatelliten auszuschalten.
In einer Mitteilung zum Bericht verweist die DIA in diesem Zusammenhang auf den Ausbau chinesischer Antisatelliten-Systeme, zu denen auch Satelliten der Baureihe Shijian gehören. Ein Raumfahrzeug dieser Serie schleppte bereits einen ausgedienten Navigationssatelliten des chinesischen Beidou-Systems in einen Friedhofsorbit, während weitere Modelle Robotergreifarme und Verfahren zur Betankung im rund 36.000 Kilometer entfernten geosynchronen Orbit testen.
Gleichzeitig zeigt die Aufnahme von Vantor eine Schattenseite für sämtliche Militärprogramme im niedrigen Erdorbit, der sich bis in eine Höhe von 2.000 Kilometern erstreckt. Da private Anbieter:innen ihre Kameras im All zunehmend für Aufnahmen von Nachbarobjekten vermarkten, lassen sich geheime Testflüge in dieser Umlaufbahn kaum noch vor externen Beobachter:innen verbergen.
Die steigende Zahl ziviler und militärischer Flugkörper vergrößert darüber hinaus die Kollisionsgefahr im erdnahen Weltraum, nachdem China allein im Jahr 2025 insgesamt 93 Raketenstarts durchgeführt und seine Flotten für die Satellitennetzwerke Xingwang und Qianfan weiter ausgebaut hat. Da im Orbit bereits mehr als 35.000 katalogisierte Objekte ab zehn Zentimetern Größe sowie bis zu 900.000 kleinere, vom Boden aus nicht verfolgbare Trümmerteile kreisen, wird das Risiko von Zusammenstößen laut den Berechnungen der DIA weiter zunehmen.

articles.title: “I don't think the world needs a new GitHub”: What GitHub's leaders really think about their new rivals
articles.text:
“I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub”: What GitHub’s leaders really think about their new rivals
At its annual Universe ’26 conference in San Francisco this week, GitHub took to the question of the platform’s stability head-on.
The code-hosting company spent a significant part of the event’s keynote to talk about the investments it is making. That includes adding 4 million cores and 160 petabytes of storage, along with a full rearchitecting of its backend infrastructure.
But at a press conference and in interviews with The New Stack after the keynote, the leadership team of Jay Parikh, the executive VP of CoreAI at Microsoft who now leads GitHub, and GitHub COO Kyle Daigle also answered questions about what GitHub’s role is in this changing developer landscape — and how they feel about some of the competition that is now popping up in response to these changes.
It’s a timely question, since former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a GitHub alternative just a few days before GitHub’s conference.
When asked about Entire, Dohmke’s startup, at the press conference — and Microsoft’s M12 investment arm funding of Entire — Daigle diplomatically noted that Microsoft often invests in tools “that compete not only with GitHub but with the entirety of the Microsoft product estate. And that’s a good thing. That’s not a bad thing.”
Daigle noted that GitHub operates at a global scale, serves more than 225 million developers, and keeps iterating to better serve them.
“I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub.”
—GitHub COO Kyle Daigle
“I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub,” he said. “They might need different tools. That’s great, but what they need is [GitHub] to evolve for the agentic era, which is what we’re doing.
“The stats for the Git layer that we showed today kind of speak for themselves.”
Daigle stressed to The New Stack the role GitHub plays in the overall software development ecosystem — spanning individual developers, large open source projects, and Fortune 100 enterprises.
Daigle argued that the conversation about new Git forges, or version control forges more broadly, focuses too narrowly on companies and the economic use of those platforms. “I think that loses a core component of the problem,” he told The New Stack.
“We’ve never been the only Git host. We’ve never been the only SCM host,” Daigle said, pointing to Perforce and other options companies have relied on for years. What sets GitHub apart, he argued, is hosting all developers together at scale, rather than focusing only on enterprises or only on open source. “I don’t see folks trying to go solve that problem. They’re trying to solve a part of the problem,” he said. “There are places where they’re very opinionated and doing it in a unique way. I think that’s always been true.”
Daigle’s argument, at its core, is that it is much easier to build tools that focus on the enterprise. At least for now, that is where Entire and most other Git forges have their focus.
More sharply, Daigle said this moment “feels similar to the end of the zero interest rate era,” when “there were a lot of really talented, interesting developer tools, but they were just incredibly narrow.” He added: “Luckily, a lot of those folks ended up joining GitHub — and doing some really great work.”
“GitHub may not think there needs to be a new GitHub, but developers clearly do.” 
—Entire CEO Thomas Dohmke
Entire’s reaction
When asked by The New Stack to comment on Daigle’s assessment that the world doesn’t need a new GitHub, Dohmke provided the following statement: “GitHub may not think there needs to be a new GitHub, but developers clearly do. Do we really want to put the future of software development and open source into the hands of a single big tech company? We are building Entire so the new home of the community is open source, scalable, and resident in many regions around the world.”
Platforms versus products
With new competition for users debuting in the form of Dohmke’s Entire platform, Parikh emphasized the importance of GitHub’s user community and the platform it offers at Wednesday’s press conference: “With how fast the world is changing around how we build and the lifecycle of software, the power of the community, I think, is more important than it’s ever been in terms of what we’re creating, how we’re sharing, how we’re learning together.”
Parikh made a similar point in a later interview with The New Stack, drawing a distinction between individual development tools and the platform that supports them when asked about the competitive landscape GitHub now faces.
“GitHub and Microsoft have always been platform companies,” he said. “So much of what’s out there are products, and yes, we have products, and we have platforms.”
For Parikh, that means offering a complete development workflow while also letting developers choose which pieces they use. Or as Daigle put it, “we’ll give you the full flow, or we’ll give you the primitives, which I think is what most companies want. Everyone’s interested in what is the one way to do this, but nobody wants to buy the only way. They want to have the optionality and the choice.”
Where agents break things
Supporting those varied workflows ended up forcing GitHub to reconsider some of the assumptions the team had made about which services were most likely to fail.
“The places that have failed are not the places we would have expected to fail historically, because agents act in such a different way than a human being,” Daigle said. “Some services that were scaling perfectly, and we thought were good to go for quite some time, had a surprising failure.”
Those failures began emerging in early summer, prompting GitHub to look beyond adding capacity as the main solution.
“It’s not just increasing the number of cores, the overall horizontal scaling, but looking at core services that need to be completely rewritten because the behavior pattern is so incredibly different,” Daigle said.
Parikh, whose experience includes scaling infrastructure at Facebook and Akamai, said the current growth rate makes incremental improvements pointless.
“You have to take a full systems look at it,” he said. “Getting five or 10% here or there, it lasts you two weeks or a week now.”
What makes all of this harder is that GitHub has to make those changes while keeping the service running and compatible with existing workflows. And in the meantime, the traffic patterns are changing, too, Parikh said.
“The traffic patterns are also not static right now … We optimized CPU, and now all of a sudden the bottleneck is going to move somewhere, and then you’re like, ‘Oh, I thought it would show up here, but it showed up here.’ Right now, the good news is you do these in staged rollouts. You test these things, and then you adjust,” he said.
One substantial architectural change the team has committed to is separating compute from storage in GitHub’s Git infrastructure. This now allows the company to more easily scale each according to demand.
“Depending on what that traffic is, time of day, who’s using it and what type of product offering sits on top of it, you can scale these things independently and optimize for how that compute workload changes and how that storage workload changes,” Parikh said at the press conference.
Moving from GitHub’s own data centers to Azure also provides more capacity, geographic flexibility and redundancy, Parikh said, which the existing facilities could not offer. But he also stressed that the work remains unfinished and includes additional changes to harden and scale GitHub Actions, for example.
“We can’t add the capacity. We don’t have the scale in those fixed data centers that GitHub has operated on, and so moving into cloud infrastructure that gives us flexibility and scale and location and redundancy and network and all that is much better for us,” Parikh told The New Stack.
Keeping free repos free
Interestingly, these architecture changes also affect the economics of hosting all open-source code and free repositories on GitHub.
Daigle said that separating compute and storage should reduce the cost of storing Git repositories, helping GitHub maintain access as developers and their agents create more work.
Daigle said GitHub has a responsibility to its community. Suddenly limiting developers to a handful of private repositories “breaks the whole contract of what GitHub is,” he said.
Daigle said anyone writing code, whether they’ve done it for years or are just starting, should have a home on GitHub. “A repo should not be hidden out on your laptop, or [be] an HTML file shared between friends,” he said. “We have a place for that.”
He did, however, distinguish that commitment from the cost of supplying AI models. GitHub cannot give everyone unlimited free tokens, he said, and has had to decide where to subsidize access.
Rethinking Git and verification
Beyond GitHub’s own infrastructure, Daigle also sees room to change Git itself. He wants the company to work with the community on its underpinnings and sees a role for something like “a porcelain layer on top of Git,” which he described as a higher-level interface that simplifies access to the underlying system.
Daigle said GitHub needs to “assert our role in the community” and work with established and new players alike to rethink some of Git’s underpinnings. “They kind of didn’t make sense before the agent change,” he said, “and now they really, really don’t make sense.”
At the same time, though, Daigle remains cautious about whether this agentic era needs an entirely different version control system.
“I want to know we need to move before we move,” he said. “I don’t think we’re done with [Git] yet. I just think we do need to lean in more.”
“You actually need to review it, you need to push it into production, you need to run other workflows, you need to do AI scanning for security issues,” Parikh said at the press conference.
Daigle expects verification — reviewing, testing, and deciding whether software should reach production — to become the next bottleneck.
Daigle expects verification — reviewing, testing, and deciding whether software should reach production — to become the next bottleneck. He argued that even unlimited CPUs wouldn’t make running every build after every agent commit desirable.
“If I have 5 or 10 agents running at a single time, I don’t actually want or need all those builds for the sake of the agent,” he said. “And that requires a change in behavior for the agents or the humans involved.”
Among the possibilities he raised were signing locally executed builds and submitting them with an agent’s work, selecting a smaller set of relevant tests, and exploring proof-driven development. The right combination of tests, evaluations and live verification will depend on the application.
“If you’re an automaker, you’re not going to say, ‘Well, I’ll let my agent check if the brake caliper was engaged or not,’” he said.

articles.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently.
This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro. Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it.
Prerequisites
Before getting started, you need:
- Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself.
- A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files.
- PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects.
- A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation).
What you will learn in this post
You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way.
Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform
Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways.
Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop
Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post.
Method 2: AWS Transform, agentic and at portfolio scale
AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘fix the loop, not the code’ apply to an autonomous run.
When each path fits
- Control and autonomy: Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests. When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines.
- Scale and novelty: Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first-of-a-kind frameworks. AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs.
- A shared feedback loop: Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa.
Solution overview: One shared brain, many projects
The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.”
The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder.
Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java.
A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain.
Discovery before translation
The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run.
The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve.
The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue.
The parity-first pipeline
Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application.
The first four phases concentrate human expertise. Phase 0 runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application.
| Phase | Name | Deliverable | 
| 0 | Assess and discover | Model manifest + inventory + cutover choice | 
| 1 | Build the judge | Parity harness runnable against PHP and Java | 
| 2 | Rulebook + gap inventory | RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md | 
| 3 | Stress-test the rulebook | Hardened rulebook, validated against representative files | 
| 4 | Scaffold | Compiling Spring Boot project | 
| 5 | Translate the data model | JPA entities + schema baseline | 
| 6 | Translate the I/O layer | Controllers, security, templates respond | 
| 7 | Convert business logic | Logic converted, tests green | 
| 8 | Prove parity and cut over | Parity report + cutover checklist | 
Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops: Phase 4 scaffolds the project, Phase 5 translates the data model from the manifest, Phase 6 translates the I/O layer (routes become controllers, middleware becomes filters, validation becomes annotated data transfer objects), Phase 7 converts business logic in batches, and Phase 8 proves parity against the harness and cuts over. Two principles govern the loop. First, the PHP code is the specification: the port is done when the referee agrees, or each mismatch is logged as an approved change. Second, you fix the loop, not the code, amending the rulebook and regenerating rather than hand-patching.
Walkthrough: From Eloquent to Spring Boot
The laravel-eloquent-sample project is a working, bounded example: a read-only slice of an open source Laravel application, with the Book, Chapter, Page, and User models migrated to Spring Boot 3.4.1 on Java 21 with Maven and an in-memory H2 database.
The mapping from PHP to Spring Boot is mechanical and traceable, as shown in the following diagram. Each manifest entry on the left maps to a Java construct on the right, producing the layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice.
The mappings are mechanical and traceable back to the manifest: a PHP namespace becomes a Java package, an Eloquent model becomes a JPA @Entity, has Many and belongs to relationships become @OneToMany and @ManyToOne, and Eloquent query scopes become Spring Data repository methods. The discipline shows in serialization: html, markdown, and text carry @JsonIgnore because the manifest recorded them in Page’s $hidden list, while Book’s description deliberately doesn’t.
The spec is candid that only 4 of 37 models were ported and, most important, that the parity harness was never built for this slice, which it calls “the single biggest gap.” Documenting where it falls short is itself part of the design.
Getting started
The complete migration engine is available in the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository.
To use it:
- Clone the repository and open its root as your Kiro workspace (open a folder and select the folder containing .kiro/). Nothing to install beyond PHP 8.0+ for the scanner and Java 21 with Maven.
- Fetch the PHP source into the project’s source-php/ folder. The README pins the exact upstream commits used for parity so anyone can reproduce the baseline.
- Ask Kiro to migrate the application. The php-to-java-migration skill activates automatically, runs the scanner first, generates a fresh spec under .kiro/specs/, and walks you through the approval gates.
- For an agentic run, point AWS Transform at the same skill files, so its agents execute the identical methodology across your portfolio.
The methodology auto-detects Laravel, Symfony, CodeIgniter, and plain PHP, and extension is additive: add a detection row and a references/<framework>-to-spring.md guide for a new framework. Because Kiro and AWS Transform read the same files, refining them once upgrades both engines.
Clean up
If you deployed the sample Spring Boot application during this walkthrough:
- Stop the running Spring Boot application (the in-memory H2 database is ephemeral and requires no separate cleanup).
- Remove the generated Java project folder from your workspace if no longer needed.
- The discovery scanner produces only a JSON manifest file. Delete the discovery scanner’s JSON manifest from your working directory if you don’t plan to reference it.
- No AWS resources are provisioned by the migration engine itself, so there are no cloud resources to deprovision.
Conclusion
We showed how to build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro that turns large-scale rewrites into a measurable, compounding process. The key principles are:
- Discovery before translation: A mechanical scanner inventories every model, field, and relationship, so you don’t guess at structure.
- Build the judge before the code: A parity harness defines done before the first line of Java is written.
- Fix the loop, not the code: When the same mistake appears across files, amend the rulebook and regenerate rather than hand-patching.
- One shared brain: The methodology is written once, shared across projects, and improves with each migration.
None of this is specific to PHP or Java. The same shape applies to other migrations where the old system is the only complete specification. Clone the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository, open it as a Kiro workspace, and explore the Skills and Steering capabilities that power it, or bring the same skill files to AWS Transform. For more about language migration patterns on AWS, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance documentation.

articles.title: PS5 : PlayStation ressuscite les manettes transparentes avec sa collection Prism
articles.text:
Les accessoires transparents font leur retour chez PlayStation avec une nouvelle collection déclinée en trois coloris. Sony proposera des manettes DualSense et des façades assorties pour personnaliser la PS5 dès février 2027.
Les amateurs de consoles aux coques translucides vont retrouver un design qui leur rappellera probablement de bons vieux souvenirs. Sony vient de dévoiler Prism, une collection d’accessoires pour la PS5 qui mise sur la transparence, avec trois associations de couleurs : Flare Orange, Emerald Green et Graphite Gray. Chaque déclinaison concerne une manette sans fil DualSense et une façade destinée à la console, toutes deux inspirées du design transparent emblématique de la fin des années 1990.
PS5 : la collection Prism remet les manettes transparentes au goût du jour
Dans un billet de blog consacré à cette nouvelle collection Prism, le constructeur japonais explique vouloir mettre en valeur les matériaux et la conception de ses accessoires en laissant apparaître une partie de leur structure. Leo Cardoso, membre de l’équipe de conception de PlayStation, précise que l’objectif était de remettre au goût du jour cette esthétique apparue à la fin des années 1990, tout en l’adaptant au design de la PS5.
Les finitions ont été travaillées pour distinguer les trois versions. Flare Orange associe un orange vif à des nuances rosées visibles à la jonction des matériaux transparents. Emerald Green mise sur un vert forêt profond, tandis que Graphite Gray adopte des tonalités grises plus froides. Sony indique également que la finition transparente brillante recouvre le dos de la DualSense, laissant entrevoir une partie de la technologie embarquée. Le bloc central bénéficie par ailleurs d’un traitement métallique qui contraste avec les surfaces translucides.
Prix, précommandes et disponibilité des accessoires PS5
La collection Prism sera commercialisée à partir du 4 février 2027. Les précommandes ouvriront le 10 novembre 2026 à 10 heures, heure française, sur le site PlayStation et auprès des revendeurs participants, sous réserve de disponibilité, bien entendu.
En France, chaque manette DualSense Prism sera proposée au prix de 84,99 euros. Les façades assorties coûteront quant à elles 74,99 euros. Ces dernières seront vendues directement par PlayStation dans les pays où sa boutique en ligne les distribue, dont la France, et pourront aussi être proposées en quantités limitées chez certains revendeurs dans d’autres régions.
Source : PlayStation Blog
- Une PS5 plus compacte, plus légère
