articles.title: MacBook Pro táctil: precio, pantalla OLED, qué chip usa y más datos
articles.text:
Apple presentó el MacBook Pro táctil, una nueva generación de portátiles profesionales con pantalla OLED en tándem, hasta 24 horas de batería y chips M5 Pro y M5 Max.
El equipo llegará en modelos de 14 y 16 pulgadas, con precios desde USD 2.899 y configuraciones enfocadas en edición de video, diseño, programación e inteligencia artificial local.
La incorporación de una pantalla táctil marca un cambio en la línea MacBook Pro. Hasta ahora, Apple concentraba la interacción en el teclado, el trackpad y los accesorios externos. El nuevo modelo añade gestos directos sobre la pantalla para mover elementos, ampliar imágenes, dibujar o controlar instrumentos virtuales, sin eliminar los métodos de trabajo habituales.
Precios y modelos disponibles
Apple abrirá las reservas el 28 de octubre y prevé iniciar la disponibilidad el viernes 6 de noviembre. La oferta inicial incluye tres configuraciones:
- MacBook Pro de 14 pulgadas con M5 Pro, desde USD 2.899.
- MacBook Pro de 16 pulgadas con M5 Pro, desde USD 3.399.
- MacBook Pro de 16 pulgadas con M5 Max, desde USD 4.799 en su configuración superior.
La marca no detalló todos los precios intermedios, que dependerán de la memoria unificada, el almacenamiento y el chip elegido. El equipo podrá configurarse con hasta 128 GB de memoria unificada y 16 TB de almacenamiento, una capacidad dirigida a cargas de trabajo con archivos grandes y programas profesionales.
El modelo de 14 pulgadas pesa 1,36 kilogramos, mientras que el de 16 alcanza 1,81 kilogramos. Apple redujo el grosor y el peso de ambas versiones, aunque mantiene una arquitectura térmica diseñada para sostener el rendimiento de los nuevos procesadores.
La pantalla PROLED XDR ofrece OLED y hasta 120 Hz
El nuevo MacBook Pro estrena la pantalla PROLED XDR, basada en tecnología OLED en tándem. El sistema utiliza dos capas de píxeles autoiluminados y alcanza hasta 2.000 nits de brillo máximo en contenidos HDR y SDR.
Apple indica que el panel ofrece una relación de contraste de 10.000.000:1, con negros profundos y mayor detalle en las zonas oscuras. También incorpora ProMotion, con una frecuencia variable que puede llegar a 120 Hz y bajar hasta 10 Hz para reducir el consumo de energía.
La pantalla admite los espacios de color P3 y Adobe RGB, dos referencias relevantes para fotografía, diseño e impresión. También supera el 80% de cobertura de Rec. 2020, un estándar utilizado en edición de video HDR.
La opción de nanotextura busca disminuir los reflejos y el deslumbramiento en espacios muy iluminados. Apple señaló que cada panel se calibra en fábrica para ajustar luminancia, punto blanco y reproducción cromática.
La pantalla táctil se suma al teclado y al trackpad
La función táctil permite desplazarse por una página, pellizcar para ampliar una fotografía, arrastrar archivos entre ventanas y tocar dos veces una aplicación para ocupar toda la pantalla. El sensor está integrado directamente en el panel, una decisión con la que Apple busca reducir la latencia.
Una bisagra rediseñada debe aportar estabilidad al tocar la pantalla. La compañía sostiene que las aplicaciones existentes podrán interpretar los toques como clics, mientras los desarrolladores podrán crear gestos específicos para macOS.
Los diseñadores podrán dibujar sobre el lienzo, los músicos tocar instrumentos de software y los desarrolladores probar funciones de iPhone y iPad. Entre las aplicaciones mencionadas como compatibles aparecen Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Shapr3D y djay Pro.
M5 Pro y M5 Max para edición, 3D e inteligencia artificial
Los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max apuntan a flujos de trabajo exigentes. Apple los orienta a edición de video ProRes 8K, animación tridimensional, composición musical, compilación de código y ejecución local de modelos de lenguaje.
El equipo incorpora tres puertos Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, lector de tarjetas SDXC, MagSafe y entrada para audífonos. La versión M5 Pro admite hasta tres pantallas externas y la M5 Max, hasta cuatro. También ofrece Wi‑Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 y carga rápida hasta el 50% en 30 minutos.
La computadora ejecutará macOS 27 Golden Gate, con Apple Intelligence, Siri AI, Isla Dinámica, Spotlight y Actividades en Vivo. La Isla Dinámica permitirá consultar actualizaciones, responder llamadas y controlar música desde la parte superior de la pantalla.
La apuesta de Apple combina más potencia y almacenamiento con una forma de interacción que antes estaba ausente en la Mac. Su adopción dependerá de si las herramientas profesionales incorporan el toque directo como una función útil dentro de sus procesos cotidianos.

articles.title: David Carracedo, ingeniero: “En 10 o 20 años, las casas pondrán la lavadora cuando haya energía solar disponible”
articles.text:
Más de 36.000 viviendas españolas instalaron placas solares en 2025, según la Unión Española Fotovoltaica (UNEF). Pero instalar placas solares en casa no siempre ahorra tanto como se puede esperar. “Depende”, responde David Carracedo, ingeniero de Caminos, Canales y Puertos, experto en hidráulica y energía. Depende de cuánto consumes, cuándo consumes y de tu vivienda.
Si consumes la electricidad que produce el sistema fotovoltaico, las placas solares ahorran electricidad; pero la instalación puede resultar poco rentable si consumes la mayoría de tu electricidad en algún otro momento, por ejemplo, si tienes una segunda vivienda a la que acudes los fines de semana. El entorno desempeña un papel importante, ya que las sombras de los edificios o los árboles pueden reducir el rendimiento; en una villa, instalar placas solares puede resultar más sencillo que en una vivienda en una comunidad de vecinos.
Una sombra se puede calcular antes de comprar las placas. Genbeta ya publicó un artículo sobre la página web ShadowCalculator, que simula la sombra que arroja un edificio o un objeto sobre el lugar donde se van a instalar las placas solares en un mapa interactivo.
El error más habitual, según Carracedo, es instalar placas sin estudiar antes a qué horas se consume la electricidad.
“La mejor instalación no es la más grande ni la que ocupa todo el tejado, sino la que está correctamente ideada para el consumo real y los horarios de la familia”, analiza Carracedo. Si pudiera realizar una sola mejora en su hogar para las próximas dos décadas, añade, centraría sus esfuerzos en el aislamiento y las obras de mejora energética de la envolvente del edificio. “La energía más barata y sostenible es la que no necesitamos consumir”.
Con el aislamiento adecuado, la cantidad de electricidad que se consume para calentar o climatizar el hogar se reduce, lo que supone un ahorro que no depende de la energía solar. Esa reducción se mantiene durante décadas.
La siguiente modificación que introduciría en una vivienda, afirma, sería el uso de sistemas de climatización más eficientes, como las bombas de calor, junto con un tamaño de instalación que se ajustara a las necesidades específicas de la familia. En cuanto a las medidas de ahorro en el consumo de agua, el ingeniero cree que las opciones sencillas, como solucionar las fugas y sustituir los grifos por otros más eficientes y las cisternas por modelos de doble descarga, son mejores opciones que los sistemas de reutilización más sofisticados.
A largo plazo, la tecnología cambiará nuestra relación con la energía y el agua. Dentro de diez o veinte años, predice Carracedo, será habitual saber casi en tiempo real cuánta electricidad y agua se gastan. La llegada de las viviendas inteligentes significará que los electrodomésticos se activarán cuando haya energía solar disponible: “Las casas pondrán en marcha el termo, la lavadora, el lavavajillas o la recarga del vehículo eléctrico cuando exista energía solar disponible”. En las comunidades de vecinos, el autoconsumo compartido permitirá que los propietarios aprovechen la energía que generan los paneles de una misma cubierta.
Para lograr la autosuficiencia energética, se necesitan placas solares y baterías suficientes para cubrir también las noches, el invierno y los días de poca producción. Además, la diferencia la marcarán los edificios con un mejor aislamiento y un diseño adaptado al clima, junto con sistemas de ventilación eficientes, capaces de mantener una temperatura confortable con mucha menos energía. “Lo que hoy puede parecernos una vivienda tecnológica o sostenible probablemente será vista, dentro de veinte años, como una vivienda completamente normal”, predice.
Qué se puede hacer ya y cuándo compensa
Pero hay algunos consejos sencillos que se pueden aplicar ahora. Muchas lavadoras y lavavajillas disponen de un inicio diferido para comenzar el ciclo de lavado en una hora determinada. Así, el usuario puede sincronizar la máquina con los momentos de menor coste de la electricidad. Según el modelo, el retraso se programa hora a hora o a saltos de varias horas. La diferencia con lo que describe Carracedo es que aquí la hora la eliges tú y la máquina no sabe si en ese momento hay sol.
Sin placas solares, el mediodía laborable cae en la franja punta, la de peajes más caros. De acuerdo con la Circular 3/2020 de la CNMC, en vigor para la península, las Islas Baleares y Canarias en el peaje 2.0TD (suministros de baja tensión con hasta 15 kW contratados), las horas punta, con los peajes más caros, son las que van de las 10:00 a las 14:00 y de las 18:00 a las 22:00 los días laborables. De 8:00 a 10:00, de 14:00 a 18:00 y de 22:00 a 24:00 es franja llano.
Y es valle de 00:00 a 08:00, así como los fines de semana y festivos nacionales. Sin placas solares para aportar electricidad adicional, los usuarios se benefician de consumir en la franja valle. El lunes a mediodía, un usuario sin placas solares se encuentra en la franja punta, la de peajes más caros.
Cuánto se ahorra con el excedente depende del tipo de acuerdos que se celebren para que la electricidad que se produce, pero no se consume, se compense con la electricidad que se compra a la red, y de la duración del periodo de liquidación.
En el caso de la compensación simplificada establecida por el Real Decreto 244/2019, que la limita a instalaciones con potencia de hasta 100 kW, la electricidad que no se consume en la factura de un mes se compensa con el importe de la electricidad comprada a la red, pero nunca en cantidades superiores a ese importe. Con la comercializadora de referencia, lo que se abona a los productores se calcula como el precio horario medio del mercado menos el coste de los desvíos.
En el autoconsumo residencial español, en 2025 se sumaron 36.330 hogares y 229 MW, un 17 % menos que los 275 MW de potencia añadida en 2024. UNEF vincula parte del frenazo al final o la incertidumbre de los incentivos. Entre los factores que se citan está también la caída continuada del precio de los excedentes en las tarifas libres.
Consumir en casa la electricidad que se genera en casa es lo que defiende el ingeniero.
Qué falta para que la lavadora se ponga sola
¿Cómo se consigue? La versión 1.4 de Matter, publicada en noviembre de 2024, incluye gestión de energía de dispositivos: permite que los aparatos que consumen energía ajusten su hora de inicio según previsiones de consumo. Además, amplía el soporte a inversores solares, baterías y bombas de calor. Que el estándar lo permita no significa que tu lavadora lo incorpore.
Se están desarrollando diferentes formas de gestionar lo que sucede en casa. El panel de energía de Home Assistant reúne los datos de la red eléctrica, los paneles solares y las baterías, así como los dispositivos individuales. Home Connect promete arrancar los electrodomésticos cuando la electricidad sea más barata o cuando los paneles generen, con un sistema solar o una tarifa flexible y el medidor P1 de HomeWizard. No está claro dónde se puede utilizar, por lo que es recomendable asegurarse de que funciona con el contador local.

articles.title: Cirquu opens AI business platform with $7 monthly subscriptions
articles.text:
Cirquu has opened its AI-powered business management platform to public sign-ups, offering African companies tools for sales, accounting and staff management with subscriptions starting at ₦9,000 ($6.70) monthly.
Michael Njoku, founder and chief executive, announced the launch at Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos on Wednesday, October 28, after about a year of operating through what he described as private placements. The first 100 people to sign up will receive three months free.
“Today, we’re opening it up to the general public, where everybody can sign up for it,” Njoku said.
The company is targeting businesses that use separate applications to manage customers, stock, finances and employees. Cirquu says its AI can configure a workspace around a company’s needs, bringing those functions into one system.
Its Starter plan includes customer relationship management, point-of-sale tools, inventory management, e-commerce, and accounting. A Growth plan, priced at ₦15,000 ($11.10) monthly, adds features including human resources, payroll, analytics and workflows.
The proposition puts Cirquu in competition with established business software providers such as Zoho and Sage. Njoku said its advantage lay in designing for local requirements, including tax, human resources, and data protection, as well as integrations with local tools and banks.
For businesses considering AI software, the handling of financial records, employee information and customer data is also central to the purchasing decision.
Asked about those concerns, Njoku said Cirquu used its own AI rather than an external platform, and that customer information remained within each user’s workspace.
“It’s not using any external AI platform; it owns its own AI,” he said. “It’s not sharing with us, not sharing with anybody.”
The company describes protections including encryption and access controls. Njoku’s comments did not provide technical details about how its AI is hosted or how customer information is isolated, leaving those claims to be assessed beyond the presentation.
Opening public sign-ups moves Cirquu from a limited rollout to a broader commercial test. Its pitch is that businesses can replace several disconnected applications with a single workspace, using AI to perform operational tasks and generate answers.
Whether that translates into adoption will depend on how well the platform handles routine work, from recording sales to running payroll, and how easily businesses can migrate their existing processes to it.

articles.title: Una empresa está creando el Tesla de las excavadoras: IA física y hasta arriba de sensores para levantar los centros de datos
articles.text:
Excavar terreno para una carretera, una fábrica o un centro de datos parece un trabajo seguro para un humano porque se sigue dependiendo de una persona a los mandos del aparato. Sin embargo, una startup de San Francisco quiere cambiar las reglas del juego y que a los mandos de esa maquinaria pesada haya una inteligencia artificial.
Se llama Bedrock Robotics, acaba de levantar 600 millones de dólares y su propuesta es la respuesta para un mundo con la pirámide demográfica invertida.
En corto. El 26 de octubre, Bedrock anunció una Serie C de 600 millones de dólares. Fundada en 2024 como una empresa de maquinaria de construcción sin conductor, tiene inversores detrás como Valor Equity, 8VC y, cómo no, Nvidia. No directamente, sino a través del brazo de riesgo de la compañía, pero evidentemente Nvidia iba a estar metiendo dinero a una empresa de IA física con cierto potencial.
La idea de la compañía es emplear el dineral captado para seguir llevando su tecnología a más máquinas de cara a reforzar el trabajo de campo y la estructura comercial y operativa. Parte de esa pasta se la ha dejado en fichar a una vicepresidenta de operaciones que ya pasó por Amazon o Uber, pero también a un directivo que se encargó de la parte legal de la división de conducción autónoma de Uber.
Meteórico. Lo llamativo es la velocidad a la que ha ocurrido todo. En julio del año pasado, la compañía salió del sigilo con 80 millones de dólares en las rondas preliminares, en febrero de este año cerró una Serie B de 270 millones. Ahí alcanzó una valoración de 1.750 millones de dólares y su financiación total superaba los 350 millones.
El cambio ha venido con la Serie C tras el anuncio de que sus excavadoras ya estaban operando de forma totalmente autónoma en obras de los clientes. Eso gustó a los inversores que se han dejado esos 600 millones en la última ronda para que la compañía alcance una valoración de 4.100 millones de dólares.
Qué vende Bedrock. Boris Sofman es el CEO y fundador de la empresa, quien ya dirigió el programa de camiones autónomos de Waymo. Sabe lo que hace en este segmento y lo que hace su nueva empresa no es fabricar maquinaria, sino sistemas que permiten convertir maquinaria pesada ya existente en autónoma.
Según la compañía, el equipo de sensores y computación se puede instalar en un día y lo bueno es que ninguno es un cambio permanente. Si no gusta, se desinstala y santas pascuas. Además, se adapta a excavadoras de 20 a 80 toneladas y de varios fabricantes.
Esa compatibilidad, unido a que ya se ha desplegado en modelos Caterpillar 352 y 336, es lo que ha resonado bien con los nuevos inversores. Ese trabajo de campo ya se ha realizado en una planta de tratamiento de agua en Nevada o movimientos de tierras en Texas.
El sistema. Y, básicamente, es como un coche autónomo. El sistema se llama 'Operator' y usa lidar, GPS y sensores de movimiento para percibir el entorno. La unidad de procesamiento recibe todos esos datos y realiza tanto la planificación de movimientos como la ejecución de las tareas complejas una vez que un jefe de obra fija el plan del día.
Y también incorpora los mismos sistemas de seguridad que un coche autónomo, como por ejemplo el detenerse sin asistencia y de manera inmediata si una persona u objeto no autorizado se acerca demasiado. Hay que decir que no hay nadie a los mandos y se encarga la IA, pero sí queda un encargado humano que es el que supervisa las operaciones e interviene si lo cree conveniente.
Por qué ahora. Según la compañía, sus clientes se han duplicado desde 2025 y tienen contratos en numerosos estados de Estados Unidos. También quieren empezar a probar a instalar el sistema en modelos aún más grandes como bulldozers gigantes o camiones articulados y la clave es que la empresa está despuntando justo cuando las grandes tecnológicas necesitan construir centros de datos a toda prisa.
El dato de Bedrock es interesado, pero afirman que se tardan cinco años en formar a un experto que conduzca estas máquinas. El dato de la patronal también coincide: necesitan 349.000 trabajadores netos en 2026 y 456.000 en 2027. No es que nadie se esté expandiendo a lo bestia, sino que llegan las jubilaciones y, además, con las políticas migratorias actuales, está en riesgo una tercera parte de la plantilla del sector al haber nacido fuera del país.
Según Bedrock, uno de cada cinco trabajadores de la construcción tiene más de 55 años y la demografía aprieta. Se necesitan obreros para levantar centros de datos y plantas energéticas, pero aunque esto pueda ser más patente en EEUU, otros países como China, Corea del Sur y Japón están probando la IA física y los robots para compensar la falta de jóvenes que realicen ciertos trabajos.
Esta carrera es a toda velocidad y en Europa tenemos a la suiza Gravis Robotics, en la que SoftBank metió 200 millones este verano.

Une caméra orientable avec vision nocturne

La vision nocturne infrarouge permet de conserver une image dans l’obscurité. Un microphone et un haut-parleur assurent la communication bidirectionnelle, pour entendre ce qui se passe dans la pièce et parler à distance.

articles.title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage.
When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions.
MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part.
In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path.
Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it.
Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work.
So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec.
That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API.
Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better.
Four constraints that shaped the architecture
Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable.
Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure to maintain.
Identity can’t be an agent’s decision. Every internal API call carries tenant, user, role, and database context. If that context is a large language model (LLM)-visible tool parameter, a model can get it wrong or be talked into changing it. MoEngage needed identity to be structurally out of the model’s reach, injected by the calling service and not surfaced as something the model can set or override.
A 400-tool catalog doesn’t fit in a context window. At roughly 50 tokens of JSON schema per tool, a full tools/list across the estate is over 20,000 tokens transmitted on every connection. That token budget is spent before the agent does anything useful, and it crowds out the context the agent actually needs to reason about the task. Client-side filtering (tool_filter in ADK or the MCP SDK) doesn’t fix this. The full catalog has already crossed the wire, and filtering by client convention isn’t an authorization boundary. An agent that is not supposed to see write operations shouldn’t receive them in the first place.
That last constraint is the one that avoided the obvious alternatives. A custom central MCP server solves the 20-servers problem but still leaves MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, none of it making MoEngage’s product better.
How AgentCore Gateway maps to those constraints
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP server. You register OpenAPI specs as targets and the gateway generates MCP tools from them, then routes calls to the backing services. Four properties mapped directly onto MoEngage’s constraints.
OpenAPI in, MCP tools out. There’s no MCP server to build or operate, and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the API. The spec teams already maintain is the tool definition. Each operation becomes a tool named Target___operationId, for example CampaignsAPI___searchCampaigns. When the spec changes, the tool changes. When a team adds an endpoint, the tool appears. When a team removes one, the tool disappears. No deployment, no protocol expertise, no coordination with the AI Platform team.
Cedar policies, evaluated before the catalog is serialized. The AgentCore policy engine uses partial evaluation to filter tools/list per principal. Each agent authenticates as its own IAM role, and its Cedar policy determines which tools it can see and call. This is what makes 400 tools tractable. It isn’t client-side filtering after the fact, but server-side scoping before the response is built.
A campaign QA bot, for example, gets read access to campaign and segment tools but can’t call a write operation:
The bot doesn’t see write tools in its tools/list response. There’s nothing to filter on the client side because the tools weren’t sent.
Managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice. The gateway reaches MoEngage’s internal services through AgentCore managed egress rather than through networking MoEngage builds and operates. Inbound, the gateway is reachable only through a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public path to it. Onboarding a new API adds a target, not a network topology change. This is the property that broke the multiply by seven Regions problem. The networking exists once and every API uses it.
Semantic search as a gateway capability. With the x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search capability, an agent can find tools by describing the task instead of naming the tool. It removed the need for a custom discovery layer. It also removed rename fragility as a side effect: if get_segment_user_count becomes get_segment_size, an agent searching for segment user count still finds it, because matching happens on description rather than identifier.
The architecture in practice
The request flow from agent to internal API is short, and every layer has a specific job. Agent services connect through a VPC interface endpoint to AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates Cedar policies and routes tool calls through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to internal APIs.
The following diagram shows how the components connect.
An agent service running on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or in a container calls the MCP client. The client can be the official MCP SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, or MoEngage’s own agent runner. The client signs the request with SigV4 using the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role the service already has. The request travels over HTTPS to a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public hop. AgentCore Gateway receives the request and evaluates Cedar policies to determine what this principal can see or call. It then routes tool invocations through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to the internal API.
MoEngage made two authentication decisions worth calling out.
First, they chose SigV4 over JWT for the internal gateway. Agents here are services that already have IAM roles. With SigV4, they can sign with credentials they already have. Nothing new to issue, rotate, or store. MoEngage’s separate public MCP server, which serves human-authenticated sessions from Claude and other clients, uses OIDC JWTs on AgentCore runtime. That is a different surface with different requirements.
Second, identity travels as headers, not as tool arguments. Tenant, user, role, and database context are converted by the client library from a small Identity object into X-MOE-* headers. The model doesn’t see them and can’t set them. One detail matters for anyone building something similar: Because SigV4 signing occupies the Authorization header, caller-forwarded bearer tokens must move elsewhere. MoEngage propagates it as a dedicated MoEngage-prefixed header. Header propagation is also capped, so the set of headers is deliberate rather than accumulated.
Discovery and execution have different identity requirements. Listing and searching tools carries no tenant identity. Only tools/call does. That separation keeps discovery cheap and makes the audit trail unambiguous. Every identity-bearing request is an actual data access.
Even with Cedar scoping an agent to a subset of the catalog, the subset can be large. MoEngage’s client library exposes a single meta-tool, search_tools, to the model. The model describes what it needs, the gateway’s semantic search returns candidates, and only those candidates become callable for the rest of the turn. The full catalog doesn’t enter context. The agent’s context contains one tool definition at the start and a handful of relevant ones after a search, instead of several hundred definitions it will never use.
Onboarding a new API
A team exposing an API as an agent tool adds a block to its existing OpenAPI spec:
Four design choices in that block are worth explaining.
Exposure is explicit opt-in. An endpoint with no x-moe-mcp block is not a tool. Continuous integration (CI) does not warn about its absence, because for most endpoints absence is the correct state. Cache-warmup routes and migration triggers are not agent tools, and nothing should nudge a team toward making them one. With the internal and external flags, a team can expose an operation to internal agents, to the public MCP server, or to both, independently.
Tool descriptions aren’t API descriptions. An API description tells a developer reading docs what an endpoint returns. A tool description tells a model when to reach for this tool and what to pass. MoEngage found that reusing API descriptions verbatim led to poor tool selection. Models picked tools based on implementation detail (“Returns a paginated list”) rather than intent (“Find campaigns by status or channel”). The tool_description and param_overrides fields exist specifically to give teams a place to write model-facing text without changing their developer-facing docs.
The CI pipeline handles everything from spec to running tool. When a team pushes a spec change, the pipeline validates the x-moe-mcp block, registers the target with AgentCore Gateway, and applies the Cedar policy. No manual steps, no tickets to the AI Platform team. A team that has never thought about MCP can have an operation available as an agent tool in the time it takes the pipeline to run.
The client library comes in two modes. A plug-in mode wraps the AgentCore Gateway MCP server inside LangChain, Google ADK, or an MCP-compatible framework as a tool provider. An agent runner mode runs a complete agent loop for teams that want a standalone agent without adopting a framework.
What MoEngage runs today
MoEngage’s AgentCore Gateway deployment runs in seven AWS Regions today. The gateway serves roughly 400 registered API operations to 10 internal agents. No product team has written MCP server code. No product team has provisioned networking for an agent integration. No product team has implemented Cedar policies. The AI Platform team owns all of that, and the cost of onboarding a new API is a spec annotation and a CI run. AgentCore feature availability varies by Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.
The system has been running in production for three months. The agents span the workflow a marketing team member touches daily. A campaign QA agent validates targeting rules and content before launch. A delivery health agent monitors send rates and bounce patterns across channels. A segment builder agent translates natural-language audience descriptions into segment queries. Each agent authenticates with its own IAM role, sees only the tools its Cedar policy permits, and discovers tools by describing the task rather than memorizing tool names. By removing the need to build and operate 20 separate MCP servers and provision per-API networking across seven Regions, MoEngage estimates the approach saved approximately six months of engineering effort. Onboarding a new API now takes hours of spec annotation instead of days of networking provisioning and security review.
The search-first pattern changed how MoEngage thinks about agent design. New agents start with zero hardcoded tool references. They describe intent, receive candidates, and call what they find. When a team renames an operation or ships a new one, existing agents pick it up without a code change.
Conclusion
The key insight behind MoEngage’s approach is a separation of concerns that maps to how engineering organizations actually work. Product teams own APIs and describe them well. A platform team owns the protocol layer, the policy layer, and the connectivity layer. AgentCore Gateway made that split practical by removing the undifferentiated work in between: no MCP server code, no per-API networking, no client-side filtering pretending to be authorization.
The result is an agent system where adding a new tool is a spec change, restricting access is a policy change, and neither requires the other team to be involved.
To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. For Cedar policy authoring, see the Cedar policy language reference. For private connectivity patterns, see the Amazon VPC Lattice documentation.
To discuss a similar architecture for your organization, contact your AWS account team or reach out to AWS.

articles.title: Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share
articles.text:
Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share
Ask a platform team what they built last year, and the list likely includes a Kubernetes controller that creates a few objects in order and copies fields between them. No business logic, just wiring. A Deployment, a Service in front of it, and a ConfigMap whose one interesting value is the hostname the Service reports in its status. Kubebuilder turns building the first controller into a pleasant afternoon. The tenth brings its own reconcile bugs, upgrade path, and on-call rotation. It’s the same controller. It’s slightly different each time, and it exists in thousands of organizations.
Every ingredient, no recipe
Kubernetes has the ingredients: CRDs define new types. Controllers give them behavior. Server-side apply tracks who owns each field. CEL evaluates expressions, and OpenAPI schemas type every field. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!
Every tool that manages a set of resources builds that piece itself, and keeps adding to it. Helm does it at render time, and Helm 4 added server-side apply and waiting on resource status. Argo CD has sync waves, hooks, and health checks because manifests cannot say what order they need or when they are done. Crossplane has compositions and functions, and v2 composes native Kubernetes resources directly. Operators do it in Go, by hand. Strip them down and the kernel is the same: a set of objects, dependencies between them, values flowing along the edges, and something that keeps re-checking whether the cluster still matches. Each recent addition reaches for a part the tool lacked: order, readiness, per-field ownership, evaluation inside the cluster.
“Kubernetes has the ingredients. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it.”
If everyone is building the same piece, the question is whether it should be shared. That is the position of kro, the Kube Resource Orchestrator, and why it moved to Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider in September 2025 as a primitive that other things build on, not another end-to-end platform.
Taking the controller apart
Kro started by taking the hand-written controller apart. API mechanics and lifecycle are the same in every one; only the wiring differs. Its answer, the ResourceGraphDefinition, writes the wiring down as data, and one controller interprets every definition. CRDs, OpenAPI, CEL, and server-side apply were already there, and kro connects them.
A ResourceGraphDefinition holds two separable things:
- The composition (the template with resources behind each instance and the CEL expressions to reference between them)
- The API (a schema, the CRD generated from it, and the instances application teams create)
The composition
kro derives the dependency graph from the references in CEL expressions (so order is never explicitly declared) and type-checks every expression against OpenAPI before an instance exists. The opening example’s ConfigMap needs the Service’s hostname, so its template names that field. That reference is the entire ordering rule: the ConfigMap reads from the Service, so the Service comes first, and nobody writes the order down. An explicitly declared order is a second description of a relationship the manifests already contain, and the two can disagree after any rename or reorder. An inferred order cannot drift, because it is derived rather than defined separately. The dependency is the reference. Wherever order is declared apart from the reference that needs it, there are two sources of truth, and an opportunity for drift.
The API
A platform team writes the ResourceGraphDefinition and application teams get a Kubernetes API like any other, with kubectl, RBAC, and GitOps working as usual. Ten glue controllers become ten definitions run by one controller. Wiring as data makes an API cheap to create, and a cheap API is still a promise. Application teams point manifests, RBAC, and pipelines at it, and from then on a removed field breaks something the platform team cannot see. kro refuses a ResourceGraphDefinition schema change that would break existing instances unless the author explicitly allows it. The cost of an abstraction moved from writing it to owning it: ten codebases gone, ten APIs left. Teams should count APIs, not controllers.
The primitive on its own
Once composition became cheap, people found more use-cases, and not all of it needed its own dedicated API. A default-deny NetworkPolicy in every labeled Namespace. Labeled Services folded into one Ingress. A DNS stack installed once and kept healthy. Nothing directly requests these; they react to what is already in the cluster. They are one-off definitions that do not need a repeatable API.
kro 0.10 adds a primitive for this case. A Graph is the composition piece alone; namespaced, with no schema, no CRD, and no instances. The Ingress case, abbreviated:
apiVersion: kro.run/v1alpha1
kind: Graph
spec:
  nodes:
    - id: services
      ref:                          # read only, never owned
        kind: Service
        metadata:
          selector: {matchLabels: {expose: "true"}}
    - id: ingress
      template:                     # created and owned
        kind: Ingress
        spec:
          rules: >-
            ${services.map(svc, {"host": svc.metadata.name + ".example.com", ...})}
Nobody creates an instance. The Services already exist, and the Graph follows them: label one and a rule appears; remove the label, and it goes.
Of the two halves, only one was ever new. The API half is a CRD, which is a primitive Kubernetes already has. ResourceGraphDefinitions make them cheaper to write, but the primitive was already there. The composition half is the piece Kubernetes lacked and every tool built for itself. Graph is that half on its own, and standing alone it shows what was easy to miss before: the API was never the input, only one kind of input. A composition reconciles against cluster state, and a new instance of a custom resource is just one of the many changes to that state it can react to. Whatever the change, the work is the kernel from earlier: objects, references between them, and a continuous declarative reconciliation loop keeping them in sync. That is the primitive. A ResourceGraphDefinition is the same primitive with a CRD in front of it.
“Strip the trigger from anything that creates objects, copies values between them, and keeps checking, and what is left is a composition.”
The split travels. Strip the trigger from anything that creates objects, copies values between them, and keeps checking, and what is left is a composition. An operator serving one custom resource is a composition with an API in front. A pipeline stage that applies manifests in order and waits for them is a composition with a commit in front, minus the loop. A runbook that creates a Namespace, its quotas, and its role bindings is a composition with a ticket in front. Seen that way, the question is no longer which tool to adopt but where composition is already happening and what is doing it.
Graphs in disguise
Kubernetes platforms are already full of resource graphs; they just aren’t written down as such. A naming convention so two manifests agree on a string. Sync waves or hooks that encode a dependency graph as step order. A script that copies a status field into another object. Each exists because the tool underneath cannot express a dependency between two objects, or cannot see what the cluster holds right now, so the dependency lives somewhere else such as a string, a step number, or a script. A composition tool puts it back as a reference between the objects. In kro that reference is a CEL expression continuously watched and evaluated inside a graph.
A familiar move
Kubernetes has grown this way before. Rolling updates were a kubectl subcommand until the Deployment controller took them over, and everything above got simpler. Composition looks due for the same move. kro, a Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider subproject on GitHub, shows what changes when the composition machinery becomes reusable, and the relationships become declarative. The question is bigger than any one project: if composition is what nearly every platform needs, should every platform have to build it for itself? Composition may be the primitive Kubernetes is missing.

articles.title: Over 41,000 DHS Employee Records Leaked Online
articles.text:
A threat actor has leaked online a database containing the personal and work information of thousands of US Department of Homeland Security employees.
The hacker, who uses the handle Department of Peace, has leaked more than 41,000 records. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the hacker wrote in a note.
According to the hacker, the data was stolen from an Okta single sign-on system used by DHS employees and contractors to access its central environment.
“We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
Most of the leaked records reportedly contain information on US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) employees.
Roughly 1,000 CISA employees, along with personnel at several other DHS agencies, had their information leaked as well.
The compromised data includes names, work email addresses and phone numbers, job titles, and office locations, as well as records showing which systems and internal applications each account can access. An online tool to search the data is also available.
“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available,” a DHS spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
According to Distributed Denial of Secrets, which obtained a copy of the database and calls it ‘Icepick’, the leaked information identifies officials in charge of covert and undercover operations and key personnel in DHS’s rendition and deportation programs.
“The most concerning part of this breach is the access information that came with it. If an attacker knows which employees have access to which systems and applications, they’ve essentially been handed a roadmap for where to go next and who to target to get there,” said Illumio public sector CTO Gary Barlet.
The incident surfaced one month after the infamous extortion group ShinyHunters breached FBI systems, and three months after the Homeland Security Information Network (HSIN) was hacked.
*Updated with statement from DHS.

articles.title: Feds to buy stake in Cohere via planned $7-billion Series E at $36-billion valuation
articles.text:
Toronto-based AI company Cohere hopes to secure as much as $7 billion CAD in new financing—which, if successful, would become the largest funding round in Canadian startup history.
The AI firm announced these plans and an initial close of its planned Series E on Thursday at Montréal AI research hub Mila, where the federal government revealed that it would take a $1.6-billion stake in Cohere as part of this round. Cohere has secured most of the target funding, a company spokesperson told BetaKit.
“We are choosing to grow Canada’s technology future instead of someone else’s.”
Cohere plans to put the capital toward computing infrastructure investment, and developing and delivering its AI models and other products to enterprises and governments. Cohere said that the fundraise is set to value the company at nearly $36 billion, post-money. This would make Cohere, Canada’s entrant in the frontier model race, the country’s most valuable private technology firm.
At the Montréal announcement, co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez said the financing will also make Cohere “the largest AI company outside of the United States.” The funds will keep Cohere headquartered in Canada, Gomez added. It will also help the more than 800-person company to create 1,000-plus “high-paying tech jobs” in the country by 2030.
“We are choosing to grow Canada’s technology future instead of someone else’s,” Gomez said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the federal investment in Cohere on the first day of the Canada-European Union Summit. Carney is hosting the event to further strengthen economic and strategic ties between Canada and the EU as it seeks to forge a middle-power alliance to decrease its dependence on the US.
Both Canadian officials and the country’s AI industry have been working more closely with European counterparts this year. AI and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced greater collaboration with Germany’s digital minister at ALL IN in September; Cohere, which recently purchased Czech cybersecurity AI startup Aisle, is in the final stages of merging with German AI peer Aleph Alpha as part of a push to create a viable, transatlantic alternative to US AI giants like Anthropic and OpenAI.
RELATED: Canada’s AI champion Cohere is standing up the load-bearing walls of our economy
Cohere said German retail giant and major Aleph Alpha shareholder Schwarz Group has committed to leading the financing, with support from new investors like the Government of Canada, Canadian telecom firm Bell’s venture capital arm, Bell Ventures, and Luxembourg’s Bullhound Capital. Existing backers, including Montréal-based Inovia Capital, US chip giant Nvidia, and Saudi Aramco-owned Prosperity7 Ventures, are also participating.
“In just seven years, Cohere has grown from a Toronto startup into a global company,” Carney said in Montréal. “It’s a Canadian success story being written before our eyes. And now, Canada has a stake in it.”
Carney said the feds would be investing on a “commercial basis.” He added that under this investment, Cohere will stay Canadian and open doors for the next generation of AI leaders through research partnerships.
“This will mean that Canadian AI companies can grow here, that Canadians will share in what they build, and that AI will serve Canadians to make their lives better,” he said.
RELATED: Cohere reaches terms with German peer Aleph Alpha to take on AI giants
In an interview on Thursday, AI and digital innovation minister Evan Solomon told BetaKit the federal investment is coming through the Canada Development Investment Corporation, a Crown corporation that manages assets on behalf of the government. It is separate from the feds’ planned $500-million Canadian Tech Growth Fund, which was announced as part of Canada’s broader AI strategy in June and will let the government provide growth capital and take stakes in promising AI companies.
The $1.6-billion investment will be “staged” and based on milestones, Solomon said. Though he declined to share the commercial terms of these stages, he said that “jobs and revenue targets are key.”
The announcement came the same day that Carney released Canada’s first national security strategy in 20 years. “Sovereignty now requires secure access to semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines, space-based communications, and artificial intelligence. Building these capabilities underpins our economic, foreign policy, and defence strategies,” he said.
This isn’t the first time Cohere has received federal money. In 2024, the feds awarded Cohere up to $240 million through its Sovereign AI Compute Strategy for a multibillion-dollar AI data centre.
Cohere to build new Canadian data centres
As part of the new agreement, Cohere will invest $1.7 billion in new computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030. Chief AI officer Joëlle Pineau told BetaKit in an interview that this is for building data centres in Canada as well as partnering with other compute infrastructure companies.
“To get compute, you need capital,” Pineau said. “Today’s announcement is going to open up a lot of opportunities in terms of what we can do. It’s a fuel that we need in order to build high-quality models and to serve them in a way that is private and secure.”
She added that Cohere is open to compute hosted in Europe, particularly to serve its global clients. For European clients who would prefer AI hosting on their own soil, lead investor Schwarz Group has a cloud services division called Stackit.
Chris Arsenault, co-founder and partner at Inovia, one of Cohere’s returning backers, called today’s investment “an important moment for Canada.” He contrasted the environment today with when Canada’s biggest tech company, Shopify, went public just over 10 years ago—and “most Canadians thought Shopify was an American company.”
“Fast forward, Cohere is the most important private Canadian technology company in valuation, in fundraising, in talent, and in global partnerships,” Arsenault asserted in an interview with BetaKit. “This is one example of what we’re becoming as an ecosystem.”
With files from Sarah Rieger.
Feature image courtesy Mark Carney via LinkedIn.

articles.title: ‘Bad actor’ cyberattack on FEC obscures political spending by donors and SuperPACs days before US midterm elections
articles.text:
‘Bad actor’ cyberattack on FEC obscures political spending by donors and SuperPACs days before US midterm elections
Millions of dollars in donations may have gone undeclared
- The FEC was hit by a cyberattack on Monday that took filing systems offline
- 24 and 48 hour donation reports couldn't be filed for almost 41 hours
- The attack has been blamed on a "bad actor", but no other details have been released
Just days before voters head to the polls in what is the most significant voting occasion in Donald Trump’s second term, the Federal Election Commission went offline for almost 41 hours to contain a cyberattack.
During that time, there was a window for big donors and SuperPACs to fund campaigns without being able to submit 24 and 48 hour funding reports, likely leaving millions of dollars undeclared.
Campaign and finance watchdogs have voiced outrage about the lack of transparency into funding at a critical time in the election cycle, especially as there are no caps on how much SuperPACs can spend to help or hinder candidates.
Funding transparency goes dark
An email sent to campaign compliance firms on Monday said that FEC services were taken down after a “bad actor” attempted to gain access to systems. Outside of this, there is little information to go on regarding who would be responsible or what their motives might be.
According to OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin, who spoke to Reuters, around $50 million was spent per day in the lead up to the FEC outage, with $250 spent on October 20 alone.
Disclosure delayed is disclosure denied,” Hilary Braseth, executive director of nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets, said in a statement during the outage. “When hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money flood political airwaves in the final days before an election, transparency is not an optional luxury, it is a fundamental public safeguard.”
As would be expected, numerous conspiracy theories surrounding the FEC outage have been floated online. Many suggested the outage would give donors a window to funnel millions of dollars of undeclared funding into candidates needing a last minute boost.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“We didn't have access to the last-minute spending, which is really ramped up as the election draws nearer,” Molly White, a crypto and Big Tech political spending tracker, told Reuters. “We have no visibility into that when the filing systems are down. It's pretty devastating this close to the election”
“It's hard to say with any real information that that's what happened, but it's certainly I think where people's minds go very quickly,” she concluded.
SuperPACs back pro-AI candidates
AI has been a hot topic ahead of the midterm elections, which take place on November 3. The huge buildout of AI data centers across the US - and the billions spent to fund it - have been met with opposition by the majority of Americans.
To counter the outrage and swing the vote in favor of AI, numerous SuperPACS have spent millions of dollars to support campaigns of pro-AI candidates and millions more to harm those critical of the technology.
President Trump has pushed an administrative policy of AI at any cost, claiming that the US economy and national security depends on continuing AI superiority over rivals such as China. To that end, the estimates on the total AI infrastructural spending range between $2.8 trillion by 2030 to $10.3 trillion by 2032, so there is certainly a lot riding on this election.
With many states enacting or considering moratoriums on AI data centers, anti-AI candidates could scupper the Trump administration's hopes for being an AI powerhouse.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Benedict is a Senior Security Writer at TechRadar Pro, where he has specialized in covering the intersection of geopolitics, cyber-warfare, and business security.
Benedict provides detailed analysis on state-sponsored threat actors, APT groups, and the protection of critical national infrastructure, with his reporting bridging the gap between technical threat intelligence and B2B security strategy.
Benedict holds an MA (Distinction) in Security, Intelligence, and Diplomacy from the University of Buckingham Centre for Security and Intelligence Studies (BUCSIS), with his specialization providing him with a robust academic framework for deconstructing complex international conflicts and intelligence operations, and the ability to translate intricate security data into actionable insights.

articles.title: Meta quietly launches an AI fashion app called Style Sketch | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch, an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads.
The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android.
Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely.
Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta. Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas.
To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style.
Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description.
The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length, and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account.
Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket, a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos.
The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.

articles.title: Bei ProSiebenSat.1 wird jetzt ein TV-Relikt der Vergangenheit abgeschaltet
articles.text:
Bei ProSiebenSat.1 wird jetzt ein TV-Relikt der Vergangenheit abgeschaltet
Der Fernsehkonzern ProSiebenSat.1 schaltet seine Videotext-Angebote ab Anfang nächstes Jahr ab. Betroffen sind neben Sat.1 und ProSieben auch Kabel Eins, Sixx, Sat.1 Gold, ProSieben Maxx und Kabel Eins Doku. Die Sender kündigen das in einer Mitteilung „in eigener Sache“ auf der ersten Seite ihrer Videotext-Angebote, die auch Teletext genannt werden, an. Das Medienmagazin DWDL.de hatte die Information entdeckt.
Kaum noch jemand schaut hin
Ein Sendersprecher begründet die Entscheidung gegenüber DWDL.de mit der geringen Nutzung: „Das Interesse der Zuschauerinnen und Zuschauer an unseren Teletext-Angeboten tangiert gegen Null.“ Als Informationsquelle habe die Website von Joyn den Videotext längst abgelöst. Joyn ist der Streamingdienst der Sendergruppe.
Schon Anfang 2025 hatte ProSiebenSat.1 den Teletext stark zusammengestrichen. Seitdem finden sich dort nur noch Programminformationen, keine redaktionellen Infos. Wer auf Seite 111 nach Nachrichten sucht, landet bei einem Verweis auf die News-Seite von Joyn. Damals erklärte die Sendergruppe, Zuschauer hätten im Teletext ohnehin fast nur noch nach dem Fernsehprogramm gesucht.
Untertitel laufen künftig anders
Mit dem Teletext fällt bei ProSiebenSat.1 auch der bisherige Weg zu den Untertiteln weg. Wer sie einblenden will, aktiviert sie künftig direkt in den Einstellungen des Fernsehers oder des Receivers. Damit folge man dem Vorgehen anderer großer Medienhäuser, sagt der Sprecher DWDL.de: „Die Untertitelung fällt nicht weg, sondern lediglich der technische Zugangsweg verändert sich.“
Andere Sender machen hingegen weiter. Das ZDF hat zwar bereits Sportnachrichten und Börsenkurse aus seinem Videotext gestrichen. Und mehrere dritte Programme betreiben kein eigenes Angebot mehr und übernehmen stattdessen den ARD-Text. Doch die Bestückung selbst endet nicht, da man besonders unter älteren Nutzer:innen noch Fans hat. Der ARD-Text wird aus Potsdam bestückt und hat dazu eine eigene Redaktion.
Die Technik stammt aus der Zeit des analogen Fernsehens. Die Sender übertrugen die Textseiten in der Austastlücke des Fernsehsignals – einem ungenutzten Teil des Bildsignals. Abrufen lassen sich die Seiten über die Eingabe von dreistelligen Seitenzahlen auf der Fernbedienung.

articles.title: GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data
articles.text:
General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers, as reported earlier by Reuters. The agreement, which resolves a complaint from a coalition of 36 US attorneys general, requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.
GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data
A coalition of 36 state attorneys general secured the settlement, which also requires GM to limit the data it collects.
The allegations surround GM’s now-discontinued Smart Driver program, which collected data about driving habits, including acceleration, braking, and trip length. GM allegedly passed this information to data brokers, enabling insurance companies to purchase the data and raise premiums. The states also accused GM of failing to notify drivers that they were enrolled in its Smart Driver program, and that the carmaker was collecting their data.
“This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices,” GM spokesperson Charlotte McCoy said in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
This settlement comes just months after GM agreed to pay $12.75 million to settle similar claims in California. Oregon AG Dan Rayfield and Washington AG Nick Brown co-led the states’ case against GM, which also included New York, Florida, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and many others.
“People bought a car, not a tracking device,” Rayfield says in a press release. “GM told drivers this program would help them drive more safely and promised it wouldn’t share their data with insurers without permission. Our investigation found GM sold that data anyway, and some drivers paid for it with higher premiums.”
Update, October 29th: Added a statement from GM.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
