articles.title: Physics-Based Validation: The Foundation Of Trustworthy Agentic EDA
articles.text:
What self-verifying agents validate their decisions against and why physics-based engines are the authority on correctness.
This is the third article in a series examining what it takes to build production-ready AI agents for EDA. The first explored the architectural decisions required for agents to operate reliably in production environments. The second examined what self-verifying means in an agentic EDA workflow: how agents continuously check their decisions as they work, rather than waiting until the end of a run.
But what exactly are those decisions being verified against?
The answer is physics. More specifically, the deterministic, physics-based EDA engines that define whether a design is correct. A self-verifying agent checks its own work, and a physics-validated workflow confirms that work is correct.
Chip design has always faced physics-based constraints. Every transistor, every wire, every timing path, and every thermal gradient is governed by the fixed laws of physics, regardless of how the design was created. This is why tapeout is binary: silicon either works or it does not.
When AI enters this domain, that physical reality does not change. The relevant question is not whether an AI system can reason about physics, but whether the outputs it produces have been confirmed by the engines that enforce that physics.
That distinction separates a model that is capable of reasoning about physics from a workflow that is physics-validated.
A physics-validated workflow is one in which every agent decision is confirmed against a deterministic, physics-based EDA engine before the next step begins. Validation does not happen only at the end of a workflow or after an entire run is complete. It happens continuously, at every step, against the engines engineers have trusted for decades.
The agent executes a step, and the engine determines whether the result meets the design’s physical constraints. If it does not, the agent identifies the issue, resolves it, and continues. Physics-validated means the engine, not the model, is the authority on correctness.
In semiconductor design, there is zero margin for unverified decisions. Tapeout dates are fixed, respins are expensive, and missed market windows do not come back.
For engineering organizations deploying agentic AI at scale, the key question is not simply whether the workflow is fast. It is whether the outcomes it produces can be trusted without requiring engineers to manually re-verify every autonomous decision.
An agentic workflow that reasons correctly about physics but does not validate its outputs against physics-based engines introduces risk at every autonomous step. The longer a workflow runs without validation, the further a design can drift from correctness before an error surfaces.
In a long-running autonomous workflow that executes across multiple tools, physical domains, and hours without human intervention, unvalidated decisions can compound. Continuous physics-based validation prevents those errors from propagating through the workflow.
In Part 2, I described an autonomous library characterization workflow in which the agent continuously checks its work against physics-based EDA engines. That workflow demonstrates the principle at a specific task level. The need for continuous validation increases when a workflow spans multiple tools and physical domains, and 3D-IC design shows why. It is the ultimate test of physics, and the clearest example of why semiconductor design is physics.
AI factories require more compute, memory bandwidth, and thermal performance within an increasingly constrained physical footprint. As power, performance, and area scaling on monolithic dies reaches practical limits, chiplet-based 2.5D and 3D architectures allow compute and memory to scale through tightly integrated packages.
That level of integration makes the physical design problem considerably more complex. Stacked active dies make heat removal and temperature interactions harder to predict, while packaging can introduce mechanical stress. Electrical, power, thermal, and mechanical effects are interconnected, so a change in one area can affect the others. Addressing these effects through manual, fragmented, and tool-intensive workflows creates frequent engineering handoffs, slows iteration, and limits the number of design alternatives teams can evaluate.
Siemens has developed an agentic engineering workflow that autonomously coordinates 3D-IC design and analysis. MCP servers and skill files for different EDA tools are connected to Fuse EDA AI Agent, which acts as an MCP aggregator that can be connected to any coding agent of choice. In this particular example, Claude Code is used as the agentic coding IDE, orchestrating a nine-stage electro-thermal workflow spanning seven Siemens EDA tools, running 100 to 200 agentic turns over more than 12 hours.
Each stage performs a distinct engineering task, from floor planning, library characterization, and power analysis to thermal signoff, system-level thermal simulation, parasitic extraction, and power- and temperature-aware SPICE simulation. Every stage is validated using signoff-grade, physics-based solvers.
The workflow runs autonomously, executing analyses, evaluating results, identifying missed targets, and continuing to refine the design. Teams can sweep heat transfer coefficient (HTC) boundaries, power budgets, and material stack-ups across 200 to 500+ design points per cycle. This enables teams to configure tools up to 20 times faster, reduce engineering effort by up to 95%, and evaluate up to 50 times more design options than a conventional manual flow.
The demo below shows the electro-thermal workflow in action:
When evaluating an agentic EDA workflow, one question determines whether its architecture is physics-validated: At each step, is the agent’s output confirmed by a deterministic, physics-based EDA engine before the workflow proceeds?
If the answer is yes, the workflow is physics-validated. The engine is the arbiter, and every autonomous decision is confirmed against the physical reality of the design.
Taken together, the three articles in this series define the requirements for production-ready agentic EDA: an architecture designed for real engineering environments, a self-verifying mechanism that continuously checks agent decisions, and a physics-validated standard that determines whether those decisions are correct.
This is the architectural standard Siemens EDA has built into the Fuse EDA AI Agent. The result is trusted autonomy: validated engineering outcomes at every step of the workflow.

articles.title: Madica secures $6m from Flourish Ventures to extend African pre-seed investment pilot - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Madica, a structured pre-seed investment programme for African startups, has secured US$6 million in additional capital from Flourish Ventures to extend its investment pilot by three years.
Launched in 2022, Madica is an Africa-focused pre-seed investment programme empowering underrepresented and underfunded mission-driven founders on the continent. The sector-agnostic platform, affiliated with Flourish Ventures, aims to empower entrepreneurs by providing funding and democratizing access to world-class company-building support.
The programme has so far backed 18 startups in 10 countries across the continent, most recently making three investments last month, and it is now set to invest in between 25 and 30 more ventures over the next three years with the additional US$6 million from Flourish Ventures.
Building on lessons learned and early signs of traction across its portfolio, Madica will also deepen its company-building support for exceptional founders underserved by established venture capital networks. The extended pilot will build further evidence for Madica’s founding conviction that these founders can build world-class businesses capable of generating venture returns when equipped with the right capital and support.
The 18 companies Madica has backed so far, across 12 sectors, have attracted, on average, twice Madica’s investment in additional funding, an early signal of investor confidence as they work towards the commercial outcomes needed to challenge prevailing assumptions about where venture-scale businesses can emerge in Africa.
The extended pilot will allow Madica to track how companies across a broader portfolio translate early traction into sustained business growth, examining the role of its investment and support model in that progress and assessing the potential to generate venture returns through exits.
“Madica was launched as an experiment to test whether pairing capital with hands-on company-building support could help overlooked founders building world-class businesses generate venture outcomes, and in many ways, our work sits at the intersection of the very many questions that underpin the state of early-stage venture investing in Africa. From the outset, we knew that gathering meaningful evidence would require years of investment, support and learning”, said Emmanuel Adegboye, head of Madica.
“Three years have given us valuable lessons and encouraging early signals, but building enduring companies and assessing venture outcomes takes longer. Flourish Ventures’ continued commitment gives us the capital to build on those lessons and test our conviction across a broader portfolio while deepening our company-building support. We want the resulting evidence to give other investors a model they can apply, shaping where funding goes and how founders are backed across Africa, well beyond Madica.”
Efayomi Carr, investment partner at Flourish Ventures and co-founder of Madica, said his company retained its conviction that with the right capital and support, exceptional talent across Africa can build world-class businesses.
“Madica’s first three years have strengthened that belief, and we are excited to continue backing the team as they help more entrepreneurs achieve that mission,” he said.

articles.title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Nano Omni, Super, Ultra, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS.
About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details:
- 120B total parameters, 12B active per token.
- Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE, and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder.
- Context length up to 1M tokens.
- Input: text, image, document, and video.
- Output: text.
- BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints.
NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. (technical report)
Model architecture
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding.
Use cases
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding:
- Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes.
- Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools.
- Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries.
- Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats.
- Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit. For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog.
Minimum GPU configurations
| vLLM (GPU Model / min count) | BF16 | NVFP4 | 
| B200/GB200 | 8 | 2 | 
| B300/GB300 | 4 | 1 | 
| H200 | 8 | 4 | 
| H100 | 16 | 8 | 
Deployment on AWS
This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family.
Deployment architecture
The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster.
NVIDIA Dynamo serves the model aggregated on a single node or disaggregated with prefill and decode on different nodes. For vision-language models, the image/video encoding stage can in addition run disaggregated on its own node.
Validation and performance
This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark.
Seeing utilization on all GPUs and traffic on all EFA adapters while the NCCL test is running, verifies that the cluster is working as expected.
You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool.
The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands.
The preceding concurrency sweep diagram reveals that the inference of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has lower TTFT and about the same ITL between aggregated and disaggregated deployments on two nodes.
A chart like this is useful when making deployment decisions. Draw your latency budget as horizontal lines, for example TTFT under 600 ms (about 1 second) and ITL under 100 ms per token. The rightmost point under both lines is the throughput one replica of this topology can serve within the service level objective (SLO), here c32, or about 320 tokens per second. To plan capacity, divide your target tokens per second by this per-replica throughput and find the number of prefill-decode pairs to deploy. Re-running the same sweep after a change (precision, TP/PP shape, aggregated versus disaggregated, a new Dynamo or vLLM release) makes the trade-off visible immediately. A curve that moves right and down is a win. Because TTFT and ITL are plotted separately, it also tells you which side to scale: rising ITL says add decode capacity, and rising TTFT says add prefill capacity.
Conclusion
This post covers the architecture and performance evaluation patterns for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM. To get started, deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in your own account, using the reference implementation. More inference blueprints are also available in the AI on EKS project. To get further hands-on experience with inference on EKS, register for our upcoming workshops.
Acknowledgements
The authors would like to convey special thanks to everyone involved in developing, validating, reviewing, and publishing this content, including but not limited to: Eliuth Triana, Jiahong Liu, Kshitiz Gupta, Abhijeet Patil, Mike Stefaniak, Chris Splinter, Sheetal Joshi, Aditya Ramakrishnan, Natarajan Kumar, Anish Maddipoti.

articles.title: Raenest wants users to earn from their money
articles.text:
Raenest, a Nigerian cross-border payments fintech, wants users to do more than receive money from abroad, its co-founder and chief executive officer, Richard Oyome, said at Moonshot 2026 in Lagos on Thursday.
Oyome traced the company’s strategy to the evolution of Africa’s fintech market, which moved from expanding access to digital banking and lending to helping people receive payments from international clients as remote work grew during the COVID-19 pandemic. As more Africans began working for foreign companies and serving customers abroad, he said, the need for financial services that connect them to global markets grew.
At Raenest Exchange 2026 on October 21, the company announced new products and features, including Raenest Vaults, a savings product offering annual yields of up to 16% on naira balances and 7% on dollar and stablecoin balances. It also expanded its USDT and USDC payment capabilities, improved its invoicing and payment links, and introduced new card options. The announcements extend the company’s services beyond cross-border payments.
“We were focused on receiving, but then again, receiving is just the beginning, not the end,” Oyome said at Moonshot. “The end is after receiving. When we started raenest, we focused on receiving not the end. Now, we’ve solved spending, now we’re focusing on the problem of earning.”
Founded in 2022, Raenest helps individuals, freelancers, creators, and businesses receive, send, store, and spend money across borders. The company says it has more than 1.5 million customers and has processed about $3 billion since inception.
Oyome said Raenest was built to help people overcome barriers to participating in the global economy by providing accounts in their own names that connect them to international markets. The company initially focused on helping users receive international payments. Its newer products are intended to address how users store their money and earn returns on it.
“Without the ability to earn or connect to global banking industries across the world, there is no opportunity to earn,” he said.
Oyome also said that the environment for companies operating in the crypto industry was also changing, with governments across Africa becoming more open to discussions about digital assets.
In July, Nigeria signed a Virtual Assets Coordination prder that established a framework to coordinate oversight among financial, revenue, and capital markets agencies. The order also provided for a regulatory sandbox in which eligible virtual-asset businesses can test products under supervision. Ghana has also introduced its Virtual Asset Service Providers Act, 2025, which provides for the licensing and supervision of businesses operating in the sector.
“Today, the governments across Africa are adopting. I think governments are happy to have conversations about crypto. It’s a success because we are coming from a very different time” Oyome said. “It’s a good time for people playing in the stablecoin space.”
The growing use of stablecoins presents an opportunity for Raenest to improve its payment operations. Oyome said stablecoins help Raenest settle payments faster.
“What we’ve seen as the biggest value is speed,” Oyome said. He explained that stablecoins allow the company to collect and settle funds faster, improving its cash flow and giving it quicker access to money that would otherwise take days to arrive.
As Raenest combines traditional currencies with stablecoins, Oyome said the company wants to shield customers from the technical complexity behind moving money across different networks.
“It can feel complicated. We don’t want it to be complicated. We have a blend of fiat and stablecoins,” he said.
He expects financial services to evolve towards a model in which users can move money without having to understand the underlying payment infrastructure or distinguish between different stablecoins.

articles.title: The Rise of Wearable Technology: Smarter Ways to Track Fitness - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Wearable technology is changing how people exercise, monitor their health, and work toward fitness goals. Modern smartwatches offer features such as GPS tracking, heart rate monitoring, sleep analysis, and personalised workout guidance.
For runners, running watches have become useful tools for tracking performance and building consistent training habits. Instead of relying only on distance or time, users can now review different measurements to better understand their workouts and daily activity.
One example of this growing trend is the Mibro AeroPace, a running smartwatch designed to support structured training and outdoor activities. As wearable technology continues to develop, Mibro demonstrates how fitness-focused devices can bring tracking, navigation, and smart features together in a convenient package. These developments are making fitness data easier to access for beginners and experienced athletes alike.
How Wearable Technology Is Transforming Fitness
Fitness tracking has moved beyond simple step counting. Modern wearable devices collect different types of information and present it in a format that users can review throughout the day. This makes it easier to understand activity levels, recognise patterns, and set realistic goals.
For beginners, a smartwatch can help establish a regular exercise routine. Daily step counts and workout summaries provide a simple way to measure activity. More experienced athletes can use pace, distance, and heart rate data to evaluate their training sessions.
Wearable technology also encourages accountability. When users can see their progress over several weeks, they may find it easier to maintain healthy habits. However, these devices should support personal goals rather than create unnecessary pressure to meet every target.
Important Features of Modern Fitness Wearables
Today’s fitness watches combine several tools to help users understand their performance. The most useful features often include:
- Heart rate monitoring: Helps users observe how their heart rate changes during exercise and recovery.
- GPS tracking: Records outdoor routes, distance, and pace to support running and cycling activities.
- Sleep tracking: Provides estimates of sleep duration and patterns, helping users become more aware of their rest habits.
- Workout modes: Allow users to record different activities, including walking, running, cycling, and strength training.
- Training guidance: Some devices provide structured workouts and progress summaries based on recorded activity.
- Smart notifications: Let users view selected phone notifications and other information without reaching for their smartphones.
The value of these features depends on how people use them. Fitness measurements are estimates, and they should not replace professional medical assessments when health concerns arise.
Smarter Training with Personalised Guidance
One challenge many runners face is knowing how to improve without training too hard. Running faster or covering longer distances every day is not always the best approach. A balanced routine usually includes different workout intensities, gradual progress, and sufficient recovery.
Modern running watches can make planning easier by presenting training information in a structured way. Some models provide suggested workouts, training plans, and performance summaries to help users follow a consistent routine.
The Mibro AeroPace includes Mibro Coach, which offers personalised training plans and workout guidance. These features can help runners organise sessions around their goals and review their progress over time. For someone preparing for a first 5K, having a structured plan may make the process feel more manageable.
Nevertheless, automated guidance should be adjusted to individual needs. Beginners should increase their activity gradually, while anyone experiencing persistent pain or unusual symptoms should stop exercising and seek appropriate medical advice.
Why GPS and Navigation Matter
GPS technology has become an important feature for people who exercise outdoors. It allows runners to record routes and compare distances across different workouts. Accurate distance information also helps users understand their average pace and track improvements over time.
Some advanced running watches offer multi-system satellite positioning and additional navigation features. These tools can be particularly useful when exploring unfamiliar routes, running in new locations, or planning longer outdoor sessions.
The Mibro AeroPace offers dual-band, multi-system satellite positioning, along with navigation features that include downloadable maps and route guidance. Such capabilities can make outdoor training more convenient.
However, GPS accuracy can vary depending on surrounding buildings, dense trees, terrain, and other environmental conditions. Runners should therefore consider long-term performance patterns instead of relying entirely on a single recorded measurement.
Making Fitness Technology Comfortable and Practical
A fitness watch should fit naturally into everyday life. Comfort, display quality, battery performance, and ease of use can all affect whether someone continues wearing a device regularly.
The Mibro AeroPace combines a lightweight design with an AMOLED display intended to make workout information easy to view. This can be helpful when checking pace, heart rate, or navigation details during a run.
Battery life also matters, especially for people who regularly use GPS. Continuous satellite tracking and other active features generally consume more power than basic timekeeping or step counting. Users should check the manufacturer’s stated battery estimates and consider their own usage patterns.
Other convenient features may include music controls, phone notifications, and Bluetooth calling. Although these functions can be useful, the best choice is a device that prioritises the features most relevant to an individual’s routine.
How Wearables Support Different Fitness Activities
Wearable technology is not limited to running. Many devices support several sports and exercise types, allowing users to record a broader range of physical activities.
For example, a weekly fitness routine might combine running with walking, cycling, strength training, and stretching. Tracking these sessions can help users maintain a balanced approach rather than focusing exclusively on one measurement.
Different activities also require different training approaches. A runner preparing for a race may focus on pace and distance, while someone interested in general wellbeing may prioritise daily movement and consistency.
Wearables can help users review these activities together, but calorie estimates and other calculated measurements should be treated as approximations. The goal is to understand general patterns, not to assume every number is perfectly accurate.
Turning Fitness Data into Better Habits
Collecting information is only useful when it leads to practical decisions. Users can get more value from fitness technology by focusing on a few achievable habits:
- Set realistic goals: Start with manageable daily activity targets and increase them gradually.
- Review weekly progress: Look for consistent changes in activity and performance instead of judging individual workouts.
- Balance exercise and recovery: Allow sufficient rest between demanding sessions and pay attention to fatigue.
- Use data as a guide: Combine watch measurements with personal experience rather than following every recommendation automatically.
- Stay consistent: Regular, sustainable activity is generally more useful than short periods of intense exercise followed by inactivity.
These simple steps help make wearable technology a practical part of a long-term fitness routine. They also reduce the risk of becoming overly focused on daily scores or comparisons with other people.
The Future of Wearable Fitness Technology
The next generation of fitness wearables is likely to place greater emphasis on personalised insights, connected applications, and easier-to-understand training recommendations. Artificial intelligence may help users interpret workout histories and identify patterns that would otherwise be difficult to recognise.
Privacy will also remain important as devices collect increasing amounts of personal activity information. Users should understand what data their devices record, which applications receive it, and how privacy settings can be managed.
The most useful wearable will not necessarily be the one with the greatest number of features. It will be the device that presents meaningful information clearly and helps users make better decisions without adding unnecessary complexity.
Conclusion
Wearable technology has changed fitness tracking by combining activity monitoring, GPS navigation, heart rate measurements, and training guidance in compact devices. These tools can help beginners establish exercise habits and enable experienced runners to review their performance more effectively.
The Mibro AeroPace is one example of a running-focused smartwatch that brings training and navigation features together. Ultimately, wearable technology is most valuable when it supports realistic goals, consistent activity, and adequate recovery. Used thoughtfully, it can help people make fitness a more informed, practical, and sustainable part of everyday life.

articles.title: Granola crunches up a dictation feature to compete with Wispr | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apps in the consumer voice AI world seem to be converging, as Granola, known for its meeting notetaker, launched a dictation feature today. This comes months after Wispr, known for its dictation tool, launched a meeting notetaker.
Granola’s dictation currently works on Mac just like any other such tool. Users can press the “Fn” key and start speaking, and the tool cleans up and formats their speech and posts the final text. This feature works across all apps, so users can post notes, dictate prompts, and reply to emails and messages.
The company said that the feature will land on iOS and Windows soon.
Granola and Wispr are valued at $1.5 billion and $2 billion, respectively. Granola is focused on meeting-related automation and notetaking. On the other hand, Wispr is trying to build its own models through a research lab, which is exploring different human-computer interfaces.
The feature mashups are not exclusive to Granola and Wispr. Other voice startups such as Fireflies, Speechify, and Monologue have converged into multifeature apps with meeting notetaking and dictation capabilities. Until earlier in the year, the play was around having a focused app that does one thing well. But now, all of these apps are thinking about how to get more out of capturing users’ speech.

articles.title: BYD avança na Bahia e quer comprar porto desativado da Ford
articles.text:
Um ano após inaugurar sua fábrica em Camaçari (BA), a BYD prevê iniciar até dezembro a produção de carros com etapas industriais realizadas integralmente no Brasil. A montadora chinesa também demonstrou interesse em adquirir o antigo porto da Ford, em Candeias (BA), para ampliar sua capacidade de exportação.
Os planos foram apresentados nesta quinta-feira (29), durante coletiva na Federação das Indústrias do Estado da Bahia (Fieb), em Salvador (BA). Segundo Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente da fábrica, os complexos de estamparia, soldagem e pintura já estão em fase de testes.
A expectativa é concluir os testes em novembro e iniciar a produção local entre novembro e dezembro. O primeiro modelo a passar pelo processo será o Atto 2, híbrido plug-in que combina motor elétrico e motor a combustão, compatível com gasolina e etanol. O veículo custa entre R$ 149.990 e R$ 166.660.
A ampliação das etapas de fabricação no país também pode ajudar a BYD a cumprir exigências de conteúdo local em acordos comerciais, como as regras do Mercosul, que exigem que pelo menos 35% do produto tenha componentes locais.
BYD mira antigo porto da Ford para exportar carros
- Além da produção nacional, a montadora demonstrou interesse no Terminal Portuário Privativo Miguel de Oliveira, conhecido como Porto da Ford. O espaço fica em Candeias, a cerca de 35 quilômetros de Camaçari, e foi construído para facilitar o escoamento dos veículos fabricados pela Ford na Bahia;
- A estrutura foi desativada após a saída da montadora estadunidense do Estado, em 2021, e atualmente pertence ao governo baiano;
- Baldy afirmou que a BYD quer construir uma operação integrada para atender diferentes mercados das Américas. A ideia é aproveitar a localização da fábrica e a infraestrutura portuária para exportar veículos produzidos na Bahia;
- “Nossa estratégia é, de fato, sermos uma empresa regional contígua entre América do Sul, Central e Norte, onde nós aproveitaríamos essa estratégia para exportar a partir da Bahia”, disse o executivo;
- A eventual aquisição do porto, porém, foi apresentada como interesse da empresa, não como negócio concluído.
Fábrica já produz cerca de 700 carros por dia
Antes da entrada em operação dos novos complexos, os veículos chegavam da China pré-montados. Na unidade baiana, eram instalados componentes essenciais, como motor e pneus. Com as novas estruturas, a maior parte do processo industrial poderá ser feita no Brasil.
A estamparia dá forma às chapas de aço que compõem a carroceria. Na etapa de soldagem, as partes são unidas, enquanto a pintura protege a estrutura contra corrosão e dá acabamento ao veículo. Depois, os carros seguem para a montagem final e passam por verificações e testes.
Atualmente, a fábrica produz cerca de 700 veículos por dia. Entre os modelos montados na unidade estão Dolphin Mini, Song Pro, Atto 2 e King.
A instalação é o maior polo da BYD fora da China. A empresa informa ter investido R$ 11 bilhões no complexo, que ocupa cerca de um milhão de metros quadrados de área construída. A expectativa é dobrar o tamanho da estrutura nos próximos anos.
Leia mais:
- BYD Dolphin Mini: o elétrico mais vendido do Brasil dá conta de uma cidade como SP?
- Especialista hackeia BYD Shark e controla funções do carro à distância
- BYD quer produzir 600 mil carros por ano em fábrica no Brasil
BYD prevê ampliar quadro de funcionários
Segundo os dados apresentados na coletiva, a fábrica gera nove mil empregos diretos, e a empresa espera alcançar dez mil postos ainda em 2026. Quando todos os investimentos previstos estiverem concluídos, a projeção é chegar a 20 mil funcionários.
O levantamento do Observatório da Indústria da Fieb aponta salário médio de R$ 3,9 mil entre os trabalhadores da fábrica, valor 24% superior à média da indústria baiana.
A parceria entre a entidade e a BYD busca mensurar os efeitos econômicos da instalação sobre Camaçari. Para isso, são analisados registros oficiais de emprego, movimentações do mercado de trabalho formal e dados empresariais, além de informações históricas da cidade.
A intenção é comparar a situação econômica do município antes e depois da chegada da montadora e projetar os impactos da operação.
Montadoras tradicionais observam avanço chinês
A expansão da BYD ocorre em momento de aumento das importações de veículos no Brasil. Segundo dados da Anfavea, o país importou 406,7 mil veículos nos oito primeiros meses de 2026, alta de 29,8% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. Mais da metade das unidades veio da China: foram 221 mil veículos, avanço de 109,9% na comparação anual.
O crescimento das marcas chinesas também foi comentado por Herlander Zola, presidente da Stellantis para a América do Sul. No início de outubro, o executivo afirmou que a indústria automotiva ocidental errou ao avaliar a velocidade com que a eletrificação ganharia espaço no mercado.
Zola também criticou as condições de competitividade no Brasil e afirmou que a falta de incentivos e previsibilidade dificulta a ampliação da cadeia de fornecedores locais. Segundo ele, componentes e matérias-primas nacionais, como aço, plásticos e pneus, podem custar mais do que os equivalentes chineses.
A ampliação da produção da BYD na Bahia pode aumentar a participação de componentes fabricados no país e abrir espaço para exportações. O alcance desse plano dependerá da entrada em operação dos novos complexos industriais e de como a empresa avançará em relação ao antigo porto da Ford.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising
articles.text:
People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science
- Summary:
- Researchers analyzing nearly 150,000 Reddit posts uncovered unexpected symptom reports linked by users to unapproved versions of retatrutide, including increased appetite, sleep disturbances, and elevated heart rates. The findings differ from clinical trial results and highlight how AI could help identify potential drug safety signals that warrant further investigation.
- Share:
An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.
The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.
Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.
One finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.
AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports
"Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.
However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.
There is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.
"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.
Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.
"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.
How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts
The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.
That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.
"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.
Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.
To investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.
The AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that users associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.
After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 users who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.
"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize."
A Surprising Appetite Paradox Emerges
The most striking difference involved hunger.
In retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.
But among Reddit users who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.
The researchers also compared the new findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.
Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.
These differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.
"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.
"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean."
Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?
Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.
Traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.
Social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.
The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.
In their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.
The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.
The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.
"That's what we hope will happen with this study," says Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing."
The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Neil K. R. Sehgal, Jena Shaw Tronieri, Benjamin Rader, Lyle Ungar, Sharath Chandra Guntuku. Self-Reported Adverse Effects Among Social Media Users Taking Nonapproved Retatrutide. JAMA Network Open, 2026; 9 (10): e2638929 DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38929

articles.title: Solink raises more than $100 million USD to help physical stores keep an eye on their business | BetaKit
articles.text:
Ottawa-based surveillance tech company Solink has raised more than $100 million USD ($140 million CAD) in a new strategic investment round to solidify itself as a global leader in what it sees as an emerging industry: AI vision intelligence.
The company announced the round, led by Toronto-based private equity firm Vertu Capital, on Thursday morning. In an interview, Solink CEO Michael Matta did not disclose how much Solink raised, but said it “may be a small rounding error” from the announced $100 million USD.
“That’s really the focus of this investment: continuing to position around where we see the puck going.”
Michael Matta, Solink
The round consisted of a mix of primary and secondary capital. More than 90 percent of the proceeds are headed to Solink’s balance sheet, and the remainder are going through employee and investor stock sales. Existing investor Goldman Sachs reinvested in Solink through the new round, citing “strong customer adoption and an ambitious product vision,” while new investors Golub Growth and Comcast Ventures also participated.
The new capital will help solidify Solink’s evolution from a cloud-connected surveillance platform for restaurants and retailers into a provider of AI-powered business intelligence for the physical world, Matta explained to BetaKit.
“The physical world is a lot more chaotic than the digital world,” Matta said. “Things don’t repeat in a certain cadence, and so that reasoning layer of being able to understand the physical world, and what the intent and context is, is really important today.”
Essentially, Matta is saying that, while data gathering is easy for an online retailer, brick-and-mortar stores are comparatively helpless. Solink helps store security teams manage and keyword search their thousands of hours of footage, but Matta also sees potential in helping those businesses extract value from the other “99 percent” of unseen surveillance footage by using AI. This includes identifying store factors, like missing products or long lines, that resulted in missed sales.
“You can go into hundreds of rabbit holes as to why we are not optimizing our physical space or the priorities that we have as a business,” Matta said. “Solink wants to be that sidekick to operators and to owners to be able to help them execute.”
Surveillance tech backlash
Solink is equipping more retailers’ surveillance cameras with its AI-powered toolkit amidst a wave of public backlash surrounding surveillance technologies, from protests against Flock cameras to the outcry against surveillance tech in billboards and M&M vending machines. That tech is also lucrative; the global AI surveillance market is expected to grow from $4 billion USD to nearly $11 billion USD by 2032. When asked how public sentiment has affected Solink, Matta stressed that the company is running a “very different business.” He explained that Solink doesn’t install any of its own cameras, only bolstering cameras that are already recording a business’ premises, and does not provide biometric data.
“The way I like to think of it is, it’s not the actor; [Solink is capturing] the actions that are happening, and being able to understand at scale what is taking place,” Matta said, adding that Solink’s tech is not identifying individuals. “It has less to do [with] us creating a viral product that’s selling anonymized information, or anything like that.”
A Solink spokesperson later added that surveillance data is confined to the business owner, and that their data doesn’t get shared with anyone, not even police, unless there is a warrant and consent from the business owner.
Data intelligence for the physical world
The last time Solink raised money was in 2023, when it secured $60 million USD in Series C funding to help take its surveillance software global. When the company expanded its Ottawa headquarters just over a year ago, Matta told BetaKit that Solink was not looking to raise any more capital, and that it still had “a lot of liquidity” from the 2023 financing.
This week, Matta said the new raise wasn’t driven by a need for liquidity; rather, Solink wants to invest in the shift from data intelligence being a strictly digital affair to a physical one.
“Today, I believe we’re operating in a trillion-dollar TAM.”
Michael Matta, Solink
“I believe in the next two to three years we’re going to continue to see that level of AI and intelligence penetrate our physical world,” Matta said. “We just wanted to be the leaders in that space, and that’s really the focus of this investment: continuing to position around where we see the puck going.”
Solink has already experienced rapid growth in recent years. Matta did not provide specific revenue numbers, but said Solink has been “scaling revenue pretty aggressively,” increasing between 40 and 50 percent year after year. On Wednesday, Solink placed 10th on Deloitte’s 2026 Enterprise–Industry Leaders list, sporting a 241-percent revenue growth rate over the past four years.
The company says its platform is in more than 35,000 customer locations (nearly double since 2023) and 500,000 cameras in 65 countries, ingesting more than 750 million hours of video every month. Its customers include stores like Gap, JYSK, Domino’s, Moose Knuckles, and Tim Hortons.
RELATED: Solink expands Ottawa headquarters as it targets 1,000 employees by 2030
To entrench its place in the market, Solink will use the new funding to execute on an AI roadmap, renew its go-to-market efforts, and explore “growth through strategic opportunities.” Solink’s AI roadmap includes an upcoming hardware launch that will provide a way for its customers to host its AI agents on premises, rather than run on an external data centre, Matta said. On the go-to-market side, an “important” reselling partnership with new investor Comcast also opens up an avenue for Solink to reach the US telecom giant’s restaurant and retailer partners.
While the physical security and security guard industries are hundred-billion-dollar businesses on their own, Matta said he believes those industries will increasingly shift their spend away from people and towards technology in the coming years. And that’s just the security side. With Solink looking to provide store managers more value from their surveillance footage than just stopping ne’er-do-wells, Matta sees his company well positioned to be a “global business that just happens to be based in Canada.”
“We used to operate in a $70 billion TAM [total addressable market],” Matta said. “Today, I believe we’re operating in a trillion-dollar TAM.”
Feature image courtesy Alex Riehl for BetaKit.

articles.title: You can generate and edit Google Docs files directly in Gemini chats now
articles.text:
Now you can generate, preview, and edit PDFs, Google Docs, Google Sheets, slide decks, Markdown files, TXT files, and code directly within Google Gemini. The new file editing capabilities are available starting today for all Gemini users, and while PDF previews/editing works on both the web and mobile, all other file formats are only in the web version for now.
You can generate and edit Google Docs files directly in Gemini chats now
Editing files you generate with Gemini no longer requires leaving the app.
Google added support for generating and downloading files in Gemini earlier this year, but now you can tweak those files without leaving the Gemini app. Google says you can expand documents to edit them in full-screen mode and highlight text in files to ask Gemini questions or prompt it to make changes to the file, like highlighting a table and asking Gemini to turn it into a graph.
You could already use Gemini to edit files with its integrations in Google’s Workspace apps, like the Gemini bar in Google Docs. Anthropic also launched a feature earlier this year that allows users to generate and edit documents and presentations in Claude chats.

Anthropics Börsengang: Ein Test für die Macht des Storytellings in der Tech-Welt
Nach wochenlangen Spekulationen hat Anthropic endlich seinen Börsenprospekt eingereicht. Das 335-seitige Dokument – etwa 100 Seiten davon befassen sich mit Risiken, die das Unternehmen für Anleger sieht – legt die Sichtweise des amerikanischen KI-Konzerns auf die von ihm entwickelte Technologie dar – und beschreibt, wie diese nach seiner Überzeugung die Welt verändern wird. Das ist alles recht speziell. Doch Anthropic feilt schon seit Jahren an seiner Fähigkeit, Narrative zu vermitteln. Tatsächlich ist die öffentliche Kommunikation des Unternehmens längst zu einer Meisterklasse im Storytelling geworden, meinen Beobachter.

articles.title: Are you still piloting?
articles.text:
There's no shortage of enthusiasm for artificial intelligence. Organizations across every sector are investing heavily, experimenting, launching proof of concepts, and finding ways to turn the latest developments into real business value.
However, there's a growing disconnect between experimentation and execution. For all the discussions of AI transforming the way we work, many AI projects never progress beyond the pilot stage. It's a familiar story. The proof of concept delivers promising results, the business case adds up, and everything looks like it's heading in the right direction.
Yet somewhere along the way the project hits a bump on the road. This can look like costs beginning to rise, confidence starting to waver, integration with existing legacy systems proving more complicated than expected, and approvals taking longer than anticipated.
VP of Insight AI at Insight.
What started out as an exciting project slowly loses its momentum. As a result, the AI initiative ends up stuck in limbo. The reason is that running a successful AI pilot and successful AI implementation are two very different things. Transitioning from a controlled environment with governed variables to a production environment brings a new set of challenges: security, governance, culture, skills, integration, and readiness.
Unfortunately, this challenge is not uncommon. Research shows that 71% of organizations remain in the pilot or proof-of-concept phase of AI transformation, highlighting just how difficult it is to turn early promise into a business reality.
This limbo is what many organizations are now experiencing: the AI implementation gap. It's the space between proving that AI can work and deploying it at scale in a way that delivers measurable value. For today's technology leaders, bridging that gap has become one of the defining challenges of AI adoption. The pressure to move beyond experimentation is growing, but doing so requires more than just increasing investment or pushing strong proof of concepts into production.
The real challenge is creating the conditions in which AI can move from an isolated trial into a sustainable part of the wider business. That requires establishing the right technical and organizational foundations, preparing people and processes, and finding the right use cases. To deliver real value, organizations need to think less about speed and more about creating something secure, scalable, and consistent.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
It isn’t a technology challenge, it’s a business one
When AI projects stall, it's seldom because of the technology itself. More often, organizations run into strategic, governance, and operational challenges that prevent encouraging pilots from becoming production-ready solutions.
One of the biggest barriers is analysis paralysis. The majority of organizations have no shortage of AI ideas, but they typically lack a clear way of understanding which use cases will deliver the greatest value. This means resources become spread across multiple proof-of-concepts, each showing promise but none receiving the attention needed to reach production. The number of pilots continues to soar while the number of live deployments stagnates.
However, some organizations make the opposite mistake by designing for scale before they've checked the concept works. Major investment is made in infrastructure, architecture, and implementation before a solution has been tested in real-world conditions. If the project then needs to change direction, the amount of investment already committed can make it tricky to adapt. As a result, organizations can end up locked into an approach that no longer delivers the value they envisioned.
Governance is another common stumbling block. For organizations operating across EMEA, navigating regulations such as the EU AI Act, GDPR, and DORA introduces understandable caution. The consequences of non-compliance can be significant, and uncertainty around an evolving regulation often slows decision-making. Many AI initiatives don't stall because the business lacks ambition, but because leaders want greater confidence that they're deploying the technology in the right way: compliantly and responsibly.
Lastly, organizations often underestimate what it will cost to move from a successful pilot to widespread deployment. AI projects that appear affordable during the proof-of-concept phase can become much more expensive once they're scaled, especially if they haven't been properly stress-tested.
That's why due diligence is critical. Yet more than half (56%) of organizations don't carry out a Total Cost of Ownership assessment before deciding where to place significant workloads. Without a clear understanding of the long-term investment required, it's easy for costs to accumulate and confidence in the project to dwindle.
Balancing certainty and speed
Closing the Implementation Gap isn't about moving faster. It's about moving with confidence and know-how.
Time and time again, organizations find themselves at one of two extremes: waiting until every unknown has been resolved before making any moves or rushing ahead with AI projects before they've been properly validated. Neither approach is sustainable. Those seeing the greatest success are the organizations finding a balance between certainty and speed - moving quickly where the evidence supports it, while building in the validation and governance needed to reduce risk.
That starts with validating ideas early. Before major investment is made, organizations need to ask the technical, commercial, and governance questions that could prevent a project from ever reaching production. It's far better to discover early that a use case won't deliver than to invest months of budget and time before uncovering the same conclusion.
Rapid prototyping also plays a crucial role. Instead of debating whether an idea might work in theory, businesses should aim to create something tangible that users can test within days. Seeing a concept in action changes the conversation from speculation to evidence, giving stakeholders the confidence to make informed decisions about where to invest next.
Equally important is maintaining transparency throughout the delivery process. AI projects shouldn't feel like a black box. Defined ownership, clear checkpoints, and agreed assessment criteria help everyone to understand where a project stands, whether it’s a success, and what comes next. Projects rarely stall because the technology isn't capable - they stall because critical decisions weren't made early enough or because expectations weren't aligned from the outset.
Bridging the implementation gap
The implementation gap isn't going to disappear overnight. With 71% of organizations still stuck between pilot and production, the challenge is clearly not a lack of willingness, technical ability or ideas. In most cases, they have all three.
Instead, it's the ability to turn experiments into solutions that actually work in the real world. That means treating the transition as a business issue, not simply a technical one. Organizations need an approach that balances speed with governance, validates value before investment is made, and gives stakeholders the confidence to scale. It also requires leaders to be confident enough to stop projects in their tracks if they're not going to deliver real value.
The organizations taking meaningful steps forward won't be those adding more pilots into the mix. They'll be those that have strong processes and capabilities in place to push the right pilots ahead. Fundamentally, closing the AI implementation gap means creating a path from pilot to production that can be followed again and again.

articles.title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act Reaches Chip And IP Suppliers
articles.text:
Determining which products may fall within the CRA’s scope and what information may need to be provided to customers.
Many of today’s electronic products connect to networks and other devices to communicate, exchange data, coordinate tasks, and receive software updates. These connections make everyday work-life tasks incredibly convenient. However, this convenience also comes with risks. Weaknesses in these products can give cyberattacks a way into trusted devices. Responding to an attack takes time and money. Even worse, reputational damage can last long after the incident. To help reduce these risks, the European Union (EU) established common cybersecurity requirements that set a baseline for product development.
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), adopted in October 2024, establishes the requirements framework. Companies supplying digital products to the EU market must consider the CRA, whether they sell directly or supply components for a customer’s finished product. The rules apply regardless of where a company is based or where development takes place.
The regulation applies to semiconductors sold separately. Manufacturers must exercise due diligence when incorporating third-party components into their products. Semiconductor intellectual property (IP) suppliers may need to provide security evaluation results and explain the assumptions for secure use.
The CRA addresses widespread product vulnerabilities, inconsistent security updates, and insufficient information for secure use. The CRA’s mandatory reporting phase took effect in September 2026. When manufacturers learn that a vulnerability in their product is being actively exploited, or that a severe incident has affected its security, an early warning must be submitted. A more detailed notification follows, with a final report explaining the findings and corrective measures. Manufacturers submit these notifications through the CRA’s Single Reporting Platform.
The CRA also lists semiconductor products such as microprocessors, microcontrollers, ASICs, and FPGAs according to core functionality, including security-related functions. The applicable category and obligations depend on the product and how it is placed on the market. Chip and IP companies need to understand which CRA responsibilities apply to their products and what information they may need to provide to customers. That determination can be challenging because commitments vary with the product’s classification. Figure 1 illustrates how suppliers may provide security evidence to support CRA reporting.
Fig. 1: Illustrative supply chain showing how component information and security evidence may move between suppliers and the product manufacturer in support of its EU CRA documentation. (Source: Arteris, Inc.)
To help companies prepare, Arteris developed the EU CRA Hardware Readiness Guide. It provides a checklist to help companies assess which products may fall within the CRA’s scope, identify who is responsible for each product, and determine what information customers may request. It also helps identify where classification, responsibility, processes, or security documentation may need further work. The guide distinguishes design-stage security evidence from a completed conformity assessment. The results can support a manufacturer’s compliance work, but it does not cover all of the manufacturer’s CRA duties.
For the security assessment, the checklist asks companies to identify assets such as keys, configuration, and debug state. Companies can also define protection boundaries and document where those assets can and cannot travel. A design that performs its specified functions does not, by itself, show that sensitive assets remain protected.
Suppliers can use the readiness guide to organize information and security evidence that may support customers as they prepare their technical documentation. Annex VII of the CRA lists what manufacturers must provide in their technical documentation. It includes cybersecurity risk assessments, relevant design and development information, and supporting evidence, where applicable. Dated, repeatable evaluations can help document the design examined, describe what was covered, and note any limitations. The guide also recommends mapping evaluation findings to named hardware weakness classes. The CRA sets security outcomes but does not mandate a specific evaluation method.
The Arteris checklist helps companies organize their preparation. In addition, Cycuity, an Arteris brand, offers Radix for hardware security verification, helping developers generate traceable security evidence. It translates security requirements into rules that can be checked in existing simulation and emulation flows. Radix-S checks those rules during simulation, and Radix-M carries them into emulation, allowing system-level analysis.
The software tracks designated assets, such as cryptographic keys and configuration data, through a design to identify flows that violate defined rules. It can also help assess whether Root of Trust features work as intended. Findings help companies locate potential weaknesses, measure security coverage, and identify areas for further testing.
December 11, 2027, marks the next major deadline. The CRA’s broader cybersecurity, conformity assessment, and documentation requirements take effect. CE marking will also be required, which declares that the product conforms to applicable EU requirements.
Before the full requirements take effect, hardware and IP suppliers can work with customers to identify which product versions are intended for the EU market. Early identification gives both sides time to align program schedules and plan necessary work while designs are still in development.
Arteris can help companies make sense of the CRA’s requirements and consider how they apply to hardware and IP products. The EU CRA Hardware Readiness Guide offers a practical starting point, and Arteris teams can help companies work through questions as they prepare.

articles.title: 500 km d’autonomie en 5 minutes : Chery dévoile sa recharge surpuissante pour terrasser BYD
articles.text:
En mars dernier, BYD avait bluffé tout le monde avec le Flash Charging : un 10 à 70 % en 5 minutes et un 10 à 97 % en 9 minutes grâce à une puissance de charge allant jusqu’à 1 500 kW en courant continu DC, c’était tout bonnement révolutionnaire. Depuis, les concurrents ne sont pas restés les bras croisés en déployant peu à peu leurs propres solutions. Ainsi, après la batterie Golden Brick de Geely, c’est au tour de Chery d’apporter une réponse au problème.
Son dispositif nommé « Volt-Dragon » promet une puissance de charge de 1 440 kW en courant continu DC. Si c’est légèrement inférieur à ce que propose BYD, Chery affirme tout de même recouvrir 500 km d’autonomie en seulement 5 minutes. Solide, d’autant plus que la recharge devrait se montrer plus constante que chez BYD, avec un 10 à 97 % de batterie annoncé en 6 minutes et 50 secondes.
CheryMind : quand l’intelligence artificielle pilote la recharge
C’est 2 minutes de moins grâce à l’implémentation de l’intelligence artificielle « CheryMind » dans le processus de recharge. Lors d’une conférence interne sur l’innovation mondiale, le constructeur considère cette innovation comme un « cerveau qui comprend le monde physique ». Celui-ci sera naturellement au cœur des Robotaxis, des systèmes de conduite autonome et de la recharge Volt-Dragon, bien évidemment.
Si la marque n’a pas véritablement précisé le fonctionnement de CheryMind appliquée au Volt-Dragon, elle explique toutefois que son écosystème de recharge Xingrui PowerMind est capable de prédire le comportement thermique pendant la charge en anticipant les variations de température des cellules 30 secondes à l’avance. Le but est d’ajuster continuellement la puissance de recharge maximale en évitant d’abimer les batteries.
Bras robotisés et stations du futur : entre promesses et réalité
Le Volt-Dragon permet donc à Chery de tenir la dragée haute face aux leaders. Seule la batterie Shenxing de troisième génération de CATL fait encore mieux, avec un 10 à 98 % de recharge annoncé en 6 minutes et 27 secondes. On sait alors ce que dira BYD face à ce panier d’annonces : il n’y a encore rien de concret contrairement aux Flash Chargers, déjà existants en Chine et très bientôt en France.
C’est tout à fait vrai. Chery lance des promesses sans encore préciser les véhicules qui seront concernés par la chose. Dans le même genre, la recharge devrait aussi être autonome grâce à des bras robotisés qui viendront automatiquement connecter le câble au véhicule. Chery confirme seulement l’ouverture de 100 stations Volt-Dragon dans 10 villes chinoises d’ici la fin de l’année. Très timide par rapport aux 20 000 Flash Chargers visés par BYD à la même échéance.
