articles.title: Freshworks acquires Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev
articles.text:
Freshworks acquires Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev
Freshworks said that this acquisition will strengthen Freshservice's capabilities, which is Freshworks’ IT service management platform, in incident management and IT operations.
SaaS major Freshworks has acquired Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev, an incident intelligence engine that uses AI to investigate technology disruptions, identify root causes, and recommend remediation actions.
In a company blogpost, Freshworks said that this acquisition will strengthen Freshservice's capabilities, which is Freshworks’ IT service management platform, in incident management and IT operations. It bridges the gap between deep diagnostic intelligence, IT service management, and modern incident orchestration.
Nasdaq-listed Freshworks did not disclose the financial details of the deal.
Founded by Natan Yellin and Arik Alon, Robusta has been heavily optimised for large scale production environments. For many of its customers, even momentary reliability issues can cause a loss of revenue. Yet operating AI Agents at that scale is challenging because of the volume of alerts and the complexity of their systems. Robusta's technology allows customers use frontier intelligence to investigate their alerts, no matter the volume.
"LLMs are fantastic at troubleshooting incidents," said Natan Yellin, co-founder and CEO of Robusta.
"Our technology lets AI Agents do that effectively in large enterprise environments, where there are so many raw events that investigating each one individually would be exorbitant from a token cost perspective. We're incredibly excited to join Freshworks, which gives us the scale and platform to bring that experience to engineering teams everywhere, while keeping humans firmly in control of decisions that touch production."

articles.title: Windows 11 KB5127936 update released with 41 changes and fixes
articles.text:
Microsoft released the KB5127936 preview cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, with 41 changes, including File Explorer and Cloud rebuild improvements.
KB5127936 is a preview update that adds new features and fixes at the end of each month, letting IT admins and users test them before they roll out to the entire user base during next month's Patch Tuesday.
However, unlike regular Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, monthly preview updates are optional and don't include security patches.
The October 2026 preview update makes the File Explorer context menu faster and easier to customize, letting users choose which app extensions and commands appear and how they're organized.
After you install KB5127936, Cloud rebuild can also reinstall Windows without USB media or a custom image, using an image and drivers downloaded directly from Windows Update, even when Windows won't start.
Microsoft also updated XBOX mode to include a refreshed Gaming Task View with quick access to key system actions like Power Options and Exit to Desktop while gaming via a new navigation bar.
You can install the KB5127936 preview update by downloading it from the Microsoft Update Catalog or by opening Settings, going to Windows Update, and selecting "Check for Updates."
Because this is an optional update, you will need to click the "Download and install" link unless you have "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" enabled (which prompts the OS to install it automatically).
Windows 11 KB5127936 highlights
Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2 devices to builds 26200.9818 and 26300.9818, respectively.
The October 2026 preview update adds further changes and improvements, some of the more important ones highlighted below:
- New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page.
- New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. Microsoft disclosed this feature last month, and it is now beginning to roll out.
- New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary clearly shows what was restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions, helps you validate your restore results, and lets you continue setup on your new device with confidence.
- New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide faster Modern Standby instant-on resumes while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation when the battery is above 80% and earlier hibernation below 10%.
This month, Microsoft also reminded users that updated Secure Boot certificates are rolling out to replace the original 2011 certificates, which will expire in late June 2027.
Microsoft first announced plans to refresh expiring Secure Boot certificates on eligible Windows 11 systems in January, after warning users and IT admins in November 2025 to update them before they expire.
The company also warned customers they may need to reboot one more time after installing the October 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next several months.
"With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process."

articles.title: The 5 essential layers of AI agent sandboxing on Kubernetes
articles.text:
The 5 essential layers of AI agent sandboxing on Kubernetes
An AI agent given autonomy to run code will inevitably run code no human has reviewed. It may install model-selected packages, run scripts generated moments earlier, and iterate until a developer’s test passes; that risk is limited to a laptop. For a company, it can extend beyond the agent’s workload to any workload deployed on shared Kubernetes infrastructure. Cluster configurations can limit a container’s system calls, but an allowed call that reaches a kernel vulnerability can still expose the underlying node.
As agents proliferate, this gap has shifted workload isolation from a niche hardening requirement to a baseline need for platforms that run agents. This is a challenge our users at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) have asked us to help solve.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon takes place in Salt Lake City, Utah, from November 9 to 12. Register now.
As expected in the cloud-native space, the community has developed solutions. These solutions exist across five layers: from the pod request, down to the node, and back up to the agent’s session. Platform teams can assemble the stack rather than reinvent it, while native provider support simplifies configuration and maintenance. Managed Kubernetes services offer sandboxed pods this way, but runtimes isolate agentic workloads differently.
The following sections cover the options and tradeoffs before showing how the components fit together.
1. The isolation layer: choosing your risk boundary
First choose between minimal isolation, a restricted kernel interface, and full VM isolation. Each option comes with trade-offs between security and performance.
runc offers the greatest performance through a shared host kernel. Seccomp-based filtering restricts the system calls a process can make.
gVisor suits use cases where a restricted kernel interface is sufficient. Its user-space application kernel handles system calls instead of booting a guest Linux kernel, so the workload reaches the host through a small interface. gVisor implements a subset of Linux, so it starts quickly and packs densely. Applications must work with the interfaces Sentry implements, which can constrain agent behavior.
“A separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents.”
Kata Containers suit use cases requiring full VM isolation. Each pod runs in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, at the cost of a VM boot and guest-kernel memory. Nearly anything that runs in a container runs in Kata. Agents exercise package managers, compilers, nested builds, and headless browsers. For that code, a separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents.
2. The node: assembling it and accounting for it
Worker nodes must be configured for the selected sandboxed runtime.
runc containers use Linux namespaces to separate process, filesystem, and network views, and cgroups to control resource use. They share the host kernel. Nodes need runc configured through a runtime such as containerd, but no guest kernel or hypervisor.
gVisor handles workload system calls in Sentry, while a separate Gofer process mediates access to host-backed files. Each eligible node needs the gVisor runtime installed and integrated with containerd.
Kata Containers place each pod in a lightweight VM. Workload system calls go to the guest Linux kernel, separated from the host by hardware-backed virtualization. This adds overhead and requires bare-metal nodes or VMs that support nested virtualization. In aKernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) setup, nodes need the Kata runtime shim, a supported virtual machine monitor (VMM), KVM and hardware virtualization, plus a guest kernel and image containing the kata-agent. You must maintain that guest image. A kernel CVE means patching two kernels. For use cases requiring flexibility and strict isolation, that burden may be necessary.
3. The access layer: limiting the agent’s reach
A sandbox protects the host from the agent, not from anything it’s handed. Code inside can still delete a writable repository, read a mounted secret, or send data wherever the network allows. Sandbox policy matters as much as the sandbox itself:
- Network: Default-deny egress with a NetworkPolicy, then allow only the destinations a task needs, such as a package mirror or model endpoint.
- Credentials: Issue short-lived credentials scoped to the task, not long-lived tokens mounted into the pod. A leaked credential expires with the task.
- Storage: Mount repositories and data read-only unless the task needs to write, and give writable workspaces their own volume.
- Remote tools: Give API endpoints and MCP servers their own authorization. They run outside the sandbox, so its boundary does not cover them.
4. The request: RuntimeClass
Kubernetes lets users retain the standard Pod API while selected pods, including agents, opt into a more isolated runtime. RuntimeClass lets pods select the security and performance balance they need without taxing non-agentic workloads.
Additional isolation affects resource consumption and pod readiness. gVisor’s Sentry processes and Kata’s guest kernel, kata-agent, and VMM add memory and CPU overhead. Add measured overhead to the RuntimeClass so the Kubernetes scheduler and resource quotas account for it. Measure your workloads rather than copying an example.
Cluster administrators create a RuntimeClass matching the node’s configured runtime. It tells Kubernetes the runtime is available, how pods select it, and what overhead it needs:
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata              # runtime name in the node's containerd config
overhead:
  podFixed:
    memory: "160Mi"        # example value; measure your own
    cpu: "250m"
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    sandbox.example.com/kata: "true"
A pod opts in through the runtimeClassName field of its spec: 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: agent-task
spec:
  runtimeClassName: kata   # or gvisor; omit for the default runc
  containers:
  - name: workspace
    image: python:3.12
Everything else stays the same. Workloads that do not need sandboxing omit the field and use the default runtime. A cluster can expose each runtime as a separate RuntimeClass.
5. The session layer: Agent Sandbox
Agent work comes in bursts. An agent runs code, then waits minutes or hours for the next interaction with a model or human. Keeping a VM running keeps it ready to resume work but consumes capacity. Tearing it down saves capacity but requires rebuilding it later. Warm pools offer a middle ground, but reserve capacity.
“Agent work comes in bursts. An agent runs code, then waits minutes or hours for the next interaction with a model or human.”
The Agent Sandbox project, owned by Kubernetes SIG Apps, standardizes this choice. Its Sandbox API creates stateful single-pod environments with stable identities and persistent storage, plus extensions for templates, claims, and warm pools. It remains runtime-agnostic and leaves isolation to the selected RuntimeClass.
Our approach: building on community projects
Community projects have helped us achieve our goal of letting users run untrusted agent code on shared infrastructure using Kubernetes tools they already know. They keep workloads portable: the same pod spec runs on any conformant cluster. Security fixes and design reviews come from a network larger than any one vendor. And frameworks that integrate with Agent Sandbox do not need a new API. Thanks to the community, users can adopt these new tools without reinventing the wheel.
We are thankful to be a part of this dynamic space and excited to see it evolve.

articles.title: Un joueur sur trois pourrait craquer pour GTA 6, tout simplement du jamais vu pour un jeu vidéo !
articles.text:
GTA 6 n'est pas encore en rayon, et il est déjà entré dans l'histoire. Selon le cabinet Circana, 29 % des joueurs américains sur console et PC comptent acheter le titre de Rockstar Games, un niveau jamais mesuré pour un jeu vidéo.
À quelques semaines de sa sortie officielle, prévue le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, GTA 6 décroche un record d'intention d'achat aux États-Unis. Après treize ans d'attente, un GTA V qui n'a jamais quitté les classements après avoir lui-même battu des records à son époque notamment en France, et des précommandes qui se comptent en millions, il faut vivre sur Mars, pour qui s'intéresse même de loin aux jeux vidéo, pour ne pas voir l'engouement. Le jeu de Rockstar s'annonce ainsi comme l'une des plus grosses sorties de l'histoire du divertissement, et comme un moteur des ventes de consoles pour les fêtes, selon une étude publiée ce 28 octobre par le cabinet américain Circana.
Un niveau d'attente record pour GTA 6
Le cabinet d'études Circana fournit des données de marché aux fabricants et aux distributeurs. Son outil PlayerPulse suit notamment l'intention d’achat des joueurs américains sur console et sur PC, c'est-à-dire la part d'entre eux qui déclarent vouloir acheter un jeu donné. Pour GTA 6, elle atteint 29 %, soit près d’un joueur sur trois. Jamais un jeu vidéo n'avait obtenu un tel score dans les relevés du cabinet. Mat Piscatella, son analyste spécialiste du jeu vidéo, parle d'un moment rare pour l'industrie, aussi culturel que commercial.
Cet appétit doit aussi beaucoup à GTA V. Le jeu reste le titre premium le plus vendu de l'historique américain de Circana, en nombre d'exemplaires, comme en dollars. Il a figuré dans le top 20 des ventes américaines chaque année, sans exception, de 2013 à 2025. L'an dernier, pour sa treizième année sur le marché, il était encore troisième en nombre de joueurs actifs sur PlayStation et Xbox. Peu d'œuvres de divertissement gardent leur public aussi longtemps.
En France, GTA 5 s'est vendu à plus de 6 millions d'exemplaires, s'imposant comme un succès historique et l'un des produits culturels les plus rentables du pays grâce à sa longévité exceptionnelle sur trois générations de consoles. Sa première semaine de lancement avait permis à Rockstar Games de vendre 1,1 million de jeux dans l'Hexagone, un record à l'époque, avec une présence dans le top 10 des meilleures ventes annuelles quasiment chaque année dans le pays.
GTA 6 va profiter à tout l'écosystème du jeu vidéo
Pour Mat Piscatella, l’effet GTA 6 ira bien au-delà des ventes du jeu. Aux États-Unis et ailleurs, comme en France, sa sortie tombe juste avant le Black Friday, fin novembre, et les enseignes se préparent déjà à une forte demande pour les fêtes. L’analyste prévoit donc une hausse des ventes de consoles, mais aussi d’accessoires (manettes, casques…) et d’abonnements liés au jeu vidéo.
GTA 6 ne tournera que sur les consoles actuelles, la PS5 et la Xbox Series. Les joueurs encore équipés d’une PS4 ou d’une Xbox One devront changer de machine pour y jouer, et beaucoup pourraient en profiter pour s’offrir une PS5. Selon lui, cet engouement montre aussi le poids croissant du jeu vidéo dans le divertissement et la tech grand public.
On retrouve d'ailleurs cette impatience dans les précommandes. D’après Sensor Tower, qui suit les ventes sur les boutiques en ligne de Sony et de Microsoft, GTA 6 cumule 6,45 millions de précommandes numériques dans le monde, dont 74 % sur PS5. Et ce score est atteint malgré un prix élevé on rappelle 79,99 euros pour l’édition standard, et 99,99 euros pour l’Ultime, plus riche en bonus. Les amateurs de support physique devront aussi s’adapter, car la boîte vendue en magasin ne contient qu’un code de téléchargement, sans disque.
Dans tous les cas, mieux vaut prévoir de la place sur sa machine, puisqu'une fuite, que Rockstar n’a pas confirmée, évoque 210 Go d'espace nécessaire sur PS5. Les versions numériques pourront être préchargées dès le 12 novembre, pour jouer dès le jour de la sortie. Une intention d’achat ne garantit pas une vente, mais tous les indicateurs pointent dans la même direction.

articles.title: Microsoft venderá bonos por al menos USD 25.000 millones para financiar la IA, algo que no hacía desde 2017
articles.text:
Microsoft, la empresa dirigida por Satya Nadella, salió a vender bonos en Estados Unidos por al menos USD 25.000 millones, su primera emisión de deuda de alta calificación en el país en más de nueve años, según Bloomberg. El dinero ayudará a costear la expansión de la infraestructura de inteligencia artificial (IA) de la empresa.
La operación se divide en hasta 10 tramos, con vencimientos de entre dos y 40 años. El tamaño definitivo no está decidido y dependerá de la demanda de los inversores. Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase y UBS organizan la colocación.
Según portales como Investing.com, que cita los términos de la oferta, la emisión incluye dos bonos de tasa variable y ocho de tasa fija. Los de dos años se ofrecían con un sobrecosto de entre 0,50 y 0,55 puntos porcentuales sobre los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense. Los de 40 años, con vencimiento en el año 2066, de entre 1,30 y 1,35 puntos.
Los fondos se destinarán a fines corporativos generales, entre ellos inversiones de capital, capital de trabajo, recompra de acciones, adquisiciones y pago de deuda existente. La liquidación está prevista para el 4 de noviembre.
Por qué es raro que Microsoft siga esta estrategia
La última emisión de Microsoft en el país fue en 2017, cuando recaudó USD 17.000 millones, según datos de Bloomberg. The Next Web precisa que esa operación, de enero de ese año, sirvió en parte para financiar la compra de LinkedIn.
Microsoft es una de las dos únicas empresas estadounidenses que cotizan en bolsa con calificación AAA, la máxima, de Moody’s y S&P Global Ratings. La otra es Johnson & Johnson. Esa nota le permite endeudarse en condiciones favorables.
Asimismo, la compañía había financiado su operación sobre todo con la caja que genera su negocio. Ahora el gasto en infraestructura cambia esa ecuación: un día antes de la venta de bonos, Microsoft dijo que invirtió USD 45.200 millones en centros de datos y equipos, incluidos arrendamientos, en los tres meses hasta septiembre.
En el mismo período, el flujo de caja libre cayó 27%, hasta USD 18.600 millones, según la información de resultados recogida por The Next Web. Los ingresos de Azure, su servicio de computación en la nube, subieron 48%, hasta USD 33.200 millones, y la empresa proyecta un crecimiento de entre 49% y 50% para el trimestre en curso.
“Todavía tenemos una demanda que supera la oferta”, dijo la directora financiera, Amy Hood, a los analistas.
Cómo las grandes tecnológicas se endeudan para la IA
Bloomberg señala que la oferta es la primera de un gigante tecnológico de primer nivel desde que Alphabet destinó USD 25.000 millones en deuda el 6 de agosto. Según la agencia, la operación será una prueba del interés de los inversores por financiar la inversión en IA, en medio de dudas sobre la sostenibilidad del gasto del sector.
The Next Web recuerda que Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft y Oracle han duplicado su deuda combinada en cinco años, hasta unos USD 350.000 millones, según datos de Bloomberg citados por el medio en julio. Alphabet dijo que planea emitir deuda en Estados Unidos dos veces al año.
No todas las emisiones tuvieron buena recepción. La venta de bonos de Amazon por USD 25.000 millones a comienzos de este año tuvo una respuesta tibia entre los inversores, y S&P rebajó la calificación de Oracle a un escalón por encima del nivel especulativo, según el mismo medio.
La emisión de Microsoft quedará liquidada el 4 de noviembre, de acuerdo con los términos citados por Investing.com. Hasta entonces, el monto final y las condiciones de cada tramo pueden cambiar según la demanda.

articles.title: Interswitch wants Nigerians to trust tap-to-pay
articles.text:
Interswitch, a Nigerian payments technology company, says consumer education is the biggest hurdle to making tap-to-pay a mainstream payment method in Nigeria, even as banks and merchants prepare to support it. Speaking at Moonshot 2026 in Lagos on Thursday, Tomi Ogunlesi, divisional head of brands, communication, content and CSR at Interswitch, said the industry must convince consumers that tapping their cards or phones to pay is secure and convenient.
“The banks are ready,” Ogunlesi said. “Where more of the work needs to be done now, from our perspective as an industry, is on the merchant side and on the consumer side, but most on the consumer side.”
His comments come after Mastercard and Interswitch announced the launch of Google Pay in Nigeria, allowing eligible Mastercard holders to add their cards to Google Wallet and pay with compatible Android phones at contactless-enabled terminals. Interswitch’ said that it was working with five Nigerian banks, including GTBank, Wema Bank, ProvidusUnity Bank, Zenith Bank, and FirstBank, to expand tokenised tap-to-pay transactions. The company said it is also working to bring more merchants into the network, including supermarket chain, Spar, had shown interest.
Contactless payments are not new to Nigeria. In 2015, Unified Payments launched PayAttitude, an NFC-based payment service, with several Nigerian banks. It used a chip-enabled tag attached to a mobile phone or another surface to make payments at compatible terminals.
A decade later, Access Bank partnered with Visa in March 2025 to launch Tap to Phone, which turns an NFC-enabled Android smartphone into a payment terminal for merchants accepting contactless card payments. In October, CashAfrica, a Nigerian contactless payments infrastructure startup, also partnered with Chicken Republic to bring mobile tap-to-pay to more than 350 outlets.
Despite these attempts, tap-to-pay has yet to become a mainstream payment method in Nigeria. Infrastructure gaps and limited consumer awareness have made it difficult for contactless payments to gain widespread adoption. Interswitch has now taken up the challenge to persuade consumers to use the technology.
Ogunlesi said Interswitch had anticipated the shift towards tokenised payments by making most of the cards it issued over the past two to three years compatible with the technology. However, he acknowledged that the simplicity of tap-to-pay could itself make some Nigerians suspicious. Ogunlesi said consumer education must explain how tokenisation protects payment details.
“At its core, tokenisation means your card details have gone through a process where the token that is replacing your card number in a tap-to-pay transaction is not your card number,” he said. “It’s more like a one-time token that is being used to mask your card number.”
Interswitch plans to support sensitisation efforts with a 15-minute documentary titled ‘Are You Tapping?,‘ which explores the evolution of payments in Nigeria and explains why tokenisation matters.
In a separate conversation at Moonshot, Ogunlesi said Nigeria embraced card payments earlier than some other African markets, where mobile money services helped drive the growth of digital payments. He pointed to Interswitch’s experience in 2009, when the Central Bank of Nigeria ordered the shutdown of magnetic-stripe cards amid fraud concerns. It forced the industry to transition towards EMV chip cards, creating an opportunity for Verve, Interswitch’s domestic card scheme.
He also argued that cards retain an advantage in areas such as international commerce and dispute resolution, where established card networks have developed processes for handling failed transactions and recovering funds. Bank transfers may work well for domestic payments, but resolving disputes involving cross-border transactions can be more complicated. He expects the physical form of cards to change as payments become digital, but believes the underlying infrastructure will remain important.
“Cards are what everybody is trying to disrupt,” he said. “But the interesting thing is that even the things that are going to disrupt cards run with the DNA of cards.”
Ogunlesi identified card rails, non-card rails such as instant bank transfers, and digital-asset rails as three broad areas of payment infrastructure that could support faster or cheaper cross-border transfers. He said Interswitch was exploring how digital-asset infrastructure could be developed in ways that are trusted and compatible with regulatory requirements. However, the company’s immediate priority is getting more Nigerians comfortable with tapping to pay.

articles.title: Paula, española trabajando en Holanda: “Puedo decir que ahorro entre 800 y 1.100 euros todos los meses”
articles.text:
Paula, una ciudadana española que lleva cerca de dos años viviendo en Holanda, ahorra “entre 800 el mes que menos gano y 1.000 o 1.100 el mes que más gano”, pagando un alquiler de unos 2.000 euros al mes, agua y electricidad incluidos, de los que su parte es de 1.000 euros. “Sí que es verdad que es caro”, admite; la dificultad para encontrar alojamiento se debe a que, en sus palabras, “La demanda aquí en Holanda es muy grande y hay muy poca oferta”, lo que hace que los precios estén, a su juicio, “un poco desorbitados”.
El seguro es obligatorio en el país de residencia y de trabajo y cuesta 142 euros al mes; se le abonan unos 129 euros del Estado, por lo que, según sus cálculos, los gastos personales de Paula ascienden a unos 11 o 12 euros al mes: la ayuda se determina en función de los ingresos de cada persona.
Su otro gasto regular es el gimnasio, con 38 euros, y la línea telefónica con datos ilimitados a cambio de una promoción para menores de 30 años, con 25 euros. Paula y su novio (con quien comparte vivienda) tienen una cuenta conjunta en la que ingresan 150 euros cada uno para la compra, pero su gasto medio en comida (tanto de ella como del novio) es de 300-350 euros al mes.
Se desplazan en un coche compartido que funciona con gas, pero consume gasolina, un gasto de 80 euros al mes, de los que se le reembolsa parte a Paula por kilómetros recorridos por su empresa. También destina entre 300 y 350 euros al mes al ocio, a lo que suma suscripciones como Netflix, Prime o Spotify. Le sobra algo de dinero, concretamente lo que no gasta de su cuenta bancaria, y ahorra 180-190 euros al mes en una cuenta de inversión. En el mejor de los casos, Paula puede ahorrar unos 1.200 euros al mes con estos dos tipos de cuenta.
Aunque Paula no menciona sus ingresos (lo que dificulta el cálculo de ahorro en función de los gastos), la suma del alquiler (1.000 euros para Paula), el seguro (11 o 12 euros, una vez descontada la ayuda), el gimnasio (38 euros), el móvil (25 euros), la mitad de los gastos de comida (150 euros; aunque más bien la mitad de 300-350 euros, ya que ella y su novio gastan esa cantidad entre los dos), la gasolina (80 euros, de los que su empresa se encarga de parte) y el ocio (300-350 euros) asciende a entre 1.600 y 1.700 euros al mes (si los 80 euros de combustible son solo los de Paula) o más (si se incluyen los de su novio). Sin duda, ahorra según sus posibilidades, restándole la suma mencionada anteriormente a su salario.
Cómo funciona la ayuda sanitaria
La prestación social parece ser la zorgtoeslag y, según la Agencia de Impuestos de los Países Bajos (Belastingdienst), en 2026 se puede acceder a ella con un ingreso anual de hasta 40.857 euros para una persona sin pareja a efectos de la prestación, y de hasta 51.142 euros entre los dos para una pareja a efectos de la prestación. El patrimonio del beneficiario a 1 de enero también está sujeto a un máximo, y asciende a 146.011 euros en el primer caso y a 184.633 euros en el segundo.
Sus pagos se reducen a medida que aumentan los ingresos. Por ejemplo, con un ingreso computable de hasta 29.500 euros en el caso de una única persona, o conjunto en el caso de dos personas, durante el año 2026, según la tabla oficial, la prestación asciende a 129 euros al mes, y a 246 euros al mes para dos personas (no 129 euros por persona). La cantidad de la prestación no depende de la prima del seguro.
Según la información facilitada por Paula, a ella se le reconoce una subvención de unos 129 euros al mes; no especifica si el Gobierno considera que ella y su novio forman parte o no de una unidad familiar a efectos del cálculo de la ayuda.
El procedimiento de solicitud es único, a través de internet y con el DigiD (identificación oficial neerlandesa); una vez concedida, se sigue cobrando cada año siempre que se cumplan las condiciones. Para ello, hay que cumplir los requisitos, entre los que se incluyen la contratación de un seguro de asistencia sanitaria básico en los Países Bajos y disponer de la nacionalidad neerlandesa o de un permiso de residencia otorgado por el Gobierno neerlandés; Paula, ciudadana española, dice que la recibe; la página web del Gobierno neerlandés no especifica cómo se concede a los ciudadanos de la UE.
Lo que no entra en sus cuentas
En las cuentas de Paula no figuran dos cuestiones más: en primer lugar, el plazo para contratar el seguro básico en caso de trabajar para un empleador neerlandés y pagar allí el impuesto sobre el salario (lo cual no se menciona expresamente), que es de cuatro meses; quien espera demasiado se arriesga a una multa, y mientras no se asegure, la atención corre por su cuenta.
También hay que tener en cuenta la franquicia que los asegurados deben sufragar antes de que el seguro cubra la atención; se trata de un pago estándar de 385 euros (en 2026) por persona de 18 años o más. Quedan fuera de la franquicia, entre otras cosas, las visitas al médico de cabecera y la enfermería a domicilio.
El coste de una vivienda en alquiler es de media un 4,4 % más alto en julio de 2026 que un año antes, con un aumento del 4,5 % en la vivienda libre y del 3,8 % en los contratos existentes sin cambio de inquilino (según el CBS, la Oficina de Estadística de Holanda). Se trata de un porcentaje inferior al registrado en este tipo de operaciones en los años anteriores: 4,9 % en 2025 y un 5,4 % en 2024.
Para situar este aumento porcentual en perspectiva, el Observatorio de Emancipación del Consejo de la Juventud de España, basándose en datos de mediados de 2024, indica que el alquiler mediano de una vivienda libre era de 1.072 euros al mes, lo que suponía el 102,3 % del salario mediano neto de una persona joven asalariada que quisiera vivir sola.
El artículo de Genbeta relacionado con esto incluía la información sobre la evolución de los sueldos frente al alquiler para los representantes de la Generación Z.
La última actualización de la información sobre el seguro y la ayuda sanitaria neerlandesa tuvo lugar el 15 de septiembre de 2026 con la publicación de los presupuestos de los Países Bajos para 2027.
Por el momento, el Gobierno neerlandés prevé que la prima media aumente en 12,50 euros, hasta situarse en 169 euros al mes en 2027; el importe máximo de la ayuda para el seguro en el caso de una persona sin pareja a efectos de la ayuda será de 140 euros, y la franquicia ascenderá a 400 euros; es decir, habrá una subida de 11 euros en la ayuda máxima frente a un aumento de 12,50 euros en la prima media del seguro; los costes individuales dependerán de la aseguradora en cada caso concreto, por lo que la situación de Paula en 2027 estará sujeta a los cambios.

articles.title: “Les gens peuvent ramasser le caca” : du gameplay de GTA 6 fait une apparition dans le dernier épisode de South Park
articles.text:
“Les gens peuvent ramasser le caca” : du gameplay de GTA 6 fait une apparition dans le dernier épisode de South Park
Dans un passage typique de son ton irrévérentieux, le dernier épisode de la série South Park montre une courte séquence de gameplay inédit de GTA 6.
Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto 6
Alors que la petite ville de South Park est devenue South America depuis le début de la saison 29, le show increvable de Comedy Central (disponible sur Canal+ en France avec un décalage de quelques jours) surfe également sur la vague GTA 6. Il faut dire qu'utiliser des éléments de l'actualité récente est devenu la spécialité de la série animée pour adultes depuis plusieurs saisons. Mais cette fois, au-delà de faire une énième référence au jeu de Rockstar et à comment il va sauver l'Amérique, une séquence de gameplay inédite a été montrée dans South Park.
"Les graphismes sont sérieusement de nouvelle génération"
Dans l'épisode 4 de la saison 29, baptisé Guinea Pig on a Stick, une femme montre une vidéo de quelques secondes à la bande, notamment composée de Cartman, Kyle, Stan ou encore Randy. Il est question d'y voir une séquence de gameplay de quelques secondes sur une plage, où un PNJ ramasse les excréments de son chien. Arrive ensuite Jason, l'un des deux personnages jouables, qui commence à se battre avec ce PNJ, avant de ramasser et de lui écraser les excréments au visage.
Here’s the FULL GTA 6 gameplay footage exclusively shown in the latest South Park episode in HD. pic.twitter.com/aMBXWtnKE3
— GTA 6 Info (@GTASixInfo) October 29, 2026
Alors que Rockstar a toujours été dans la retenue concernant le fait de montrer du gameplay de GTA 6, sa participation visiblement volontaire à cet épisode de South Park est assez étonnante. Le développeur est bel et bien crédité en fin d'épisode, mais il n'a visiblement pas de problème à être ainsi moqué pour sa volonté peut-être un peu absurde de réalisme.
Malgré le ton moqueur, il s'agit cependant d'un bon coup de pub pour le jeu, s'il en avait seulement besoin. Les personnages de la série sont en tout cas épatés par ces "graphismes de nouvelle génération" comme le dit la femme, incitant probablement les spectateurs à l'être aussi. Après avoir dévoilé le trailer principal de GTA 6 en exclusivité sur Netflix, Rockstar semble bien décidé à faire sa promotion autrement.
Pour South Park, ce n'est pas la première fois qu'un jeu vidéo est central dans son intrigue. Par le passé, World of Warcraft a notamment été utilisé à plusieurs reprises, de même que Red Dead Redemption 2, déjà chez Rockstar. Ne manque aujourd'hui plus qu'un jeu vidéo South Park inspiré de GTA pour boucler la boucle.

articles.title: ASRock Industrial AI Box-A395 Review: Taking Strix Halo to Work
articles.text:
When AMD first announced its high-end Ryzen AI Max (Ryzen Halo) chips at the start of last year, the company aimed to use them across a wide range of computing markets, including laptops and desktop PCs. The product ecosystem built around AMD’s powerful integrated chips has turned out far wilder than the company expected, largely because demand for local AI inference systems has exploded. We have not seen as many laptops, but the desktop mini-PC space with these has grown like crazy since these make great local AI boxes to run agents and models in an always-on fashion.
As a result, when one of AMD’s partners does something with the Ryzen AI Max that isn’t just a small black box, it can turn some heads. That is exactly what we are seeing today with the latest Ryzen AI Max+ 395 mini-PC to cross our labs, this time coming from ASRock Industrial. The Taiwanese vendor’s industrial arm, ASRock Industrial, has a reputation for building no-nonsense machines with a few extra features for the industrial market. This gives us a chance to see what they think a no-nonsense Ryzen AI Max box should look like.
| ASRock Industrial AI Box-A395 Key Specs (As Configured) |  | 
| Processors | AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 16C/32T (5.1GHz) | 
| Operating System | None: Barebones (As Tested: Ubuntu Linux 26.04) | 
| Memory | 128GB LPDDR5X-8000, Soldered | 
| Drive Bays | 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Empty) 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Empty) | 
| GPU | Radeon 8060S Graphics (40 CUs) | 
| PSU | 400W Internal PSU | 
| Form Factor | Small Tower PC | 
| Dimensions | 200 x 100 x 232 mm (7.87 x 3.94 x 9.13 in) | 
| Weight | 2.8kg (6.2 lbs) | 
| Wireless | Wi-Fi 7 (2×2) + Bluetooth 5.4 (MT7925) | 
| Color | Aluminum | 
| Ports | Top: 2x USB-A 480Mbps Rear: 2x USB-C 40Gbps, 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 2x USB-A 10Gbps, 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x 10GbE (RJ45, AQC113), 1x 2.5GbE LAN (RJ45, RTL8125BG), 1x 3.5mm Line-Out, 1x 3.5mm Mic-In | 
Officially, ASRock Industrial promotes the barebones AI BOX-A395 as an AI workstation PC. While it can certainly be used as one, as we will see when we talk about its build and configuration, that marketing spin is probably a bit too optimistic. Instead, the AI BOX-A395 is best framed as a portable Ryzen AI Max system for industrial environments. It is a Ryzen mini-PC meant for on-the-go use or environments where it can run on its own without babysitting.
If you wanted to find the ASRock Industrial AI Box-A395 online, here is a Newegg affiliate link.
ASRock Industrial AI Box-A395 External Hardware Overview
Starting with a look at ASRock Industrial’s Ryzen AI Max+ 395 mini-PC from the outside, you will immediately notice this is not the usual low-profile, wide-and-low mini-PC design. Instead, ASRock has opted for a more micro-tower style configuration, with the system’s motherboard sitting vertically. This makes it very space-efficient in terms of 2D floor space.
The other thing you will notice is the system’s aluminum body. There is also a large collection of vent holes on the left side of the system. Now install the optional carrying handle along the top side of the system, and it bears more than a passing resemblance to Apple’s 2003 Power Mac G5, otherwise (lovingly) known as the cheese grater. Between the unpainted metallic case and the small vertical vent holes, you cannot escape the comparison. If nothing else, it is a very distinctive design in a market flooded with a mix of colorful gaming-adjacent designs or minimalistic corporate designs. The one design that we looked at which is roughly a similar size and orientation is the Framework desktop, which we went over a bit in the video.
Even with this tower design, ASRock Industrial has taken the interesting route of not bothering to use the system’s front at all. Not for I/O ports or cooling. The only thing on the front is the company’s logo. Once we take a look at the internals, the whys of this will become a bit clearer, but for now it serves to underscore how this is not a traditional mini-PC in terms of design, cooling, or how it is meant to be used.
So if there are no I/O ports or buttons on the front of the system, where are they? As it turns out, it is all on top. In front of another large collection of vent holes (and mounting points for the handle), ASRock Industrial placed the system’s power button and a pair of USB-A ports at the top, as far forward as possible.
The USB ports here are one of a few different surprises with this mini-PC. The black ports are not (just) a design choice. These are not SuperSpeed USB 3.x ports. Instead, these are classic 480Mbps USB 2.x ports. As the only two ports not on the rear of the system, this means there are no high-speed I/O ports on the front. This system assumes you will plug in basic peripherals at the top, and that is it. This is one of a few reasons why, despite ASRock Industrial’s “workstation” marketing, this is much closer to the kind of industrial PC design the group is better known for.
Moving on, if we stand the system up again and rotate it slightly to the left, we can see the right side. Like the front face, this side is blank. There are no vent holes or other notable features. Some screws hold the panel on and let you remove it to access the back side of the motherboard.
For the rest of the story on the A395’s chassis, we need to turn to the rear side of the system, which immediately illustrates just what kind of a system we are looking at.
Right off the bat, we see the familiar rim of an ATX I/O shield. The A395 is sold as a barebones PC, and it certainly lives up to those expectations. ASRock has not designed a highly custom case just to fit the Ryzen AI Max+ processor, but instead we are looking at AMD’s high-end AI chip placed inside of a standing mini-ITX form factor case. An integrated power supply, no less.
Looking at the port configuration of the system, to the right of the obligatory mic-in/line-out 3.5mm audio ports, we have a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports driven by the Ryzen AI Max+ 395’s integrated Radeon 8060S iGPU. That iGPU can drive up to two HDMI-style ports, and many PC vendors have opted to implement both, including ASRock Industrial.
If you need a DisplayPort-type output, ASRock Industrial also covers this via DP Alt Mode. There are three USB-C ports on the system, and all of them can be used for display outputs, taking advantage of the chip’s ability to drive up to four monitors at once.
Otherwise, we are looking at a mix of USB 3 and USB4 ports. The left-most USB-C port is a 10Gbps USB 3.x port, while the right two USB-C ports are the two blazing 40Gbps USB-C ports that the Strix Halo silicon natively supports. These are likely to be the last ports you use for display outputs unless necessary, as doing so will eat up one (or both) of the system’s fastest USB I/O ports.
For older peripherals and drives, ASRock Industrial also added a pair of USB-A ports on the rear of this system. Both of these are 10Gbps ports, using the industry-standard cyan coloring. And while ASRock Industrial did not use the USB-IF’s official logos here, the fact that they have otherwise clearly labeled the performance and capabilities of each USB port is greatly appreciated as it is something that other vendors have struggled with.
As for non-USB I/O, ASRock Industrial has equipped the A395 with a pair of Ethernet ports. First up, we have a 10GbE port with an RJ45 jack, driven by Marvell’s nearly ubiquitous AQC113 controller. For the price and performance capabilities of Ryzen AI Max+ 395 systems, 10Gb Ethernet ports have been rarer than we would like to see. So it is good to see that one is included here.
To the right of that is the second Ethernet port, a 2.5GbE port driven by Realtek’s RTL8125BG controller. Some Strix Halo systems ship with two 10GbE ports. We have also seen many, including the previously mentioned Framework Desktop, ship with only a single 5GbE or 2.5GbE port. Having 10Gb + 2.5GbE is a solid compromise here. Besides labeling each port with its max speed, ASRock has also used blue plastic with the 2.5GbE port to further distinguish the system’s two Ethernet jacks.
Meanwhile, if you instead need wireless networking, ASRock Industrial has that covered as well. The metal case makes internal antennas impractical, so the company added a pair of antenna connectors on the rear of the system that lead back to the Wi-Fi 7 radio. The antennas are included, of course.
Meanwhile, here is a quick look at the system’s internal power supply from the outside. With the extra volume afforded by the standing system, and to keep it portable, ASRock Industrial opted for an internal power supply. So there is no need to haul around an external power brick here. The A395 can be powered with any standard C13 power cable. Assuming the system will run in headless mode (common for industrial PCs), this makes the A395 entirely self-contained.
Finally, we will take a quick look at the bottom of the system. Although it lacks ventilation on its right side, the A395 is designed to be operated in a standing position, and the case design reinforces this. The included rubber feet keep the system elevated to keep the power supply intake clear and avoid scratching any surfaces. This is also where ASRock Industrial has placed the required stickers, including the model info, serial number, HDMI logo, and regulatory information.
Now that we have taken a look at the outside of the AI Box-A395, let us dig into the guts of the system.

articles.title: Medio Ambiente autoriza a Amazon a gastar un 48 % más de agua en su centro de datos de El Burgo de Ebro (Zaragoza)
articles.text:
El Instituto Aragonés de Gestión Ambiental (Inaga) ha autorizado a Amazon Web Services a aumentar un 48 % la dotación de agua de su centro de datos de El Burgo de Ebro. Según El Periódico de Aragón, el organismo no aprecia efectos significativos sobre el medio ambiente (aunque sospechamos que muchos agricultores no estarán de acuerdo) y da por hecho que la misma medida se extenderá a los complejos de Villanueva de Gállego y Huesca, para los que la compañía pidió lo mismo. La resolución se publicará en el Boletín Oficial de Aragón en los próximos días.
Cómo hemos llegado hasta aquí. Empecemos con un resumen breve:
- 2022: entran en servicio los primeros centros de AWS en Aragón.
- 2023: el Gobierno aragonés modifica el PIGA para ampliar su capacidad energética.
- Finales de 2024: AWS pide modificar su evaluación ambiental simplificada.
- Enero de 2026: Ecologistas en Acción anuncia un contencioso contra el PIGA.
- Finales de agosto: el Gobierno central presenta un borrador de decreto más exigente.
- 15 de septiembre: nueva restricción de riego en el Gállego.
- 2 de octubre: Heraldo revela que AWS paga el IAE en Madrid.
- 8 de octubre: AWS anuncia que pagará el impuesto en los municipios.
- 26 y 27 de octubre: el Gobierno suaviza el decreto.
Qué ha resuelto ahora. El proyecto no tendrá que pasar por una evaluación de impacto ambiental ordinaria. Eso no significa vía libre sin más: AWS deberá modificar su autorización ambiental integrada y aportar información detallada sobre consumos previstos, caudales de abastecimiento, volúmenes de aguas residuales, sistemas de tratamiento y capacidad de los depósitos. También tendrá que cumplir la normativa contra la legionelosis y de protección contra incendios, aplicar un plan de vigilancia ambiental con seguimiento continuo y restaurar el terreno cuando se desmantele la instalación.
Por qué piden más agua. AWS solicitó el cambio a finales de 2024. El diseño original calculaba 555 horas al año de uso de agua para refrigeración. La memoria, elaborada por la consultora Tauw Iberia, dispara esa cifra a 900 horas. La empresa sostiene que, tras dos años de funcionamiento, los valores aprobados no reflejan con exactitud las últimas condiciones climáticas del emplazamiento. A cambio, ha retrasado el umbral al que el sistema pasa del free cooling a la refrigeración con agua, de 28,3 a 29,4 ºC, lo que, según el documento, reduce el uso.
El número que importa. Los 53.961 m³ no son lo que gastará AWS en la zona. Con la ampliación de la región de datos, el agregado máximo asciende a 917.603 m³ al año, es decir, 0,92 hectómetros cúbicos. Para ponerlo en contexto, el diario recuerda que las papeleras de la Ribera Baja superan los 20 hectómetros cúbicos.
AWS añade que el centro de El Burgo de Ebro toma agua del Canal Imperial de Aragón y que su demanda actual, de 36.662 m³, supone el 0,009 % del total. Esa cifra queda 201 m³ por encima del tope anterior (y el texto no explica por qué). Un estudio ambiental previo hablaba de unos 755.000 m³ para las nuevas instalaciones, y Ecologistas en Acción ya avisaba de que sería difícil comprobar cuánta agua se extrae.
Las medidas de AWS. La compañía ha fusionado dos plantas de tratamiento previstas en una sola, con nanofiltración, que debería recuperar cerca del 70 % del agua, y ampliará el almacenamiento in situ hasta 72 horas. Aparte, el diario enumera dos proyectos relacionados: tres tanques de tormentas en los nuevos centros y la financiación de 25 kilómetros de renovación del Canal Imperial para evitar fugas. Las cifras de ahorro de AWS, más de 10.000 millones de litros al año en 2030, son de la propia empresa.
Las alegaciones. Ecologistas en Acción y Tu Nube Seca Mi Río argumentaron que el cambio climático ya debía estar en la solicitud original. Recordaron además que una investigación de El País estimó que el centro de Huesca consumió casi el doble de lo concedido. Piden controles independientes, porque la regulación no obliga a las empresas a informar de lo que gastan. AWS defiende que necesita margen para años anómalos como 2022, y asegura que sus centros solo usan agua por encima de los 30 grados.
Regantes contra la nube. El 15 de septiembre, la acequia de Camarera, en la cuenca del Gállego, vio recortada su concesión al 35 %. Era la segunda restricción del verano, tras el 60 % de agosto, y afectaba a unas 4.500 hectáreas. El colectivo No es sequía, es saqueo lo vincula con los proyectos de Villanueva de Gállego, Villamayor y La Puebla de Alfindén, y sostiene que los centros conectados a redes urbanas tienen prioridad legal sobre el riego.
El de El Burgo de Ebro no está en esa zona, pero bebe del Canal Imperial, una infraestructura de regadío cuya comunidad de usuarios colabora con AWS en el proyecto de modernización. En Teruel, la comunidad de regantes de Gaén mantiene bloqueadas las negociaciones sobre ceder agua del Ebro.
¿Y la respuesta? Ese mismo 15 de septiembre, Jorge Azcón defendió en un foro organizado por AWS que la industria del dato aporta más agua de la que consume. Los críticos contestan que ahorrar en el campo no elimina el consumo del centro.
Impuestos y calle. Cuando se supo lo del IAE, el alcalde de El Burgo de Ebro, Vicente Royo, habló de algo “lamentable y vergonzoso”. Después hubo manifestaciones y marchas. Ya había precedentes: en Cuarte, los vecinos lograron que Amazon desviara una línea de alta tensión, y en Walqa (Huesca) rechazaron un centro en la primera consulta vecinal de Aragón. AWS prometió pagar el IAE en los municipios y abonar cuatro años de atrasos, sin dar cifras. Según la prensa aragonesa, también saldó 194.000 euros de IBI pendientes en El Burgo de Ebro.
Un decreto más blando. El borrador de agosto aplicaba las normas a partir de 1 MW. Según Reuters, el umbral sube ahora a 10 MW, con el 80 % de suministro renovable y un régimen transitorio de hasta cinco años. El Gobierno de Aragón había presentado cinco alegaciones al texto. Los colectivos del agua señalan que fija parámetros de eficiencia, pero no límites al consumo en sequía.
Lo que está en juego. AWS calcula una inversión global de 33.700 millones de euros hasta 2035. Los centros emplean a pocos trabajadores directos y, a pleno rendimiento, consumirían más electricidad que toda la comunidad. Las preguntas abiertas son tres: quién mide cuánta agua usa cada centro, qué prioridad tendrá el regadío en una restricción y qué dirá la justicia sobre el PIGA.
En la misma cuenca del Ebro, el embalse riojano de Mansilla, que sirve a riego y energía, tiene expuestas ahora calles enteras de su antiguo pueblo sumergido. Esa es la imagen de un otoño seco, el mismo en el que Aragón ha permitido ampliar el agua de un centro de datos. Al menos podremos preguntarle a Alexa qué tiempo hará mañana.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Freiburg’s VUSE XR raises €1.2 million to bring AI-powered mixed reality training to enterprises | EU-Startups
articles.text:
VUSE XR, a Freiburg-based startup developing enterprise software for mixed reality training, today announced the closing of a €1.2 million pre-Seed financing round.
The round was led by IACD, a Düsseldorf-based business angel network, with additional participation from individual business angels.
“From an investor’s perspective, VUSE XR brings together everything we look for at this stage: an exceptional team, defensible AI-driven technology, and strong commercial traction. The company has demonstrated its ability to turn a technically demanding product into a scalable software business with considerable growth potential, further accelerated by continuous AI-powered feature enrichment,” said Markus Roithmeier, IACD member and Chairman of the VUSE XR Advisory Board.
Founded in November 2023 by cousins Niclas Matthias and Dr. Paul Matthias, VUSE XR develops the VUSE XR Hub, an enterprise software platform that enables industrial and life sciences companies to create, manage and deploy immersive mixed reality training for complex products and processes.
While mixed reality hardware has matured rapidly, producing the training content to run on it has remained expensive and difficult to scale; VUSE XR is addressing this problem. The startup replaces the traditional model of costly, agency-led custom mixed reality projects with a standardised, AI-assisted workflow that allows companies to build, update and distribute training content themselves, across products and locations.
The biggest selling point here is the ease with which VUSE XR helps enterprises to create mixed reality training content. The VUSE XR Hub works by converting existing CAD models, engineering data and product documentation into photorealistic 3D models, which users can then arrange into interactive training sequences using AI-assisted tools or drag-and-drop functionality.
“Mixed reality hardware is advancing rapidly, but creating mixed reality training content remains the biggest barrier to broader enterprise adoption. The VUSE XR Hub removes this bottleneck, enabling companies to unlock significant business value from mixed reality,” said Niclas Matthias, co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of VUSE XR.
Once the content is created, training can be delivered via a web browser, mobile devices, or fully immersive XR headsets such as Meta Quest. The results are tracked centrally, and content can be updated and redeployed across an organisation at any time.
The company already counts some of the major names in the industrial and life sciences space as its customers. Its customer base includes ZEISS, Hologic, Badenova, Scheidt & Bachmann, WITRON, University Medical Centre Hamburg-Eppendorf (UKE) and Sartorius. VUSE XR has won the smartXautomation Award 2025, the AI Champions Award 2025 from the German state of Baden-Württemberg, and the pitch competition at Black Forest Space 2026.
Andreas Goss, IACD member and former Chief Executive Officer of thyssenkrupp Steel, said, “Effective training is critical to productivity, knowledge transfer and the safe operation of increasingly complex products and processes. The technology developed by VUSE XR has the potential to fundamentally change how companies deliver training, making it more accessible and scalable across products and locations.”
Alongside the funding, VUSE XR is strengthening its commercial leadership team with two senior appointments: Jan Hendrik Degner, who joins as Chief Commercial Officer, bringing experience from J.P. Morgan and CEWE Group, and Robert Günther, whose background includes senior positions at Meta and Unity, takes the role of Vice President of Sales and Service Delivery.
The startup says it will use the pre-Seed capital to advance its enterprise mixed reality training platform VUSE XR Hub, expand its AI-assisted creation capabilities and accelerate commercial growth. “With this funding and our expanded commercial team, we are ready to build VUSE XR into the category leader in enterprise mixed reality training,” Matthias added.

articles.title: Hackers Steal 2.6 Million Records From Sony’s Japanese ISP So-net
articles.text:
Hackers have stolen the personal information of current and former So-net and Plala internet subscribers in Japan, Sony Network Communications announced on October 27. Nearly 2.6 million records were impacted.
The attackers broke into the So-net member database on October 19. The company first spotted the intrusion on October 23, then took the targeted server offline and cut off traffic coming from the attackers.
By the following day, its investigators had confirmed that personal data had been taken and determined the scope of the leak.
The stolen information includes names, dates of birth, gender, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, and the IDs customers use to connect to the internet.
Of the roughly 2.6 million exposed records, 2.14 million belong to So-net subscribers and 443,000 to Plala (S Course) subscribers. Roughly 293,000 of them relate to people who left the services in March 2026 or later, as their details are kept for some time to handle final bills and support requests.
The hackers also obtained approximately 54,000 email addresses, along with their passwords, belonging to four additional mail services: Mail Service (G), A-Box, So-net VAIO Mail, and the PostPet email account service. So-net has not identified any password leak for the free basic mailbox that comes with a subscription.
On October 27, the company began resetting the passwords for the impacted email addresses, forcing users to set new ones before they could resume using the services.
“Due to the leak of email addresses and email address passwords, a third party who obtained the information was in a position to view, send, and receive emails using email software and So-net Webmail. We implemented these measures as an emergency step to prevent unauthorized use of customers’ email addresses,” reads a translation of an FAQ issued by So-net.
The breach also impacted 16 records containing bank account details, such as the bank and branch, account type, account number, and account holder’s name. So-net says it does not hold the PINs for these accounts.
Credit card data is not involved, because So-net does not store it. NURO and the company’s other offerings do not appear to be affected.
How the attackers got in has not been disclosed. So-net lists the cause as unauthorized access by a third party and says it is still investigating. The incident has been reported to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

articles.title: Bot Food secures $1.5 million to give AI users more control over their data | BetaKit
articles.text:
The team that built and sold Toronto’s Wysdom has launched a new software startup that aims to give individuals greater control and ownership over how much they share with powerful AI systems, and when they share it.
Bot Food Corporation announced on Thursday that it has secured $1.5 million CAD in pre-seed funding from fellow Toronto firm GreenSky Ventures to build “one personal context library that works across every AI product.” It also launched a beta version of its application.
“One day, people are going to realize, ‘I want to take back control of that [personal context].’”
Bot Food co-founder and CEO Ian Collins co-founded Wysdom as CEO in 2012 with former president and CTO Jeff Brunet, working alongside ex-COO Nitin Singhal. That startup, which was initially named CrowdCare, built an AI evaluation platform to help customer service chatbot operators improve their performance, before selling to Minneapolis-based Calabrio in 2024.
During his time at Wysdom, Collins said he and his colleagues grasped the importance of context in AI. “As we measured and evaluated all these bots and their performance, it was almost always a context problem,” he told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
Collins said that while it has become clear that the more knowledge these systems possess about the individuals using them, the better they perform, many have yet to realize how valuable their personal context actually is. As AI companies race to capture as much personal context on their users as possible to improve their performance and keep them locked in, Collins envisions what he sees as a better path forward.
With Bot Food, Collins and Singhal have teamed up again to give individuals control and ownership over that context, and Brunet, now managing partner at GreenSky, has bought into their vision. Brunet has joined Bot Food’s board of directors as part of its all-equity, all-primary capital pre-seed round, which closed in October and brings the startup’s total funding to $3 million. Collins did not share its valuation.
RELATED: Bot management software startup Wysdom acquired by US-based Calabrio
Brunet told BetaKit over email that GreenSky likes to invest in startups building tech other products will depend upon. “We believe a universal personal context layer could become a critical piece of infrastructure for the entire AI ecosystem,” he added. “Backing proven founders I trust, with a bold vision for the future of AI, was an easy decision.”
Collins argued that sharing detailed personal context with AI will soon become a prerequisite for anyone who wants agentic systems “to do great things” for them. “A lot of people are resisting [AI],” he posited, “but we’re all going to give in eventually; the productivity is just going to be too great.”
For his part, Collins has been using Muse, US tech giant Meta’s fast-growing personal AI agent, since it became available in Canada last month. “It’s pretty amazing, and it’s getting to know me so much,” he said. “It’s just sucking up the data at this massive pace.”
As AI usage grows, these systems will amass deep libraries of information about the individuals using them over time. AI users may not possess access to or rights over their own usage data, Collins said, from rich details about their digital shopping history to the TV shows and movies they’ve watched, the music they listen to, and the places they’ve worked and travelled. At the moment, many major AI labs are using this personal context they have gathered for customer retention.
RELATED: GreenSky closes $23.5-million sixth fund with help from new managing partner Jeff Brunet
Bot Food is betting that some portion of the population will eventually recognize that all of this personal context is a tremendous asset. “One day, people are going to realize, ‘I want to take back control of that,’” Collins said. “‘I should own that thing. It’s rich, it’s valuable, [and] I could probably … get paid for it if I wanted to.’”
Bot Food aims to give its users that power, along with greater choice over how much they share about themselves, with which systems, and when. Those libraries will be collected and managed by Bot Food’s AI assistant RaLHF (pronounced like the common name Ralph), which Collins said will sign into the apps that customers use and catalogue what it finds into a private, encrypted digital library that they can view, edit, and selectively share from with the systems they are using.
The now seven-person startup, which has brought on former ThinkData Works CTO Brendan Stennett as CTO, plans to put its pre-seed funding largely towards go-to-market testing.
“A lot of people are resisting [AI], but we’re all going to give in eventually; the productivity is just going to be too great.”
When asked why individuals should trust a small startup like Bot Food to responsibly store their info instead of a large AI lab, Collins said Bot Food’s terms of service make clear that the company does not hold any rights to the data stored on its platform and cannot do anything with it. He also argued that Bot Food’s product architecture and Stennett’s experience in enterprise data security will help the company keep its clients’ context secure.
Bot Food’s beta features a simple on/off switch that users can click to allow or bar certain AI systems from accessing their data. Its next version will likely include permission for certain AI systems to draw relevant context from select apps.
Collins envisions a final product that can not only send personal context back into its library, but one that features more granular buckets as its own agent improves. He said the startup is also testing its capacity to allow individuals to grant AI access to their information for some tasks and then forget about it afterwards.
Cyberattacks are on the rise thanks to agentic AI, and Collins acknowledged that there could come a day where, if Bot Food achieves success building these sorts of libraries, it becomes a prime target for bad actors, human or machine.
“It’s key to us that we build trust like a 1Password, and have a level of security that we can offer like they do because [Bot Food] will become a target one day,” Collins said.
UPDATE (10/29/26): This story has been updated to clarify Jeff Brunet’s role at Wysdom.
Feature image courtesy Bot Food Corporation.

articles.title: Sam Altman zu Gen Z: Probiert etwas Neues
articles.text:
Neue Arbeitswelt: Wieso Sam Altman von der Gen Z enttäuscht ist
Die KI-Revolution sorgt schon jetzt dafür, dass die Zahl der Stellenangebote für Berufseinsteiger:innen rapide abnimmt – auch in Deutschland, wie eine Analyse des Jobportals Indeed kürzlich gezeigt hat. Vor allem Angehörige der sogenannten Gen Z, also zwischen 1997 und 2012 geborene Personen, fürchten, durch den zunehmenden Einsatz von KI-Tools ersetzt zu werden.
Sam Altman: Anhaltend enttäuscht von Gen Z
Sam Altman will solche Sorgen nicht gelten lassen. Im Sommer 2025 prognostizierte der OpenAI-Chef Uni-Absolvent:innen einen Arbeitsalltag der Zukunft, in dem dank KI „einfach alles besser“ ist – „astronomische Gehälter“ inklusive. Die Gen Z teilt Altmans Begeisterung offenbar nicht, was diesen „anhaltend enttäusche“, wie Fortune berichtet.
In einem Interview mit der Stanford Graduate School of Business erklärte Altman, dass die Studierenden lieber machten, was vor fünf Jahren cool war statt etwas Neues auszuprobieren. Dabei, so der KI-Verfechter, sei genau jetzt die richtige Zeit um neue Wege zu gehen.
KI-Revolution bietet auch Chancen
Es sei vollkommen richtig, dass KI eine große Zahl von Dingen, die heute noch Menschen erledigen, künftig besser, günstiger und schneller mache. Zudem übernehme die KI große Bereiche aktueller Tätigkeiten komplett. Aber: Der Umbruch biete auch Chancen für ambitionierte Arbeitskräfte, so Altman. Dazu müsse man aber bereit sein zu überlegen, welche neuen Geschäftsmodelle sich mithilfe von KI entwickeln ließen.
Die Ausgangslage sei so offen wie nie zuvor. Die KI öffne Unternehmer:innen ein seltenes Zeitfenster, um Bereiche aufzubauen, die noch vor wenigen Jahren schwierig oder gar unmöglich gewesen seien, so Altman. Auf Basis der Technologie, so der OpenAI-Chef, ließen sich Unternehmen entwickeln, die weitaus größer und bedeutender sein könnten als OpenAI selbst.
Karriere in Zeiten des größten Wandels
„Wenn ihr euch jetzt in die Welt hinausbegebt, um an etwas zu arbeiten – dann beginnt ihr eure Karriere vermutlich in einer Zeit des größten Wandels“, gab Altman den Stanford-Studierenden mit auf den Weg. Menschen mit großem Potenzial, Tatendrang, Ideen, einer neuen Sichtweise auf die Dinge sowie neuen Fähigkeiten kämen tendenziell besonders gut zurecht, „wenn der Boden am stärksten bebt“.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity | TechCrunch
articles.text:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month.
The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.
Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”
The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.
Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.
The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.
“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”
The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.
Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves.
“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.
Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem.
While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”
Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting.
“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.
