articles.title: Africa’s Creator Economy Needs Better Infrastructure to Grow
articles.text:
Africa’s creative industries have no shortage of talent or stories to tell. What they lack is the commercial infrastructure to distribute their work, reach audiences and get paid for it.
That was the central argument at a Creative Economy Stage panel at Moonshot by TechCabal on Thursday where executives from film, live entertainment, payments and television production discussed what it will take for African companies to build an economy that allows creators to capture more value.
“There isn’t a challenge in creativity, and there isn’t a challenge in talent. There’s an abundance of stories that just haven’t even begun to be told,” said Kene Okwuosa, group chief executive officer (CEO) of Filmhouse Group, a cinema operator and film distributor. “But are creators capturing the value that their talent and their creativity should capture? The truth is that we still have quite a way to go.”
Africa’s creator economy is worth about $3 billion and could exceed $17 billion by 2030, according to the Africa Creator Economy Report. But growth in the sector does not automatically translate into better earnings for creators. Distribution channels, access to international payments and the infrastructure needed to produce and monetise content remain critical links in the value chain.
For Okwuosa, one of the biggest gaps is distribution. With relatively few streaming platforms and other buyers competing for African content, creators have limited options for selling their work. More distribution channels could give them greater bargaining power and help keep more revenue within the continent’s creative industries.
Filmhouse has sought to address that gap by expanding across the film value chain. The company produces films, operates what Okwuosa described as the largest cinema chain in the market and distributes content to 26 or 27 airlines. It also supplies streaming platforms including Netflix and Amazon. In 2025, it launched Kava, a subscription streaming service, in partnership with Inkblot Studios.
The strategy comes as the West African cinema market records growth. Cinemas in the region generated a record ₦15.6 billion ($11.6 million) in revenue in 2025, while Nollywood films outsold Hollywood titles at the box office for the first time, according to FilmOne’s annual scorecard.
While Filmhouse is building routes to audiences, Darey Art Alade, co-founder and chief creative officer of live entertainment company Livespot360, said his business emerged from a different infrastructure gap: the technical capacity to stage large-scale productions.
When the team first attempted to organise a major live show, it struggled to find local providers capable of delivering the production it envisioned. Rather than abandon the idea, Livespot360 built the lighting, staging and technical capabilities it needed. That infrastructure now supports platforms such as the Born in Africa Festival and Detty December.
“Those problems have given birth to solutions,” Alade said.
For creators working across borders, however, even a successful project can fall apart if they cannot receive their earnings.
Richard Oyome, co-founder and chief operating officer of cross-border payments company Raenest, recalled a creator who lost an international job because he did not have a bank account capable of receiving the payment. The example illustrated how gaps in financial infrastructure can prevent African talent from participating in a global market, regardless of the quality of their work.
Raenest, which has processed more than $1 billion for over 700,000 users, connects creators in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana to payment partners in the United States, the United Kingdom and Europe.
“If you do not have access, you are locked out of the economy,” Oyome said.
Kopano Cowen, CEO of South African television production company Connect Channel, also participated in the discussion, which examined how businesses can build the systems creators need to produce, distribute and monetise their work.
Taken together, the discussion pointed to an infrastructure problem that extends well beyond any single platform or service. Creators need buyers willing to pay for their work, venues and production capabilities to bring it to life, distribution channels to reach audiences, and payment systems that allow them to collect their earnings.
Oyome highlighted another part of that equation: the relationship between creators and their audiences. He said brands increasingly value genuine audience relationships over follower counts alone, making audience trust and engagement important assets for creators seeking commercial partnerships.
Africa’s creative infrastructure is taking shape, from cinema screens and live stages to streaming platforms and payment rails. The question is whether creators will finally see more money reach their pockets when the curtain falls.

articles.title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
articles.text:
This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.
For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?
It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.
These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?
A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.
The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.
Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.
Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.
With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.
The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.
The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:
- True wireless earbuds – 3 hours
- Wireless headphones – 3 hours
- Smart glasses – 5 hours
- Audio glasses – 6 hours
- Smartwatches – 9 hours
- Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours
Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control.
Consumer Trust Is Hard-Won
But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.
The top reported issues around adoption are privacy, security, and user control. The data points to a certain amount of caution around deeply personal use cases, like voice, health, and location, as almost 60 percent of respondents want to keep data from their wearables private, or at least insist on gaining approval before it gets shared.
In other words, even though premium features like high-quality audio, perception sensing, battery life, and comfort whet consumer appetites (and agentic AI capabilities drive upgrade intent), true adoption will come only with consumer trust. They want security, privacy, transparency and control.
Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.
The Industry Remains Fluid
The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.
Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.
The Rise of Personal AI in Intelligent Wearables
Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.
Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.
The Opportunity
The industry for intelligent wearables is exciting. It’s clear that consumer demand for Personal AI is high, and this report dives deeply into the specifics of what respondents want out of it. They want AI that is personal and understands their context, and they want it to be proactive and helpful instead of merely reactive. They’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control.
Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.
Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.
All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.
Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

articles.title: Auriga Partners reaches €80 million interim close for second fund dedicated to cybersecurity | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Auriga Partners, a Paris-based asset management firm specialising in venture capital and innovation investment, has announced an €80 million interim close for Auriga Cyber Ventures II, its second fund dedicated exclusively to cybersecurity.
Auriga Cyber Ventures II is backed by Bpifrance through the French National Seed Fund No. 3, managed on behalf of the French State as part of the France 2030 investment plan. It also benefits from the support of the European Union under the InvestEU fund, through the European Investment Fund (EIF), as well as an Equity Guarantee managed by Bpifrance’s Investor Partnerships and Guarantees team.
“Given the economic, industrial and sovereignty challenges posed by cybersecurity, Europe must equip itself to develop global leaders. We have a particularly dynamic pool of talent, technologies and startups, but they need both substantial capital and specialised support to realise their potential,” said Geoffroy Rosset, Managing Partner, Auriga Partners.
Founded in 1998 by Jacques Chatain, Bernard Daugeras, and Patrick Bamas, Auriga Partners calls itself a pioneer in venture capital in France. Since its inception, it has backed more than 150 companies, including Neolane, Nexthink, Wallix, Vade and Vestiaire Collective. The latter two investments enabled Auriga to distribute more than €500 million to its investors over the 2025-26 period alone.
The firm’s cybersecurity approach is built on the expertise of a network of industry founders, including Jean-Noël de Galzain, founder of Wallix; Georges Lotigier, founder of Vade; Thierry Rouquet, founder of Sentryo, which was acquired by Cisco; and Édouard de Rémur, co-founder of Oodrive and Virtual Browser.
“Our community of experts and entrepreneurs, which we continuously strive to expand, provides startups with more than just capital. It brings collective intelligence, combining in-depth market knowledge, privileged access to industry decision-makers, support for business development and expertise in international expansion. In cybersecurity, the ability to provide hands-on support is just as critical as funding,” said William Lecat, Managing Partner, Auriga Partners.
Auriga Partners’ second dedicated fund for cybersecurity firms comes amidst the escalating urgency around digital security. With more than 30 billion connected devices globally, a cyberattack occurs every 39 seconds, and the global cost of cybercrime is estimated at $10.5 trillion in 2025, equivalent to the world’s third-largest economy.
The Auriga Cyber Ventures II fund has a target of €100 million and a hard cap of €120 million, and it builds on the success of Auriga’s first €55 million cybersecurity vehicle launched in 2022. The fund primarily targets early-stage European startups, from pre-Seed to Series A, with investment tickets ranging from €500,000 to €5 million.
It will take minority equity stakes and plans to allocate roughly half its capital to follow-on investments in its most promising portfolio companies. The fund aims to back around 30 startups, with a focus on two high-priority segments: artificial intelligence security (protecting AI models, data and emerging applications) and identity and data protection, which addresses increasingly sophisticated fraud and digital access proliferation.
Since 2022, Auriga says its teams have analysed more than 2,000 European cybersecurity startups, and it has already deployed capital from the new fund into four startups: Finovox (document fraud prevention), Fleuret (AI-powered automated penetration testing), Mankind’s (AI systems auditing and compliance), and Nextident (AI agent security). It plans two to three further investments before the end of 2026.
Over the past five years, the firm has backed 30 European companies spanning the full cybersecurity value chain, including Tenancy, Patrowl, Emproof, Cytix and Mindflow. Auriga Partners has already established what it describes as Europe’s largest dedicated cybersecurity startup portfolio, and with Auriga Cyber Ventures II, the firm plans to build on that portfolio.

articles.title: Jetzt auch Apple: Wieso Laptops mit Touchscreen für mich sinnlos sind
articles.text:
Jetzt auch Apple: Wieso Laptops mit Touchscreen für mich sinnlos sind
Und plötzlich touchen alle am Bildschirm. Denn das ist bei Apples neuem Macbook Pro so gewollt. Es ist nicht nur mit einem OLED-Display ausgestattet, sondern eben auch berührungsempfindlich. Dabei hatte Steve Jobs schon vor 25 Jahren bei einem Mac-Event darüber gesprochen, dass Touchscreens an Laptops ergonomische Albträume sind. „Nach längerer Zeit wird Ihnen der Arm abfallen“, so Jobs damals.
Sicher, solche Ansichten können sich über die Zeit überholen. Schließlich stellte es sich auch als falsch heraus, dass 3,5 Zoll immer die perfekte Größe für Smartphone-Bildschirme bleiben wird. Und so gut wie jeder Windows-Hersteller hat ja ebenfalls Geräte mit Touchscreen im Portfolio. Warum also nicht Apple?
Apple lässt Kreative in der Video-App touchen
Profitieren sollen davon kreative Nutzer:innen. Für die ist so ein Pro-Macbook gedacht. Entsprechend sieht man sie auf Apples eigenen Bildern und Videos jetzt ständig an den Bildschirm greifen, um Fotos zu vergrößern oder in der Video-App Clips hin und her zu schieben. Dinge, die man prima und wahrscheinlich präziser mit der Maus oder dem Multitouch-Trackpad hinbekommt – Apples einstmaligen Argument gegen Touchscreen-Laptops.
Die App-Auswahl bestätigt meinen Eindruck, dass die „neue“ Eingabemethode wahrscheinlich erstmal auch selten bei Nutzer:innen ankommen wird. Neben Apples eigenen Apps werden zum Start ausgewählte Anwendungen neue Touchgesten unterstützen. Dazu zählen neben Notion und Canva etwa Word, Outlook und Excel. Bürosoftware also. In einer Pressemeldung ist von „intuitiven Erlebnissen“ die Rede. Bei der Nutzung auf dem iPad kann ich sagen: Es ist immer noch leichter, mit der Maus eine Textstelle gezielt auszuwählen oder Text zu markieren, als es auf dem Touchbildschirm zu versuchen.
Fairerweise muss man dazu sagen, dass Bildbearbeitungs-Apps wie Lightroom oder Videoschnitt-Anwendungen wie Davinci Resolve ebenfalls als kompatibel genanntwerden. Dass jemand mal schnell ein Foto großzieht oder per Drag-and-Drop ein paar Dateien verschiebt, kann ich mir noch vorstellen. Dass aber jetzt unheimlich viele Musiker:innen ihre Stücke direkt via Touchscreen einspielen oder selbige Grafik-Tablets ersetzen? Vermutlich eher nicht. Schließlich unterstützen die Macbooks den Apple Pencil auch nicht.
Zudem kommt das Henne-Ei-Problem. Alle Apps, die nicht auf die Touchbedienung ausgelegt sind, interpretieren Eingaben schlicht als Klicks. Ob sich das ändert, wird auch davon abhängen, wie viel Zuspruch die neuen Geräte vom Publikum erhalten. Heißt: Sind die Touch-Macbooks eher weniger beliebt, gibt es keinen Grund, Arbeit in Funktionen zu investieren, die dann nicht genutzt werden. Das war auch eines der Probleme bei der Touch Bar.
Wann sich das neue Macbook wirklich lohnt
Uninteressant ist das Gerät dennoch nicht. Da wäre eben jenes OLED-Display, das für kräftige Farben und satte Kontraste sorgen dürfte. Die Displaytechnologie ist dabei dieselbe wie beim iPad Pro. Apple setzt auf ein Tandem-Display, bei dem zwei Schichten übereinander liegen. Das sorgt für ein sehr helles Bild. Zudem sind die neuen Geräte laut Apple leichter. Das 14-Zoll-Gerät wiegt 230, die 16-Zoll-Version sogar 320 Gramm weniger als die Modelle ohne OLED.
Dazu kommen die leistungsstarken Prozessoren, Möglichkeiten zur Kalibrierung und andere nützliche Funktionen für Kreative. Gute Gründe das Gerät zu kaufen. Aber der Touchscreen gehört nicht dazu.

articles.title: ¿Estrés o emoción? Por qué tu reloj inteligente no distingue la diferencia
articles.text: Un hombre consulta su ritmo cardíaco en un reloj inteligente. Los relojes inteligentes o smartwatches y las pulseras de actividad se han consolidado como herramientas del sector del bienestar para registrar pasos, ejercicio, sueño y otros indicadores de salud. La Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) publicó en noviembre de 2024 que el 34,8 % de las personas con teléfono inteligente en España había utilizado un reloj inteligente o una pulsera de actividad, es decir, aproximadamente una de cada tres. Pero, más allá de su uso para monitorizar la actividad física, las investigaciones estudian ahora hasta qué punto estos dispositivos pueden aportar información sobre el estado de ánimo. ¿Cómo funcionan y qué pueden decirnos realmente sobre nuestras emociones? articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.
Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial.
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.
Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.
Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗
Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.
Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.
Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗
Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training.
Explore the Onshape importer guide.
Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗
Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.
The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.
Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.
Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗
A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.
The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect.
Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, C. J. Ballance, R. Srinivas, D. M. Lucas, A. Bermúdez. Aharonov–Bohm interference in a $${\\pmb{\\mathbb{Z}}}_{\\bf{2}}$$ lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6
- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

articles.title: US investigated Chinese spy plot aimed at Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.
The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.
The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.
But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”
In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

articles.title: Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
articles.text:
The new MacBook Pro brings with it a bunch of firsts for Apple laptops, the two flashiest being an OLED display and touchscreen functionality. But as an image-accuracy enthusiast, trained calibrator, and resident display expert, what excites me most about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the technology it uses to display an accurate picture. It’s the first laptop, and only the second product overall, to support Apple CMF 2026 color modes. It could be the future for displays.
Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
CMFs, or color-matching functions, mathematically represent how we perceive color, and there are a few different variations. The specification that’s been the standard for years is CIE 1931 (CIE stands for Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage, or International Commission on Illumination). For nearly a century, CIE 1931 has been a reliable calibration target, and most of the reference modes on the new MacBook use it.
But with the development of new display technologies over the past 20 years that have ultra-narrow band spectra — such as OLED, LEDs with KSF phosphors, and quantum dots — CIE 1931’s shortcomings are increasingly apparent. Even when calibrated to the same D65 white point, the same image on an OLED and quantum dot LED can look identical to one person, but different to another because of biological variations in our eyes. We all have small discrepancies in our eyes — such as the sensitivity of the cones in our eyes, which allow us to see color — and those can change as we age. CIE 1931 doesn’t properly handle that and was created based on only 17 test subjects. It’s not ideal in a professional setting where content needs to look the same regardless of the screen technology it’s on or who’s viewing it. Apple CMF 2026 addresses that, so that displays look the same regardless of the technology they use.
Apple first included its new CMF on the Studio Display XDR, which I reviewed earlier this year and found to be an excellent, albeit expensive, monitor for color professionals because of Apple CMF 2026 and the reference color modes. But the fact that this technology is now on a laptop that’s portable and not just a standalone monitor living on a desk is a big help for professionals on the move.
As on the Studio Display XDR, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has two Apple CMF 2026 reference modes — one for P3 color primaries and one that includes both P3 and Adobe RGB color primaries for more flexibility. Peak brightness with both HDR and SDR content is 2,000 nits (on the XDR monitor peak SDR luminance is up to 1,000 nits), and the True Tone setting automatically adjusts HDR tone mapping, brightness, and white point based on ambient lighting. (An option to disable True Tone is in Displays preferences.)
The MacBook doesn’t require using Apple CMF 2026, as there are 14 more reference color modes that use the CIE 1931 color space — it is still the standard, after all — including DICOM for medical imaging (which is cool, but only useful to those in the medical field). The MacBook also supports Apple Pro Display Calibrator, which includes three calibration methods to adjust the reference color modes, or a custom mode, if necessary. There are options for a full calibration or to fine-tune a calibration with the proper measurement gear, or to visually fine-tune the display.
Color science and display technologies have come a long way since 1931, when the CIE 1931 color space was established. Apple’s development of the Apple CMF 2026 and its standardization efforts — the company is currently working with a CIE technical committee on a proposed standard — is an important step to make sure current display technologies look the same to as many people as possible.
Extending support to the new MacBook expands the user base considerably (let’s face it, more people are buying a touchscreen MacBook, even at $2,900, than a $3,300 professional monitor). And more importantly, it gives professionals that can get the most out of it easier, portable access.

articles.title: Galaxy Watch und Ring erkennen Schlafapnoe jetzt genauer
articles.text:
Auch für einige ältere Smartwatches: Samsung bringt neue KI-Gesundheitsfunktion
Allein in Deutschland sollen laut AOK etwa drei Prozent der Frauen und fünf Prozent der Männer an sogenannter obstruktiver Schlafapnoe leiden. Die nächtlichen Atemaussetzer sorgen für Müdigkeit und Konzentrationsstörungen am Tag. Bei Betroffenen steigt aber auch das Risiko für Folgeerkrankungen wie Diabetes Typ-2, Herzinfarkt oder Depressionen.
Samsung: KI-Update für Schlafapnoe-Funktion
Smartwatches von Samsung verfügen seit dem Start der Galaxy Watch 4 über eine Funktion zur Erkennung von Schlafapnoe. Seit Juni 2025 ist die Schlafapnoe-Funktion auch in Deutschland verfügbar. Bisher ließ sich so aber lediglich erkennen, ob eine Person in der Nacht Atemaussetzer hat. Mit dem aktuellen Update geht Samsung jetzt einen Schritt weiter.
Wie das Unternehmen mitteilt, nutzt die erweiterte Schlafapnoe-Funktion auf Galaxy-Geräten wie Watch und Ring einen KI-Algorithmus. Damit sollen sich die Atemstörungen in drei Schweregrade einteilen lassen: leicht, gelegentlich und häufig. Dazu sind mindestens zwei nächtliche Messeinheiten innerhalb von zehn Tagen notwendig, in denen Ring oder Uhr jeweils fünf Stunden getragen werden.
Start auf Smartwatches in Südkorea
Nach einer Freigabe durch die Gesundheitsbehörde FDA in den USA im Juli 2026 hat Samsung jetzt auch die Genehmigung der südkoreanischen Behörde für Lebensmittel- und Arzneimittelsicherheit erhalten. Entsprechend will Samsung das Update der Schlafapnoe-Funktion schon im November 2026 für Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 9 und Galaxy Ring in Südkorea ausspielen.
Die USA könnten innerhalb kurzer Zeit folgen, wie Androidpolice schreibt. Für einen möglichen Europa-Start der KI-gestützten Schlafapnoe-Funktion für Samsung-Smartwatches gibt es derweil bisher keinen offiziellen Termin. Die CE-Freigabe der europäischen Behörden steht noch aus.
Ältere Geräte bis Galaxy Watch 7 folgen
Ebenfalls unklar ist, wann Samsung die Funktion für ältere Modelle freischaltet. Dabei soll es sich um Galaxy Watch Ultra, Galaxy Watch 8 und Galaxy Watch 7 handeln. Auf noch älteren Smartwatches soll laut Samsung zumindest die bisherige Schlafapnoe-Funktion verfügbar bleiben.

articles.title: Windows 11: So reduzierst du das überladene Rechtsklickmenü
articles.text:
Windows 11: So kannst du jetzt das Rechtsklickmenü selbst einrichten
Da Microsoft die Funktion schrittweise ausrollt, ist sie nach der Installation des optionalen Updates KB5127936 vom Oktober möglicherweise nicht sofort sichtbar. Sie lässt sich mithilfe des kostenlosen Open-Source-Werkzeugs „ViVeTool“ aber in wenigen Minuten aktivieren – und zwar so.
So bekommt ihr das kostenlose Open-Source-Werkzeug „ViVeTool“
Als erstes müsst ihr „Einstellungen“ > „Windows Update“ öffnen und auf „Nach Updates suchen“ klicken. Falls das Update KB5127936 nicht angezeigt wird, aktiviert die Option „Die neuesten Updates erhalten, sobald sie verfügbar sind“ und sucht erneut. Sobald ihr das Update KB5127936 installiert habt, startet ihr den PC neu. Führt auch den Befehl „winver“ aus, um sicherzustellen, dass ihr Build 26200.9818 oder 26300.9818 verwendet.
Dann klickt ihr im Datei-Explorer mit der rechten Maustaste auf eine beliebige Datei. Wenn ihr unten den Eintrag „Menü anpassen“ seht, habt ihr laut windowslatest.com Glück – in diesem Fall benötigt ihr ViVeTool nicht. Falls die Funktion bei euch, wie wohl bei den meisten Nutzer:innen, noch nicht vorhanden ist, müsst ihr ViVeTool von der offiziellen Github-Seite herunterladen. Entpackt die ZIP-Datei dabei so, dass sich die Datei „ViVeTool.exe“ unter „C:\ViVeTool“ befindet.
Zwei Befehle müssen ausgeführt werden
Klickt dann mit der rechten Maustaste auf die Start-Schaltfläche, öffnet das Terminal als Administrator:in und führt nacheinander die folgenden beiden Befehle aus:
cd C:\ViVeTool
vivetool /enable /id:60813048
Wenn die Meldung „Successfully set feature configuration(s)“ erscheint, könnt ihr den PC neu starten und erneut mit der rechten Maustaste auf eine Datei klicken.
Software-Nostalgie: Kennt ihr diese Programme noch?
Statt 25 Einträgen nur noch acht
Das neue Menü enthält am unteren Rand die Schaltfläche „Menü anpassen“, die direkt zu den Einstellungen unter „Personalisierung > Kontextmenü“ führt. Laut Microsoft ist für die Nutzung der Standardkonfiguration kein weiteres Handeln erforderlich. Wer dennoch das alte Menü im Stil von Windows 10 bevorzugt, kann dies weiterhin aufrufen, indem er beim Rechtsklick auf den Desktop oder eine Datei die Umschalttaste gedrückt hält.
Vor dem Update erschienen laut windowslatest.com bei einem Rechtsklick auf eine Bilddatei unterhalb der Symbole für „Ausschneiden“, „Kopieren“, „Umbenennen“, „Freigeben“ und „Löschen“ 20 weitere Einträge. Diese überladen wirkende Systematik könnt ihr dann beispielsweise so anpassen, dass das neue Standardmenü für eine solche Bilddatei nur noch acht Einträge enthält.

articles.title: Los hackers norcoreanos del grupo Lazarus se blindan con IA y cifrado poscuántico
articles.text:
Los hackers norcoreanos del grupo Lazarus se blindan con IA y cifrado poscuántico
El brazo cibernético de Pyongyang empieza a proteger sus ataques contra la potente computación cuántica, llamada a revolucionar la informática
La computación cuántica, todavía en fase experimental, está llamada a revolucionar la informática. Se supone que multiplicará exponencialmente la capacidad de cómputo de los ordenadores. Eso es una muy buena noticia para la investigación y los desarrolladores, pero también tiene algunas implicaciones en el campo de la seguridad: los ordenadores cuánticos serán tan potentes que, presumiblemente, serán capaces de romper el cifrado (es decir, conseguir la clave) de muchas de las comunicaciones consideradas hoy bien protegidas. Este problema lleva tiempo anticipándose en el campo de la ciberseguridad, que busca estrategias para desarrollar sistemas de criptografía que puedan resistir a ordenadores cuánticos.
Pero los buenos no son los únicos que se preparan para la era cuántica: también lo hacen los malos. La empresa de ciberseguridad Kaspersky ha detectado que el grupo Lazarus, que en realidad es una amalgama de varios equipos de hackers de élite patrocinados extraoficialmente por Corea del Norte, ha empezado a usar encriptación poscuántica. “Se considera la criptografía del futuro, está diseñada para seguir siendo segura contra computadoras cuánticas. Eso nos demuestra que ya han comenzado a prevenir sus futuras vulnerabilidades frente a dichos ataques”, explica desde Seúl por videollamada Sojun Ryu, investigador de Kaspersky.
La encriptación consiste en codificar un archivo: la clave para abrirlo es solucionar un problema matemático. Los mensajes de WhatsApp, por ejemplo, están cifrados de extremo a extremo, lo que significa que se encriptan en el momento de enviarlos y solo el receptor recibe la clave para abrirlo. Se puede encriptar cualquier archivo, o incluso el acceso a un ordenado. Las claves de ese cifrado suelen ser extensas series alfanuméricas, virtualmente imposibles de conseguir con ordenadores convencionales. La computación cuántica puede cambiar eso.
Ryu y sus colegas investigaban una campaña de ciberespionaje lanzada por Lazarus sobre compañías surcoreanas. Los atacantes usaron sofisticadas técnicas de phishing, una modalidad de ciberataque que consiste en descargar programas maliciosos a través del engaño, para hacerse con datos sensibles de empresas dedicadas a la construcción, el software y la fabricación de equipos de telecomunicaciones. Los atacantes usaron inteligencia artificial (IA) para crear identidades ficticias de supuestos trabajadores y correos electrónicos que contenían enlaces a falsos currículums. Cuando las víctimas pinchaban en ellos, se les descargaba una serie de programas espía muy difíciles de detectar con los que los hackers robaban información de los equipos.
Este tipo de ataque sofisticado ya se había visto anteriormente. Lo que es nuevo es que las comunicaciones entre los equipos infectados y los atacantes se cifraron con mecanismos criptográficos poscuánticos. Eso hace que prácticamente nadie, menos los atacantes, puedan recuperar esos datos.
“La seguridad criptográfica se basa en problemas difíciles de resolver. Por ejemplo, dado un número muy, muy grande N = p*q, es difícil saber qué dos números primos p y q se utilizaron para crear N. Este problema, que es difícil hoy en día, y en el que se basan muchos algoritmos criptográficos, sería fácil de resolver si aparece una computadora cuántica”, explica Carmela Troncoso, profesora en la Escuela Politécnica de Lausana (Suiza) y directora científica en el Instituto Max Planck para la Seguridad y Privacidad (Alemania).
“La criptografía poscuántica está basada en problemas difíciles incluso para ordenadores cuánticos”, añade la científica española. Esa tecnología, dice, está al alcance de muy pocos.
El primer ciberataque con cifrado poscuántico del que se tiene constancia es de marzo de este año. Fue en un ransomware, una modalidad de ataque en la que los cibercriminales cifran (secuestran) los archivos de un equipo y luego piden un rescate para liberarlos. Se le atribuyó a Kyber, un grupo relativamente nuevo del que todavía se desconoce si está patrocinado por algún estado. Medio año después, Lazarus ya ha sido capaz de incorporar esta tecnología puntera a su arsenal, dando una muestra más de su capacidad.
Anna Širokova, analista de Rapid7, la empresa de ciberseguridad que descubrió el uso que hacía de esta tecnología Kyber, lo considera una operación de marketing: “Decir que se ha usado cifrado poscuántico suena mucho más intimidante que decir ‘utilizamos AES’ [un algoritmo de encriptación muy usado] , sobre todo para los directivos sin conocimientos técnicos que podrían estar valorando si deben pagar el rescate. Es un truco psicológico. No les preocupa que alguien lo descifre dentro de una década, ellos quieren que se les pague en un plazo de 72 horas”, dijo en una entrevista.
Sea o no una operación estética, esta tecnología no está al alcance de todo el mundo. “Mi primera impresión al ver que Lazarus usa la criptografía postcuántica fue pensar que se toman muy en serio la mejora de su conjunto de herramientas de malware”, apunta Ryu. “Que hayan sido capaces de desarrollar esta herramienta quiere decir que han dedicado un equipo exclusivamente a mejorarla”, añade. Desde su punto de vista, eso habla muy bien de la sofisticada organización de este grupo criminal. “Podemos considerar que tienen equipos dedicados para las operaciones, otros a los ataques dirigidos y otros a desarrollar herramientas especializadas”.
Todavía faltan años (los expertos suelen hablar de décadas) antes de que los ordenadores cuánticos pasen del ámbito experimental al comercial. Precisamente por eso, el hecho de que Lazarus esté ya protegiéndose de algo que no existe indica su planificación a largo plazo. “Realmente no quieren que sus cargas maliciosas queden expuestas ante defensores o investigadores”, concluye Ryu.
Robar para el Amado y Respetado Líder
Países como la mencionada China, Rusia, Irán, Israel o EE UU patrocinan extraoficialmente a equipos de hackers de élite para que realicen sabotajes o consigan información de valor. En el sector son conocidos como APT (amenazas avanzadas persistentes). Se trata de organizaciones muy bien estructuradas y con profesionales de primer nivel, cuyas capacidades suelen estar a la par o por encima de los servicios secretos de las grandes potencias.
El caso de Pyongyang es llamativo por dos motivos: porque su peso en la arena cibernética es desproporcionadamente mayor que el que le presupondría por el tamaño de su economía y porque utiliza a sus distintos grupos de expertos informáticos, agrupados bajo el nombre en clave Lazarus, no tanto en labores de inteligencia como para hacer dinero. El Amado y Respetado Líder —una de las formas oficiales de referirse a Kim Jong-un— apostó hace años por el cibercrimen como una fuente de ingresos que le permita sobrevivir a las duras sanciones internacionales a las que está sometido su país. Funcionó: Lazarus es especialmente temible entre las criptomonedas, sector en el que ha protagnizado sonoros golpes, incluyendo el mayor robo de la historia: el de Bybit, a quien sustrajo 1.500 millones de dólares en un solo día.

articles.title: Scaling Autonomous Root Cause Analysis For Regression Triage
articles.text:
Solving difficult bugs while intelligently deciding what to investigate, what to rerun, and where to spend compute.
As semiconductor designs grow larger and more complex, debugging is becoming increasingly difficult to scale.
At DVCon earlier this year, Nvidia’s Stuart Oberman described first-silicon success as approaching a “statistical impossibility.” Semiconductor Engineering cites that debugging accounts for 44% of verification effort; a number reported in 2018, before the scale and complexity of today’s designs.
As designs get larger and design spaces are expanding, engineers are working across systems containing millions of gates. If design complexity continues to scale, debugging needs a fundamentally different approach. In this article, we will explain an AI-native approach to root cause analysis (RCA) and regression triage.
There are two important ways that debugging effort scales.
The first is bug difficulty.
Some bugs require deep tracing across design hierarchies, long pipelines, large waveforms, and multiple interacting components before the actual root cause becomes clear.
ChipAgents RCA was designed specifically for this axis. Rather than treating debugging as a simple question-answering problem, the system approaches RCA as a search problem. It explores high-probability traces, executes across different hypotheses, ranks the resulting explanations, and provides confidence scores to the engineer.
Consider one bug encountered in a real customer environment.
The design contained a bidirectional serialization interface between a manager and subordinate. During a transaction, a reset was triggered by the subordinate while the manager continued transmitting a frame beyond the reset grace period.
Part of the transmitted data happened to contain the same value used to represent the protocol’s start code. The subordinate interpreted that payload as the beginning of a new frame, eventually causing a downstream failure.
Several conditions had to coincide: a reset needed to occur during the transaction, the data needed to resemble the start code, and the transmission needed to outlive the reset grace period.
This is the type of bug where autonomous RCA becomes particularly valuable because identifying the root cause requires reasoning through a long chain of events.
But difficulty is only one dimension.
The second is bug quantity.
A regression may contain hundreds of simulations across many test cases and seeds. Multiple simulations can fail simultaneously, and those failures may represent different bugs—or many apparently different failures may actually originate from the same root cause.
The most challenging case lies at the intersection of these two axes: hard bugs at scale.
Now the problem is no longer simply finding one root cause. The system must determine how many distinct problems actually exist, decide which failures are related, identify which simulations contain the information needed to debug them, and orchestrate RCA across those problems efficiently.
Regression debugging creates a fundamentally different scaling challenge.
There can be an arbitrary number of bugs with varying levels of difficulty. Fixing one problem may expose another. Hundreds of simulations may be running across different test cases and seeds.
And every simulation generates data.
Individual debug cases can already involve enormous logs and waveforms. At regression scale, that data multiplies across every failing simulation.
The naive approach would be to apply an agent to every failure, rerun simulations whenever more information is needed, generate waveforms for every failing test, attempt fixes, and then rerun the entire regression.
But this quickly becomes inefficient.
For autonomous regression triage to work at commercial scale, the system needs to minimize the amount of expensive work it performs.
That means being selective about which failures actually need independent investigation and which simulations actually need to be rerun.
It also means that the underlying RCA system needs to be highly reliable. If an autonomous system proposes an incorrect fix, reruns a simulation, fails again, tries another hypothesis, and repeats the process across dozens of failures, the compute cost can grow quickly.
Accuracy and efficiency therefore become tightly coupled.
The first step is understanding how many distinct bugs actually exist.
Traditional regression systems already use binning techniques, often relying on deterministic scripts and pattern matching to group failures with similar signatures. These methods remain useful.
But there is an opportunity to go further.
Two simulations may produce different log signatures while still sharing the same underlying root cause. An intelligent system should therefore be able to collapse failures beyond what deterministic pattern matching alone can identify.
ChipAgents RCA Triage uses a secondary pass after conventional binning to identify failures that are most likely related by a common root cause.
Instead of treating every failing simulation as an independent debugging task, the system attempts to reduce the regression into a smaller set of meaningful failure groups.
That creates a much more manageable problem for the RCA system.
The same principle applies to waveform generation.
One straightforward approach would be to rerun every failing simulation and dump a waveform for each one.
But that is expensive and often unnecessary.
Instead, the system can identify a minimum set of witness simulations capable of explaining the failures represented by each bin.
Those witness simulations are then rerun with waveform dumping enabled.
The goal is not to collect every possible piece of debugging information. It is to collect the smallest amount of information necessary to explain the regression failures.
This is an important distinction because regression triage is a long-horizon task. A regression might take minutes or hours to execute. Every unnecessary simulation adds cost and delays the final result.
Binning and selective waveform reruns already represent forms of automation.
But automation does not have to stop there.
Once the regression has been reduced into meaningful failure groups and the necessary witness simulations have been identified, those debug packages can be handed directly into autonomous RCA.
The RCA system investigates the root cause for each bin, generates potential fixes, and performs verification.
If verification succeeds, the system gains another signal that the proposed fix is correct. Combined with RCA confidence scoring and the result of the witness simulation, the system can determine whether the fix is likely ready for a final regression run.
The final step is to rerun the regression and verify that the failures have actually been resolved.
This creates an end-to-end workflow:
Regression → intelligent binning → witness selection → waveform rerun → autonomous RCA → fix → verification → final regression.
Instead of an engineer waking up after an overnight regression, discovering a collection of failures, and beginning the triage process manually, the regression can become the beginning of an autonomous debugging workflow.
By the time the engineer returns, the system could have resolved some or all of those failures. If some remain unresolved, the engineer can receive a report showing what was fixed and what still requires investigation.
The paradigm shifts from starting regression triage to reviewing the results of regression triage.
There is another challenge that becomes increasingly important as these systems scale: cost.
Multi-agent systems naturally consume more resources than a single agent because they execute the agent primitive multiple times. That tradeoff exists for a reason: parallel exploration can improve performance and accuracy.
But simply spending more compute is not a sustainable path to better engineering results.
The objective should be to gain the accuracy advantages of multi-agent reasoning while improving token and cost efficiency.
In our internal benchmarks, ChipAgents’ multi-agent systems achieve state-of-the-art performance while operating at costs comparable to traditional single-agent systems.
That is an important direction for autonomous semiconductor engineering.
As agents take on longer-horizon workflows, the question will increasingly move beyond whether an agent can perform a task.
The question becomes whether the system can perform that task reliably, efficiently, and economically across the scale of real semiconductor development.
Regression triage is a useful example of that transition.
Solving one difficult bug autonomously is valuable.
Solving difficult bugs across an entire regression while intelligently deciding what to investigate, what to rerun, and where to spend compute is the next step toward autonomous debugging at commercial scale.

articles.title: Découvrez la « queue de chat » le résultat d'une énorme collision cosmique
articles.text:
Galaxie roue de chariot ou sombrero, nébuleuse nœud de cravate ou de la tête de sorcière… Les astronomes aiment parfois donner des noms insolites aux différents objets cosmiques qu’ils découvrent. Il faut dire que pour ces structures distantes parfois de quelques dizaines à plusieurs millions d’années-lumière, nous disposons de peu d’informations à part une vague idée de leur forme, ce qui peut laisser libre cours à l’imagination.
Toujours dans cette optique, voici donc la queue de chat. Il s’agit d’une protubérance visible dans la constellation du Peintre, que l’on peut voir uniquement depuis l’hémisphère sud, et qui interroge les scientifiques depuis sa découverte début 2024. Elle fait l’objet d’une étude parue dans The Astrophysical Journal Letters qui tente d’expliquer son origine.
Le fruit d’une collision
D’une forme rappelant effectivement la queue d’un chat, la structure se situe dans le disque de poussière de Beta Pictoris, à 63 années-lumière de la Terre. Cette étoile jeune abrite un système planétaire en formation qui n’existe que depuis quelques millions d’années. Il s’agit d’un disque très étudié, repéré en 1983 par le satellite infrarouge IRAS puis photographié pour la première fois en 1984 depuis l’observatoire de Las Campanas, au Chili, ce qui en fait d’ailleurs le tout premier disque circumstellaire à avoir été imagé.
Mais en 2024, avec un niveau de détail jamais atteint auparavant, le télescope James Webb découvre cette queue de chat qui semble sortir du disque. Dans une étude parue dans la revue The Astronomical Journal, les scientifiques évoquent une structure de poussière qui pourrait être le résultat d’une collision.
On retrouve d’ailleurs dans ces nouveaux travaux quelques auteurs de l’étude de 2024, comme Isabel Rebollido, du Centre d’astrobiologie de Madrid, ou Christopher Stark, du Goddard Space Flight Center de la Nasa. Leur objectif était de retracer l’évolution de la queue de chat ces dernières années. Les astronomes ont pour cela combiné les nouvelles images de Hubble avec des observations plus anciennes, qui remontent sur 14 ans, afin de mieux cerner la position exacte et la nature de cette structure.
200 000 milliards de chats
D’après leurs résultats, l’hypothèse d’une collision déjà envisagée en 2024 était bien la bonne : la queue de chat serait le résultat d’un impact entre deux astres qui pourraient être gros comme Pluton. La poussière issue du choc serait presque entièrement faite de matière organique riche en carbone, qui absorbe la lumière visible. Elle est donc très sombre, ce qui explique pourquoi seul James Webb et son œil infrarouge l’avait captée jusqu’ici, avant ces nouvelles observations de Hubble en lumière visible.
De plus, la queue de chat serait constituée de grains de poussière minuscules, de l’ordre du micron (un millième de millimètre) et très poreux. L’ensemble pourrait s’étendre sur un millier d’unités astronomiques (une unité correspond à la distance moyenne entre la Terre et le Soleil), soit environ 150 milliards de kilomètres, ou comme le précise le communiqué qui accompagne l’étude, environ 200 000 milliards de chats mis bout à bout. Une image magnifique ou cauchemardesque selon les sensibilités de chacun. Cette porosité intrigue les chercheurs. Selon Kevin Wagner, coauteur de l’étude et chercheur à l’observatoire Steward de l’université de l’Arizona, les vitesses en jeu lors de la collision ont pu être si élevées que les grains de carbone se sont vaporisés, avant de se recondenser en refroidissant, d’où leur structure poreuse.
L’étude de ce système et de cette queue de chat est intéressante pour comprendre notre propre Système solaire car ces collisions présentes dans cet ensemble jeune auraient pu également avoir lieu chez nous avant que la Terre et les autres planètes ne se forment définitivement.
