articles.title: Unlocking Tensor Core Performance for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Atomistic simulations help researchers understand how molecules and materials behave, from chemical reactions and phase transitions to mechanical failure. These simulations come with a cost-accuracy trade-off. Quantum-mechanical methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can provide accurate energies and forces, but their computational cost often limits their use for large systems or long simulations. Classical interatomic potentials are much faster, but their fixed functional forms limit accuracy and generalizability across different atomic environments. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) help bridge this gap. They use neural networks to predict potential energies and interatomic forces at a fraction of the cost, enabling researchers to study larger systems and longer timescales while retaining much of the required accuracy.
Running an MLIP efficiently, however, presents its own challenge. Atomistic simulations are sensitive to small errors that can accumulate over time and are most visible when computing forces, which are obtained by differentiating the predicted energy. During molecular dynamics simulations, these forces guide updates to atomic velocities and positions over many timesteps, making numerical precision important not only for physical accuracy but also for the stability of the resulting trajectory.
For this reason, many MLIPs continue to run inference in FP32, even though modern NVIDIA GPUs offer substantially higher matrix-multiplication throughput through low-precision Tensor Core operations. Tensor Core methods for FP32 matrix multiplication offer a way to narrow that gap. They decompose each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, evaluate their cross-products on Tensor Cores, and recombine the results in FP32. This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture.
In this post, we evaluate how Tensor Core FP32 methods perform in practice on the Point Edge Transformer (PET), a transformer-based MLIP developed by Lab COSMO at EPFL. PET spends much of its runtime in highly optimized general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), leaving limited headroom for further optimization and making it a demanding test case of whether these methods can deliver additional performance gains.
We evaluate BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, comparing kernel and end-to-end molecular dynamics performance and trajectory-level behavior. We further test the TF32x3 method for potential-energy smoothness, energy conservation, and structural relaxation. We show how these methods can accelerate MLIP inference while retaining behavior close to the FP32 baseline and outline how to evaluate them on other precision-sensitive scientific machine learning workloads.
How Tensor Core FP32 closes the hardware gap
Modern NVIDIA GPUs deliver substantially higher Tensor Core throughput for BF16 and TF32 than for FP32 matrix multiplication, creating a gap between the available throughput at lower precision and the precision requirements of many scientific workloads. Tensor Core FP32 methods help narrow this gap by decomposing FP32 operands into lower-precision components, evaluating selected products on Tensor Cores, and recombining them with FP32 accumulation. Depending on the method and workload, this can deliver accuracy at or near native FP32 while taking advantage of higher Tensor Core throughput.
On Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA cuBLAS provides a BF16x9 Tensor Core path (Figure 1). Each FP32 operand is decomposed into three BF16 components, and nine pairwise products are recombined with the required scaling. cuBLAS can enable this path through the CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 environment variable, so compatible PyTorch GEMMs can use it without changing the model architecture or implementing a custom GEMM.
Because this approach changes how GEMMs are evaluated, it may provide additional gains when combined with optimized graph construction, fused operations, custom kernels, and NVIDIA CUDA graphs. We did not measure the combined gain in this evaluation; it should be established end to end for each workload.
The TF32x3 method applies the same principle on Ampere GPUs (Figure 2). TF32x3 represents each FP32 operand using a leading TF32 component and a residual TF32 component. Unlike BF16x9, our TF32x3 implementation does not use scaling factors. It evaluates three cross-products and omits the residual-by-residual term, as shown in the following equation
NVIDIA CUTLASS provides this approach through the OpMultiplyAddFastF32 operator. Inputs and outputs remain in FP32. Tensor Cores execute the three TF32 products with accumulation in FP32.
Benchmarking Tensor Core FP32 matrix math on PET
We evaluated the 26M-parameter PET-MAD small checkpoint (pet-mad-s-v1.6.0-nn-32) on a 192-atom water box and a 17,280-atom supercell. We also evaluated the 255M-parameter large checkpoint (pet-mad-m-v1.6.0) on the 192-atom system. We compared predicted energies, forces, and stresses with those from the native FP32 path.
BF16x9 method on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs
On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 10.0 or 10.3, cuBLAS supports enabling BF16x9 through an environment variable, math mode, or compute type (requested with CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_EMULATED_16BFX9, CUBLAS_FP32_EMULATED_BF16X9_MATH, or CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1). No model-code changes are required to use this path for single-precision general matrix multiplication (SGEMM).
With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in PET were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload (Figure 3). Figure 4 compares MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager strategies against compiled FP32.
- 192-atom system: The performant strategy sped up the MD step by 1.2x, while the eager strategy achieved 1.1x.
- 17,280-atom system: The performant strategy achieved a 1.7x speedup, while the eager strategy achieved 1.4x.
The performant strategy uses BF16x9 when cuBLAS expects it to be faster; the eager strategy uses it whenever the operation supports it. Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism. This result is significant because PET already expresses much of its runtime as optimized GEMM work, and yet the BF16x9 path exposed performance headroom without retraining the model, changing its transformer architecture, or writing custom kernels.
TF32x3 method on Ampere GPUs
On Ampere GPUs, we implemented TF32x3 by replacing PET’s standard nn.Linear layers with a custom TF32Linear layer that calls a CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel.
CUTLASS C++ provides a reference implementation of this approach in Example 27. The key setting in the PET implementation is:
C++
cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32
This selects CUTLASS’s fast, accurate FP32 multiplication mode. The kernel represents each FP32 operand as leading and residual TF32 components. Tensor Cores then evaluate three products—leading-by-leading and the two leading-by-residual products—and accumulate them in FP32. The smallest residual-by-residual product is omitted. The CUTLASS C++ operator is declared with float inputs and outputs. PET therefore continues to supply ordinary FP32 activations and weights and receives an FP32 result; from the rest of the model’s perspective, the layer behaves like a standard nn.Linear. Only the implementation of the underlying matrix multiplication changes. The C++ example is written for sm80 (Ampere) and can also be compiled for sm90 (Hopper).
The custom TF32Linear module replaces compatible PyTorch linear layers and performs their matrix multiplications using the CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel while preserving the trained weights, bias, and input shape.
Because PET calculates forces by differentiating predicted energies, TF32x3 is also used to propagate gradients to the layer inputs. This ensures that both energy and force calculations use TF32x3 Tensor Core arithmetic. Weight gradients use the standard PyTorch path, but they are not required during fixed-weight inference.
Across PET’s major linear-layer shapes on A100, TF32x3 accelerated GEMMs by approximately 1.7–1.9x (Figure 5). Figure 6 compares MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its corresponding FP32 baseline. One-pass TF32 achieved higher speedups, but at a greater cost to accuracy and trajectory stability (Figures 6–7).
- Small checkpoint (26M parameters): Results are shown for a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell. TF32x3 kept the force error to roughly three times the difference between FP32 runs after recompilation and sped up the MD step by 1.5x on the larger system.
- Large checkpoint (255M parameters): On the 192-atom system, TF32x3 achieved a 1.4x speedup, compared with 1.2x for the small checkpoint. Its force error was 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV/Å, essentially unchanged from the small checkpoint.
Validating physical consistency
For molecular simulation, matching isolated energy and force predictions is only the first test of numerical fidelity. Forces are gradients of the learned potential-energy surface and are integrated over many timesteps, so even small numerical irregularities can roughen the surface, destabilize trajectories, or produce unphysical energy drift. The promise of the Tensor Core FP32 method is therefore especially compelling: it can unlock Tensor Core performance for matrix multiplications while preserving the smooth and stable behavior expected from FP32.
We tested potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation using two separate tests (Figure 7). To test energy smoothness, we dragged a single CO molecule rigidly away from an on-top site of a Pt(111) slab and evaluated the total energy at 60 carbon heights from 1.2 to 6.0 Å in steps of 8.1 × 10⁻² Å. TF32x3 followed the smooth FP32 CO/Pt(111) energy curve, while one-pass TF32 introduced visible point-to-point variations.
In a separate NVE simulation of a 192-atom water box, FP32 and TF32x3 showed comparable bounded energy fluctuations, while one-pass TF32 showed a larger systematic drift. These results show that TF32x3 preserved potential-energy smoothness and maintained energy conservation in the tested systems, not just single-point accuracy.
Testing structural relaxation
Structural relaxation also tests numerical fidelity as the optimizer repeatedly uses predicted forces to update the atomic geometry. Small force inconsistencies can alter the optimization path, increase the number of steps required, or prevent the system from reaching the desired force tolerance. We relaxed a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. Across three replicates, FP32 converged in 218 steps and TF32x3 in 218–222 steps; every run reached the 1.0 × 10⁻³ eV/Å force tolerance. With one-pass TF32, all three replicates failed to converge within the 500-step limit, and forces plateaued around 1.2 × 10⁻³ eV/Å.
TF32x3 accelerated each optimization step by 1.5x while matching the FP32 convergence rate and criterion (Figure 8). One-pass TF32 achieved a 2.0x per-step speedup but failed to converge even after doubling the optimization step limit to 1,000 steps.
These results highlight the practical value of the Tensor Core path: substantial acceleration without sacrificing the convergence behavior of the FP32 workflow.
Limitations and decision criteria
End-to-end gains depend on system size and the share of runtime spent in GEMMs. Small systems generally benefit less because launch overhead, neighbor processing, graph operations, and other non-GEMM work make up a larger portion of the runtime. Larger systems benefit more when GEMMs account for more of the work. TF32x3’s performance also depends on kernel tuning for the model’s matrix shapes and hardware.
Numerical behavior depends on the Tensor Core strategy used. In matrix-multiplication tests, BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy against an FP64 reference, supporting its use as a drop-in replacement for FP32 GEMMs on supported hardware. TF32x3 has a slightly different accuracy profile and should be validated against the model’s accuracy and physical-stability requirements.
Conclusion
Tensor Core FP32 methods improved PET performance without retraining or changing the model architecture. TF32x3 accelerated major GEMMs on A100 by up to 1.9x and the complete molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x. BF16x9 accelerated major GEMMs on an NVIDIA B300 Tensor Core GPU by up to 2.5x and the complete step by up to 1.7x. As demonstrated for TF32x3, Tensor Core methods preserve behavior close to FP32 in the tested energy-conservation and structural-relaxation workflows.
These results support evaluating the methods in other MLIPs and precision-sensitive scientific machine learning models whose runtime is dominated by large FP32 GEMMs. Neither of the Tensor Core FP32 strategies requires retraining or an architectural redesign. Each can therefore be evaluated as an independent performance layer and combined with other software optimizations when the workload supports it.
Try TF32x3 or BF16x9 Tensor Core methods with your model today—no retraining or architectural changes needed. Learn more in the cuBLAS documentation and the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit documentation. Explore the PET models in the UPET repository.
Acknowledgments
We’d like to thank Nikita Fedik, Harun Bayraktar, Gregory Thomsen, and Vamsi Sripathi for their contributions to this post.

articles.title: Nokia 1100: cuánto cuesta hoy el celular más vendido de la historia
articles.text:
El Nokia 1100, considerado el teléfono móvil más vendido de la historia, puede encontrarse hoy desde USD 70 en plataformas de segunda mano como eBay. Más de 20 años después de su lanzamiento, el modelo sigue despertando interés por una combinación que marcó su época: bajo coste, resistencia y funciones básicas que resolvían una necesidad concreta.
El dispositivo llegó al mercado en 2003 con un precio cercano a USD 100. Su éxito se relacionó con la posibilidad de acceder a llamadas y mensajes sin depender de cámaras, conexión a internet o pantallas a color. En 2026, conseguir una unidad nueva resulta casi imposible, pero el interés por los teléfonos clásicos mantiene activos los anuncios de ejemplares usados.
El Nokia 1100 superó los 250 millones de unidades vendidas
El alcance comercial del Nokia 1100 no ha sido superado por otro celular. Según datos de Visual Capitalist, basados en informes de Yahoo Finance y Omdia, el modelo vendió más de 250 millones de unidades en todo el mundo.
El segundo puesto también pertenece a Nokia. El Nokia 1110 alcanzó 248 millones de equipos vendidos, mientras que el iPhone 6 y el iPhone 6 Plus sumaron 222 millones de unidades. La distancia ilustra el impacto que tuvo el modelo lanzado en 2003.
Más de 250 millones de unidades convierten al Nokia 1100 en el celular más vendido de la historia. La cifra se explica, en buena medida, por su llegada a mercados emergentes y por una propuesta dirigida a usuarios que buscaban un aparato fiable, económico y sencillo.
Para millones de personas, el Nokia 1100 fue el primer teléfono móvil propio. La estrategia de la compañía consistió en priorizar la accesibilidad y la durabilidad, dos factores que facilitaron la expansión de la telefonía móvil durante los primeros años de la década de 2000.
Un celular diseñado para llamadas, mensajes y autonomía
El equipo fue concebido para cumplir tareas esenciales. No tenía cámara, acceso a internet ni pantalla a color. Su objetivo era permitir llamadas y mensajes SMS en distintas condiciones, con un diseño orientado a resistir el uso cotidiano.
Entre sus elementos principales estaban:
- Batería con autonomía de hasta una semana.
- Linterna LED integrada.
- Carcasa robusta con superficie antideslizante.
- Teclado de silicona.
- Pantalla monocromática.
- Despertador, calculadora y calendario.
- Juegos básicos, entre ellos Snake.
La batería de larga duración fue una de las características que diferenciaron al modelo frente a otros teléfonos de su época. La posibilidad de utilizarlo durante varios días sin recargarlo resultaba útil para usuarios con acceso limitado a electricidad o para quienes necesitaban un aparato centrado en la comunicación.
La linterna también se convirtió en una función reconocible. Junto con el teclado físico y la carcasa resistente, aportó una imagen asociada a un equipo preparado para funcionar sin depender de accesorios o configuraciones complejas.
El precio actual depende del estado del dispositivo
En plataformas de segunda mano, los ejemplares del Nokia 1100 aparecen desde USD 70. El valor puede variar según el estado físico, el funcionamiento de la batería, la presencia de cargador y accesorios, o si conserva su caja original.
El precio actual supera el coste aproximado de lanzamiento, aunque no responde a prestaciones modernas. Su valor está vinculado al interés de coleccionistas, la nostalgia y la búsqueda de equipos que representan una etapa anterior de la telefonía móvil.
Encontrar una unidad nueva es casi imposible después de más de dos décadas desde su llegada al mercado. Por eso, la mayoría de los teléfonos disponibles pertenecen al circuito de reventa y pueden presentar desgaste, problemas de batería o falta de componentes originales.
Utilizar un Nokia 1100 como teléfono principal presenta obstáculos. El modelo solo funciona con redes 2G, una tecnología que ha sido desactivada en gran parte de Estados Unidos, Europa y varios países de Latinoamérica para dar paso al 4G y al 5G.
Sin cobertura 2G, el dispositivo no puede realizar llamadas ni enviar mensajes. En muchas zonas urbanas, queda reducido a funciones locales como la linterna, el despertador, la calculadora y los juegos.
Tampoco permite utilizar aplicaciones, acceder a internet, enviar fotos o almacenar una gran cantidad de contactos. La memoria interna admite menos de 50 números, una capacidad alejada de las necesidades actuales.
Aun con esas limitaciones, el Nokia 1100 conserva cualidades que contrastan con los teléfonos inteligentes: es difícil de hackear y su batería puede durar hasta una semana.

articles.title: Safaricom fires 118 staff for fraud even as incidents fall 82%
articles.text:
Safaricom dismissed 118 employees for fraud in the year to March, even as fraud incidents fell 82%, pointing to a declining insider threat amid an intensified crackdown at Kenya’s largest telecoms operator.
The figure, disclosed in the company’s 2026 Sustainable Business Report released on Tuesday at its Nairobi headquarters, is more than four times the 28 dismissals recorded in the year to March 2021. It equates to about 2% of the 5,648 people the report lists as employees.
Earlier disclosures put the tally at 95 in the year to March 2024 and 113 in the year to March 2025, so the climb has been steady rather than a one-off spike.
Insider conduct carries unusual weight at Safaricom as staff sit close to customer data, SIM registration and the agent network that moves money across M-PESA, Kenya’s dominant mobile-money platform. The report treats theft, falsifying company records, and unauthorised access to customer call records as gross misconduct that can result in dismissal.
“Our customers entrust us with their personal information, communications and financial transactions and expect our services to be secure, reliable and responsible,” Safaricom said in the report.
The report lists 118 fraud cases investigated and 118 dismissals, along with three disciplinary warnings, up from none the prior year. Referrals to law enforcement doubled from seven to 14. Fraud was the most common concern raised through Safaricom’s anonymous ethics hotline.
The rise comes as the company says its anti-fraud push is working. It cut fraud incidents by 82%, short of a 90% target, and recovered 46% of reported fraud losses. Monitoring and analytics also recovered KES 953 million ($7.4 million) linked to inflated agent commissions.
Safaricom said it moved from an investigation-led model to real-time detection covering internal, distributor and mobile-money fraud. The report does not break down dismissals by role, value internal losses, or say how many cases led to charges.
According to the report, fraud awareness training reached 5,643 people across staff, call centres, M-PESA, distributors and brand ambassadors, and 98% of employees completed the annual ethics programme.
Group Chief Risk Officer Nicholas Mulila said the company is committed to “embedding accountability across our operations.” Safaricom named in-person social engineering as the largest source of customer fraud.
Crackdown on insider threats
The staff dismissals over fraud mirror what is happening in the banking industry, where sharper detection has also pushed dismissals higher. KCB Group, Kenya’s largest bank by assets, dismissed 60 staff for fraud in 2025, up from 34 in 2024, even as reported fraud incidents fell to 201 from 339, according to its sustainability report. Most of the 50 dismissals were in Kenya.
In May 2025, Equity Group’s chief executive officer, James Mwangi, said the lender had dismissed more than 1,200 employees after an audit of staff transactions, including personal M-PESA activity. Mwangi said the company would make such conduct audits a permanent practice, similar to performance appraisals.
Equity treated receiving money from customers as grounds for dismissal, a conflict-of-interest test wider than outright fraud. Safaricom’s figure covers only cases it investigated as fraud.
Outside finance, Kenya Power dismissed at least 20 employees over irregularities in the year to June 2025, including three who colluded with guards and drivers in a diesel-theft scheme that cost it KES 207.6 million ($1.5 million).

articles.title: Why Africa needs its own AI off switch
articles.text:
Imagine that it is 6 a.m. in the wholesale markets of Nairobi. Merchants are delivering vegetables from up-country farms to the retailers who sell to the city’s households. Everyone is using M-Pesa, Safaricom’s mobile money platform, when suddenly, the system crashes, bringing the market to a standstill. Imagine that across the continent in Accra, MTN’s MoMo has also crashed, and business in Makola Market has all but stopped.
With the growing number of cyberattacks caused by artificial intelligence, these are highly plausible scenarios. In both these cases, Safaricom, MTN, and the Kenyan and Ghanaian governments need an off switch, or the technical ability and know-how to stop a rogue AI agent from executing its code on their payment systems.
Currently, the conversation on AI agents revolves around China versus the U.S., open versus closed models, and who will dominate the AI race. But in Africa’s capitals, the distinction that will ultimately matter is not whose product was used to build a system, or who dominates whom, but rather whether AI can serve its purpose and be controlled locally. So how can Africa build with agency, and with control over the code and makeup of its own systems, even though they are built on foreign technology?
African countries are already building AI for digital transformation, as outlined in the African Union’s continental AI strategy and country-specific AI strategies. Policymakers are building AI infrastructure but rarely discuss how AI delivers economic growth in a safe environment. Developers across Africa are creating AI-powered innovations that sit on the continent’s digital infrastructure — chief among them is mobile money. These innovations bring new opportunities, but also new threats. In July, AI agents running inside an OpenAI evaluation attacked the production infrastructure of Hugging Face. In September, rogue OpenAI agents breached Australian government websites. Africa, the home of mobile money, which has brought financial inclusion to hundreds of millions, may be the next target.
In countries like Kenya and Ghana, mobile money is not simply another digital service; it is infrastructure for everyday economic activity. It is how small traders receive payments, households move money, and bills are settled. The scale is significant: More than $2 trillion flowed through mobile money globally in 2025, of which $1.4 trillion, roughly two-thirds, was transacted in sub-Saharan Africa. East Africa alone accounted for $806 billion and West Africa for $498 billion. An agent capable of disrupting transactions, manipulating accounts, or disabling access at scale could therefore disrupt livelihoods and economic activity very quickly, and a single point of failure can have outsize effects, with far-reaching consequences for people who have little to fall back on.
Small-scale traders mostly live on what they sell each day, rarely have credit, and in most African societies lack robust social welfare to cushion the loss. For a trader in Nairobi or Accra, losing a day’s income would be devastating, and the disruption can run back up the chain to farmers, and to the households and families who depend on the market.
So how do we protect it?
Building differently
The answer lies in how Africa builds its AI systems, and who controls them. Whether a rogue agent can simply be switched off depends on how the AI model is deployed. If it runs on a centrally controlled cloud service, the provider may be able to revoke access, disable credentials, or shut the system down; that is the closed-model case. If the underlying model is an open-weight one that has been downloaded, modified, and deployed independently across multiple systems, containment becomes much harder. The loss of control is therefore less about a machine suddenly becoming omnipotent and more about humans losing the ability to understand, interrupt, or reverse actions occurring across interconnected systems quickly enough.
African developers are building largely on open models, which are arguably cheaper and can be run locally. But they present a trade-off: Open models give developers more control over their own systems, but less protection when someone else misuses them. Closed models carry a cost of their own. When Hugging Face investigated the July intrusion, it had to run the forensic analysis on a Chinese open-weight model because the U.S. models blocked requests containing real attack code. The same central control that lets a closed model be switched off also constrains the people defending against it. This means both open- and closed-weight models carry their own vulnerabilities that must be addressed when building Africa’s AI economy.
This means building differently, beginning with partnerships that position Africa as a technology developer and not only a consumer, and through which it builds its own capability to design systems where the user is in control. Such partnerships are essential to ensure that the end user, and the state, retain control over access, and that dependency is not recreated. This also moves the narrative toward building African AI not around the U.S. or China but around avoiding lock-in to a single vendor or stack. The goal is solutions built with agency, which use imported technologies to develop homegrown solutions, with applications that are robust and equipped with the necessary security measures.
Those security measures are how Africa should insulate itself from crippling disruptions. African countries have limited cybersecurity and incident-response capacity, and they depend on foreign providers. So another key issue is capacity: Do African governments and firms have the monitoring systems, technical expertise, and redundancy needed to detect an autonomous system behaving unexpectedly and contain it quickly? Hugging Face detected and contained its intrusion, but its own automated systems initially failed to escalate the alert. It is one of the best-resourced AI companies in the world. Very few African public or private institutions have anything close to that capability. Africa must build its own cybersecurity defenses fit for the agentic AI age.
Building them demands a refocus in African AI policy, so that it treats resilience as seriously as adoption. As governments digitize and build AI on critical systems, they need human override mechanisms, segmentation, auditability, incident response, and credible offline fallbacks designed in from the beginning. That is the off switch, and on the day that M-Pesa and MoMo crash, it has to be in the hands of those who are responsible for protecting their citizens and their platforms.

articles.title: Why Physics Needs To Move At The Pace Of Design
articles.text:
Physics-based analysis becomes more consequential as chips, packages, boards, and systems are designed together.
Every hardware design contains decisions made before the team fully understands their physical consequences. An architecture is chosen. Components are placed. Materials are selected. Engineers bring experience and judgment to those choices, but the detailed physics often arrives later, when changing course is harder and more expensive.
That order of work limits what engineers can build. When every answer requires substantial preparation, compute and specialist time, teams have to decide which questions are worth asking. Promising ideas can be set aside because there is no practical way to investigate them within the schedule.
We built Vinci to change that. We recently announced a $250 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. The investment gives us the resources to accelerate a goal that reaches well beyond any single analysis: shortening the distance between what engineers can imagine and what they can build.
The cost of slow analysis extends into decisions made long before a simulation begins. Teams simplify designs so they can evaluate them. They add margin where uncertainty remains. They carry assumptions forward because testing every alternative would take too long.
Consider a change in component placement. It may improve one aspect of a design while changing how heat moves through the board. Differences in temperature and material expansion can also affect warpage. The engineer needs to understand those interactions while the placement is still a choice. If that understanding arrives after other decisions depend on it, even a small change can require substantial rework.
This becomes more consequential as engineers design chips, packages, boards and systems together. A decision about power affects cooling requirements. A packaging choice changes the physical constraints elsewhere. The number of interactions grows, while the time available to investigate them remains limited.
AI adds urgency to this problem. As engineering workflows become increasingly automated and agentic, they will be able to propose and act on more design choices. Each of those choices still has physical consequences. Generating possibilities is useful only if engineers can determine which ones will work.
Continuous Physics Reasoning makes trustworthy physical understanding available throughout design. Engineers can investigate a change, understand its consequences and use that understanding to decide what to do next, while the design is still moving.
Making this practical requires changes to the entire computational process. Vinci automates design understanding and preparation, combining agentic orchestration with our Foundation Model for Physics and GPU-native physics kernels. The platform delivers deterministic, solver-accurate results at manufacturing resolution and works across new designs without customer-specific training or fine-tuning.
Those properties matter together. Engineers need enough physical detail to evaluate the design they intend to manufacture. They need repeatable answers they can trust. And they need to investigate a new design without first building a model trained specifically for it.
We chose semiconductors as our first proving ground because their physical demands leave little room for compromise. Vinci is already running on production engineering programs, with commercial capabilities across thermal, thermo-mechanical and convective fluid behavior. Manufacturing-scale analyses that once required hours or days can be completed in minutes.
For an engineering team, that changes how much it can learn before committing. More alternatives become practical to evaluate. A question that would once have been deferred can inform the next design decision. Engineers can pursue ideas that would otherwise have been too costly or time-consuming to investigate.
Continuous Physics Reasoning gives us the foundation for a broader ambition. Once physical understanding can keep pace with design, we can work toward helping engineers determine what should change to improve a product, and eventually toward creating designs from human intent.
That is a demanding engineering problem. A useful recommendation has to account for how changing one part of a system affects the rest. It must work within constraints imposed by materials, manufacturing and the other disciplines involved in building a product. Extending physical understanding into that kind of engineering intelligence is central to our long-term work.
This financing will accelerate progress across both physics and engineering. We will expand physical coverage beyond the capabilities available today, develop more capable agentic engineering workflows and deepen integrations with the systems our customers use. We will also invest in the people and computing infrastructure needed to bring Vinci into more production programs.
The need extends well beyond semiconductors. Engineers developing vehicles, aircraft and satellites face different physical problems, but they share the need to understand the consequences of decisions while those decisions can still change. Our ambition is to make that understanding part of the infrastructure on which hardware engineering runs.
I am grateful to our customers, investors and team for helping us pursue this work. Our customers are putting Vinci to use on real engineering programs, where the value of an answer depends on whether it can inform the work in front of them.
That is the standard we intend to keep building toward. Engineers should be able to pursue an idea because they can investigate it, understand its constraints and improve it. Giving them that ability throughout design can expand the range of products they are able to create. That is what this next chapter of Vinci is for.

articles.title: Ein Hauch von Apple-Store: Bei Mediamarkt kannst du jetzt auch beim Verkäufer bezahlen
articles.text:
Der Verkäufer wird zur Kasse: Was sich bei Mediamarkt und Saturn jetzt bei der Bezahlung ändert
Was Kund:innen im stationären Handel immer noch am meisten nervt, ist das Anstehen an der Kasse. Dass die Warterei zum Problem werden kann, zeigt eine aktuelle Studie des Zahlungsdienstleisters Adyen: 16 Prozent der Deutschen haben innerhalb von sechs Monaten mindestens einmal einen Einkauf im Supermarkt abgebrochen, weil ihnen die Wartezeit an der Kasse zu lang war. Selbst im Elektronikfachhandel waren es acht Prozent.
Ein mobiles Gerät als Kartenterminal
Die Elektronikketten Mediamarkt und Saturn setzen hier an und wollen das in Zukunft ändern. Denn wer hier einen neuen Fernseher, eine Waschmaschine oder ein Notebook beim Berater oder der Beraterin kauft, kann dort in Zukunft auch gleich sein Gerät bezahlen.
Möglich wird das über eine Soft-POS-Lösung, also ein mobiles Gerät, das als Kartenterminal funktioniert und den passenden Kassenzettel gleich mit auswirft oder an einen nahegelegenen Drucker sendet. Profitieren könnten davon sowohl die Kund:innen, weil sie nicht mehr anstehen müssen als auch das Verkaufspersonal, das nicht riskiert, dass der Kunde sich auf dem Weg zur Kasse doch noch umentscheidet.
Gleichzeitig kann der Einkauf natürlich schneller werden und die Beratung kann psychologisch angenehm in den Kaufabschluss übergehen. Eher nebenbei werden so natürlich auch die weiter bestehenden Kassen entlastet, weil die Warteschlangen dort kürzer werden. Mediamarkt arbeitet hier ja aus gutem Grund schon in den meisten Filialen mit mehreren Kassen und einer Sammelschlange – auch ein psychologischer Kniff, damit Kund:innen nicht den Eindruck haben, dass es überall schneller geht als in der eigenen Warteschlange.
Bundesweit in 400 Märkten
Die Elektronikkette hatte das Konzept unter dem Namen „Pay-on-Shopfloor“ schon vor einigen Wochen angekündigt. Nach einer Pilotphase in einigen Filialen ist die neue Bezahlmöglichkeit jetzt bundesweit in 400 Märkten verfügbar. Das Onboarding habe jeweils nur zwei Tage gedauert, erklären die Beteiligten. Komplett ersetzen wie im Apple Store will man die Kassenzone allerdings nicht, sondern sie eher ergänzen.
Die Kund:innen können und sollen also weiterhin auch an regulären Kassen und Selbstbedienungskassen bezahlen. Mit der zusätzlichen mobilen Bezahlmöglichkeit könne man das Einkaufserlebnis aber flexibler gestalten, erklärt das Unternehmen.
Technisch basiert das Konzept auf einer SoftPOS-Lösung des Zahlungsdienstleisters CCV. Die Software ermöglicht es, geeignete mobile Geräte zur Annahme von Kartenzahlungen zu nutzen. Der Payment-Anbieter Computop hat die Lösung in die bestehende Zahlungsinfrastruktur von Mediamarkt und Saturn integriert und übernimmt die zentrale Steuerung der Transaktionen. Die gemeinsame Infrastruktur kombiniert dabei unter anderem den Onlinehandel, klassische Kassensysteme und Self-Checkout-Lösungen. Das ermöglicht, es, zusätzliche Bezahlmöglichkeiten einführen, ohne jeweils eine vollständig neue Zahlungsarchitektur aufbauen zu müssen.
Auffällig ist aber, dass die Lösung einmal mehr ein Schritt hin zu bargeldlosem Bezahlen ist – denn naturgemäß funktioniert das Pay-on-Shopfloor-Konzept nur mit Karte oder Wearable, während Kund:innen, die mit Bargeld zahlen wollen, weiterhin anstehen müssen. Je nachdem, wie das System in Deutschland ankommt, wolle man die Lösung auch in den internationalen Filialen von Mediamarkt und Saturn einsetzen, heißt es. Genauere Angaben dazu gibt es allerdings bislang nicht.

articles.title: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.
Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago, as development costs have surged.
“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.
Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.
If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”
While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.
The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.
Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.
While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings.
Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

articles.title: Risco de colapso de correntes do Atlântico é ignorado em planos climáticos; Brasil é exceção
articles.text:
Um sistema de correntes oceânicas essencial para regular o clima da Terra pode sofrer um enfraquecimento significativo até o fim do século, mas o risco ainda é ignorado pela maioria dos governos em seus planos de adaptação climática. De 91 planos nacionais apresentados à Convenção das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima, apenas dois mencionam a possibilidade de colapso dessas correntes — e nenhum deles prevê medidas concretas para enfrentar o cenário.
O alerta foi publicado em artigo na revista Nature Sustainability, elaborado por pesquisadores que analisaram como os países se preparam para possíveis mudanças na circulação do Oceano Atlântico.
O sistema em questão é a Circulação Meridional de Revolvimento do Atlântico, conhecida pela sigla AMOC. Ela funciona como uma espécie de esteira transportadora oceânica: leva águas quentes da superfície em direção ao norte do Atlântico e devolve águas mais frias para o sul em camadas profundas.
Esse movimento redistribui calor pelo planeta e influencia temperaturas e padrões de chuva em regiões muito distantes do oceano. Com o aquecimento global, a circulação está enfraquecendo e pode continuar a perder força ao longo deste século.
Os pesquisadores ressaltam, porém, que um colapso completo é considerado improvável antes de 2100. Um estudo recente citado pelos autores projetou redução de 50% na intensidade da AMOC até o fim do século em cenário intermediário de emissões.
O que aconteceria se as correntes enfraquecessem ainda mais?
Uma redução acentuada da circulação poderia provocar mudanças importantes no clima de diferentes regiões. No norte da Europa, por exemplo, a diminuição do transporte de calor vindo dos trópicos poderia favorecer episódios de frio extremo durante o inverno. Simulações climáticas com a AMOC desligada indicaram a possibilidade de temperaturas de até -20 °C em Londres (Inglaterra).
Os efeitos também poderiam atingir regiões que dependem das chuvas de monção. Experimentos com modelos climáticos apontaram enfraquecimento médio de 29% das monções da África Ocidental e de 19% das monções de verão da Índia em cenários de interrupção da circulação.
Essas alterações aumentariam os riscos para o abastecimento de água e a produção de alimentos em áreas dependentes dessas chuvas. Outros estudos mencionados no artigo apontam maior risco de secas severas em partes da América Central, da África Ocidental e da região amazônica.
A pesca e o nível do mar também poderiam ser afetados. Mudanças nas temperaturas oceânicas e na distribuição das águas teriam consequências para comunidades costeiras, estoques pesqueiros e estruturas de proteção contra a elevação do mar.
Leia mais:
- Cientistas descobrem como prever El Niño com até um ano de antecedência
- Como as mudanças climáticas favorecem doenças infecciosas no Brasil
- Relatório da ONU revela novo recorde de gases de efeito estufa
Brasil menciona o risco, mas preparação ainda é um desafio
- Entre os 91 planos nacionais analisados, o Brasil está entre os dois países que mencionam a AMOC. O plano brasileiro inclui alerta de que o desligamento do sistema poderia deslocar a faixa de chuvas do Atlântico para o sul e contribuir para levar a Floresta Amazônica a ponto de colapso;
- A Irlanda é o outro país citado. Como depende da circulação para manter seu clima relativamente ameno, o documento irlandês reconhece que a adaptação, por si só, pode não ser suficiente diante de um colapso. O plano também conclui que nenhum planejamento nacional consegue se preparar plenamente para pontos de inflexão climática desse tipo;
- Ainda assim, os autores avaliam que mencionar o risco não basta. Nenhum dos dois planos apresenta ações concretas para responder à possibilidade de colapso da circulação;
- O problema é que muitos investimentos em infraestrutura, abastecimento de água e proteção costeira são planejados para durar décadas. Se as mudanças climáticas forem diferentes das previstas inicialmente, essas estruturas podem deixar de cumprir sua função e gerar prejuízos elevados — especialmente em países com menos recursos para reagir a situações inesperadas.
Como os países podem se preparar?
Os pesquisadores propõem cinco medidas para incorporar o risco da AMOC ao planejamento climático: identificar países e investimentos mais vulneráveis; testar projetos com simulações que considerem o colapso da circulação; priorizar soluções flexíveis, que possam ser adaptadas ao longo do tempo; manter o monitoramento das correntes oceânicas; e revisar as projeções climáticas globais.
O objetivo não é prever exatamente quando — ou mesmo se — ocorrerá um colapso, mas verificar se decisões tomadas hoje continuariam funcionando em diferentes cenários climáticos.
Os autores também ressaltam que preparar-se para esse risco não deve desviar recursos do combate aos impactos já observados, como ondas de calor, secas e enchentes. A redução rápida das emissões de gases de efeito estufa continua sendo fundamental.
A AMOC já passou por mudanças drásticas no passado. Estudos indicam que o sistema esteve perto de interrupção quase completa há cerca de 17,5 mil anos, após o período mais frio da última era glacial. O histórico mostra que alterações profundas são possíveis, embora não determine quando ou se uma nova interrupção acontecerá.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: J'ai essayé la Peugeot E-208 GTi : 281 ch de pur plaisir, mais seulement 200 km pour en profiter
articles.text:
Ressusciter un blason disparu est un pari risqué, surtout quand il a cristallisé la passion automobile sur plusieurs générations. S’il n’y a que les plus férus qui se souviendront de la toute première GTi chez Peugeot avec la 604, la plus marquante restera la 205 GTi.
Au fil des années, les modèles se sont succédé, chaque fois accompagnés d’une déclinaison sportive : 309, 106, 306, 206/207 (baptisées RC en France), 308 et enfin 208. Sauf que depuis son restylage de 2019, la petite dernière n’avait pas encore le droit à sa version pimentée, la faute aux normes CO2. L’idée d’avoir une variante électrique sportive sous le badge PSE (Peugeot Sport Engineered) était alors dans les cartons. Finalement avorté, le projet ne se concrétisera qu’en 2025, avec le retour inespéré du célèbre blason GTi.
GTi et électrique, l’association sacrilège ? Il n’y aura que ceux qui ne l’auront pas essayé (ou n’auront pas lu d’essais) qui scanderont à la traitrise. Moi, c’est avec le cœur enjoué que je me suis rendu près des Highlands en Écosse pour voir ce que la nouvelle Peugeot E-208 GTi avait dans le ventre. Ça fait longtemps que je n’avais pas eu un tel sourire au volant !
| Caractéristique | Donnée | 
|---|---|
| Modèle / Version testée | Peugeot E-208 GTi | 
| Prix (à partir de / version testée) | 42 900 € | 
| Autonomie WLTP | 353 km/375 km* | 
| Autonomie constatée (essai) | ~200 km | 
| Consommation relevée | 25 kWh/100 km | 
| Capacité batterie | 51 kWh (utiles) | 
| Puissance / Couple | 281 ch / 345 Nm | 
| 0 à 100 km/h | 5,5 s | 
| Vitesse max | 180 km/h | 
| Puissance de charge max (DC) | 100 kW | 
| Temps de charge 20-80 % (DC) | 27 min | 
| Temps de charge 20-80 % (AC) | 3h10 (11 kW) / 4h40 (7,4 kW) | 
| Dimensions (L x l x h) | 4,10 m x 1,77 m x 1,40 m | 
| Coffre (litres) | 309 | 
Design extérieur de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : sportive discrète
De loin, la E-208 GTi ressemble à n’importe quelle banale 208 électrique. À mesure que l’on s’approche de la bête, on se rend compte qu’il y a de nombreux détails indiquant qu’il ne s’agit pas du modèle de monsieur et madame tout le monde. Une sportivité discrète parfaitement en adéquation avec l’esprit GTi et sa couleur indissociable : le rouge.
Commençons par la face avant, où de fines barettes viennent habiller les bordures de la calandre. Ces éléments vifs soulignent également le blason au milieu ainsi que les lentilles des phares. Sur le profil, le liseré rouge de la 205 GTi est réinterprété ici au niveau des passages de roues, sans oublier la présence du badge en trois lettres avec un effet translucide pour un effet différenciant. À l’arrière, le rouge s’invite aussi sous le spoiler.
Tout ce cocktail fonctionne remarquablement bien avec la teinte Rouge Élixir, Noir Perla Nera ou encore le Blanc Okénite de mon modèle d’essai, lui donnant un look rallye. En revanche, j’ai plus de doute sur l’association avec les autres couleurs au catalogue, notamment le jaune fluo.
Mais l’arrivée du blason sportif n’est pas que poudre aux yeux. Les voies ont été élargies de 56 mm à l’avant et 28 mm à l’arrière, tandis que la caisse a été abaissée de 25 mm. Cela se voit visuellement, la citadine paraît nettement plus ramassée.
Aux quatre coins, la 208 GTi électrique s’appuie sur des jantes spécifiques de 18 pouces singeant les jantes percées de son aïeule, les trous laissant apercevoir d’immenses disques de 355 mm, pincés par des étriers… rouges bien sûr !
Design intérieur de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : ça sent bon le sport !
Même si j’avais déjà vu à quoi ressemblait l’intérieur, le voir « pour de vrai » n’est pas pareil. J’ouvre la porte et oh, quelle merveilleuse moquette rouge. Le genre de détail qui fait immédiatement la différence et qui apporte une bonne dose de muscle. Rajoutez à ça des sièges baquets vous enveloppant bien comme il faut, une sellerie bi-matière intéressante, des touches de rouge (encore) et de l’Alcantara sur le volant. J’adore l’ambiance.
Mais je ne peux pas m’empêcher de tiquer sur des détails. Hormis le revêtement légèrement moussé imitant la fibre de carbone, courant le long de la planche de bord, le reste de l’habitacle est couvert de plastique dur noir.
Il y en a partout : un gros bloc sur les portes, sur les côtés du compartiment central. Je comprends qu’il faille rationnaliser, mais Peugeot aurait tout de même pu pousser les matériaux plus loin sur une version aussi spéciale, avec un ciel de toit en suédine par exemple.
Technologies embarquées de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : une interface relookée
La partie info-divertissement est identique à la 208 standard avec le compteur numérique en 3D « i-Cockpit » accompagné d’un écran tactile de 10 pouces. Cependant, l’interface se met dans le thème grâce à un affichage tout de rouge vêtu ainsi qu’un menu alignant plusieurs compteurs évoquant les cadrans d’époque.
L’ensemble souffre malheureusement de quelques latences à l’utilisation. Un défaut sur toutes les versions du modèle, pas uniquement la GTi. On privilégiera donc plutôt la connexion Apple CarPlay/Android Auto livrée de série.
Côté aides à la conduite, sont livrés d’office la conduite semi-autonome (régulateur de vitesse + maintien dans la voie) et la caméra 360°. Là aussi, la résolution d’image de cette dernière n’est pas plus au rendez-vous que sur les autres versions.
Au volant de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : c’est de la balle
Bon, même si cela réhausse l’expérience globale, une voiture affublée d’un blason comme GTi ne s’évalue pas par la réactivité de ses écrans ou ses aides à la conduite (qu’on désactivera volontiers ici), mais évidemment par la conduite.
Avec ses 281 ch pour 345 Nm de couple, la 208 GTi est une vraie bombe. Non sérieusement, quel pied ! Il y a amplement de quoi s’amuser sur petites routes, alors que l’on trouve un vrai esprit de petites sportives thermiques. Peugeot promet un 0 à 100 km/h en 5,5 secondes et des reprises de 80 km/h à 120 km/h en 3,2 secondes. Ou quand le lion se transforme en guépard.
Le toucher de route est bien au rendez-vous avec un train avant précis et une direction prouvant qu’il est possible d’avoir du ressenti au volant d’une voiture électrique. Forcément, sur les chaussées humides écossaises de ma boucle d’essai, le nez cherche (très) légèrement sa trajectoire quand on met brutalement le pied dedans. Honnêtement, on s’en moque que la motricité puisse parfois être ainsi. Car ce qui prime ici, c’est le plaisir. J’ai été surpris de retrouver un réel côté joueur où le train arrière peut se dérober dans les virages serrés, donnant du piment dans la conduite, tout en restant totalement maîtrisable.
La E-208 GTi s’illustre surtout par son différentiel autobloquant mécanique type Torsen. Autrement dit, le félin peut passer dans les courbes à des allures auxquelles on ne s’attendait pas, sans broncher.
Le châssis garni d’une barre antiroulis arrière de 31 mm sur cette version GTi déballe toute sa rigueur et me voilà en train de bondir de virages en virages sans le moindre mouvement de caisse. On peut applaudir le travail des liaisons au sol qui nous offre une adhérence phénoménale, comme le bitume abrasif des routes écossaises aidant aussi un peu à garder stable la citadine malgré l’humidité. Il faudrait être fou pour troquer les pneumatiques Michelin Pilot Sport 4S livrés d’office pour les Hankook Ventus S1 Evo3 en option gratuite. Tant pis pour les kilomètres grapillés, le grip apporté est bien trop jouissif à la conduite.
Ce que je reproche à cette voiture si engageante, c’est son freinage. Alors qu’on a souvent tendance à regretter le manque de feeling au niveau de la pédale, pour une fois il est bon ici, grâce à une excellente gestion de la répartition hydraulique/régénératif. En fait, c’est plutôt le mordant qui manque. La faute n’est pas à rejeter sur les disques, carrément généreux avec 355 mm de diamètre, mais sur le maître cylindre sous dimensionné qui n’envoie donc pas assez de pression dans les étriers. Et ne comptez pas sur le freinage récupératif au lever de pied (position B) pour vous ralentir énormément, il est désactivé en mode Sport. D’ailleurs, cette fameuse position B ne permet pas d’aller jusqu’à l’arrêt, pourtant vendue comme One Pedal. Étrange.
Et en conduite tranquille alors, la lionne devient-elle un chaton mignon ? C’est bien là le débat. À rythme soutenu, la citadine enchante, mais à allure plus polie l’emballement peut vite s’effondrer, revers de son amortissement raffermie spécifiquement, qui se traduit par des secousses dès la moindre bosse ou bouche d’égout survolée. S’ajoutent à cela une insonorisation peu poussée avec un léger sifflement perceptible du moteur électrique et des bruits d’air venant notamment du toit vitré. Ces derniers sont réduits un fois le pare-soleil fermé, mais le mieux serait finalement de ne pas opter pour cette option à 650 € (pour une fois). L’intérieur de la cabine peut aussi se montrer très bruyant sur revêtement dégradé en raison de bruits de roulement prononcés.
Autant d’éléments qui rendraient une utilisation quotidienne potentiellement plus éreintante sur le long terme comparé à ses concurrentes. Une Mini John Cooper Works E, déjà radicale en roulage « pépère », paraît bien plus docile, et je ne parle même pas de l’Alpine A290. Mais ces deux-là ne proposent pas un comportement aussi affûté que cette délicieuse Peugeot E-208 GTi.
Autonomie et consommation de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : vite, une borne
La réelle contrainte à l’usage de la 208 GTi électrique viendra de son autonomie. Avec sa batterie NMC de 51 kWh utiles, la citadine sportive promet 353 km WLTP d’autonomie avec les pneus Michelin et jusqu’à 375 km équipés des gommes Hankook mentionnés plus haut.
Parti à 100 %, le tableau de bord m’annonce 350 km d’autonomie. Sauf qu’après 167 bornes et une conduite digne d’une GTi, il ne me reste que 18 % de batterie et à peine 39 km d’autonomie. Consommation moyenne : 25 kWh/100 km, soit environ 200 km d’autonomie réelle, en siphonnant intégralement la capacité disponible. Autant dire que la plage d’utilisation idéale 10-80% est assez réduite.
Il faudra donc penser à bien connaître son environnement de jeu si l’on prévoit des virées loin du domicile. Sur borne rapide, le 10 à 80 % demande 27 minutes, à une puissance maximale de 100 kW.
Prix et concurrence de la Peugeot E-208 GTi : on signe ?
Alors, conquis ? D’accord, ça vous fera donc 42 900 € ! Gloups. Heureusement, Peugeot offre d’ores et déjà une remise de 1 850 €, à laquelle on peut ajouter 3 600 € de prime CEE (montant minimum). Le prix frontal tombe ainsi à 37 450 €, ce qui reste conséquent compte tenu de l’autonomie.
Du côté de la concurrence, la Mini John Cooper Works E avec ses 258 ch et 371 km WLTP est vendue 42 600 €, mais est inéligible aux aides à cause de sa fabrication en Chine. L’Alpine A290 réclame quant à elle 39 500 € en version GT de 180 ch (382 km WLTP) et 42 700 € en version GT Performance de 220 ch (365 km WLTP). Enfin, la Volkswagen Polo GTI offre 226 ch, 431 km WLTP pour 41 450 €.
Au sein du groupe Stellantis, il y a aussi les cousines techniques :
- Lancia Ypsilon HF : même prix, même prime CEE, mais pas de remise
- Opel Corsa GSE : 39 990 €, 4 300 € de remise et 3 600 € de prime CEE = 32 090 €
Le verdict
Peugeot E-208 GTi
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Châssis diablement efficace
- Puissance à gogo pour une citadine
- Du fun et encore du fun au volant
- Look GTi charmant (surtout les moquettes rouges)
On a moins aimé
- Autonomie trop limitée en conduite sportive
- Certains détails de finition intérieure à revoir

articles.title: 4 millions de coeurs CPU en plus : GitHub muscle son infrastructure pour faire face au code généré par IA — Frandroid
articles.text:
Il y a quelques mois, les agents IA étaient encore un outil que les développeurs testaient avec espoir ou méfiance suivant les mentalités. Mais la situation semble avoir bien évolué : en septembre, ces outils étaient à l’origine de plus de 40 % des pull requests ouvertes sur GitHub, contre 17 % en mars.
Du moins selon les chiffres publiés par la plateforme à l’occasion d’Universe, et de son rapport annuel Octoverse, qui donnent tous deux la mesure du phénomène. Sur les douze mois achevés fin septembre, les développeurs ont poussé du code 17,9 milliards de fois, plus qu’en 2024 et 2025 réunis, détaille GitHub sur son blog.
Les commits, ces instantanés de modifications, ont atteint le nombre de 34,3 milliards, contre 12,9 milliards un an plus tôt. La courbe s’est surtout cabrée à partir de juin : en septembre, GitHub enregistrait environ six fois plus de commits qu’en septembre 2025. Une montée en charge qu’on a d’ailleurs pu observer (ou subir) cet été avec les « quelques » ralentissements de la plateforme.
Quatre millions de cœurs CPU de plus, et ça ne suffira pas
Pour suivre la cadence, GitHub a ajouté depuis janvier 4 millions de cœurs CPU à son infrastructure, 160 pétaoctets de stockage haute vitesse et 50 Tb/s de capacité réseau. Mais le volume de code n’est ici qu’une partie du problème : chaque commit ou pull request déclenche en effet une cascade de tâches automatisées (tests, vérifications de style, analyses de sécurité). GitHub Actions, l’outil d’automatisation maison, a ainsi exécuté 45,4 milliards de tâches en un an, plus de trois fois plus que l’an passé, soit 1 440 par seconde.
Empiler les serveurs ne suffirait donc plus. GitHub a dû revoir l’architecture de Git en simplifiant les briques de base, en séparant le stockage du calcul et en réduisant la coordination entre les systèmes. En parallèle, la plateforme bascule vers un déploiement multirégion sur Azure, le cloud de Microsoft, une migration qu’elle compte boucler début 2027.
    Pour aller plus loin
Fini la lenteur et les pubs : j’ai redonné une seconde jeunesse à ma Google TV en 10 minutes
            
Plus de code ne veut pas dire plus de travail abattu
L’un des éléments les plus intéressants du billet de GitHub, c’est peut-être qu’il distingue le volume de code du travail « utile ». Les dépôts créés cette année et dotés d’un fichier de configuration pour agent affichent en moyenne huit fois plus de commits que les autres. Un écart qui en dit sans doute autant sur la propension des agents à multiplier les petites modifications que sur le travail réellement accompli. La plateforme le reconnaît d’ailleurs elle-même en ouverture de son billet : ce qui compte, c’est le travail terminé, pas la quantité de code.
Le travail fourni par les agents n’est toutefois pas à jeter : en septembre, 90 % de leurs pull requests étaient fusionnées sous deux semaines, contre environ 86 % pour les autres. Enfin, côté langages utilisés, TypeScript, Python et Rust, les communautés qui grossissent le plus vite, sont aussi celles où l’IA intervient le plus, dans 40 à 44 % des pull requests fusionnées.
    Pour aller plus loin
QUELLE IA : on a lancé un comparateur gratuit de 252 modèles pour trouver le bon selon votre usage
            
Il n’y a plus qu’à voir comment l’IA va encore chambouler les investissements de GitHub dans les mois et années à venir. En attendant, la plateforme parie que tout le code écrit à ce jour représentera moins de 1 % de celui des cinq prochaines années. Autant dire que les 4 millions de cœurs ajoutés cette année ne seront clairement pas suffisants.

articles.title: Nouveautés HBO Max : les films et séries à ne pas rater en streaming en novembre 2026
articles.text:
Nouveautés HBO Max : les films et séries à ne pas rater en streaming en novembre 2026
Abonnés à HBO Max et en quête de nouveaux films et séries à regarder ? Ça tombe bien, la plateforme de streaming vient de dévoiler les nouveautés de son catalogue pour le mois de novembre 2026.
Après un mois d'octobre bien fourni - avec notamment Crystal Lake et le dernier Destination Finale - la plateforme de streaming HBO Max garde le rythme au mois de novembre 2026 avec de nouveaux films, séries et documentaires ajoutés à son généreux catalogue.
Et il y a de quoi ravir une fois de plus un peu tout le monde ce mois-ci, avec la nouvelle saison de The Gilded Age, la série The Good daughter, ou encore les films Les Trois Mousquetaires, Apocalypse Now, Wolf Man et Les filles du Docteur March.
Mais avant de vous présenter la liste des nouveautés de HBO Max en novembre 2026, on a sélectionné pour vous les deux événements du mois sur le service de streaming.
La série du mois sur HBO Max
The Gilded Age - Saison 4
Après avoir ébranlé l'ordre établi de la haute société, Bertha Russell doit désormais composer avec les conséquences de ses choix. Alors qu'Agnes van Rhijn tente de reprendre la place qui lui revenait autrefois, Marian poursuit sa quête d'indépendance et Peggy cherche à se faire accepter par sa future belle-famille. Dans un monde en pleine mutation, où ambitions et aspirations se heurtent à la réalité, chacun apprendra qu'il faut parfois se méfier de ce que l'on souhaite.
Le créateur de la série culte Downton Abbey, Julian Fellowes, quitte la noblesse anglaise et rend visite à l’aristocratie américaine avec cette série pleine de décors flamboyants, de costumes fabuleux et de dialogues pinçants. La série revient ce mois-ci avec une saison 4 où ses personnages sont plus que jamais prêts à se battre pour être à la tête de la haute société, coûte que coûte.
À partir du 4 novembre sur HBO Max.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Le film du mois sur HBO Max
Les Trois Mousquetaires : D'Artagnan
Du Louvre au Palais de Buckingham, des bas-fonds de Paris au siège de La Rochelle… dans un Royaume divisé par les guerres de religion et menacé d’invasion par l’Angleterre, une poignée d’hommes et de femmes vont croiser leurs épées et lier leur destin à celui de la France.
Cette nouvelle adaptation du classique d'Alexandre Dumas arrive à remettre au goût du jour une histoire pourtant bien connue. Le réalisateur Mathieu Bourboulon livre une aventure nerveuse et flamboyante, dôtée d'un souffle épique non négligeable grâce à une production soignée. Du grand spectacle qui ne réussit pas tout ce qu'il entreprend, mais qui reste hautement divertissant, avec (pour ne rien gâcher) un casting cinq étoiles : Romain Duris, François Civil, Vincent Cassel, Eva Green, Lyna Khoudri...
Disponible le 8 novembre sur HBO Max.

articles.title: Slice Into GFN Thursday: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches on GeForce NOW
articles.text:
This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats.
Something wicked this blade comes. S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches on GeForce NOW today, bringing a scarily good blend of martial arts and punk fantasy to the cloud.
There’s also something on the horizon for adventurers: World of Warcraft: Forever arrives Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 3 p.m. PST, with a launch-week access reward coming for GeForce NOW members.
This week’s lineup also includes nine games streaming from the GeForce NOW library, alongside new mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. That means more options to play, with no downloads or installs to haunt gamers’ devices.
There’s another sweet update for gamers in India: The option to sign up for four-month Performance and Ultimate memberships is launching tomorrow. Visit the GeForce NOW website for more information.
Cold Steel Meets Cloud Power
Framed for his master’s murder and gravely wounded, a warrior named Soul has 66 days to uncover a conspiracy threatening the martial world in S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero. Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the game combines wuxia storytelling with cinematic action.
Master more than 30 primary weapons and over 20 Phantom Edges, chaining evasions, deflections and counterattacks into fluid combat. Traditional Chinese martial arts meet mechanical prosthetics, industrial ruins and rock music in a distinctive kungfupunk world.
Ultimate members can wield GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, compatible TVs and more. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage, leaving more time for the next clash. Soul’s clock is ticking, but the download bar doesn’t have to. Cut to the chase and hop into the game today.
Azeroth Awaits
Get ready for Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever, arriving Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 3 p.m. PT, on GeForce NOW. Explore an iconic world reimagined with new and expanded zones, new gameplay enhancements, upgraded graphics and more.
A new reward will give eligible GeForce NOW members access to join beginning at launch and ending Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT. The reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers for new WoW users who don’t already have a subscription, while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis.
Once available, members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem. Mark the calendar and gather the party — launch week is approaching.
New Tricks and Treats
Familiar favorites have a few new tricks, too: Mod.io support is now available directly in game for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered, bringing more ways to make Night City and the Continent feel different.
And the treats keep coming with the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:
- Phantom Blade Zero (New release on Steam, Oct. 28)
- ATMOSFAR (New release on Steam, Oct. 29)
- Hunting Simulator 3 (New release on Steam, Oct. 29)
- Queen’s Domain (New release on Steam, Oct. 30)
- Dimraeth (Steam)
- Dressmaker (Steam)
- Halloween (Epic Games Store)
- Hell Let Loose: Vietnam (Epic Games Store)
- The Seance of Blake Manor (Steam)
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.
Settle in for a scary-good gaming session: Grab a day pass to experience Performance or Ultimate cloud gaming. Gamers can then apply the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership upgrade.
What’s haunting the gaming playlist this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

articles.title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
articles.text:
Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One, Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network.
Key insights
- Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure.
- Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.
- Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment.
Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour
Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer.
More swarms, fewer giants
Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025:
- 96% ended in under 10 minutes
- 98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website
On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad.
Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot. Mirai-classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21.
Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP
The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3.
Meanwhile, DNS amplification surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open DNS resolvers in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other UDP floods climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources.
Most-attacked industry
While Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively.
Most-attacked locations
Geographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranks
Adding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries.
Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year.
Top 10
The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift.
Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the Internet
Cloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by free, unmetered DDoS protection that runs at every one of our 330+ cities globally, backed by 500 Tbps of network capacity. Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention. And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter.
To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers.
Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit Cloudflare Radar.
About Cloudforce One
Driven by a mission to help defend the Internet, Cloudforce One draws on telemetry from Cloudflare's global network — which protects more than 20% of the web — to drive threat research and operational response, protecting critical systems for millions of organizations worldwide.

articles.title: Wenn Werbung schützt: So nutzen Non-Profits KI als ethisches Werkzeug
articles.text:
Wenn Werbung schützt: So nutzen Non-Profits KI als ethisches Werkzeug
Ein Kind berichtet von häuslicher Gewalt, ein Jugendlicher erzählt von seiner Flucht, ein Mädchen schildert seinen Alltag in Armut: Solche Geschichten können Menschen berühren und Spenden mobilisieren. Für Hilfsorganisationen entsteht dabei jedoch ein Dilemma: Werden die betroffenen Menschen durch Fotos, Videos oder persönliche Details erkennbar, riskieren sie Stigmatisierung, Anfeindungen oder Eingriffe in ihre Privatsphäre – möglicherweise noch Jahre nach der Kampagne. Insbesondere Kinder und Jugendliche benötigen besonderen Schutz. Werden ihre Gesichter und Lebensgeschichten öffentlich, können sie identifiziert werden. Selbst wenn eine Einwilligung vorliegt, lassen sich die langfristigen Folgen kaum abschätzen.
